acceptedAnswer.text: A senior React Native engineer costs $150,000+ per year in salary alone — before benefits, equity, recruiting fees, and onboarding time. With our subscription, you get a specialized React Native team available immediately, with no hiring risk and no overhead. You can pause or cancel at any time, which is impossible with a full-time hire.

mainEntity.name: How is hiring a React Native development service different from hiring a full-time mobile developer?

acceptedAnswer.text: We embed directly into your GitHub workflow from day one. We join your existing repositories, follow your branching conventions, and deliver pull requests your team reviews and merges. Most clients have us shipping code within 48 hours of subscribing — no lengthy onboarding, no knowledge transfer sessions that delay delivery.

mainEntity.name: How quickly can your React Native developers integrate with our existing engineering team?

acceptedAnswer.text: You work directly with David Leuliette, a top 20 Stack Overflow contributor with 10+ years of React Native experience, and Matthys Ducroq, our lead developer. No account managers, no rotating junior contractors. The same senior developers who scope your tasks are the ones writing your production code.

mainEntity.name: Who will be working on our React Native codebase?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, 100%. All code we write is committed directly to your private repository. There are no licensing restrictions, no proprietary tooling lock-in, and no clauses that retain ownership on our end. The moment we push the code, it belongs entirely to you.

mainEntity.name: Do we retain full ownership of the code and IP?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. We handle greenfield React Native projects, new feature sprints, performance audits, library upgrades, and legacy codebase migrations — including upgrades from the old React Native architecture to the New Architecture with Fabric and TurboModules. We regularly work on codebases we did not start from scratch.

mainEntity.name: Can you handle both new React Native feature development and legacy code maintenance?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can upgrade, downgrade, pause, or cancel your subscription at any time with no penalty. If your roadmap accelerates, we can increase throughput. If you’re in a quiet period, pause and restart when you’re ready. We’re designed to flex with your engineering needs, not lock you into a fixed contract.

mainEntity.name: What happens if we need to scale up or scale down the engagement?

acceptedAnswer.text: We manage the full release pipeline — TestFlight builds, Google Play internal tracks, Expo EAS submissions, and production rollouts. We set up automated CI/CD if you don’t have it, handle code signing and provisioning profiles, and notify your team on Slack when each build is ready for review or live in the stores.

mainEntity.name: How do you handle App Store submissions and production deployments?

acceptedAnswer.text: React Native releases major versions regularly, and Apple and Google enforce SDK requirements that can block your app from the stores. Falling behind on upgrades — React Native version, Expo SDK, or native dependencies — can require months of remediation work or, in severe cases, a full rebuild. Staying current is significantly cheaper than catching up.

mainEntity.name: Why is keeping a React Native app up to date a critical engineering concern?

acceptedAnswer.text: You organize your backlog as GitHub Issues in your repository. We triage, prioritize, and work through tasks one at a time, focusing on production-ready delivery rather than partially completed work. You get automatic Slack notifications when a task is in review and when it’s shipped to production.

mainEntity.name: How is our backlog managed and how do we track progress?

acceptedAnswer.text: That’s exactly who we built this for. We act as your embedded React Native experts — reviewing architectural decisions, mentoring your existing developers, and delivering features your team doesn’t have the mobile depth to build confidently. We’ve helped CTOs at funded startups and scale-ups ship iOS and Android apps without hiring a full mobile team.

acceptedAnswer.text: Oui, à condition d’avoir 1h à 2h par semaine à investir et de venir construire un actif concret (newsletter, podcast, offre productisée, sponsoring, SaaS). Au tarif affilié (1 490 € HT), le rapport qualité-prix est très bon : c’est moins cher qu’un coach individuel sur un mois et tu accèdes à une communauté de 300+ solopreneurs investis. Au tarif public (2 400 € HT), le verdict est plus nuancé — voir la section « Rapport qualité-prix » plus bas.

mainEntity.name: L’Incubateur Solopreneur, ça vaut le coup en 2026 ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Marketing Mania (Stan Leloup) est principalement un format formation : 6 à 8 semaines, vidéos structurées, focus copywriting / marketing direct. L’Incubateur Solopreneur de Flavie Prevot est un format communauté + sprints mensuels : 12 mois, lives hebdomadaires, focus passage à l’action et construction d’actifs durables (newsletter, podcast, sponsoring, IA). Si tu veux apprendre la persuasion écrite, Marketing Mania. Si tu veux te mettre en mouvement dans la durée avec un cercle de pairs, l’Incubateur.

mainEntity.name: Quelle différence entre l’Incubateur Solopreneur et le Bootcamp de Marketing Mania ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Le format est conçu autour d’une heure le vendredi (le live « atelier ») et d’un Sprint mensuel qui demande 2 à 4 heures réparties dans le mois. À l’aise avec 1h à 3h par semaine, tu es dans le rythme. En-dessous, tu auras du mal à finir les Sprints. Au-dessus, tu peux aussi consommer les replays, les office hours et les canaux thématiques.

mainEntity.name: Combien de temps faut-il consacrer par semaine ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Concrètement, sur 6 mois, j’ai relancé mon podcast vidéo, structuré une offre productisée, identifié 3 pistes de sponsoring pour ma newsletter, et automatisé une partie de ma prospection. La promesse n’est pas « tu vas faire 10k MRR » — c’est « tu vas shipper des actifs et tu seras dans un cercle qui te tient le rythme ». Les résultats financiers dépendent de ce que tu construis, pas du programme.

mainEntity.name: Quels résultats peut-on espérer en 6 mois ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flavie Prevot a construit plusieurs business avant l’Incubateur. Elle a une newsletter qui dépasse les 30 000 abonnés, un podcast écouté, et anime la communauté de manière très présente (lives chaque vendredi, office hours, réponses dans les canaux). Le contenu n’est pas délégué : c’est elle qui orchestre les Sprints et qui anime. Aucun signal d’arnaque ni de promesse irréaliste dans ses contenus publics. Pour un profil détaillé de son parcours, de son écosystème et de sa réputation publique, voir la page dédiée /flavie-prevot-avis sur ce site.

mainEntity.name: Est-ce que Flavie Prevot est sérieuse ? Quel est son parcours ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pas obligatoirement, mais c’est mieux. L’Incubateur n’apprend pas « comment devenir solopreneur partant de zéro ». Il aide les solopreneurs déjà en activité (freelance, consultant, créateur, SaaS solo) à construire des actifs et à sortir du modèle 100 % temps facturé. Si tu es salarié sans aucune activité side, commence par poser ton premier projet avant de rejoindre.

mainEntity.name: Faut-il être déjà solopreneur pour rejoindre ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Oui — et c’est probablement le meilleur programme du paysage FR pour un dev solopreneur. Le tech est explicitement présent dans les Sprints (IA/Claude, Custom GPT’s, automation, SaaS solo), et le format « un actif construit chaque vendredi en live » colle exactement à la façon dont un dev avance. Effet levier concret : ce qui prend 3 semaines à un non-dev (mettre en place un agent, déployer un mini-SaaS, connecter une chaîne d’outils) te prend l’après-midi. Ton edge tech compose avec le programme. Bon point d’entrée : le Sprint « Solo SaaS » d’octobre 2026, détaillé sur /sprint-solo-saas.

mainEntity.name: L’Incubateur est-il adapté aux développeurs / SaaS solo ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Le tarif est verrouillé sur 12 mois sans engagement de reconduction tacite. En fin d’année, tu décides simplement de repartir ou non pour un nouveau cycle. Il n’y a pas de période d’essai et pas de remboursement après inscription — c’est l’une des limites à connaître avant d’acheter (voir « Points faibles »).

mainEntity.name: Comment résilier ou ne pas reconduire ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sur 300+ incubés affichés, j’estime à environ un tiers ceux qui se présentent régulièrement aux lives et postent des wins dans la communauté. C’est cohérent avec la plupart des communautés payantes. Le noyau actif (50 à 80 personnes) crée la vraie valeur : entraide, échanges asynchrones, retours sur les actifs en construction.

mainEntity.name: Combien d’incubés sont vraiment actifs ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Oui, Flavie Prevot a une fiche Trustpilot avec des avis vérifiés positifs (note moyenne supérieure à 4,5/5). Les avis pointent surtout la qualité de l’animation et la dynamique communautaire. Pour un retour plus détaillé que les avis Trustpilot, cette page synthétise mon expérience après 6 mois d’incubation.

mainEntity.name: Combien d'économies avec le code réduction Solopreneur ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Chaque Sprint est vendu à deux prix : le Sprint seul (1 mois) autour de 1 490 € HT, ou le Sprint + 12 mois d'Incubateur autour de 1 990 € HT. Le tarif affilié est plus simple : 1 490 € HT pour les 12 mois, Sprint en cours inclus. Autrement dit, tu paies le prix du Sprint seul et tu obtiens l'année entière. C'est le prix « sous le manteau » que Flavie réserve aux personnes recommandées par un incubé, et qu'elle n'affiche nulle part.

mainEntity.name: Le code réduction Solopreneur fonctionne aussi sur le Sprint mensuel ?

Pour ceux qui veulent une heure par semaine vraiment dédiée à leur business plutôt qu'à leurs clients. Et pour celles et ceux qui veulent construire des actifs (newsletter, podcast, offre, SaaS, sponsoring) brique après brique, dans une communauté qui pousse au shipping.

Mais à ce prix-là, le tarif affilié te donne l'année entière, donc le Sprint seul n'a d'intérêt que si tu es sûr de ne pas vouloir continuer.

mainEntity.name: Puis-je avoir un essai ou un remboursement ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Le Sprint « Solo SaaS : construire un SaaS qui bosse à ta place » du 9 au 30 octobre 2026, animé avec Pierre Thomassina (développeur agentique). 4 lives : trouver la bonne idée de SaaS, installer son environnement de vibe coding (base de données, déploiement, sécurité), construire les premières features, puis organiser un bêta-test pour trouver ses premiers utilisateurs. Ensuite : « Client Express » (4 semaines pour trouver 10 clients) en novembre, puis « Indé blindé » (optimisation fiscale, financière et rémunération) en fin d'année. Il y a 12 Sprints par an : tu rejoins pour un Sprint, les 11 autres sont inclus. Voir le détail sur /sprint-solo-saas.

mainEntity.name: Quel est le prochain Sprint de l’Incubateur Solopreneur ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Oui, c'est le vrai critère de filtrage. L'Incubateur va vite : une app communautaire (Mighty), des prompts à copier-coller, des outils comme Claude, Codex, Notion ou n8n manipulés en live. Ce n'est pas un programme materné : si tu as besoin qu'on te tienne la main sur chaque clic, tu vas te sentir perdu. Si tu utilises déjà un peu l'IA au quotidien et que tu aimes apprendre en faisant, tu es dans la cible.

mainEntity.name: Faut-il être à l’aise avec les outils digitaux et l’IA ?

jsonLd.description: Tarif affilié pour l'Incubateur Solopreneur de Flavie Prevot. 12 mois d'incubation avec Sprints mensuels, lives, communauté de 300+ solopreneurs et experts invités. Prix le plus bas du marché : 1 490 € HT au lieu de 2 400 € HT.

/flavie-prevot-avis.title: Flavie Prevot : avis et parcours (2026) — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Qui est Flavie Prevot ? Parcours, écosystème (newsletter 30k+ abonnés, podcast, Incubateur Solopreneur), avis publics, réputation Trustpilot et LinkedIn. Analyse neutre par un incubé actif.
og:description: Qui est Flavie Prevot ? Parcours, écosystème (newsletter 30k+ abonnés, podcast, Incubateur Solopreneur), avis publics, réputation Trustpilot et LinkedIn. Analyse neutre par un incubé actif.
og:image:alt: Profil de Flavie Prevot, fondatrice de l’Incubateur Solopreneur
og:title: Flavie Prevot : avis et parcours (2026)
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

acceptedAnswer.text: Flavie Prevot est une entrepreneure française spécialisée dans l'accompagnement des solopreneurs. Elle a construit plusieurs business avant de lancer l'Incubateur Solopreneur en 2023. Son écosystème actuel repose sur trois piliers : une newsletter hebdomadaire (30 000+ abonnés), un podcast interviewant des solopreneurs francophones, et l'Incubateur Solopreneur (communauté payante + Sprints mensuels).

mainEntity.name: Qui est Flavie Prevot ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Non. Rien dans son parcours public ne pointe vers une arnaque : aucune promesse de revenus irréalistes, aucun upsell caché à 5 000 €, aucun avis Trustpilot négatif significatif, paiements gérés sur incubateursolopreneur.fr avec un programme de parrainage officiel et traçable. Le terme « arnaque » revient dans les recherches simplement parce que le tarif de l'Incubateur (2 400 € HT) déclenche une vérification réflexe — c'est sain. Ma propre expérience après 6 mois d'incubation confirme : le programme livre ce qu'il annonce.

mainEntity.name: Flavie Prevot, arnaque ou pas ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flavie a occupé des postes dans le retail et le marketing digital avant de basculer dans l'entrepreneuriat. Elle a lancé et développé plusieurs activités (conseil, formation, communauté) avant de structurer l'Incubateur Solopreneur en 2023. Sa légitimité vient à la fois de son expérience personnelle (elle a été solopreneur avant d'accompagner d'autres solopreneurs) et de la traction de sa newsletter et de son podcast.

mainEntity.name: Quel est le parcours de Flavie Prevot avant l’Incubateur ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Trois canaux gratuits pour découvrir son approche avant de payer : (1) sa newsletter hebdomadaire (études de cas de solopreneurs, tactiques concrètes), (2) son podcast (interviews longues de solopreneurs francophones), (3) ses posts LinkedIn (réflexions courtes, format hebdo). C'est le meilleur point d'entrée si tu hésites à rejoindre l'Incubateur payant.

mainEntity.name: Que propose Flavie Prevot en gratuit ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Deux formules payantes principales. Le Sprint mensuel : autour de 1 490 € HT pour 1 mois seul, ou 1 990 € HT avec les 12 mois d'Incubateur. L'Incubateur Solopreneur annuel : 2 400 € HT au tarif public, 1 900 € HT en remise VSL (3-4 jours après la vidéo), 1 490 € HT via lien affilié (le tarif plancher). Le tarif affilié à 1 490 € HT est verrouillé par Flavie : aucune promo publique ne descend en-dessous.

mainEntity.name: Combien coûtent les programmes de Flavie Prevot ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Oui pour les solopreneurs déjà en activité qui veulent construire des actifs (newsletter, podcast, offre, sponsoring, SaaS solo) avec un cercle de pairs. Le format « atelier » du vendredi et les Sprints mensuels poussent au shipping. À éviter si tu cherches un cours vidéo passif ou si tu n'as pas 1h/semaine garantie. Mon avis détaillé après 6 mois d'incubation est disponible sur la page dédiée.

mainEntity.name: L’Incubateur Solopreneur de Flavie Prevot, ça vaut le coup ?

acceptedAnswer.text: LinkedIn est son canal principal (posts hebdomadaires, threads sur le solopreneuriat). Elle publie aussi sur Instagram et sa newsletter est le point d'entrée le plus dense en valeur. Son podcast est disponible sur toutes les plateformes (Spotify, Apple Podcasts, YouTube). Elle est peu active sur X/Twitter.

mainEntity.name: Où trouver Flavie Prevot sur les réseaux ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Suivre en gratuit d'abord : newsletter + podcast pendant 2-3 mois. Ça te donne une vraie idée de son style et de son approche. Rejoindre la communauté payante si tu veux passer du contenu passif à la construction active d'actifs avec un cercle de pairs. La bascule gratuit → payant est plus efficace que l'inverse.

mainEntity.name: Faut-il rejoindre la communauté payante ou suivre en gratuit ?

/incubateur-solopreneur-vs-marketing-man.title: Incubateur Solopreneur vs Marketing Mania — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Comparaison indépendante entre l'Incubateur Solopreneur (Flavie Prevot) et le Bootcamp Marketing Mania (Stan Leloup) : format, prix, rythme, communauté, résultats. Recommandation par cas d'usage.
og:description: Comparaison indépendante entre l'Incubateur Solopreneur (Flavie Prevot) et le Bootcamp Marketing Mania (Stan Leloup) : format, prix, rythme, communauté, résultats. Recommandation par cas d'usage.
og:image:alt: Comparaison Incubateur Solopreneur vs Bootcamp Marketing Mania — quelle formation choisir en 2026 ?
og:title: Incubateur Solopreneur vs Marketing Mania
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

acceptedAnswer.text: Si tu veux apprendre la persuasion écrite, le copywriting et les mécaniques marketing pointues (VSL, funnels, YouTube) : Marketing Mania de Stan Leloup. Si tu es déjà solopreneur en activité et que tu veux construire des actifs (newsletter, podcast, offre, sponsoring, SaaS solo) dans la durée avec un cercle de pairs qui pousse au shipping : Incubateur Solopreneur de Flavie Prevot. Les deux sont sérieux — le bon choix dépend de ton objectif, pas du prix.

mainEntity.name: Marketing Mania ou Incubateur Solopreneur : lequel choisir en 2026 ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Marketing Mania est un format formation (contenus structurés, cohorte intensive de quelques semaines, focus tactique marketing). L'Incubateur Solopreneur est un format communauté + Sprints mensuels sur 12 mois (rythme long, format atelier, focus construction d'actifs et passage à l'action). L'un t'apprend, l'autre te met en mouvement.

mainEntity.name: Quelle est la différence principale entre les deux ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Le Bootcamp Marketing Mania est historiquement positionné autour de 1 000 à 1 500 € HT selon les éditions, avec des variantes en fonction des modules inclus (copywriting, YouTube, offres). Le tarif exact évolue à chaque nouvelle cohorte — vérifier sur la page officielle avant achat. Stan Leloup propose aussi des formations plus courtes et des ressources gratuites (chaîne YouTube).

mainEntity.name: Combien coûte Marketing Mania ?

acceptedAnswer.text: 2 400 € HT au tarif public sur la page de vente, 1 900 € HT en remise VSL (3–4 jours après la vidéo), 1 490 € HT via lien affilié (le tarif plancher verrouillé par Flavie). Le tarif couvre 12 mois d'accès complet à la communauté, aux Sprints mensuels, aux lives et aux experts invités. Aucun upsell caché.

mainEntity.name: Combien coûte l'Incubateur Solopreneur ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Marketing Mania : format bootcamp intensif, généralement 6 à 8 semaines avec un rythme dense (plusieurs heures par semaine). L'Incubateur Solopreneur : 12 mois avec un rythme modéré (1 à 3 heures par semaine, un live le vendredi, un Sprint par mois). Marketing Mania demande un sprint d'effort concentré, l'Incubateur demande de la régularité dans la durée.

mainEntity.name: Combien de temps chaque programme prend-il ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Oui, et c'est cohérent. Beaucoup d'incubés Solopreneur ont fait Marketing Mania avant (ou l'envisagent après). L'ordre logique : Marketing Mania d'abord pour poser les fondamentaux marketing (copywriting, persuasion, funnels), puis l'Incubateur pour appliquer ces fondamentaux à un actif construit dans la durée. Compte 3 000 à 4 000 € HT cumulés — investissement significatif mais pas déraisonnable si tu es solopreneur à temps plein.

mainEntity.name: Peut-on faire les deux ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Oui, mais pas seulement. Le Bootcamp attire des solopreneurs, des marketers en entreprise, des indépendants du service (agences, freelances) et des créateurs. Le focus reste sur la mécanique marketing / persuasion — moins sur le business creator complet. Si tu cherches un cadre solopreneur global (offre, sponsoring, communauté, positionnement), l'Incubateur est plus adapté.

mainEntity.name: Marketing Mania est-il adapté aux solopreneurs ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Partiellement. La communauté est composée majoritairement de solopreneurs en activité (créateurs, freelances, consultants, SaaS solo), pas de marketers en poste. Si tu es marketer employé qui prépare une transition, l'Incubateur reste utile pour la partie business / positionnement. Mais Marketing Mania sera plus dense sur les compétences techniques marketing.

mainEntity.name: L’Incubateur Solopreneur est-il adapté aux marketers ?

acceptedAnswer.text: L'Incubateur Solopreneur, sans hésiter. Le programme contient des Sprints IA/Claude, Custom GPT’s, automation et SaaS solo — le tech est déjà dans le format, tu n'as qu'à l'appliquer. Un dev qui rejoint l'Incubateur obtient un effet 10x sur ces Sprints : ce qui prend 3 semaines à un non-dev te prend l'après-midi (mise en place d'un agent, déploiement d'un mini-SaaS, automation d'une chaîne d'outils). Marketing Mania reste utile pour la persuasion et le copywriting, mais son terrain n'est pas la construction tech.

mainEntity.name: Je suis développeur / builder — lequel choisir pour un effet levier ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Oui : Livementor (formations multi-thématiques), Le Board (communauté leaders femmes), Solopreneur.fr (communauté gratuite), Copywriting Mafia et autres formations copywriting spécialisées. Chaque programme cible un profil légèrement différent. Marketing Mania et l'Incubateur Solopreneur restent parmi les plus reconnus du paysage FR pour leur qualité d'exécution.

mainEntity.name: Y a-t-il des alternatives à ces deux programmes ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stan Leloup (Marketing Mania) : profil intellectuel, référence Cialdini, ton analytique, YouTube long-format, focus mécaniques de persuasion. Flavie Prevot (Incubateur Solopreneur) : profil entrepreneure-praticienne, ton direct et pragmatique, LinkedIn + podcast + lives, focus passage à l'action. Deux excellents opérateurs avec des styles très différents. La question n'est pas « qui est meilleur » mais « à quel style tu adhères ».

author: David Leuliette
description: Paste a Google Play link to see if an app is built with React Native, Expo or Flutter. We read the APK file list and show the proof. Free, no sign-up.
og:description: Paste a Google Play link to see if an app is built with React Native, Expo or Flutter. We read the APK file list and show the proof. Free, no sign-up.
og:image:alt: Is this app built with React Native? — weshipit.today
og:title: Is This App Built with React Native?
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

@graph.description: Paste a Google Play link to see if an app is built with React Native, Expo or Flutter. We read the APK file list and show the proof. Free, no sign-up.
@graph.name: Is this app built with React Native?

acceptedAnswer.text: Every React Native Android app ships the React Native runtime as native libraries (libreactnative.so, or libreactnativejni.so on older versions) and a JavaScript bundle (index.android.bundle). We list the files inside the APK from Google Play and look for them.

mainEntity.name: How do you know if an app is built with React Native?

acceptedAnswer.text: Discord, Bluesky, Coinbase, Tesla, Microsoft Outlook and Microsoft Teams all ship React Native in their Android app. Bluesky, Coinbase and Tesla also use Expo.

mainEntity.name: Which popular apps are built with React Native?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. An APK is a ZIP file, and its table of contents sits at the end. We read only that part with HTTP range requests, usually a few hundred KB out of a 50 MB app.

mainEntity.name: Do you download the whole app?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Expo modules leave their own native files in the APK (expo-modules-core, expo-*.kotlin_module). If they are present, the app uses Expo.

mainEntity.name: Can it tell if the app uses Expo?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flutter apps ship libflutter.so and a flutter_assets folder. The checker detects Flutter, Capacitor, Cordova, .NET MAUI / Xamarin, NativeScript and Unity. If none of them match, the app is native Android (Kotlin or Java).

mainEntity.name: How can I tell if an app uses Flutter instead?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rarely. A company can rename or merge the React Native libraries in a custom build. The files we look for are then missing and the app shows as native.

mainEntity.name: Can the result be wrong?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not yet. iOS apps are encrypted on the App Store, so they cannot be inspected the same way. Most apps ship with the same stack on both stores: paste the Google Play link instead.

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, 100%. All code we write is committed directly to your private repository. There are no licensing restrictions, no proprietary tooling lock-in, and no clauses that retain ownership on our end. The moment we push the code, it belongs entirely to you.

mainEntity.name: Do we retain full ownership of the code and IP?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can upgrade, downgrade, pause, or cancel your subscription at any time with no penalty. If your roadmap accelerates, we can increase throughput. If you’re in a quiet period, pause and restart when you’re ready. We’re designed to flex with your engineering needs, not lock you into a fixed contract.

mainEntity.name: What happens if we need to scale up or scale down the engagement?

We triage, prioritize, and work through tasks one at a time, focusing on production-ready delivery rather than partially completed work. You get automatic Slack notifications when a task is in review and when it’s shipped to production.

author: David Leuliette
description: 252 React Native terms explained in plain English for developers new to the ecosystem — Expo, Metro, JSX, Flexbox, Hermes, the New Architecture, Fabric and TurboModules.
og:description: 252 React Native terms explained in plain English for developers new to the ecosystem — Expo, Metro, JSX, Flexbox, Hermes, the New Architecture, Fabric and TurboModules.
og:title: React Native Glossary
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Plain-English definitions of 252 React Native terms, written for developers new to the ecosystem.

hasDefinedTerm.description: Absolute positioning takes a React Native view out of the flexbox flow and places it with top, right, bottom and left offsets relative to its parent view.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Absolute Positioning

hasDefinedTerm.description: An accessibility label is the text a screen reader speaks for an element; in React Native you set it with accessibilityLabel or aria-label on views and controls.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Accessibility Label

hasDefinedTerm.description: An accessibility role tells screen readers what kind of element something is, such as a button, header or link, set with the accessibilityRole or role prop.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Accessibility Role

hasDefinedTerm.description: ActivityIndicator is React Native’s core loading spinner, rendering the native indeterminate progress indicator on iOS and Android with configurable size and colour.
hasDefinedTerm.name: ActivityIndicator

hasDefinedTerm.description: ADB (Android Debug Bridge) is the command-line tool that talks to Android devices and emulators to install apps, read logs, forward ports and open a shell.
hasDefinedTerm.name: ADB

hasDefinedTerm.description: Alert is the React Native API that shows a native system dialog with a title, message and up to a few buttons, using UIAlertController on iOS and AlertDialog on Android.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Alert

hasDefinedTerm.description: An Android App Bundle (.aab) is the format you upload to Google Play, which then generates smaller device-specific APKs for each user instead of one universal file.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Android App Bundle

hasDefinedTerm.description: Android App Links are verified https links that open your Android app directly, without a chooser dialog, once an assetlinks.json file on your domain proves you own both.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Android App Links

hasDefinedTerm.description: The Android Emulator runs a virtual Android device on your computer from an AVD profile, letting you install and debug a React Native app without a real phone.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Android Emulator

hasDefinedTerm.description: An Android keystore is the password-protected file holding the private key that signs your app; Google Play rejects updates signed with a different key.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Android Keystore

hasDefinedTerm.description: Android Studio is Google’s official Android IDE; React Native developers use it to install the Android SDK, manage emulators, read Logcat and debug native builds.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Android Studio

hasDefinedTerm.description: AndroidManifest.xml declares an Android app’s identity to the OS: its activities, permissions, intent filters for deep links, and how the main activity behaves.
hasDefinedTerm.name: AndroidManifest.xml

hasDefinedTerm.description: An animated component is a React Native view whose style values are driven by an animation library — Reanimated or the built-in Animated API — rather than by plain state.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Animated Component

hasDefinedTerm.description: Any API key embedded in a React Native app ships to every user and can be extracted. Only public, restricted keys belong in the app; true secrets stay on a server.
hasDefinedTerm.name: API Keys in Mobile Apps

hasDefinedTerm.description: API routes are Expo Router files ending in +api.ts that export HTTP handlers, letting a React Native project ship server endpoints in the same codebase as its app.
hasDefinedTerm.name: API Routes

hasDefinedTerm.description: An APK (.apk) is the Android package file that installs directly on a device or emulator, holding the compiled code, resources, native libraries and JavaScript bundle.
hasDefinedTerm.name: APK

hasDefinedTerm.description: App config is the app.json or app.config.js/ts file where an Expo project declares its name, identifiers, icons, permissions and plugins for native generation.
hasDefinedTerm.name: App Config

hasDefinedTerm.description: The app icon is the image representing your React Native app on the home screen and in stores, built from platform-specific assets such as Android’s adaptive icon.
hasDefinedTerm.name: App Icon

hasDefinedTerm.description: App permissions are the user approvals iOS and Android require before an app can use sensitive features such as the camera, location, contacts or notifications.
hasDefinedTerm.name: App Permissions

hasDefinedTerm.description: App Store Connect is Apple’s web portal for publishing iOS apps: you create the app record, upload builds, run TestFlight, write the listing and submit for review.
hasDefinedTerm.name: App Store Connect

hasDefinedTerm.description: App Store Review is Apple’s check of every app version against the App Store Review Guidelines before release; failing it means a rejection you must fix and resubmit.
hasDefinedTerm.name: App Store Review

hasDefinedTerm.description: App versioning is managing the two numbers each store build carries: a user-facing version such as 1.4.0 and a build number that must increase with every upload.
hasDefinedTerm.name: App Versioning

hasDefinedTerm.description: Appearance is the React Native API, with its useColorScheme hook, that reports whether the user has chosen light or dark mode and notifies the app when that changes.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Appearance

hasDefinedTerm.description: AppState is the React Native API that reports whether the app is active in the foreground, inactive, or in the background, and emits an event whenever that changes.
hasDefinedTerm.name: AppState

hasDefinedTerm.description: AsyncStorage is an unencrypted, asynchronous key-value store that persists strings on the device, maintained as @react-native-async-storage/async-storage.
hasDefinedTerm.name: AsyncStorage

hasDefinedTerm.description: Autolinking is the build step that finds native code in your installed npm packages and wires it into the iOS and Android projects, so you never link libraries by hand.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Autolinking

hasDefinedTerm.description: Babel is the JavaScript compiler Metro runs on every file to turn JSX, TypeScript and modern syntax into code the React Native JavaScript engine can execute.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Babel

hasDefinedTerm.description: Background tasks let a React Native app run short pieces of work while it is not on screen, scheduled by iOS and Android rather than by your own timers.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Background Tasks

hasDefinedTerm.description: BackHandler is the React Native API for intercepting the Android back button and back gesture, letting a screen close a sheet or confirm before leaving.
hasDefinedTerm.name: BackHandler

hasDefinedTerm.description: The bridge was React Native’s original asynchronous, JSON-serialised channel between JavaScript and native code. The New Architecture replaces it with JSI.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Bridge

hasDefinedTerm.description: Bridgeless mode runs React Native with the legacy bridge removed entirely, so JavaScript talks to native code only through JSI. It is the default New Architecture setup.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Bridgeless Mode

alternateName: Add React Native to existing app
hasDefinedTerm.description: A brownfield app is an existing native iOS or Android app that adds React Native for some screens, rather than being built in React Native from scratch.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Brownfield App

hasDefinedTerm.description: A bundle identifier is the unique reverse-DNS ID, such as com.acme.shop, that iOS, Android and the app stores use to tell your app apart from every other app.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Bundle Identifier

hasDefinedTerm.description: Bundle size is the weight of a React Native app: the JavaScript bundle plus native code and assets, which together set download size and affect startup time.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Bundle Size

hasDefinedTerm.description: A C++ TurboModule is a native module written once in C++ and shared by iOS and Android, called from JavaScript through JSI without Swift, Kotlin or Java glue code.
hasDefinedTerm.name: C++ TurboModule

hasDefinedTerm.description: Capacitor is Ionic’s open-source runtime that packages a web app inside a native iOS or Android shell and exposes device features to it through plugins.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Capacitor

hasDefinedTerm.description: The children prop holds whatever JSX you nest between a component’s opening and closing tags, letting you build wrappers like cards, screens and providers by composition.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Children Prop

hasDefinedTerm.description: CI/CD for React Native means automatically testing every change and building, signing and delivering iOS and Android binaries or OTA updates without manual steps.
hasDefinedTerm.name: CI/CD

hasDefinedTerm.description: CocoaPods is the Ruby-based iOS dependency manager React Native uses to install its own native code and the iOS side of every native library into your Xcode project.
hasDefinedTerm.name: CocoaPods

hasDefinedTerm.description: Code coverage measures which lines, branches and functions of a React Native app run during tests. It finds untested code but does not prove it is correct.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Code Coverage

hasDefinedTerm.description: Code obfuscation makes a shipped React Native app harder to read and reverse engineer by renaming and scrambling code. It slows attackers down but hides nothing for good.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Code Obfuscation

hasDefinedTerm.description: Code signing cryptographically stamps an iOS or Android build with your identity, so the OS and app stores can verify who made it and that it is unaltered.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Code Signing

hasDefinedTerm.description: Codegen generates the native C++, Java and Objective-C binding code for TurboModules and Fabric components from TypeScript spec files, at build time.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Codegen

hasDefinedTerm.description: CodePush was Microsoft’s over-the-air update service for React Native, part of App Center, pushing new JavaScript to installed apps until its retirement in March 2025.
hasDefinedTerm.name: CodePush

hasDefinedTerm.description: The communication layer is everything that lets JavaScript talk to native platform code — historically the bridge, and today JSI, TurboModules and Codegen.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Communication Layer

hasDefinedTerm.description: The component lifecycle is the sequence a React component goes through: it mounts onto the screen, updates when state or props change, and unmounts when removed.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Component Lifecycle

hasDefinedTerm.description: Concurrent rendering lets React prepare an update in the background and interrupt it for urgent input, using startTransition, useTransition and useDeferredValue.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Concurrent Rendering

hasDefinedTerm.description: A config plugin is a JavaScript function that edits the native iOS and Android projects during Expo prebuild, so native setup lives in app config, not hand edits.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Config Plugin

hasDefinedTerm.description: Context is React’s way to pass a value such as a theme, user or locale to any component below a provider without threading it through every level of props.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Context

hasDefinedTerm.description: Continuous Native Generation (CNG) regenerates the ios and android folders from app config and config plugins, so native projects become build output, not hand-edited source.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Continuous Native Generation

hasDefinedTerm.description: A controlled component is an input whose current value comes from React state through props, so React rather than the native view is the source of truth.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Controlled Component

hasDefinedTerm.description: Core components are the built-in building blocks React Native ships with — View, Text, Image, ScrollView, TextInput — each backed by a real native view on iOS and Android.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Core Components

hasDefinedTerm.description: Crash reporting captures errors and crashes from users’ devices with stack traces and context, so a React Native team can fix problems it never reproduced locally.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Crash Reporting

hasDefinedTerm.description: Cross-platform development means building one app for several operating systems, such as iOS and Android, from a largely shared codebase instead of one per platform.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Cross-Platform Development

hasDefinedTerm.description: Custom fonts are typeface files you bundle with a React Native app, either embedded at build time or loaded at runtime with expo-font, then used through fontFamily.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Custom Fonts

hasDefinedTerm.description: A custom hook is your own function, named with a use prefix, that combines built-in hooks so several React Native components can reuse the same stateful logic.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Custom Hook

hasDefinedTerm.description: Deep linking lets a URL open a React Native app on a specific screen, such as myapp://post/42, instead of just launching it on the home screen.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Deep Linking

hasDefinedTerm.description: Density-independent pixels are the unitless numbers React Native uses for sizes, mapped to iOS points and Android dp so layouts look the same size on any screen density.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Density-Independent Pixels

hasDefinedTerm.description: Design tokens are named values for colour, spacing, typography and radius that a React Native app’s theme reads, so one change updates the design everywhere.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Design Tokens

hasDefinedTerm.description: Detox is an end-to-end testing framework for React Native that drives a real app build on a simulator or emulator and automatically waits for the app to go idle.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Detox

hasDefinedTerm.description: The dev menu is the in-app debugging panel available in development builds, offering reload, the element inspector, performance monitor and debugger connection.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Dev Menu

hasDefinedTerm.description: A development build is a debug build of your app with its native dependencies and the Expo dev client, so it loads JavaScript from Metro and runs any native library.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Development Build

hasDefinedTerm.description: A drawer navigator hides the app’s main destinations in a side panel that slides in from the screen edge, opened by a swipe or a menu button in the header.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Drawer Navigator

hasDefinedTerm.description: EAS (Expo Application Services) is Expo’s hosted cloud service for building, submitting and updating React Native apps without running your own Xcode and Gradle machines.
hasDefinedTerm.name: EAS

hasDefinedTerm.description: EAS Build is Expo’s cloud build service: it compiles and signs your React Native app into an installable .ipa, .apk or .aab on hosted macOS and Linux machines.
hasDefinedTerm.name: EAS Build

hasDefinedTerm.description: EAS Submit is Expo’s service for uploading a finished React Native binary to App Store Connect or Google Play from the command line or CI, without opening Xcode.
hasDefinedTerm.name: EAS Submit

hasDefinedTerm.description: EAS Update is Expo’s hosted over-the-air update service: the expo-updates library in your app downloads new JavaScript and assets published with eas update.
hasDefinedTerm.name: EAS Update

hasDefinedTerm.description: EAS Workflows is Expo’s CI/CD service: YAML files in .eas/workflows chain builds, submissions, OTA updates and tests on Expo’s infrastructure when your repo changes.
hasDefinedTerm.name: EAS Workflows

hasDefinedTerm.description: End-to-end testing runs a real build of a React Native app on a simulator or device and drives it like a user, checking that whole flows work from screen to backend.
hasDefinedTerm.name: End-to-End Testing

hasDefinedTerm.description: Entitlements are signed key-value permissions in an iOS app that unlock Apple capabilities such as push notifications, App Groups, Sign in with Apple and Universal Links.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Entitlements

hasDefinedTerm.description: In React Native, environment variables are build-time values, such as an API URL, inlined into the JavaScript bundle; they configure an app but never keep a secret.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Environment Variables

hasDefinedTerm.description: An error boundary is a React component that catches errors thrown while rendering its children and shows a fallback UI instead of letting the whole app go down.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Error Boundary

hasDefinedTerm.description: ESLint is the JavaScript linter React Native projects use to catch bugs and enforce conventions, most importantly the Rules of Hooks and effect dependencies.
hasDefinedTerm.name: ESLint

hasDefinedTerm.description: An event emitter lets native code push events to JavaScript, such as download progress or sensor readings, which components receive by subscribing to a listener.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Event Emitter

hasDefinedTerm.description: The event loop is how React Native’s JavaScript thread schedules work: it runs one task at a time, drains the microtask queue after each, and then lets rendering update.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Event Loop

hasDefinedTerm.description: Expo is a framework and toolchain built on React Native. It supplies routing, native modules, build services and updates so teams do not assemble that stack themselves.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Expo

hasDefinedTerm.description: Expo Doctor is a command-line check, run with npx expo-doctor, that finds dependency, config and native setup problems in an Expo project before they break a build.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Expo Doctor

hasDefinedTerm.description: Expo DOM components are React files marked with a ‘use dom’ directive that render web DOM code inside a native WebView on iOS and Android, and as plain DOM on web.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Expo DOM Components

hasDefinedTerm.description: Expo Go is a free sandbox app from the App Store and Google Play that runs Expo projects instantly, with a fixed set of native modules and no custom native code.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Expo Go

hasDefinedTerm.description: The Expo Modules API is a Swift and Kotlin DSL for writing native modules and views for React Native, built on JSI and usable in Expo and bare React Native apps.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Expo Modules API

hasDefinedTerm.description: Expo Router is a file-based routing library for React Native. Files in the app directory become routes, with deep links and typed navigation derived automatically.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Expo Router

hasDefinedTerm.description: The Expo SDK version is the numbered release of the expo package that pins a matching React Native version and a tested set of Expo library versions.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Expo SDK Version

hasDefinedTerm.description: A Fabric Native Component is a platform view, such as a map or video player, exposed to React Native as a component through a Codegen spec and the Fabric renderer.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Fabric Native Component

hasDefinedTerm.description: Fabric is React Native’s rendering system. It builds the view tree in C++ and mounts real native views, replacing the legacy Paper renderer.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Fabric Renderer

hasDefinedTerm.description: Fast Refresh reloads edited React components in a running app within a second, preserving component state where it safely can.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Fast Refresh

hasDefinedTerm.description: Fastlane is an open-source Ruby tool that automates building, signing and uploading iOS and Android apps, with scripted lanes that replace manual Xcode and store steps.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Fastlane

hasDefinedTerm.description: The Fetch API is React Native’s built-in global fetch() for HTTP requests, implemented over the native networking stacks of iOS and Android rather than a browser.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Fetch API

hasDefinedTerm.description: Firebase is Google’s app backend platform; React Native apps use it through React Native Firebase, which wraps the native SDKs, or through the Firebase JavaScript SDK.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Firebase

hasDefinedTerm.description: FlashList is Shopify’s high-performance list component for React Native. It recycles mounted cells instead of unmounting them, with an API close to FlatList.
hasDefinedTerm.name: FlashList

hasDefinedTerm.description: FlatList is React Native’s virtualised list component. It renders only the rows near the viewport, keeping memory flat no matter how long the data is.
hasDefinedTerm.name: FlatList

hasDefinedTerm.description: Flexbox is the layout system React Native uses for every view. It matches CSS Flexbox closely, with a column default direction and a few React Native specific differences.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Flexbox

hasDefinedTerm.description: Flipper is Meta’s desktop debugging platform for mobile apps, once bundled with every React Native project and removed from the default template in 0.74.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Flipper

hasDefinedTerm.description: Flow is Meta’s static type checker for JavaScript; React Native’s own source code is written in it, though most apps today use TypeScript instead.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Flow

hasDefinedTerm.description: Flutter is Google’s open-source UI toolkit that builds cross-platform apps in Dart and draws its own widgets with its own rendering engine instead of native views.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Flutter

hasDefinedTerm.description: Font scaling is React Native’s support for the user’s system text size, such as iOS Dynamic Type and Android font size, which enlarges Text by default.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Font Scaling

hasDefinedTerm.description: A Fragment groups several React elements without adding a wrapper, so a component can return siblings without creating an extra native View in the hierarchy.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Fragment

hasDefinedTerm.description: Frame rate is how many frames per second a React Native app draws. At 60 FPS each frame has about 16.7 ms of work; on 120 Hz screens only 8.3 ms.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Frame Rate

hasDefinedTerm.description: Garbage collection is how the JavaScript engine reclaims memory from objects nothing references any more. In React Native, Hermes runs a mostly concurrent collector.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Garbage Collection

hasDefinedTerm.description: React Native Gesture Handler recognises touches and gestures natively on the UI thread, replacing the JS-based responder system for pans, swipes and pinches.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Gesture Handler

hasDefinedTerm.description: getItemLayout is a FlatList prop that tells the list each item’s height and offset in advance, so it can skip measuring rows and jump straight to any index.
hasDefinedTerm.name: getItemLayout

hasDefinedTerm.description: Google Play Console is Google’s web dashboard for publishing Android apps: it holds the store listing, release tracks, app signing, policy forms and Android vitals.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Google Play Console

hasDefinedTerm.description: Gradle is the build system that compiles the Android side of a React Native app, resolving native dependencies and producing the APK or AAB you install or ship.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Gradle

hasDefinedTerm.description: Headless JS is an Android-only React Native feature that runs a JavaScript task from a native service while no UI is showing, for work such as syncing data.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Headless JS

hasDefinedTerm.description: Hermes is the JavaScript engine Meta built for React Native. Default since version 0.70, it precompiles code to bytecode for faster startup and lower memory use.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Hermes

hasDefinedTerm.description: Hermes bytecode is the precompiled binary form of your JavaScript bundle that Hermes executes in release builds, so the device skips parsing source code at launch.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Hermes Bytecode

hasDefinedTerm.description: Hooks are React functions such as useState and useEffect that let a function component hold state, run side effects and reach React features without a class.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Hooks

hasDefinedTerm.description: The host platform is the operating system embedding React Native — iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, tvOS or the web — and the source of the real views your components render to.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Host Platform

hasDefinedTerm.description: A hybrid app is a web app written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript that runs inside a WebView in a native shell, distributed through the app stores like any other app.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Hybrid App

hasDefinedTerm.description: Image caching keeps downloaded images in memory or on disk so a React Native app can show them again instantly without re-downloading or re-decoding them.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Image Caching

hasDefinedTerm.description: Image is the React Native core component for displaying bundled, remote or base64 pictures; expo-image is the popular drop-in with stronger caching and placeholders.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Image Component

hasDefinedTerm.description: Info.plist is the iOS property list holding an app’s configuration: display name, version, URL schemes, fonts and the permission usage messages users see.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Info.plist

hasDefinedTerm.description: InteractionManager is a legacy React Native API that defers expensive JavaScript work until running animations and touches finish, using runAfterInteractions.
hasDefinedTerm.name: InteractionManager

hasDefinedTerm.description: The internal testing track is Google Play’s fastest release channel, delivering a build to up to 100 invited testers within minutes, ahead of the closed and open tracks.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Internal Testing Track

hasDefinedTerm.description: Internationalisation (i18n) is preparing a React Native app to support several languages and regions, and localisation (l10n) is adding the translations and formats.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Internationalization

hasDefinedTerm.description: The interop layer lets native modules and view components written for the legacy architecture run unchanged inside a New Architecture React Native app.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Interop Layer

hasDefinedTerm.description: The iOS Simulator is the Mac app bundled with Xcode that runs iPhone and iPad builds of your React Native app on your computer, without a physical device.
hasDefinedTerm.name: iOS Simulator

hasDefinedTerm.description: An IPA (.ipa) is the signed archive that packages an iOS app for distribution, the file you upload to App Store Connect or install on registered test devices.
hasDefinedTerm.name: IPA

hasDefinedTerm.description: Jailbreak and root detection lets a React Native app check whether it runs on a modified iOS or Android device, where its security protections can be bypassed.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Jailbreak and Root Detection

hasDefinedTerm.description: Jank is visible stutter in a React Native app, caused when the UI or JavaScript thread misses its frame deadline and frames are dropped or delivered late.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Jank

hasDefinedTerm.description: The JavaScript bundle is the single file Metro produces from your source code. It ships inside the app binary and is what the JavaScript engine actually executes.
hasDefinedTerm.name: JavaScript Bundle

hasDefinedTerm.description: The JavaScript runtime is the engine that executes your app’s JavaScript on the device. React Native ships Hermes by default, with JavaScriptCore as the alternative.
hasDefinedTerm.name: JavaScript Runtime

hasDefinedTerm.description: The JavaScript thread is where your React components, business logic and event handlers run. Blocking it makes the app feel frozen even though native rendering continues.
hasDefinedTerm.name: JavaScript Thread

hasDefinedTerm.description: JavaScriptCore is Apple’s JavaScript engine from Safari. It was React Native’s original engine and is now an opt-in alternative to Hermes, maintained by the community.
hasDefinedTerm.name: JavaScriptCore

hasDefinedTerm.description: Jest is the JavaScript test runner most React Native projects use for unit and component tests. It runs tests in Node.js, not on a device, with mocks and snapshots.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Jest

hasDefinedTerm.description: JNI (Java Native Interface) is the JVM bridge between Java or Kotlin and C++ code, which React Native’s Android side uses to reach Hermes, JSI and the Fabric renderer.
hasDefinedTerm.name: JNI

hasDefinedTerm.description: JSI (JavaScript Interface) is a lightweight C++ API that lets JavaScript hold direct references to native objects and call them synchronously, replacing the bridge.
hasDefinedTerm.name: JSI

hasDefinedTerm.description: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that lets you write UI markup directly inside component code. React Native compiles it to plain function calls.
hasDefinedTerm.name: JSX

hasDefinedTerm.description: KeyboardAvoidingView is a React Native core component that moves or shrinks its content when the software keyboard opens, so inputs and buttons stay visible.
hasDefinedTerm.name: KeyboardAvoidingView

hasDefinedTerm.description: A key is a stable identifier you give each item in a rendered list so React can tell which item is which across renders instead of re-creating them all.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Keys

hasDefinedTerm.description: Kotlin is Google’s preferred language for Android; React Native’s Android template is written in it, and it is the usual choice for writing Android native modules.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Kotlin

hasDefinedTerm.description: Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) is JetBrains’ technology for sharing Kotlin code across Android, iOS and other targets, usually business logic, while keeping native UIs.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Kotlin Multiplatform

hasDefinedTerm.description: Layout animations are Reanimated’s entering, exiting and layout props, which animate a component automatically when it mounts, unmounts or changes position in the layout.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Layout Animations

hasDefinedTerm.description: LayoutAnimation is a React Native API that animates every layout change in the next render automatically, with one line of code and no animated values to manage.
hasDefinedTerm.name: LayoutAnimation

hasDefinedTerm.description: Lazy loading delays loading or running code until it is needed. In React Native that mostly means inline requires and React.lazy, which defer module evaluation.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Lazy Loading

hasDefinedTerm.description: The New Architecture replaces the asynchronous bridge with JSI, Fabric and TurboModules. It has been the default since React Native 0.76.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Legacy vs New Architecture

hasDefinedTerm.description: Linking is the React Native API for opening URLs in other apps, such as the browser, phone or maps, and for receiving the URLs that open your own app via deep links.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Linking API

hasDefinedTerm.description: LogBox is React Native’s in-app overlay for development builds that shows errors full screen and warnings as dismissible notifications, with readable stack traces.
hasDefinedTerm.name: LogBox

hasDefinedTerm.description: Lottie is a format for vector animations exported from After Effects as JSON; lottie-react-native plays them in React Native apps using the native Lottie players.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Lottie

hasDefinedTerm.description: Maestro is a mobile end-to-end testing tool where tests are short YAML flows that tap, type and assert on a running app, with no changes needed inside the app.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Maestro

hasDefinedTerm.description: Memoization caches the result of a computation and reuses it while its inputs stay the same. In React Native it is used to skip wasted renders and repeated work.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Memoization

hasDefinedTerm.description: A memory leak is memory a React Native app keeps holding after it is no longer needed, so usage grows until the app slows down or the OS kills it.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Memory Leak

hasDefinedTerm.description: Metro is React Native’s JavaScript bundler. It resolves imports, transforms code, serves the bundle to the app in development and powers Fast Refresh.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Metro

hasDefinedTerm.description: MMKV is a fast, synchronous key-value storage library for React Native, built on Tencent’s memory-mapped MMKV engine and exposed through JSI as react-native-mmkv.
hasDefinedTerm.name: MMKV

hasDefinedTerm.description: Mocking replaces a real dependency, such as a native module, network call or timer, with a controlled fake so React Native code can be tested in Jest without a device.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Mocking

hasDefinedTerm.description: Modal is React Native’s core component for presenting content above the rest of the app in a separate native window, with slide or fade animations and iOS sheet styles.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Modal

hasDefinedTerm.description: A monorepo keeps a React Native app alongside other apps and shared packages in one repository, linked together with npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun workspaces.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Monorepo

hasDefinedTerm.description: A native app is a mobile app built with each platform’s own SDK and languages, Swift or Objective-C on iOS and Kotlin or Java on Android, installed from a store.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Native App

hasDefinedTerm.description: The native driver, useNativeDriver: true in React Native’s Animated API, hands an animation to native code once so it runs on the UI thread without JavaScript.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Native Driver

hasDefinedTerm.description: A native module is platform code — Swift, Kotlin, Objective-C, Java or C++ — exposed to JavaScript, letting an app reach APIs React Native does not wrap itself.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Native Module

hasDefinedTerm.description: NativeWind lets you style React Native components with Tailwind CSS utility classes through a className prop, compiled into native styles at build time.
hasDefinedTerm.name: NativeWind

hasDefinedTerm.description: Navigation state is the plain object a React Native navigator keeps describing which screens exist, which one is focused and the params each received.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Navigation State

hasDefinedTerm.description: Node.js is the JavaScript runtime that powers React Native’s development tools such as Metro, Expo CLI and the React Native CLI, though your app itself never runs on it.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Node.js

hasDefinedTerm.description: Objective-C is Apple’s older iOS language; much of React Native’s iOS core and many libraries still use it, often as Objective-C++ to reach C++ code like JSI.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Objective-C

hasDefinedTerm.description: Offline-first is an architecture where a React Native app reads and writes a local database first and syncs in the background, so it works without a connection.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Offline-First

hasDefinedTerm.description: An out-of-tree platform is a React Native target maintained outside the core repository, such as React Native Windows, React Native macOS or react-native-tvos.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Out-of-Tree Platform

hasDefinedTerm.description: An over-the-air update ships new JavaScript and assets straight to installed apps, skipping app store review. Native code changes still require a new store build.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Over-the-Air Update

hasDefinedTerm.description: OWASP MASVS is the open Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, a checklist of security requirements used to audit iOS, Android and React Native apps.
hasDefinedTerm.name: OWASP MASVS

hasDefinedTerm.description: A package manager such as npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun installs a React Native project’s dependencies into node_modules and records exact versions in a lockfile.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Package Manager

hasDefinedTerm.description: PanResponder is React Native’s built-in API for tracking drag gestures in JavaScript, wrapping the gesture responder system to report distance and velocity.
hasDefinedTerm.name: PanResponder

hasDefinedTerm.description: patch-package is a tool that saves your edits to a library inside node_modules as a patch file and reapplies them after every install, until an upstream fix ships.
hasDefinedTerm.name: patch-package

hasDefinedTerm.description: Peer dependencies are packages a library expects your app to provide, such as react and react-native, so that only one shared copy exists in the project.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Peer Dependencies

hasDefinedTerm.description: PixelRatio is the React Native API that exposes the device’s pixel density and font scale, used to request sharp images and to round layout values to physical pixels.
hasDefinedTerm.name: PixelRatio

hasDefinedTerm.description: Platform-specific code lets one codebase behave differently per platform, via the Platform module or file extensions like Button.ios.tsx that Metro resolves.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Platform-Specific Code

hasDefinedTerm.description: The Podfile is the Ruby file in ios/ that tells CocoaPods which native iOS dependencies to install; Podfile.lock records the exact versions it resolved.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Podfile

hasDefinedTerm.description: Pressable is React Native’s core component for handling taps and long presses, exposing a pressed state for feedback; it supersedes the older Touchables.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Pressable

hasDefinedTerm.description: A privacy manifest is the PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file Apple requires in iOS apps and SDKs, declaring the data they collect and why they use certain sensitive APIs.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Privacy Manifest

hasDefinedTerm.description: Profiling is measuring where a React Native app spends time and memory, using tools that record JS, React renders and native threads, so you fix real bottlenecks.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Profiling

hasDefinedTerm.description: A Progressive Web App (PWA) is a website that can be installed to the home screen and work offline, using a web app manifest and a service worker instead of a store.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Progressive Web App

hasDefinedTerm.description: Props are the read-only inputs a component receives from its parent. State is the data a component owns and can change, triggering a re-render.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Props and State

hasDefinedTerm.description: Push notifications are messages a server sends to a device through Apple’s APNs or Google’s FCM, shown by the OS even when the React Native app is closed.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Push Notifications

hasDefinedTerm.description: R8 is Android’s code shrinker and obfuscator, the successor to ProGuard; it removes unused Java and Kotlin code from release builds and renames what remains.
hasDefinedTerm.name: R8 and ProGuard

hasDefinedTerm.description: A re-render is React calling a component function again to compute new output. It does not always change the screen, but too many of them slow a React Native app.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Re-render

hasDefinedTerm.description: React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that memoises components and hooks automatically, removing most hand-written useMemo, useCallback and memo.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React Compiler

hasDefinedTerm.description: React DevTools is the React team’s inspector for browsing the component tree, reading props, state and hooks, and profiling why and how long components render.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React DevTools

hasDefinedTerm.description: A React element is a lightweight plain-object description of what should appear on screen. React compares elements between renders to work out the smallest native update.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React Elements

hasDefinedTerm.description: The React Native CLI is the community-maintained command-line tool for creating, running and building React Native apps that you manage without a framework.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React Native CLI

hasDefinedTerm.description: React Native DevTools is the official debugger for React Native apps, a Chrome DevTools-based window for console logs, breakpoints, React components and profiling.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React Native DevTools

hasDefinedTerm.description: React Native Directory is a searchable catalogue of React Native libraries showing platform support, New Architecture compatibility, maintenance activity and popularity.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React Native Directory

hasDefinedTerm.description: React Native SVG is the library that renders SVG graphics natively, exposing elements such as Svg, Path and Circle as React components on iOS and Android.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React Native SVG

hasDefinedTerm.description: React Native Testing Library (RNTL) renders components in Jest and queries them by text, role or label, so tests check what users see rather than internal state.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React Native Testing Library

hasDefinedTerm.description: React Native Web is a library that implements React Native’s components and APIs with React DOM, so the same View, Text and StyleSheet code renders as a website.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React Native Web

hasDefinedTerm.description: React Navigation is the standard navigation library for React Native, providing stack, tab and drawer navigators built on native primitives.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React Navigation

hasDefinedTerm.description: React.memo wraps a component so React skips re-rendering it when its props are shallowly equal to last time, a common fix for slow lists in React Native.
hasDefinedTerm.name: React.memo

hasDefinedTerm.description: Reactotron is a free desktop app from Infinite Red for inspecting a React Native app in development: logs, network requests, state, storage and custom commands.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Reactotron

hasDefinedTerm.description: Reanimated is the standard React Native animation library. It runs animation logic as worklets on the UI thread, so motion stays smooth while JavaScript is busy.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Reanimated

hasDefinedTerm.description: Reconciliation is React’s process of comparing the new element tree with the previous one to work out the minimal set of changes to apply to the native views.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Reconciliation

hasDefinedTerm.description: Redux is a predictable global state library where a single store is updated by dispatched actions. Redux Toolkit is its official, modern way to write it in React Native.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Redux

hasDefinedTerm.description: A ref is an escape hatch that holds a mutable value or points at a native component instance, letting you call imperative methods without triggering a re-render.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Refs

hasDefinedTerm.description: A release build is the optimised, production-signed React Native app with JavaScript bundled in and developer tooling removed, unlike the debug build you develop with.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Release Build

hasDefinedTerm.description: A renderer is the part of React that turns components into output for one platform. React Native ships its own renderer, so the same React core drives native views.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Renderer

hasDefinedTerm.description: Responsive design in React Native means layouts that adapt to window size, orientation and device type, from small phones to tablets, foldables and split screens.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Responsive Design

hasDefinedTerm.description: Right-to-left (RTL) layout mirrors a React Native interface for languages such as Arabic and Hebrew, controlled through the I18nManager API and start/end styles.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Right-to-Left Layout

hasDefinedTerm.description: A runtime version is a label describing an app binary’s native layer. Expo’s OTA updates only install on builds with the exact same runtime version string.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Runtime Version

hasDefinedTerm.description: The safe area is the part of the screen not covered by the notch, status bar, home indicator or rounded corners. Content must be inset to stay usable.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Safe Area

hasDefinedTerm.description: A screen reader is assistive software, VoiceOver on iOS and TalkBack on Android, that speaks the interface aloud and lets people navigate an app by swipes and taps.
hasDefinedTerm.name: Screen Reader
