/react-native-glossary/absolute-position.title: Absolute Positioning in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Absolute positioning takes a React Native view out of the flexbox flow and places it with top, right, bottom and left offsets relative to its parent view.
og:description: Absolute positioning takes a React Native view out of the flexbox flow and places it with top, right, bottom and left offsets relative to its parent view.
og:title: Absolute Positioning in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Absolute positioning takes a React Native view out of the flexbox flow and places it with top, right, bottom and left offsets relative to its parent view.
jsonLd.name: Absolute Positioning

jsonLd.articleBody: Absolute positioning removes a view from the normal flexbox layout and places it at fixed offsets with top, right, bottom and left. Its siblings lay out as if it did not exist. It is how you build badges, floating action buttons, overlays and image captions. The big difference from CSS: in React Native every view is position: 'relative' by default, so an absolutely positioned child is always placed relative to its direct parent, not to the nearest positioned ancestor or the screen. StyleSheet.absoluteFill is a shortcut for "cover the whole parent", handy for overlays and backgrounds. zIndex controls stacking, with rules that surprise people: It only orders siblings. A child cannot escape its parent’s stacking, however high its zIndex. Without it, later siblings draw on top of earlier ones. On Android, elevation also affects drawing order, so a view with a shadow can cover a sibling that has a higher zIndex. Give both the same elevation or set it explicitly. The most common gotcha is touches. A child positioned outside its parent’s bounds, like the badge above, may be visible but not tappable on Android, because touches are only delivered inside the parent’s frame. Make the parent large enough, or move the floating element higher up the tree. Reach for absolute positioning sparingly. Hard-coded offsets break with font scaling, translations and different screen sizes, where a flex layout would adapt.
jsonLd.description: Absolute positioning takes a React Native view out of the flexbox flow and places it with top, right, bottom and left offsets relative to its parent view.
jsonLd.headline: What is Absolute Positioning in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/accessibility-lab.title: Accessibility Label in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: An accessibility label is the text a screen reader speaks for an element; in React Native you set it with accessibilityLabel or aria-label on views and controls.
og:description: An accessibility label is the text a screen reader speaks for an element; in React Native you set it with accessibilityLabel or aria-label on views and controls.
og:title: Accessibility Label in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An accessibility label is the text a screen reader speaks for an element; in React Native you set it with accessibilityLabel or aria-label on views and controls.
jsonLd.name: Accessibility Label

jsonLd.articleBody: An accessibility label is the name a screen reader announces when the user focuses an element. In React Native you provide it with the accessibilityLabel prop, or the web-style aria-label alias, on components such as View, Text, Image and Pressable. Text elements usually do not need one, because the screen reader reads their content. Labels matter for everything that has no readable text: icon buttons, images, avatars, and controls whose visible text is ambiguous out of context. The related accessible prop decides what becomes a single focus stop. When accessible is true, the element and all its children are grouped and read as one item, and by default the screen reader combines the children’s text. Touchable components are accessible by default; a plain View is not, so a card built from several Text nodes is read piece by piece unless you group it. Practical rules: Describe the purpose, not the appearance: "Search", not "Magnifying glass icon". Do not repeat the role. With accessibilityRole="button" the reader already says "button", so a label of "Delete button" is read twice. Keep it short, and use accessibilityHint for extra context about the outcome. Translate it. Labels are user-facing text and belong in your localisation files. The most common mistake is grouping too much. Setting accessible on a container that holds several buttons makes them unreachable as separate targets. Labels are also what React Native Testing Library queries with getByLabelText, so good labels make tests more readable too.
jsonLd.description: An accessibility label is the text a screen reader speaks for an element; in React Native you set it with accessibilityLabel or aria-label on views and controls.
jsonLd.headline: What is Accessibility Label in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/accessibility-rol.title: Accessibility Role in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: An accessibility role tells screen readers what kind of element something is, such as a button, header or link, set with the accessibilityRole or role prop.
og:description: An accessibility role tells screen readers what kind of element something is, such as a button, header or link, set with the accessibilityRole or role prop.
og:title: Accessibility Role in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An accessibility role tells screen readers what kind of element something is, such as a button, header or link, set with the accessibilityRole or role prop.
jsonLd.name: Accessibility Role

jsonLd.articleBody: An accessibility role tells assistive technology what an element is and how it can be used. In React Native you set it with accessibilityRole or the web-style role prop, and the screen reader announces it after the label: "Settings, button" or "Notifications, heading". Roles matter because React Native builds most controls from generic views. A Pressable is just a touchable view with no role by default, so without one VoiceOver and TalkBack read only its text and give no hint that it can be activated. The built-in Button sets the button role for you; custom buttons must set it themselves. Commonly used values include button, link, header, image, text, search, checkbox, switch, tab, tablist, adjustable and none. The role prop accepts web-style names, such as heading and img, and takes precedence over accessibilityRole when both are set. A role usually needs a state to be complete. Checkboxes, switches and tabs should pass accessibilityState (or the matching aria-checked, aria-selected, aria-disabled props) so the reader says "checked" or "selected" and updates when it changes. Headers deserve a special mention. Screen reader users jump between headings to skim a screen, so marking section titles as header is one of the cheapest, highest-impact accessibility fixes in any app. The common mistake is choosing a role for its look rather than its behaviour. Something that navigates to another screen is a button in most apps, while link is better reserved for text that opens a URL. A row that toggles a setting is a switch, not a button. Match the role to what happens on activation.
jsonLd.description: An accessibility role tells screen readers what kind of element something is, such as a button, header or link, set with the accessibilityRole or role prop.
jsonLd.headline: What is Accessibility Role in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: ActivityIndicator is React Native’s core loading spinner, rendering the native indeterminate progress indicator on iOS and Android with configurable size and colour.
og:description: ActivityIndicator is React Native’s core loading spinner, rendering the native indeterminate progress indicator on iOS and Android with configurable size and colour.
og:title: ActivityIndicator in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: ActivityIndicator is React Native’s core loading spinner, rendering the native indeterminate progress indicator on iOS and Android with configurable size and colour.
jsonLd.name: ActivityIndicator

jsonLd.articleBody: ActivityIndicator is the core component that shows a circular loading spinner. It renders the platform’s own control, UIActivityIndicatorView on iOS and an indeterminate ProgressBar on Android, so it looks native on each without styling. The props are deliberately few: size — 'small' or 'large'. A numeric size works on Android only; iOS ignores it, so scale with a transform if you need a custom size there. color — the spinner colour. The defaults differ per platform, so set it to match your theme, especially in dark mode. animating — whether it spins. On iOS, hidesWhenStopped (true by default) hides it when it stops. It is indeterminate only: it says “something is happening” but never “how much”. For uploads or downloads with known progress, use a progress bar from a library or a View whose width you animate. The most common UX mistake is flashing a spinner for requests that finish in 100 ms. A spinner that appears and vanishes instantly feels slower than nothing. Delay it by a few hundred milliseconds, or show skeleton placeholders shaped like the content, which keeps layout stable. Data libraries such as TanStack Query expose separate “first load” and “background refetch” flags so you can show a full spinner only the first time. A full-screen spinner also says nothing to a screen reader user. Add an accessibilityLabel such as “Loading orders” so the state is announced, and consider whether Suspense fallbacks can own loading states declaratively instead of scattering spinners through components.
jsonLd.description: ActivityIndicator is React Native’s core loading spinner, rendering the native indeterminate progress indicator on iOS and Android with configurable size and colour.
jsonLd.headline: What is ActivityIndicator in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/adb.title: ADB in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: ADB (Android Debug Bridge) is the command-line tool that talks to Android devices and emulators to install apps, read logs, forward ports and open a shell.
og:description: ADB (Android Debug Bridge) is the command-line tool that talks to Android devices and emulators to install apps, read logs, forward ports and open a shell.
og:title: ADB in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: ADB (Android Debug Bridge) is the command-line tool that talks to Android devices and emulators to install apps, read logs, forward ports and open a shell.
jsonLd.name: ADB

jsonLd.articleBody: ADB, the Android Debug Bridge, is the command-line tool from the Android SDK platform-tools that connects your computer to Android devices and the Android Emulator. Every time a React Native app is installed or launched on Android during development, ADB is doing the work underneath. It has three parts: the adb client you type commands into, a background server on your machine, and a daemon running on each device. The commands a React Native developer uses most: adb reverse matters most. A phone’s localhost is the phone itself, so without that port mapping the app cannot download the bundle from Metro. The CLI runs it automatically, but it resets when a USB cable is reconnected or the server restarts; rerun it when you hit "could not connect to development server". With several devices attached, add -s <serial> to target one. adb logcat is the first place to look when an Android build crashes on launch before JavaScript runs: native exceptions never reach the JS console. Common gotchas: "adb server version doesn’t match this client" means two copies of ADB are installed, often one from Android Studio and one from Homebrew. Keep one on your PATH. "unauthorized" devices need the USB debugging prompt accepted on the phone. Physical devices need Developer options and USB debugging switched on first. See the ADB docs.
jsonLd.description: ADB (Android Debug Bridge) is the command-line tool that talks to Android devices and emulators to install apps, read logs, forward ports and open a shell.
jsonLd.headline: What is ADB in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/alert-api.title: Alert in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Alert is the React Native API that shows a native system dialog with a title, message and up to a few buttons, using UIAlertController on iOS and AlertDialog on Android.
og:description: Alert is the React Native API that shows a native system dialog with a title, message and up to a few buttons, using UIAlertController on iOS and AlertDialog on Android.
og:title: Alert in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Alert is the React Native API that shows a native system dialog with a title, message and up to a few buttons, using UIAlertController on iOS and AlertDialog on Android.
jsonLd.name: Alert

jsonLd.articleBody: Alert is the core API for native dialogs. Alert.alert(title, message, buttons, options) shows the platform’s own dialog, UIAlertController on iOS and an AlertDialog on Android, so it matches system styling and dark mode without any work. Behaviour differs per platform more than the one-line API suggests: Button styles cancel and destructive affect presentation on iOS (bold, red). Android ignores them. Button count: Android shows at most three buttons (neutral, negative, positive). Extra ones are dropped. Dismissal: on Android the user can tap outside or press back if you pass { cancelable: true }, and onDismiss tells you it happened. iOS alerts can only be closed with a button. Alert.prompt, which asks for text input, exists on iOS only. Alert.alert is fire-and-forget: it returns immediately rather than waiting for the user. If you want await confirm(), wrap it in a Promise that resolves from each button’s onPress. The common gotcha is cross-platform reach. On React Native Web, Alert does nothing at all, so a confirmation that guards a destructive action silently disappears. Wrap it in your own helper with a web fallback. For anything beyond a short question, such as custom layout, images, forms or branded styling, build a Modal or bottom sheet instead. Alerts work best when they are rare, short and native.
jsonLd.description: Alert is the React Native API that shows a native system dialog with a title, message and up to a few buttons, using UIAlertController on iOS and AlertDialog on Android.
jsonLd.headline: What is Alert in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/android-app-bundl.title: Android App Bundle in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: An Android App Bundle (.aab) is the format you upload to Google Play, which then generates smaller device-specific APKs for each user instead of one universal file.
og:description: An Android App Bundle (.aab) is the format you upload to Google Play, which then generates smaller device-specific APKs for each user instead of one universal file.
og:title: Android App Bundle in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An Android App Bundle (.aab) is the format you upload to Google Play, which then generates smaller device-specific APKs for each user instead of one universal file.
jsonLd.name: Android App Bundle

jsonLd.articleBody: An Android App Bundle is the file a React Native app uploads to Google Play. It contains all of the app’s compiled code, resources and native libraries, but it is not installable on its own. Google Play uses it to build optimised APKs for each device that downloads the app. New apps on Play have been required to use bundles since 2021. The benefit matters more for React Native than for many native apps. The app ships native libraries, Hermes and the framework itself among them, for several CPU architectures. From a bundle, Play delivers only the architecture, screen density and languages the device needs, which noticeably cuts download size compared with a universal APK. See bundle size. You build one with the release Gradle task, or eas build for Android, which produces bundles by default: The bundle is signed with your upload key. With Play App Signing, Google verifies that signature, then re-signs the generated APKs with the app signing key it holds. Losing the upload key is recoverable through Play Console; it is not the end of the app. Common confusion: You cannot install an .aab by dragging it onto a phone. To test exactly what Play would deliver, use Google’s bundletool to generate and install APKs from it, or upload to an internal testing track. Bundles are a Play format. Sideloading, enterprise distribution and some other stores still expect an APK, so keep a build profile for that. The JavaScript bundle inside is unrelated to the term "App Bundle"; it is just one asset among many.
jsonLd.description: An Android App Bundle (.aab) is the format you upload to Google Play, which then generates smaller device-specific APKs for each user instead of one universal file.
jsonLd.headline: What is Android App Bundle in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/android-app-links.title: Android App Links in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Android App Links are verified https links that open your Android app directly, without a chooser dialog, once an assetlinks.json file on your domain proves you own both.
og:description: Android App Links are verified https links that open your Android app directly, without a chooser dialog, once an assetlinks.json file on your domain proves you own both.
og:title: Android App Links in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Android App Links are verified https links that open your Android app directly, without a chooser dialog, once an assetlinks.json file on your domain proves you own both.
jsonLd.name: Android App Links

jsonLd.articleBody: Android App Links are https:// links that Android hands straight to your app because it has verified you own the domain. They are the Android counterpart of iOS Universal Links, and the public-facing form of deep linking. The app declares the domain with an intent filter marked autoVerify in AndroidManifest.xml, or android.intentFilters in an Expo app config: The website publishes /.well-known/assetlinks.json, listing the app’s package name and the SHA-256 fingerprint of the certificate that signs it. Android checks the file when the app is installed. The mistake almost everyone makes once is the fingerprint. With Play App Signing, Google re-signs your app, so the fingerprint users’ devices see is Google’s app signing key, shown in Play Console, not your upload key from the keystore. Debug builds use yet another certificate. Put every fingerprint you need in the file. Other things worth knowing: Without verification, recent Android versions open the link in the browser rather than offering your app, so a failed check looks like "links just open Chrome". Every host in a verified intent filter must pass, including subdomains you list. You can inspect and re-trigger verification on a device: See Android App Links.
jsonLd.description: Android App Links are verified https links that open your Android app directly, without a chooser dialog, once an assetlinks.json file on your domain proves you own both.
jsonLd.headline: What is Android App Links in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/android-emulator.title: Android Emulator in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The Android Emulator runs a virtual Android device on your computer from an AVD profile, letting you install and debug a React Native app without a real phone.
og:description: The Android Emulator runs a virtual Android device on your computer from an AVD profile, letting you install and debug a React Native app without a real phone.
og:title: Android Emulator in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The Android Emulator runs a virtual Android device on your computer from an AVD profile, letting you install and debug a React Native app without a real phone.
jsonLd.name: Android Emulator

jsonLd.articleBody: The Android Emulator is a virtual Android device that runs on macOS, Windows or Linux. Each device is defined by an AVD (Android Virtual Device): a profile combining a screen size, an Android version and a system image. You create AVDs in the Device Manager of Android Studio. Unlike the iOS Simulator, it genuinely emulates a device and runs a full Android system image, accelerated by your machine’s hypervisor. That makes it closer to a real phone, but also heavier on RAM and CPU. Things that trip React Native developers up: localhost is the emulator, not your computer. The app reaches Metro because the tooling runs adb reverse tcp:8081 tcp:8081 for you; if that mapping is lost, you get a red "could not connect to development server" screen. The host machine is also reachable at 10.0.2.2. Pick a system image with Google Play if your app relies on Play Services, such as Firebase Cloud Messaging or Google sign-in. Match the CPU architecture. On Apple silicon use arm64 images; x86 images are slow or will not start. The Dev Menu opens with Cmd+M (macOS) or Ctrl+M, and pressing R twice reloads. You drive and inspect it with ADB, exactly as you would a USB-connected phone: adb devices lists it as emulator-5554 or similar. The gotcha is trusting it for performance or device quirks. Manufacturer skins, low-end memory pressure, and aggressive battery savers that kill background work only appear on real hardware.
jsonLd.description: The Android Emulator runs a virtual Android device on your computer from an AVD profile, letting you install and debug a React Native app without a real phone.
jsonLd.headline: What is Android Emulator in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: An Android keystore is the password-protected file holding the private key that signs your app; Google Play rejects updates signed with a different key.
og:description: An Android keystore is the password-protected file holding the private key that signs your app; Google Play rejects updates signed with a different key.
og:title: Android Keystore in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An Android keystore is the password-protected file holding the private key that signs your app; Google Play rejects updates signed with a different key.
jsonLd.name: Android Keystore

jsonLd.articleBody: An Android keystore is a password-protected file, usually ending in .jks or .keystore, that holds the private key used to sign your Android build. Every React Native release you send to Google Play is signed with a key from this file. With Play App Signing, which new apps published as an Android App Bundle must use, there are two keys: The upload key, which you keep. You sign each .aab with it before uploading. The app signing key, which Google keeps and uses to sign the APKs delivered to users. That split is a safety net. If you lose the upload key, you can ask Google through the Google Play Console to register a new one. Older apps that never enrolled are not so lucky: lose that key and you can never ship an update to the same listing. You create a key with the JDK’s keytool and point Gradle at it in a signingConfigs block: Common gotchas: The React Native template signs release builds with the shared debug.keystore until you change it. Builds signed with the debug key are rejected by Play. Never commit the keystore or its passwords. Keep passwords in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties or CI secrets, and store a backup of the file somewhere other than your laptop. Services such as EAS can generate and hold the keystore for you; download a copy anyway. Do not confuse this file with the Android Keystore system, the on-device API apps use to store cryptographic keys securely at runtime. Same name, different thing.

author: David Leuliette
description: AndroidManifest.xml declares an Android app’s identity to the OS: its activities, permissions, intent filters for deep links, and how the main activity behaves.
og:description: AndroidManifest.xml declares an Android app’s identity to the OS: its activities, permissions, intent filters for deep links, and how the main activity behaves.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: AndroidManifest.xml declares an Android app’s identity to the OS: its activities, permissions, intent filters for deep links, and how the main activity behaves.
jsonLd.name: AndroidManifest.xml

jsonLd.articleBody: AndroidManifest.xml is the file that describes an Android app to the operating system. In a React Native project it lives at android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml and declares the main activity that hosts your React Native views, the permissions the app may request and which URLs or intents it responds to. It is the Android counterpart of iOS’s Info.plist. Edits React Native developers commonly make: Permissions — a <uses-permission> line for the camera, location or notifications. Dangerous permissions still need a runtime request; see App Permissions. Intent filters — so the app opens for a custom scheme or verified Android App Links. android:windowSoftInputMode — controls whether the window resizes when the keyboard opens, which affects every keyboard-handling bug you will chase. android:configChanges — the React Native template lists orientation, screen size and similar changes so the activity is not destroyed and your JavaScript state survives a rotation. A frequent surprise is manifest merging. Every library ships its own manifest, and Gradle merges them into yours at build time, so the final app can request permissions you never wrote. Inspect the merged manifest in Android Studio when Google Play flags a permission you did not expect. You can strip one with tools:node="remove". Another gotcha: since Android 12, any activity with an intent filter must set android:exported explicitly, or the build fails. In Expo projects using Continuous Native Generation, the manifest is generated from app.json (android.permissions, android.intentFilters) and config plugins, so hand edits are lost on the next prebuild.

description: Android Studio is Google’s official Android IDE; React Native developers use it to install the Android SDK, manage emulators, read Logcat and debug native builds.
og:description: Android Studio is Google’s official Android IDE; React Native developers use it to install the Android SDK, manage emulators, read Logcat and debug native builds.
og:title: Android Studio in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Android Studio is Google’s official Android IDE; React Native developers use it to install the Android SDK, manage emulators, read Logcat and debug native builds.
jsonLd.name: Android Studio

jsonLd.articleBody: Android Studio is Google’s integrated development environment for Android, built on IntelliJ IDEA. Most React Native developers write their JavaScript elsewhere, but still need Android Studio because it is the easiest way to install and manage the pieces an Android build depends on. What it gives a React Native developer: SDK Manager — installs Android SDK platforms, build tools, the NDK and command-line tools that Gradle needs. Device Manager — creates and launches virtual devices for the Android Emulator. Logcat — the full native log, including the Java or Kotlin stack trace when an app crashes before JavaScript even loads. Gradle sync and build output — clearer errors than the terminal when a native dependency fails to compile. Profilers and the Layout Inspector — for native memory, CPU and view hierarchy investigation. The usual mistake is opening the wrong folder. Open the android/ directory of your project, not the repository root; otherwise Android Studio does not see a Gradle project and offers nothing useful. Environment setup is the other source of pain. The React Native CLI and Expo find the SDK through the ANDROID_HOME environment variable and expect platform-tools (which contains ADB) on your PATH. Android Studio installs the SDK but does not set these variables for your shell. Builds also need a compatible JDK, so follow the version your React Native release documents rather than whatever Java happens to be installed. You do not need Android Studio to ship: EAS Build or a CI machine can build with command-line tools alone. But when a release build crashes on launch, Logcat in Android Studio is usually the fastest way to see why. The official Android Studio documentation covers installation per platform.

og:description: An animated component is a React Native view whose style values are driven by an animation library — Reanimated or the built-in Animated API — rather than by plain state.

jsonLd.description: An animated component is a React Native view whose style values are driven by an animation library — Reanimated or the built-in Animated API — rather than by plain state.
jsonLd.name: Animated Component

jsonLd.articleBody: An animated component is a view whose styles are driven frame by frame by an animation library instead of by ordinary re-renders. Animating through useState would re-render the tree on every frame, so React Native provides purpose-built wrappers. There are two options, and newcomers should know which they are reading about: The built-in Animated API ships with React Native. You animate Animated.Value objects and render Animated.View, Animated.Text, and friends. With useNativeDriver: true the animation is handed to the native side so it keeps running when JavaScript is busy. Reanimated is the community standard for anything non-trivial. It runs animation logic as worklets directly on the UI thread, so gestures and scroll-linked effects stay smooth. The failure mode to recognise: an animation that stutters only in release-mode-with-work-happening usually means it is running on the JavaScript thread rather than natively.

/react-native-glossary/api-keys.title: API Keys in Mobile Apps in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Any API key embedded in a React Native app ships to every user and can be extracted. Only public, restricted keys belong in the app; true secrets stay on a server.
og:description: Any API key embedded in a React Native app ships to every user and can be extracted. Only public, restricted keys belong in the app; true secrets stay on a server.
og:image:alt: API Keys in Mobile Apps — weshipit.today
og:title: API Keys in Mobile Apps in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Any API key embedded in a React Native app ships to every user and can be extracted. Only public, restricted keys belong in the app; true secrets stay on a server.
jsonLd.name: API Keys in Mobile Apps

jsonLd.articleBody: An API key in a mobile app is a credential compiled into the app so it can call a third-party service: maps, analytics, payments, an AI model. The core rule for React Native is simple and widely misunderstood: anything shipped in the app is public. Your JavaScript bundle sits inside every .ipa and .apk, and it can be unpacked and searched for strings, even when compiled to Hermes bytecode. Environment variables do not change this. Variables prefixed with EXPO_PUBLIC_, or values read through libraries like react-native-config, are inlined into the build at compile time; a .env file keeps a value out of git, not out of the app. Keys fall into two groups: Publishable keys are designed to be public: a Stripe publishable key, a Firebase web config, a Supabase anon key protected by row-level security. Shipping them is fine. Secret keys grant real power or cost money: a Stripe secret key, an OpenAI or Anthropic API key, an admin token. They must never be in the app. For secrets, put a backend in between. The app calls your server or a serverless function, which authenticates the user, applies rate limits and calls the third-party API with the secret. For publishable keys, use the provider's restrictions: limit a Google Maps key to your bundle identifier and Android signing certificate, and set quotas so abuse is capped. The common mistake is reaching for obfuscation or secure storage to hide a secret. Obfuscation only delays extraction, and the Keychain and Keystore protect data your app receives at runtime, such as a user's session token, not a value baked into the package. If a secret key has already shipped, rotate it.
jsonLd.description: Any API key embedded in a React Native app ships to every user and can be extracted. Only public, restricted keys belong in the app; true secrets stay on a server.
jsonLd.headline: What is API Keys in Mobile Apps in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: API routes are Expo Router files ending in +api.ts that export HTTP handlers, letting a React Native project ship server endpoints in the same codebase as its app.
og:description: API routes are Expo Router files ending in +api.ts that export HTTP handlers, letting a React Native project ship server endpoints in the same codebase as its app.
og:title: API Routes in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: API routes are Expo Router files ending in +api.ts that export HTTP handlers, letting a React Native project ship server endpoints in the same codebase as its app.
jsonLd.name: API Routes

jsonLd.articleBody: API routes are server endpoints you write inside an Expo Router project. Any file in app/ whose name ends in +api.ts becomes an HTTP route, and the functions it exports, named after HTTP methods, handle requests using the standard Request and Response objects. The reason they matter in a mobile app is secrets. Everything in a JavaScript bundle can be extracted from the installed app, so a third-party key that must stay private (a payment provider, an LLM provider, an admin database key) cannot live in the client. An API route runs on a server, so it can hold that key and expose only the narrow operation the app needs. See API keys in mobile apps. In practice: The project needs server output (web.output: "server" in app config), and the routes are deployed separately from the app binary, to EAS Hosting or another host through an adapter. The app calls them with fetch. A relative URL works against the dev server in development, but a production build needs to know the deployed origin, which you configure for Expo Router. Route files are never bundled into the native app. The common mistake is forgetting that the app and the API now ship on different schedules. A store build in users’ hands for months will keep calling the endpoint shapes it was built with, so changing a route’s request or response format can break older installs. Version or extend routes rather than reshaping them. See the API routes docs.
jsonLd.description: API routes are Expo Router files ending in +api.ts that export HTTP handlers, letting a React Native project ship server endpoints in the same codebase as its app.
jsonLd.headline: What is API Routes in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: An APK (.apk) is the Android package file that installs directly on a device or emulator, holding the compiled code, resources, native libraries and JavaScript bundle.
og:description: An APK (.apk) is the Android package file that installs directly on a device or emulator, holding the compiled code, resources, native libraries and JavaScript bundle.
og:title: APK in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An APK (.apk) is the Android package file that installs directly on a device or emulator, holding the compiled code, resources, native libraries and JavaScript bundle.
jsonLd.name: APK

jsonLd.articleBody: An APK is the installable unit of Android: a ZIP archive containing compiled Kotlin and Java code (classes.dex), resources, the binary AndroidManifest.xml, native libraries under lib/<abi>/, and in a React Native release build the JavaScript bundle under assets/. Every Android app on a device was installed as one or more APKs. For React Native developers APKs are the everyday testing format, because they install directly: That makes them the right choice for sharing a build with a tester outside the Play Store, installing on an emulator in CI for end-to-end tests, or distributing internally. With EAS, setting "buildType": "apk" in an Android build profile produces one instead of the default bundle. For Google Play itself you upload an Android App Bundle, and Play generates the APKs. Things that surprise people: A debug APK may contain no JavaScript. It expects to fetch the bundle from Metro, so on a device without a Metro connection it shows a red error screen. Build a release variant to share. Universal APKs are large. They include native libraries for every CPU architecture. Limiting reactNativeArchitectures in gradle.properties speeds up local builds, but only ship what real devices need. Signatures must match to update. Installing a release APK over a debug one fails with INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE, because they are signed with different keys. Uninstall first with ADB. The template’s release build is signed with the debug keystore until you configure your own, which is fine for testing but never for a store.

jsonLd.headline: What is APK in React Native?

description: App config is the app.json or app.config.js/ts file where an Expo project declares its name, identifiers, icons, permissions and plugins for native generation.
og:description: App config is the app.json or app.config.js/ts file where an Expo project declares its name, identifiers, icons, permissions and plugins for native generation.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: App config is the app.json or app.config.js/ts file where an Expo project declares its name, identifiers, icons, permissions and plugins for native generation.
jsonLd.name: App Config

jsonLd.articleBody: App config is the file at the root of an Expo project, app.json or its dynamic form app.config.js / app.config.ts, that describes the app: display name, version, icon, splash screen, bundle identifier, permissions and the list of config plugins. It matters because it is the source of truth for the native projects. With Continuous Native Generation, npx expo prebuild reads app config and writes Info.plist, AndroidManifest.xml and the rest, running each config plugin along the way. EAS Build, Expo CLI and Expo Router read it too. The dynamic form is plain code, which helps when values depend on the build: The config argument contains whatever is in app.json, so the two files can coexist. Run npx expo config to print the fully resolved result. Common gotchas: Changing native fields such as permissions, icons or the bundle identifier needs a new native build. A JavaScript reload will not pick them up. If you commit your own ios/ and android/ folders and never run prebuild, most native fields in app config are ignored, which Expo Doctor warns about. Anything placed under extra ends up readable inside the app bundle. It is not a place for secrets.

/react-native-glossary/app-icon.title: App Icon in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The app icon is the image representing your React Native app on the home screen and in stores, built from platform-specific assets such as Android’s adaptive icon.
og:description: The app icon is the image representing your React Native app on the home screen and in stores, built from platform-specific assets such as Android’s adaptive icon.
og:title: App Icon in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The app icon is the image representing your React Native app on the home screen and in stores, built from platform-specific assets such as Android’s adaptive icon.
jsonLd.name: App Icon

jsonLd.articleBody: The app icon is the image people tap on the home screen and see in the App Store and Google Play. It is a native asset baked into the binary, so React Native code never renders it; you supply files in the formats each platform expects. iOS needs a single 1024×1024 square image in the asset catalog, from which Xcode derives every size. It must be fully opaque: an icon with a transparent background is rejected at upload. Do not round the corners yourself, the system applies its own mask. Recent iOS versions also let users pick dark and tinted home screens, for which you can provide variants. Android uses the adaptive icon, introduced in Android 8.0. Instead of one bitmap you provide two layers: A foreground image, usually your logo on transparency. A background colour or image. The launcher masks the combined layers into a circle, squircle or whatever shape the device uses, and can animate them slightly. The layers are 108dp square, but only the central area is guaranteed to be visible, so keep the logo well inside that safe zone. A monochrome layer powers themed icons on Android 13 and later. With Expo all of this lives in your app config: The usual mistakes, often caught late in App Store review or on a real launcher: putting a full-bleed square logo in the foreground layer, so the launcher crops it; forgetting the icon changes only after a fresh native build; and expecting to swap it with an over-the-air update. Alternate icons the user can choose at runtime are possible, but must be bundled ahead of time.

jsonLd.headline: What is App Icon in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/app-permissions.title: App Permissions in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: App permissions are the user approvals iOS and Android require before an app can use sensitive features such as the camera, location, contacts or notifications.
og:description: App permissions are the user approvals iOS and Android require before an app can use sensitive features such as the camera, location, contacts or notifications.
og:title: App Permissions in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: App permissions are the user approvals iOS and Android require before an app can use sensitive features such as the camera, location, contacts or notifications.
jsonLd.name: App Permissions

jsonLd.articleBody: App permissions are the approvals a user grants before a React Native app can touch sensitive data or hardware: camera, microphone, photos, location, contacts, Bluetooth, notifications. Both platforms need a declaration in native config plus a request at runtime, and they handle each differently. iOS requires a usage description string in Info.plist, such as NSCameraUsageDescription, explaining why you need access. If the key is missing, the app crashes the moment it asks. The system shows the prompt once; after a denial, the only way back is the Settings app. Android requires each permission in AndroidManifest.xml. Normal permissions such as internet access are granted at install. Dangerous ones, such as camera or fine location, must also be requested at runtime, and since Android 13 notifications are one of them. After repeated denials the system stops showing the dialog and silently returns "denied". In React Native you request permissions through the module that uses the feature (Expo modules expose requestPermissionsAsync), through the core PermissionsAndroid API, or through the cross-platform react-native-permissions library. With Expo, the native declarations are usually added by each library’s config plugin. Practical advice: Ask in context, right before the feature is used, never in a wall of prompts at launch. A denial on iOS is close to permanent. Always handle "denied" and "limited" (iOS photo access can be partial) and offer a path to Settings with the Linking API. Write honest, specific usage strings. Vague ones are a frequent App Store review rejection.
jsonLd.description: App permissions are the user approvals iOS and Android require before an app can use sensitive features such as the camera, location, contacts or notifications.
jsonLd.headline: What is App Permissions in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/app-store-connect.title: App Store Connect in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: App Store Connect is Apple’s web portal for publishing iOS apps: you create the app record, upload builds, run TestFlight, write the listing and submit for review.
og:description: App Store Connect is Apple’s web portal for publishing iOS apps: you create the app record, upload builds, run TestFlight, write the listing and submit for review.
og:title: App Store Connect in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: App Store Connect is Apple’s web portal for publishing iOS apps: you create the app record, upload builds, run TestFlight, write the listing and submit for review.
jsonLd.name: App Store Connect

jsonLd.articleBody: App Store Connect is where an iOS build becomes an App Store app. It was called iTunes Connect until 2018, which is why older guides and some error messages still use that name. Using it requires a paid Apple Developer Program membership. A React Native release passes through it in a fixed order: Register the bundle identifier in the developer portal, then create an app record in App Store Connect that uses it. Upload a signed IPA from Xcode, Apple’s Transporter app, fastlane or EAS Submit. The build then spends some minutes "processing" before it appears. Distribute it to testers through TestFlight. Fill in the version’s metadata: screenshots, description, keywords, privacy details, age rating. Attach the build and submit it for review. It also holds sales, crash and usage analytics, pricing, in-app purchase products and team roles. For automation, create an App Store Connect API key (a .p8 file with a key ID and issuer ID). EAS, fastlane and CI pipelines use it to upload builds without anyone’s Apple ID or two-factor code. Keep it out of the repository; anyone holding it can act on your apps. Gotchas that slow first releases: Every upload needs a build number higher than the last one for that version, or it is rejected. Builds can sit as "Missing Compliance" until you answer the encryption question. Setting ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption in Info.plist answers it once for every build. The app record’s name is reserved globally, so a name another developer already uses is unavailable.
jsonLd.description: App Store Connect is Apple’s web portal for publishing iOS apps: you create the app record, upload builds, run TestFlight, write the listing and submit for review.
jsonLd.headline: What is App Store Connect in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/app-store-review.title: App Store Review in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: App Store Review is Apple’s check of every app version against the App Store Review Guidelines before release; failing it means a rejection you must fix and resubmit.
og:description: App Store Review is Apple’s check of every app version against the App Store Review Guidelines before release; failing it means a rejection you must fix and resubmit.
og:title: App Store Review in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: App Store Review is Apple’s check of every app version against the App Store Review Guidelines before release; failing it means a rejection you must fix and resubmit.
jsonLd.name: App Store Review

jsonLd.articleBody: App Store Review is the step between submitting a version in App Store Connect and its release. Apple combines automated checks with a human reviewer who installs the build and tests it against the App Store Review Guidelines. Most reviews finish within a day or two. Being a React Native app is not a problem in itself. Rejections come from the same places as for native apps, and a few appear again and again: App completeness (2.1): crashes, placeholder content, broken links, or a login wall with no demo account in the review notes. Always provide working credentials. Minimum functionality (4.2): an app that is mostly a website in a WebView is often rejected as offering nothing an app should. Account deletion: if users can create an account in the app, they must be able to delete it from within the app. Payments (3.1.1): digital goods and subscriptions unlocked in the app generally have to use in-app purchase. Privacy: purpose strings for every permission, an accurate privacy label, and a valid privacy manifest for the SDKs you ship. Login services (4.8): offering only third-party social login can trigger a request to add a privacy-focused alternative such as Sign in with Apple. React Native teams should also know where over-the-air updates stand: Apple tolerates JavaScript updates that fix bugs or adjust content, but using them to change the app’s main purpose after review breaks the rules and risks removal. When rejected, the reviewer’s message in the Resolution Center cites the guideline. You can reply, fix and resubmit, or appeal to the App Review Board. Replying calmly with a screen recording often resolves misunderstandings faster than a new build. Google Play has its own review, mostly automated and policy-driven, so passing one store says little about the other. See the App Store Review Guidelines.
jsonLd.description: App Store Review is Apple’s check of every app version against the App Store Review Guidelines before release; failing it means a rejection you must fix and resubmit.
jsonLd.headline: What is App Store Review in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: App versioning is managing the two numbers each store build carries: a user-facing version such as 1.4.0 and a build number that must increase with every upload.
og:description: App versioning is managing the two numbers each store build carries: a user-facing version such as 1.4.0 and a build number that must increase with every upload.
og:title: App Versioning in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: App versioning is managing the two numbers each store build carries: a user-facing version such as 1.4.0 and a build number that must increase with every upload.
jsonLd.name: App Versioning

jsonLd.articleBody: Every native build of a React Native app carries two separate numbers per platform, and the stores enforce rules on both: Purpose iOS Android Shown to users CFBundleShortVersionString versionName Build number CFBundleVersion versionCode (an integer) The user-facing version is up to you; most teams follow semantic versioning. The build number is what the stores actually compare. Google Play rejects any versionCode it has seen before, on any track. App Store Connect requires each upload to have a build number higher than the previous one for that version. In an Expo project they live in the app config: In a bare project they are Xcode’s MARKETING_VERSION and CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION build settings and the defaultConfig block of android/app/build.gradle. If you use Continuous Native Generation, edit the config, not the generated native files, or your change is overwritten. The usual pain is remembering to bump the build number. Let tooling do it: EAS can store versions remotely (appVersionSource: "remote") and increment them on each build with autoIncrement, and fastlane has actions for both platforms. Read build numbers from CI rather than from a developer’s machine so two people never upload the same number. The common misconception is that an over-the-air update changes the version. It does not; the binary keeps its numbers. What links updates to binaries is the runtime version, so keep the store version for native releases and track update versions separately.
jsonLd.description: App versioning is managing the two numbers each store build carries: a user-facing version such as 1.4.0 and a build number that must increase with every upload.
jsonLd.headline: What is App Versioning in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Appearance is the React Native API, with its useColorScheme hook, that reports whether the user has chosen light or dark mode and notifies the app when that changes.
og:description: Appearance is the React Native API, with its useColorScheme hook, that reports whether the user has chosen light or dark mode and notifies the app when that changes.
og:title: Appearance in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Appearance is the React Native API, with its useColorScheme hook, that reports whether the user has chosen light or dark mode and notifies the app when that changes.
jsonLd.name: Appearance

jsonLd.articleBody: Appearance is the core API for the system colour scheme. Appearance.getColorScheme() returns 'light' or 'dark' (or nothing when no preference is available), and the useColorScheme() hook gives the same value inside components, re-rendering when the user switches mode. React Native does not theme your app automatically. Unlike system UI, your own Views and Text keep whatever colours you gave them, so dark mode means choosing colours from the scheme yourself, usually through a theme context and design tokens rather than ternaries scattered through every style. Appearance.setColorScheme() lets an app override the system choice, which is how an in-app “Light / Dark / System” setting can also switch native elements such as alerts, date pickers and the keyboard to match. The most common “dark mode doesn’t work” report is configuration, not code. The hook always returns light when the app has opted out of dark mode at the native level: On iOS, UIUserInterfaceStyle set to Light in Info.plist locks the app to light. In Expo, the userInterfaceStyle field in app config must be automatic for the app to follow the system; with light it never changes. Android may also need the expo-system-ui package for that setting to apply. Other things to remember: Update the status bar style with the scheme, or icons disappear against dark headers. Images and illustrations may need dark variants, not just backgrounds. Test switching while the app is running, not only at launch, since some screens cache styles computed at import time.
jsonLd.description: Appearance is the React Native API, with its useColorScheme hook, that reports whether the user has chosen light or dark mode and notifies the app when that changes.
jsonLd.headline: What is Appearance in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/appstate.title: AppState in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: AppState is the React Native API that reports whether the app is active in the foreground, inactive, or in the background, and emits an event whenever that changes.
og:description: AppState is the React Native API that reports whether the app is active in the foreground, inactive, or in the background, and emits an event whenever that changes.
og:title: AppState in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: AppState is the React Native API that reports whether the app is active in the foreground, inactive, or in the background, and emits an event whenever that changes.
jsonLd.name: AppState

jsonLd.articleBody: AppState is the core API for knowing whether your app is in the foreground. AppState.currentState holds the current value, and a change listener fires on every transition. The states you will see: active — in the foreground and receiving input. background — the user switched away, went home or locked the phone. inactive — iOS only, a brief in-between state: pulling down Notification Centre, the app switcher, an incoming call, a system permission dialog. Typical uses are refreshing data when the user returns, pausing video or timers when they leave, locking a banking screen, or flushing analytics. Data libraries such as TanStack Query can wire AppState into their “refetch on focus” behaviour, since React Native has no browser visibilitychange event. Common mistakes: Treating inactive as background. A system permission prompt makes iOS apps inactive, so logging out on inactive logs users out mid-flow. Decide which transitions you actually care about. Expecting code to keep running in the background. Once backgrounded, the OS may suspend the JavaScript thread within seconds; timers and pending work stop. Real background work needs the platform’s background task mechanisms. Forgetting cleanup. Not removing the subscription in the useEffect cleanup leaks listeners every time the component remounts. AppState describes the whole app, not one screen. To react when a particular screen gains or loses focus inside the app, use your navigator’s focus events instead.
jsonLd.description: AppState is the React Native API that reports whether the app is active in the foreground, inactive, or in the background, and emits an event whenever that changes.
jsonLd.headline: What is AppState in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/asyncstorage.title: AsyncStorage in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: AsyncStorage is an unencrypted, asynchronous key-value store that persists strings on the device, maintained as @react-native-async-storage/async-storage.
og:description: AsyncStorage is an unencrypted, asynchronous key-value store that persists strings on the device, maintained as @react-native-async-storage/async-storage.
og:title: AsyncStorage in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: AsyncStorage is an unencrypted, asynchronous key-value store that persists strings on the device, maintained as @react-native-async-storage/async-storage.
jsonLd.name: AsyncStorage

jsonLd.articleBody: AsyncStorage is the long-standing simple way to save small amounts of data on a device in React Native. It stores string values under string keys, every call returns a promise, and the data survives app restarts. It once shipped inside React Native itself; it now lives in the community package @react-native-async-storage/async-storage, and old import { AsyncStorage } from 'react-native' code no longer works. It is the default persistence adapter in a lot of library documentation (state persistence, auth session storage), and it works in Expo Go, on web and everywhere else, which is why it remains common. How it behaves in practice: Strings only. Objects must be serialised with JSON.stringify and parsed back, and getItem returns null for a missing key. Always asynchronous. You cannot read a value during the first render, so anything that depends on it (a theme, a logged-in flag) needs a loading state. Batch your reads. Many sequential getItem calls at startup add up; multiGet fetches several keys in one round trip. Size limits. On Android it is backed by SQLite with a default total size cap of around 6 MB, so it is not a place for caches of images or large API responses. The serious mistake is storing secrets. AsyncStorage is not encrypted: on a rooted or jailbroken device, or from an unencrypted backup, auth tokens stored there can be read directly. Keep tokens and keys in secure storage. For performance-sensitive or synchronous access, MMKV is the usual upgrade, and structured data that needs querying belongs in SQLite. See the Async Storage docs.
jsonLd.description: AsyncStorage is an unencrypted, asynchronous key-value store that persists strings on the device, maintained as @react-native-async-storage/async-storage.
jsonLd.headline: What is AsyncStorage in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/autolinking.title: Autolinking in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Autolinking is the build step that finds native code in your installed npm packages and wires it into the iOS and Android projects, so you never link libraries by hand.
og:description: Autolinking is the build step that finds native code in your installed npm packages and wires it into the iOS and Android projects, so you never link libraries by hand.
og:title: Autolinking in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Autolinking is the build step that finds native code in your installed npm packages and wires it into the iOS and Android projects, so you never link libraries by hand.
jsonLd.name: Autolinking

jsonLd.articleBody: Autolinking is the mechanism that scans your dependencies for native code and adds it to the iOS and Android builds automatically. Install a library such as react-native-mmkv, rebuild, and its native module is available without touching Xcode or Gradle files. It works at build time, on both platforms: iOS — the Podfile calls use_native_modules! (and use_expo_modules! in Expo projects), which finds each library’s podspec in node_modules and hands it to CocoaPods. Android — the Gradle settings call into the same discovery logic, include each library as a Gradle project and generate the code that registers its packages. There are two implementations: the React Native Community CLI’s, configured through react-native.config.js, and Expo’s, which also discovers modules built with the Expo Modules API. Expo projects use both. The key point newcomers miss: autolinking only runs when the native app is built. Installing a native library and reloading JavaScript is not enough. You must rebuild: Skip that step and you get an error like TurboModuleRegistry.getEnforcing(...): 'X' could not be found, or a “native module is null” message from older libraries. For the same reason a library with custom native code cannot work in Expo Go; it needs a development build. You can opt a package out per platform in react-native.config.js: Before autolinking, every install meant manually editing the Xcode project, settings.gradle and MainApplication, which is why old READMEs still mention react-native link.
jsonLd.description: Autolinking is the build step that finds native code in your installed npm packages and wires it into the iOS and Android projects, so you never link libraries by hand.

/react-native-glossary/babel.title: Babel in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Babel is the JavaScript compiler Metro runs on every file to turn JSX, TypeScript and modern syntax into code the React Native JavaScript engine can execute.
og:description: Babel is the JavaScript compiler Metro runs on every file to turn JSX, TypeScript and modern syntax into code the React Native JavaScript engine can execute.
og:title: Babel in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Babel is the JavaScript compiler Metro runs on every file to turn JSX, TypeScript and modern syntax into code the React Native JavaScript engine can execute.
jsonLd.name: Babel

jsonLd.articleBody: Babel is a JavaScript compiler. In React Native it runs inside Metro: every file Metro bundles passes through Babel, which strips TypeScript and Flow types, turns JSX into function calls and applies any plugins you configure. Most projects never touch it beyond a short babel.config.js that loads a preset. Expo projects use babel-preset-expo; projects on the React Native CLI use @react-native/babel-preset. Babel matters because several libraries do their work at compile time. Reanimated’s worklets, the React Compiler, import aliases and some styling libraries all ship Babel plugins that rewrite your code before it runs. How it behaves in practice: Babel only transforms. It does not type-check, so a TypeScript error will still bundle and run. Type checking is a separate tsc step. Plugin order matters. Plugins run before presets, in the order listed, and some must come last; Reanimated’s plugin is the classic example. Babel output is cached by Metro. That last point causes the most common gotcha: you edit babel.config.js, reload, and nothing changes. Restart Metro with its cache cleared (npx expo start --clear or npx react-native start --reset-cache) after any Babel config change. Another frequent mistake is adding a plugin that a preset already includes. Recent versions of babel-preset-expo configure Reanimated and other common plugins automatically, so adding them again can produce confusing duplicate-transform errors.
jsonLd.description: Babel is the JavaScript compiler Metro runs on every file to turn JSX, TypeScript and modern syntax into code the React Native JavaScript engine can execute.
jsonLd.headline: What is Babel in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/background-tasks.title: Background Tasks in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Background tasks let a React Native app run short pieces of work while it is not on screen, scheduled by iOS and Android rather than by your own timers.
og:description: Background tasks let a React Native app run short pieces of work while it is not on screen, scheduled by iOS and Android rather than by your own timers.
og:title: Background Tasks in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Background tasks let a React Native app run short pieces of work while it is not on screen, scheduled by iOS and Android rather than by your own timers.
jsonLd.name: Background Tasks

jsonLd.articleBody: A background task is work your React Native app performs while it is not in the foreground: syncing data, uploading a queued photo, refreshing content before the user opens the app. Mobile operating systems aggressively suspend apps to save battery, so background work only happens on the OS’s terms. When the app moves to the background, AppState reports it and, within seconds, the JavaScript thread is effectively frozen. setInterval stops firing. To run later you must register work with the platform scheduler: iOS uses BGTaskScheduler, with short app refresh tasks and longer processing tasks. The system decides when to wake you based on battery, network and how often the user opens the app. Android uses WorkManager, where periodic work runs at most every 15 minutes and can be deferred further by Doze and manufacturer battery savers. Headless JS is the older React Native mechanism for running JavaScript without a UI. In practice you reach these through a library: Expo’s expo-background-task with expo-task-manager, or community packages such as react-native-background-fetch. Separate APIs exist for specific jobs like location tracking, audio playback and large downloads, which each have their own platform modes. Common gotchas: Timing is a hint, not a promise. You cannot schedule "every five minutes", and iOS may not run your task for hours. A force-quit app on iOS generally does not get background refresh until the user opens it again. Define tasks at module top level, outside components, because the OS may launch your app headlessly and no screen will mount. For anything time-sensitive, send a push notification from your server instead of hoping a background task wakes up.
jsonLd.description: Background tasks let a React Native app run short pieces of work while it is not on screen, scheduled by iOS and Android rather than by your own timers.
jsonLd.headline: What is Background Tasks in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/backhandler.title: BackHandler in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: BackHandler is the React Native API for intercepting the Android back button and back gesture, letting a screen close a sheet or confirm before leaving.
og:description: BackHandler is the React Native API for intercepting the Android back button and back gesture, letting a screen close a sheet or confirm before leaving.
og:title: BackHandler in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: BackHandler is the React Native API for intercepting the Android back button and back gesture, letting a screen close a sheet or confirm before leaving.
jsonLd.name: BackHandler

jsonLd.articleBody: BackHandler is the core API for responding to Android’s system back action, whether it comes from the navigation bar button or the edge-swipe gesture. iOS has no equivalent system back event, so this is Android-specific behaviour. You subscribe to hardwareBackPress. Handlers run in reverse order of registration, most recent first, and the return value decides what happens next: return true — you handled it; stop here. return false — pass it on to the previous handler, and ultimately the default behaviour, which closes the activity. BackHandler.exitApp() closes the app, though Google’s guidelines discourage custom exit flows. In practice you rarely need it for navigation. React Navigation and Expo Router already wire back to “pop the current screen” in a stack navigator, and a core Modal routes back to its onRequestClose prop instead. BackHandler is for what sits outside those: closing a custom bottom sheet, leaving a selection mode, or warning about unsaved changes. Common mistakes: Registering globally in a screen that stays mounted. In stack and tab navigators, unfocused screens are still mounted, so their handlers keep swallowing back presses. Register inside React Navigation’s useFocusEffect so the handler exists only while the screen is focused. Forgetting to remove the subscription, which leaves stale handlers that capture old state. Always returning true. That traps the user on a screen with no way out via back, a frustrating experience. For unsaved-changes prompts, React Navigation’s beforeRemove event is often a better fit, because it also catches header buttons and iOS swipe-back, not just Android’s back action.
jsonLd.description: BackHandler is the React Native API for intercepting the Android back button and back gesture, letting a screen close a sheet or confirm before leaving.
jsonLd.headline: What is BackHandler in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/bridge.title: Bridge in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The bridge was React Native’s original asynchronous, JSON-serialised channel between JavaScript and native code. The New Architecture replaces it with JSI.
og:description: The bridge was React Native’s original asynchronous, JSON-serialised channel between JavaScript and native code. The New Architecture replaces it with JSI.
og:title: Bridge in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The bridge was React Native’s original asynchronous, JSON-serialised channel between JavaScript and native code. The New Architecture replaces it with JSI.
jsonLd.name: Bridge

jsonLd.articleBody: The bridge was the original mechanism connecting JavaScript to native code in React Native. Every interaction — mounting a view, calling a native module, delivering a touch event — was serialised to JSON, placed on a queue, and processed asynchronously on the other side. That design bought thread safety and simplicity, but it had three well-known costs: Serialisation overhead on every call, which grew with payload size. No synchronous reads. JavaScript could never ask native code a question and get an immediate answer, which is why measuring a view was awkward. Congestion. A busy queue — a fast scroll driving many events — meant frames arriving late. The bridge is gone in bridgeless mode, the default since React Native 0.76, replaced by JSI. Newcomers still meet the word constantly because a decade of blog posts, conference talks, and library READMEs describe React Native in bridge terms. If an article's central claim is "the bridge is the bottleneck", it predates late 2024.
jsonLd.description: The bridge was React Native’s original asynchronous, JSON-serialised channel between JavaScript and native code. The New Architecture replaces it with JSI.
jsonLd.headline: What is Bridge in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/bridgeless-mode.title: Bridgeless Mode in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Bridgeless mode runs React Native with the legacy bridge removed entirely, so JavaScript talks to native code only through JSI. It is the default New Architecture setup.
og:description: Bridgeless mode runs React Native with the legacy bridge removed entirely, so JavaScript talks to native code only through JSI. It is the default New Architecture setup.
og:title: Bridgeless Mode in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Bridgeless mode runs React Native with the legacy bridge removed entirely, so JavaScript talks to native code only through JSI. It is the default New Architecture setup.
jsonLd.name: Bridgeless Mode

jsonLd.articleBody: Bridgeless mode is the last step of the New Architecture migration: the app starts without creating the bridge at all. Fabric and TurboModules had already moved rendering and native modules onto JSI, but early New Architecture apps still booted a bridge for everything else. Bridgeless mode removes that remaining infrastructure, and it is part of the default setup since React Native 0.76. The leftovers it had to replace were not glamorous but they were everywhere: Runtime start-up and teardown. The bridge object owned the JavaScript runtime. Bridgeless apps create it through a new host object instead: RCTHost on iOS and ReactHost on Android. Timers, error handling and event delivery, which used to route through bridge queues. Module lookup. Every native module is reached through the TurboModule system rather than through a bridge registry. For app developers the visible effect is mostly indirect: faster start-up and no hidden bridge traffic. For anyone maintaining native code it is concrete, because APIs that assumed a bridge are gone. Native code that reached for self.bridge in an iOS module, or the CatalystInstance on Android, to dispatch events or find another module has to be updated to the bridgeless equivalents. Those are the libraries that crash or log "bridge is nil" after an upgrade. Two misconceptions are worth clearing up: Bridgeless does not mean legacy modules stop working. Modules written against the old API usually keep running through the interop layer, which emulates enough of the old environment for them. Direct bridge access is what breaks. Bridgeless is not a separate option you choose any more. On current React Native versions the legacy architecture cannot be enabled, so bridgeless is simply how React Native runs. If an older article explains a bug by "bridge congestion", it is describing a system your app no longer has.
jsonLd.description: Bridgeless mode runs React Native with the legacy bridge removed entirely, so JavaScript talks to native code only through JSI. It is the default New Architecture setup.
jsonLd.headline: What is Bridgeless Mode in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/brownfield-app.title: Brownfield App in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A brownfield app is an existing native iOS or Android app that adds React Native for some screens, rather than being built in React Native from scratch.
og:description: A brownfield app is an existing native iOS or Android app that adds React Native for some screens, rather than being built in React Native from scratch.
og:title: Brownfield App in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

alternateName: Add React Native to existing app
jsonLd.description: A brownfield app is an existing native iOS or Android app that adds React Native for some screens, rather than being built in React Native from scratch.
jsonLd.name: Brownfield App

jsonLd.articleBody: A brownfield app is an existing native app, written in Swift, Objective-C, Kotlin or Java, that embeds React Native for part of its interface. The opposite, an app started in React Native from day one, is called greenfield. It is how many large companies adopt React Native: one new feature or a settings flow ships in React Native while the rest of the app stays native. The native host creates a React Native instance and displays a root view, or an Android activity or fragment, for each React screen it wants to show. Why teams choose it: No risky rewrite. React Native proves itself on one screen at a time. Shared features across iOS and Android, built by one team. Product screens can receive over-the-air JavaScript updates while the native shell stays stable. Where it gets hard: Build integration. The native project must pull in React Native through CocoaPods and Gradle, and every native developer suddenly needs Node and Metro. Many teams instead package the React Native part as a prebuilt XCFramework or AAR so the native build stays unchanged. Navigation across the boundary. Back buttons, deep links and transitions between native and React screens need a deliberate contract. Shared state and services, such as auth tokens or analytics, must be exposed through native modules in both directions. Upgrades touch two codebases at once, and dependency versions on the native side can clash with what React Native libraries expect. The common mistake is treating each React screen as fully independent and starting several React Native instances. One shared instance keeps memory and startup cost down and lets screens share JavaScript state. See the official integration guide.
jsonLd.description: A brownfield app is an existing native iOS or Android app that adds React Native for some screens, rather than being built in React Native from scratch.
jsonLd.headline: What is Brownfield App in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/bundle-identifier.title: Bundle Identifier in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A bundle identifier is the unique reverse-DNS ID, such as com.acme.shop, that iOS, Android and the app stores use to tell your app apart from every other app.
og:description: A bundle identifier is the unique reverse-DNS ID, such as com.acme.shop, that iOS, Android and the app stores use to tell your app apart from every other app.
og:title: Bundle Identifier in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A bundle identifier is the unique reverse-DNS ID, such as com.acme.shop, that iOS, Android and the app stores use to tell your app apart from every other app.
jsonLd.name: Bundle Identifier

jsonLd.articleBody: A bundle identifier is the permanent, unique ID of your app, written in reverse-domain style such as com.acme.shop. iOS calls it the bundle identifier; Android calls it the application ID, often still called the package name. Both platforms and both stores use it to decide whether two builds are the same app. Where it is set in a React Native project: iOS — PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER in the Xcode build settings. Android — applicationId in android/app/build.gradle. Expo — ios.bundleIdentifier and android.package in your app config. Why it matters: once you upload a build to App Store Connect or the Google Play Console, the identifier is locked to that listing. Changing it later means publishing a brand-new app, losing reviews, downloads and existing users’ upgrade path. Pick it deliberately before the first upload. It also ties into other systems. iOS provisioning profiles and push certificates are issued per bundle ID, so code signing fails when the two disagree. Firebase config files, OAuth redirect setups and Universal Links all reference it too. Common confusions: On Android, applicationId and the Gradle namespace (the Kotlin package of your source code) are separate. You can change the store ID without renaming source folders. Installing a debug and a release build side by side requires different IDs, often done with a suffix such as .dev. The iOS and Android IDs do not have to match, but keeping them identical saves confusion in every dashboard.
