jsonLd.headline: What is Bundle Identifier in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/bundle-size.title: Bundle Size in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Bundle size is the weight of a React Native app: the JavaScript bundle plus native code and assets, which together set download size and affect startup time.
og:description: Bundle size is the weight of a React Native app: the JavaScript bundle plus native code and assets, which together set download size and affect startup time.
og:title: Bundle Size in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Bundle size is the weight of a React Native app: the JavaScript bundle plus native code and assets, which together set download size and affect startup time.
jsonLd.name: Bundle Size

jsonLd.articleBody: Bundle size describes how big your app is. In React Native the word covers two different things, and conflating them is the most common source of confusion: The JavaScript bundle — the file Metro produces from your code and npm dependencies, shipped as Hermes bytecode in release builds. The binary size — the full .ipa or .aab: the JavaScript bundle plus the React Native runtime, every native library your dependencies pull in, fonts, images and other assets. The JavaScript bundle matters for startup time, because more code generally means more to load and run at launch. The binary matters for download size, store limits on cellular downloads, and conversion: users on slow connections or small phones abandon large installs. What users actually download is usually smaller than your build output. Google Play generates device-specific APKs from an Android App Bundle, and the App Store thins iOS builds per device. Check the sizes reported by App Store Connect and the Play Console rather than the file on your disk. Practical levers: Audit dependencies. A single convenience package can drag in a large native SDK or a whole utility library. Import only what you use, and avoid barrel files that re-export an entire package. Enable R8 shrinking for the Android native side. Compress and correctly size images; ship vector icons rather than PNGs at three densities. A frequent gotcha is assuming the JavaScript bundle is tree-shaken like a web build. Metro has traditionally included every module you import, so unused exports still ship. Tools such as Expo Atlas or a bundle visualiser show exactly which packages dominate.
jsonLd.description: Bundle size is the weight of a React Native app: the JavaScript bundle plus native code and assets, which together set download size and affect startup time.
jsonLd.headline: What is Bundle Size in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/capacitor.title: Capacitor in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Capacitor is Ionic’s open-source runtime that packages a web app inside a native iOS or Android shell and exposes device features to it through plugins.
og:description: Capacitor is Ionic’s open-source runtime that packages a web app inside a native iOS or Android shell and exposes device features to it through plugins.
og:title: Capacitor in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Capacitor is Ionic’s open-source runtime that packages a web app inside a native iOS or Android shell and exposes device features to it through plugins.
jsonLd.name: Capacitor

jsonLd.articleBody: Capacitor is an open-source native runtime from the Ionic team. It takes a web app built with any framework (React, Vue, Angular, Svelte or plain HTML) and runs it inside a native iOS or Android project, rendering the UI in the system WebView and bridging to native APIs through plugins. It is the modern successor to Apache Cordova and the usual way to build a hybrid app today. Ionic Framework, a separate UI component library, is often used with it but is optional. How it compares with React Native, factually: Rendering. Capacitor renders HTML and CSS in a browser engine. React Native renders platform-native views; there is no DOM. Reuse. Capacitor can wrap an existing web app almost unchanged, so the same code serves the browser and the stores. React Native shares React knowledge and logic with the web, but UI components must use React Native primitives (or React Native Web in the other direction). Native projects. Capacitor commits real Xcode and Android Studio projects to your repo, and you edit them directly when needed. Native features. Both reach camera, files, push and so on through plugins written in Swift and Kotlin. Capacitor is a strong fit when you already have a solid web app, or when the app is mostly content and forms. It is a weaker fit for interfaces that depend on native gestures, heavy animation or very long lists, where WebView performance and platform feel become noticeable. A frequent mistake is assuming an app will pass store review just because it is wrapped. Apple’s guidelines reject apps that are little more than a repackaged website, so a Capacitor app still needs to offer an app-like experience.
jsonLd.description: Capacitor is Ionic’s open-source runtime that packages a web app inside a native iOS or Android shell and exposes device features to it through plugins.
jsonLd.headline: What is Capacitor in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/children-prop.title: Children Prop in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The children prop holds whatever JSX you nest between a component’s opening and closing tags, letting you build wrappers like cards, screens and providers by composition.
og:description: The children prop holds whatever JSX you nest between a component’s opening and closing tags, letting you build wrappers like cards, screens and providers by composition.
og:title: Children Prop in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The children prop holds whatever JSX you nest between a component’s opening and closing tags, letting you build wrappers like cards, screens and providers by composition.
jsonLd.name: Children Prop

jsonLd.articleBody: children is a special prop React fills with whatever you place between a component’s tags. <Card><Text>Hi</Text></Card> calls Card with props.children set to that Text element. It is the basis of composition: building generic containers that render content they know nothing about. Most React Native wrappers work this way: a screen layout with safe-area padding, a Pressable row, a context provider at the root of the app. Composition is usually the better alternative to adding a variant prop for every new case, or to threading data through layers of props. Children are also a quiet performance tool. Elements passed as children are created by the component that wrote them, not by the wrapper. If the wrapper has state of its own — an animated header that tracks scroll, a collapsible panel — its updates do not re-create the children: When CollapsiblePanel toggles its own state, React reuses the same ExpensiveChart element and skips it. Moving content into children is often the simplest fix for a re-render problem. React Native specifics and gotchas: Raw strings need a Text. A string passed as children to a View-based wrapper triggers "Text strings must be rendered within a <Text> component". If your component accepts text, wrap children in a Text component. Nested Text inherits style. Children of a Text can be more Text elements, which inherit font and colour from the parent; nested Views do not. Treat children as opaque. It might be one element, an array, a string or null. Avoid inspecting or cloning it; pass explicit props or a render function when the wrapper needs to inject data.
jsonLd.description: The children prop holds whatever JSX you nest between a component’s opening and closing tags, letting you build wrappers like cards, screens and providers by composition.
jsonLd.headline: What is Children Prop in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/ci-cd.title: CI/CD in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: CI/CD for React Native means automatically testing every change and building, signing and delivering iOS and Android binaries or OTA updates without manual steps.
og:description: CI/CD for React Native means automatically testing every change and building, signing and delivering iOS and Android binaries or OTA updates without manual steps.
og:title: CI/CD in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: CI/CD for React Native means automatically testing every change and building, signing and delivering iOS and Android binaries or OTA updates without manual steps.
jsonLd.name: CI/CD

jsonLd.articleBody: Continuous integration (CI) runs checks on every pull request; continuous delivery (CD) turns merged code into something users or testers can install. In React Native the CI half looks like any JavaScript project. The CD half is where mobile gets hard, because it involves two native toolchains, signing and two app stores. A typical pipeline: On each pull request: install dependencies, run TypeScript, ESLint and Jest, and optionally build the app and run end-to-end tests on a simulator or emulator. On merge: build signed binaries, upload them to TestFlight and a Play testing track, and tag the release. For JavaScript-only changes: publish an over-the-air update to a channel instead of a store build. Deciding between those last two automatically is the React Native-specific trick. Tools that hash the native parts of a project, such as Expo’s fingerprint, tell the pipeline whether native code changed and a new binary is needed. Common runners are GitHub Actions, Bitrise, CircleCI and EAS Workflows, which runs builds on Expo’s infrastructure. Mix and match: many teams run tests on GitHub Actions and hand builds to EAS Build. The gotchas: iOS builds need macOS. macOS runners are slower to start and cost several times more per minute than Linux ones, so run iOS builds only when needed. Signing is the hardest part. Certificates, provisioning profiles, the Android keystore and store API keys must live in CI secrets, never in the repository. Fastlane match and EAS managed credentials exist to solve exactly this; see code signing. Cache aggressively: package manager cache, CocoaPods and Gradle. Uncached native builds are where most pipeline time goes. Pin Node, Xcode and Java versions so a runner image update does not break a release day.
jsonLd.description: CI/CD for React Native means automatically testing every change and building, signing and delivering iOS and Android binaries or OTA updates without manual steps.
jsonLd.headline: What is CI/CD in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/cocoapods.title: CocoaPods in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: CocoaPods is the Ruby-based iOS dependency manager React Native uses to install its own native code and the iOS side of every native library into your Xcode project.
og:description: CocoaPods is the Ruby-based iOS dependency manager React Native uses to install its own native code and the iOS side of every native library into your Xcode project.
og:title: CocoaPods in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: CocoaPods is the Ruby-based iOS dependency manager React Native uses to install its own native code and the iOS side of every native library into your Xcode project.
jsonLd.name: CocoaPods

jsonLd.articleBody: CocoaPods is a dependency manager for iOS, written in Ruby. React Native uses it to pull React Native’s own iOS code, Hermes and the native half of every library you install into an Xcode workspace. The result lives in ios/Pods/. The everyday command is pod install, run from the ios/ folder. It reads the Podfile, resolves versions, writes Podfile.lock and regenerates YourApp.xcworkspace. Each library describes itself in a .podspec file, and autolinking finds those podspecs in node_modules so you don’t list them by hand. When to run it: After adding, removing or upgrading any package that contains native iOS code. After upgrading React Native or the Expo SDK. After pulling a branch where someone else changed native dependencies. If you forget, the JavaScript side expects a module the binary doesn’t contain, and the app fails at launch or when that module is first used. Common pitfalls: Ruby version drift. Use the project’s Gemfile and run bundle exec pod install so everyone uses the same CocoaPods version. Stale spec cache. “Could not find compatible versions” often needs pod install --repo-update. Opening the wrong file. After CocoaPods runs, build from the .xcworkspace in Xcode. With Expo’s Continuous Native Generation, npx expo prebuild and npx expo run:ios run pod install for you, and EAS Build does it in the cloud. CocoaPods is in maintenance mode, and its maintainers have announced that the central Specs repository will become read-only. Apple’s Swift Package Manager is the long-term direction, and the React Native ecosystem is gradually preparing for it, but today most React Native iOS builds still go through CocoaPods.
jsonLd.description: CocoaPods is the Ruby-based iOS dependency manager React Native uses to install its own native code and the iOS side of every native library into your Xcode project.
jsonLd.headline: What is CocoaPods in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/code-coverage.title: Code Coverage in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Code coverage measures which lines, branches and functions of a React Native app run during tests. It finds untested code but does not prove it is correct.
og:description: Code coverage measures which lines, branches and functions of a React Native app run during tests. It finds untested code but does not prove it is correct.
og:title: Code Coverage in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Code coverage measures which lines, branches and functions of a React Native app run during tests. It finds untested code but does not prove it is correct.
jsonLd.name: Code Coverage

jsonLd.articleBody: Code coverage is a metric that reports how much of your source code was executed while your test suite ran. In React Native projects it comes from Jest: run jest --coverage and you get a table per file plus an HTML report that highlights every line that never ran. Jest reports four numbers: Statements and lines: how much of the code executed. Functions: how many functions were called at least once. Branches: whether both sides of every if, ternary and && were taken. This is usually the most revealing figure, because error paths and edge cases live in branches. You can make the build fail below a threshold, which is common in CI/CD pipelines: Know what the number leaves out. Jest coverage only measures JavaScript and TypeScript run by Jest. Swift, Kotlin, native module code and anything exercised only by end-to-end tests count as zero, so the figure describes your JavaScript unit test suite, not how well tested the app is. The main misconception is that high coverage means good tests. Coverage records that a line ran, not that anything checked its result. A test that renders a screen without a single assertion can mark hundreds of lines as covered. Teams chasing a 100% target often end up with exactly those tests, plus brittle tests of trivial code. Use coverage as a map, not a score. Look at the report for important logic, such as payment or authentication, that has no tests at all, and leave generated files, configuration and simple presentational components out of the calculation.
jsonLd.description: Code coverage measures which lines, branches and functions of a React Native app run during tests. It finds untested code but does not prove it is correct.
jsonLd.headline: What is Code Coverage in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/code-obfuscation.title: Code Obfuscation in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Code obfuscation makes a shipped React Native app harder to read and reverse engineer by renaming and scrambling code. It slows attackers down but hides nothing for good.
og:description: Code obfuscation makes a shipped React Native app harder to read and reverse engineer by renaming and scrambling code. It slows attackers down but hides nothing for good.
og:title: Code Obfuscation in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Code obfuscation makes a shipped React Native app harder to read and reverse engineer by renaming and scrambling code. It slows attackers down but hides nothing for good.
jsonLd.name: Code Obfuscation

jsonLd.articleBody: Code obfuscation transforms your shipped code so it still runs the same way but is much harder for a person to understand: meaningful names become single letters, control flow is rearranged and strings are encoded. Its purpose is to raise the cost of reverse engineering. Anyone can download your app and unpack it. An .apk or .ipa is an archive, and inside it sits your JavaScript bundle. In a React Native app there are three layers to consider: JavaScript. Release builds are minified, and with Hermes the bundle ships as Hermes bytecode rather than source. Bytecode is less readable but not secret: open-source disassemblers and decompilers recover a lot of your logic, strings and API endpoints. Android native code. R8 shrinks and renames Java and Kotlin classes when enabled. It does nothing to your JavaScript, which is a common misunderstanding. iOS native code. Compiled Swift and Objective-C are harder to read than JavaScript, but class and method names often remain visible. Dedicated JavaScript obfuscators and commercial app-hardening products go further, with string encryption, control-flow flattening and tamper checks. They add build complexity, can slow the app down, and can break code that relies on function or class names. The essential point: obfuscation is not encryption. Everything the app needs at runtime is in the package, so a determined attacker will eventually find it. Never rely on it to hide API keys, secrets or business rules that must not be bypassed. Those belong on your server. Treat obfuscation as a speed bump that protects intellectual property and makes casual tampering less attractive, alongside real server-side checks.
jsonLd.description: Code obfuscation makes a shipped React Native app harder to read and reverse engineer by renaming and scrambling code. It slows attackers down but hides nothing for good.
jsonLd.headline: What is Code Obfuscation in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/code-signing.title: Code Signing in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Code signing cryptographically stamps an iOS or Android build with your identity, so the OS and app stores can verify who made it and that it is unaltered.
og:description: Code signing cryptographically stamps an iOS or Android build with your identity, so the OS and app stores can verify who made it and that it is unaltered.
og:title: Code Signing in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Code signing cryptographically stamps an iOS or Android build with your identity, so the OS and app stores can verify who made it and that it is unaltered.
jsonLd.name: Code Signing

jsonLd.articleBody: Code signing attaches a cryptographic signature to your compiled app so that iOS, Android and the app stores can confirm who built it and that nobody modified it afterwards. A React Native app cannot be installed on a real device or uploaded to a store unless it is signed. The two platforms work differently. iOS needs two pieces that must agree: A signing certificate (Apple Development or Apple Distribution), whose private key lives in your keychain or in a build service. A provisioning profile, issued by Apple, that ties together the certificate, the app’s bundle identifier, the allowed entitlements and, for development and ad hoc builds, the list of device UDIDs. Android is simpler: you sign the APK or App Bundle with a private key stored in a keystore file. There are no profiles; see Android Keystore for how upload keys and Play App Signing fit together. In practice most signing errors are mismatches. On iOS that means a profile that does not include the device, lacks a capability you just enabled such as push notifications, or belongs to a different team or bundle identifier. Xcode’s automatic signing handles this for solo developers; teams and CI usually centralise credentials instead, for example with EAS Build managing them or Fastlane match storing them in a private repository. The common misconception is that signing is a one-off setup step. Distribution certificates and profiles expire, so iOS builds can fail months later without a single code change. Treat credentials as shared infrastructure: back them up, document who owns them, and never leave them only on one laptop.
jsonLd.description: Code signing cryptographically stamps an iOS or Android build with your identity, so the OS and app stores can verify who made it and that it is unaltered.
jsonLd.headline: What is Code Signing in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/codegen.title: Codegen in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Codegen generates the native C++, Java and Objective-C binding code for TurboModules and Fabric components from TypeScript spec files, at build time.
og:description: Codegen generates the native C++, Java and Objective-C binding code for TurboModules and Fabric components from TypeScript spec files, at build time.
og:title: Codegen in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Codegen generates the native C++, Java and Objective-C binding code for TurboModules and Fabric components from TypeScript spec files, at build time.
jsonLd.name: Codegen

jsonLd.articleBody: Codegen is the build-time tool that turns a TypeScript interface into the native glue code both sides need. You describe a module or component once; Codegen emits the C++, Java, and Objective-C scaffolding. A spec file looks like ordinary TypeScript: From that, Codegen produces the interfaces a TurboModule or Fabric component must implement. The point is catching mismatches early. Under the legacy architecture, bindings were hand-written on both sides and a renamed method or a changed argument type surfaced as an undefined-is-not-a-function crash on device. With Codegen the compiler rejects it. Codegen runs automatically during a native build, so app developers rarely invoke it directly — but it explains why adding a New Architecture library requires a native rebuild rather than a JavaScript reload.

/react-native-glossary/codepush.title: CodePush in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: CodePush was Microsoft’s over-the-air update service for React Native, part of App Center, pushing new JavaScript to installed apps until its retirement in March 2025.
og:description: CodePush was Microsoft’s over-the-air update service for React Native, part of App Center, pushing new JavaScript to installed apps until its retirement in March 2025.
og:title: CodePush in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: CodePush was Microsoft’s over-the-air update service for React Native, part of App Center, pushing new JavaScript to installed apps until its retirement in March 2025.
jsonLd.name: CodePush

jsonLd.articleBody: CodePush was the service that made over-the-air updates mainstream in React Native. Developers released a new JavaScript bundle with a CLI command, and the react-native-code-push library inside the app downloaded it and applied it on the next restart or immediately. It ran as part of Microsoft’s App Center, which was retired on 31 March 2025, taking the hosted CodePush service with it. Its vocabulary still shows up in older codebases and job descriptions: Deployments such as Staging and Production, each with its own key baked into the binary. Target binary version: the store version an update was compatible with, the same idea Expo calls a runtime version. Mandatory updates, rollout percentages, and automatic rollback if an update crashed before signalling success. codePush.sync(), the call that checked for, downloaded and installed an update. Why it still matters: apps released before the shutdown may still contain the SDK, calling a service that no longer answers. Nothing visibly breaks, but those apps can no longer receive hotfixes, which a team usually discovers on the day it urgently needs one. If you inherit such an app, plan the migration before the next incident. The common replacements: EAS Update, Expo’s hosted service, which works in bare React Native projects as well as Expo ones. Self-hosting a CodePush-compatible server, including the server code Microsoft published as open source ahead of the retirement, or one of several third-party services built to accept existing CodePush clients. Whichever you choose, switching requires a new store build, because the update client lives in native code. Users stay on the old client until they install it.

/react-native-glossary/communication-lay.title: Communication Layer in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The communication layer is everything that lets JavaScript talk to native platform code — historically the bridge, and today JSI, TurboModules and Codegen.
og:description: The communication layer is everything that lets JavaScript talk to native platform code — historically the bridge, and today JSI, TurboModules and Codegen.
og:title: Communication Layer in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The communication layer is everything that lets JavaScript talk to native platform code — historically the bridge, and today JSI, TurboModules and Codegen.
jsonLd.name: Communication Layer

jsonLd.articleBody: The communication layer is the machinery that carries calls between your JavaScript and the platform's native code — reading a file, opening the camera, or pushing a layout update. Its pieces, in the order they arrived: The bridge — the legacy transport. Every call was serialised to JSON and queued asynchronously, so nothing could be read back synchronously. JSI — a C++ interface that lets JavaScript hold a direct reference to a native object and invoke it without serialisation. TurboModules — native modules built on JSI and loaded lazily, so startup no longer pays for modules the app never uses. Codegen — generates the C++, Java and Objective-C glue from TypeScript specs, so both sides agree on types at build time. An EventEmitter sits alongside these for the reverse direction, letting native code push events up to JavaScript. Newcomers meet this layer the first time a library needs npx expo prebuild or a native rebuild: that is native code entering the app, not just JavaScript.
jsonLd.description: The communication layer is everything that lets JavaScript talk to native platform code — historically the bridge, and today JSI, TurboModules and Codegen.
jsonLd.headline: What is Communication Layer in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/component-lifecyc.title: Component Lifecycle in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The component lifecycle is the sequence a React component goes through: it mounts onto the screen, updates when state or props change, and unmounts when removed.
og:description: The component lifecycle is the sequence a React component goes through: it mounts onto the screen, updates when state or props change, and unmounts when removed.
og:title: Component Lifecycle in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The component lifecycle is the sequence a React component goes through: it mounts onto the screen, updates when state or props change, and unmounts when removed.
jsonLd.name: Component Lifecycle

jsonLd.articleBody: Every React component goes through three phases. It mounts when React first adds it to the tree and creates its native views, it updates each time it re-renders with new state, props or context, and it unmounts when React removes it and destroys its views. State lives exactly as long as the component stays mounted. Class components expose these as lifecycle methods: componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate and componentWillUnmount. Function components express the same thing with hooks: A useEffect with dependencies covers the update case. Hooks encourage thinking in terms of "keep this in sync with that" rather than "what happens on mount", but the phases underneath are unchanged. In React Native the lifecycle diverges from what web developers expect in two places: Navigating away does not unmount. In a stack navigator, pushing a new screen keeps the previous one mounted underneath so the back gesture can reveal it instantly. Tabs stay mounted once visited. Code in a mount effect therefore runs once, not every time the screen appears. To run work when a screen gains or loses focus, React Navigation provides useFocusEffect and useIsFocused. Backgrounding the app does not unmount. When the user switches apps, your components stay mounted and frozen. To pause a video or refresh data on return, listen to AppState. The usual bug is subscriptions that outlive their component because no cleanup was returned. The opposite surprise also happens: a screen that unmounts and remounts — after a key change or a conditional render — loses all its local state, including scroll position and text input values. If state must survive, lift it above the component that comes and goes.
jsonLd.description: The component lifecycle is the sequence a React component goes through: it mounts onto the screen, updates when state or props change, and unmounts when removed.
jsonLd.headline: What is Component Lifecycle in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/concurrent-render.title: Concurrent Rendering in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Concurrent rendering lets React prepare an update in the background and interrupt it for urgent input, using startTransition, useTransition and useDeferredValue.
og:description: Concurrent rendering lets React prepare an update in the background and interrupt it for urgent input, using startTransition, useTransition and useDeferredValue.
og:title: Concurrent Rendering in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Concurrent rendering lets React prepare an update in the background and interrupt it for urgent input, using startTransition, useTransition and useDeferredValue.
jsonLd.name: Concurrent Rendering

jsonLd.articleBody: Concurrent rendering is React’s ability to work on a render without committing it straight away, pause it, and throw it away if something more urgent arrives. It arrived with React 18, and in React Native it requires the New Architecture, because only the Fabric renderer and its immutable Shadow Tree can hold more than one version of the UI at a time. You opt in per update by marking it as non-urgent: Typing stays responsive while the filtered list renders in the background. If the user types again before it finishes, React abandons the stale render and starts the new one. isPending lets you dim the list meanwhile. useDeferredValue(value) achieves the same thing when you only control the value, not the setter. Concurrent React also brings automatic batching, which merges several state updates from a timer, promise or native event into a single re-render, and makes Suspense transitions keep the old screen visible instead of flashing a fallback. The misconception to avoid: concurrency does not add threads. Rendering still happens on the single JavaScript thread. React yields between components so input can be handled, but one component that takes 200 ms to render still blocks for 200 ms, and work outside rendering — a big JSON.parse, a sort inside an event handler — is not interruptible at all. Transitions also cannot wrap a controlled TextInput value; keep that update urgent. If you upgraded from the legacy architecture and transitions seem to do nothing, check that the New Architecture is actually enabled. See useTransition.
jsonLd.description: Concurrent rendering lets React prepare an update in the background and interrupt it for urgent input, using startTransition, useTransition and useDeferredValue.
jsonLd.headline: What is Concurrent Rendering in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/config-plugin.title: Config Plugin in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A config plugin is a JavaScript function that edits the native iOS and Android projects during Expo prebuild, so native setup lives in app config, not hand edits.
og:description: A config plugin is a JavaScript function that edits the native iOS and Android projects during Expo prebuild, so native setup lives in app config, not hand edits.
og:title: Config Plugin in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A config plugin is a JavaScript function that edits the native iOS and Android projects during Expo prebuild, so native setup lives in app config, not hand edits.
jsonLd.name: Config Plugin

jsonLd.articleBody: A config plugin is a plain JavaScript function that takes your Expo config and returns a modified one, describing changes to the native ios/ and android/ projects. Expo runs every plugin when it generates those projects with npx expo prebuild. It exists because of Continuous Native Generation: if the native folders are regenerated from scratch, any manual edit to Xcode or Gradle files would be wiped. Plugins make those edits repeatable and reviewable. Most libraries that need native setup ship one, and you enable it in the plugins array of your app config: Under the hood a plugin chains mods: small modifiers such as withInfoPlist, withAndroidManifest or withPodfile, each of which receives one native file in a parsed form and returns the edited version. Writing your own is a few lines when you need a key in Info.plist or a permission in AndroidManifest.xml that no library adds for you. Common gotchas: Plugins run only at prebuild time. Changing a plugin option does nothing until you regenerate and rebuild the native app; an over-the-air update cannot apply it. They never run inside Expo Go, which has a fixed native binary. "Dangerous" mods that patch files with string replacement are fragile across SDK upgrades. Prefer the typed mods and re-test plugins after every upgrade. If you commit native folders and edit them by hand, plugins and your edits can fight. Pick one source of truth. See the config plugins docs.
jsonLd.description: A config plugin is a JavaScript function that edits the native iOS and Android projects during Expo prebuild, so native setup lives in app config, not hand edits.
jsonLd.headline: What is Config Plugin in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/context.title: Context in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Context is React’s way to pass a value such as a theme, user or locale to any component below a provider without threading it through every level of props.
og:description: Context is React’s way to pass a value such as a theme, user or locale to any component below a provider without threading it through every level of props.
og:title: Context in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Context is React’s way to pass a value such as a theme, user or locale to any component below a provider without threading it through every level of props.
jsonLd.name: Context

jsonLd.articleBody: Context lets a parent make a value available to its whole subtree. You create it with createContext, provide it near the top of the tree, and read it anywhere below with useContext (or use in React 19). It replaces "prop drilling": passing the same prop through five components that do not need it. In React 19 the context object can be rendered directly as the provider, as above; earlier versions use <ThemeContext.Provider value={...}>. React Native apps are built on context more than most developers realise. React Navigation, safe area insets, gesture handler roots and most data libraries expose their state through providers, which is why "must be used within a Provider" errors are so common: the hook is being called outside the subtree, often in a component rendered above NavigationContainer. The performance gotcha is that every component reading a context re-renders when its value changes, compared by identity. Two consequences: Passing an inline object, value={{ user, setUser }}, creates a new value on every render of the provider and re-renders every consumer. Wrap it in useMemo. One large context holding many unrelated fields re-renders everything when any field changes. Split it into smaller contexts, or keep fast-changing data elsewhere. React.memo does not stop a context-driven re-render, because the update comes from inside the component, not from its props. The common misconception is that context is a state management library. It is a transport for a value; it has no selectors and no subscriptions to slices. It suits values that change rarely — theme, locale, the signed-in user. For frequently changing shared state, a store such as Zustand or Redux re-renders only the components that select what changed. See useContext.
jsonLd.description: Context is React’s way to pass a value such as a theme, user or locale to any component below a provider without threading it through every level of props.
jsonLd.headline: What is Context in React Native?

jsonLd.name: Continuous Native Generation

jsonLd.articleBody: Continuous Native Generation is the practice of treating the ios/ and android/ directories as generated output rather than source you maintain. Running npx expo prebuild recreates them from app.json plus a set of config plugins. Without CNG, adding a library that needs a permission means editing Info.plist and AndroidManifest.xml by hand — and then resolving conflicts in those files on every React Native upgrade. With CNG you declare the intent once: A config plugin is the function that applies one library's native changes during prebuild. Most Expo SDK packages ship one; community libraries increasingly do too. The payoff is upgrades. Because the native folders are regenerated, bumping React Native does not mean merging someone else's changes into your Podfile. You can still drop out and manage native folders manually — the "bare" approach — but you lose that upgrade property. See prebuild.

/react-native-glossary/controlled-compon.title: Controlled Component in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette

jsonLd.description: A controlled component is an input whose current value comes from React state through props, so React rather than the native view is the source of truth.
jsonLd.name: Controlled Component

jsonLd.articleBody: A controlled component is an input that displays exactly what React tells it to. In React Native that usually means a TextInput with a value prop and an onChangeText handler that writes back to state. An uncontrolled component keeps its own value inside the native view; you give it a starting defaultValue and read it when you need it, typically through a ref or the last change event. Controlled inputs are the default choice because the value is always available for validation, formatting and conditional UI, and resetting a form is just resetting state. The React Native twist is that the text really lives in a native UITextField or EditText. Each keystroke travels to JavaScript, updates state, re-renders, and sends the value back. Usually that is invisible. It shows when the JavaScript thread is busy, or when your handler rewrites the text — forcing uppercase, inserting spaces in a card number — where the native field and React can briefly disagree, causing flicker or a jumping cursor. The New Architecture reduced this, but heavy formatting on every keystroke is still worth testing on a low-end Android device. Other gotchas: The value snaps back. If onChangeText does not update the state behind value, the input reverts. The same applies to Switch, which is controlled-only: a Switch without an onValueChange that updates value flips and returns. Switching modes. Starting with value={undefined} and later passing a string turns an uncontrolled input into a controlled one, which React warns about. Initialise with ''. Large forms. Controlling twenty fields in one component re-renders all of them on every keystroke; form libraries such as React Hook Form lean on uncontrolled inputs for that reason.

/react-native-glossary/cpp-turbomodule.title: C++ TurboModule in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A C++ TurboModule is a native module written once in C++ and shared by iOS and Android, called from JavaScript through JSI without Swift, Kotlin or Java glue code.
og:description: A C++ TurboModule is a native module written once in C++ and shared by iOS and Android, called from JavaScript through JSI without Swift, Kotlin or Java glue code.
og:title: C++ TurboModule in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A C++ TurboModule is a native module written once in C++ and shared by iOS and Android, called from JavaScript through JSI without Swift, Kotlin or Java glue code.
jsonLd.name: C++ TurboModule

jsonLd.articleBody: A C++ TurboModule is a TurboModule implemented entirely in C++ rather than separately in Objective-C or Swift for iOS and Java or Kotlin for Android. You write one implementation, both platforms compile it, and JavaScript calls it directly through JSI. The workflow mirrors any other TurboModule. You declare the interface in a TypeScript spec file, and Codegen generates a C++ base class for it, whose name ends in CxxSpec. Your class extends that base and implements the methods, receiving and returning JSI values that Codegen converts to and from ordinary C++ types. A small amount of per-platform registration code tells each app how to find the module. Why teams reach for one: One codebase for logic that is not platform-specific. Parsing, encryption, compression, maths, a rules engine: there is no reason to write it twice. Reusing existing C or C++ libraries. SQLite, image codecs, audio processing, cryptography and ML runtimes are written in C or C++, and a C++ module can call them without a Java or Objective-C layer in between. Speed and synchronous calls. No hop through another language, and synchronous return values are cheap. Some of the fastest storage and crypto libraries in the ecosystem are built this way. The gotchas: No platform APIs for free. C++ cannot directly show a dialog, read the iOS keychain or request an Android permission. Anything platform-specific still needs Objective-C, Swift, Kotlin or Java, often via a regular TurboModule. Threading is your problem. Calls arrive on the JavaScript thread. Long work blocks the UI, and touching the JSI runtime from another thread crashes. Do heavy work elsewhere and hop back to deliver results. Two toolchains to debug. Build failures surface through CMake and the Android NDK on one side and Xcode on the other, which is a steeper learning curve than a Kotlin or Swift module. See cross-platform native modules (C++).
jsonLd.description: A C++ TurboModule is a native module written once in C++ and shared by iOS and Android, called from JavaScript through JSI without Swift, Kotlin or Java glue code.
jsonLd.headline: What is C++ TurboModule in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/crash-reporting.title: Crash Reporting in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Crash reporting captures errors and crashes from users’ devices with stack traces and context, so a React Native team can fix problems it never reproduced locally.
og:description: Crash reporting captures errors and crashes from users’ devices with stack traces and context, so a React Native team can fix problems it never reproduced locally.
og:title: Crash Reporting in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Crash reporting captures errors and crashes from users’ devices with stack traces and context, so a React Native team can fix problems it never reproduced locally.
jsonLd.name: Crash Reporting

jsonLd.articleBody: Crash reporting means installing an SDK that records errors on users’ devices and sends them, with a stack trace, device details and recent breadcrumbs, to a dashboard. The common choices in React Native are Sentry (@sentry/react-native), Firebase Crashlytics through React Native Firebase, and Bugsnag. React Native apps fail in two layers, and a useful tool covers both: JavaScript errors: an unhandled exception in your code. In a release build, a fatal JavaScript error closes the app, so it looks like a crash to the user. Native crashes: an exception or signal in Objective-C, Swift, Java, Kotlin or C++ code, often from a library or the framework itself, plus ANRs (frozen apps) on Android. The step teams skip is symbolication. Production code is minified and compiled, so raw stack traces are unreadable. Each layer needs its own file uploaded for every build: JavaScript: source maps, composed with Hermes’s own map when bytecode is used. iOS: dSYM files from the archive. Android: the mapping.txt from R8. Upload them automatically from CI or your build service, or you will receive thousands of reports reading index.android.bundle:1:84721. Over-the-air updates add a twist: each update ships a new bundle, so it needs its own source maps and should be tagged as its own release. Otherwise errors from an update are attributed to the store version and mapped against the wrong code. Tag reports with the release, the update id and the user’s app version, and wrap screens in an error boundary that reports the error and shows a fallback instead of a blank screen. The crash-free sessions rate those tools compute is also the signal to watch during a staged rollout.
jsonLd.description: Crash reporting captures errors and crashes from users’ devices with stack traces and context, so a React Native team can fix problems it never reproduced locally.
jsonLd.headline: What is Crash Reporting in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/cross-platform-de.title: Cross-Platform Development in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Cross-platform development means building one app for several operating systems, such as iOS and Android, from a largely shared codebase instead of one per platform.
og:description: Cross-platform development means building one app for several operating systems, such as iOS and Android, from a largely shared codebase instead of one per platform.
og:title: Cross-Platform Development in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Cross-platform development means building one app for several operating systems, such as iOS and Android, from a largely shared codebase instead of one per platform.
jsonLd.name: Cross-Platform Development

jsonLd.articleBody: Cross-platform development is the practice of shipping one product to several operating systems from a mostly shared codebase. In React Native that means writing components and business logic once in JavaScript or TypeScript and running them on iOS and Android, with optional targets such as the web or desktop. Frameworks differ in what they share. React Native shares the code but renders each platform’s own native views. Flutter shares the code and draws its own UI. Kotlin Multiplatform usually shares business logic and lets the UI stay native. WebView-based tools share a web app. None of these is universally better; they trade sharing against platform fidelity in different places. Why it matters to a React Native team: One team and one language can cover both stores, and most features land on both platforms at once. Platform differences do not disappear. Permissions, push notifications, back navigation, keyboard handling and store rules still differ, so you will write some platform-specific code and occasionally a native module. Your team still needs someone comfortable opening Xcode and Android Studio when a build breaks. The most common misconception is "write once, run anywhere". React Native’s original slogan was deliberately different: "learn once, write anywhere". The aim is a shared mental model and a large shared codebase, while still letting each platform look and behave the way its users expect. A cross-platform app that ignores platform conventions, such as using iOS-style navigation on Android, tends to feel wrong on both. How much code you actually share depends on the app. Content and form-heavy apps share almost everything; apps built around a device feature such as the camera, Bluetooth or widgets share less.
jsonLd.description: Cross-platform development means building one app for several operating systems, such as iOS and Android, from a largely shared codebase instead of one per platform.
jsonLd.headline: What is Cross-Platform Development in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/custom-fonts.title: Custom Fonts in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Custom fonts are typeface files you bundle with a React Native app, either embedded at build time or loaded at runtime with expo-font, then used through fontFamily.
og:description: Custom fonts are typeface files you bundle with a React Native app, either embedded at build time or loaded at runtime with expo-font, then used through fontFamily.
og:title: Custom Fonts in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Custom fonts are typeface files you bundle with a React Native app, either embedded at build time or loaded at runtime with expo-font, then used through fontFamily.
jsonLd.name: Custom Fonts

jsonLd.articleBody: Custom fonts are .ttf or .otf files you ship with your React Native app so Text can use a typeface other than the system font. Once registered, you reference one through the fontFamily style. There are two ways to get the file into the app: Embed at build time. The font is copied into the native project and registered with the OS. With Expo this is the expo-font config plugin; in a bare project you list asset folders in react-native.config.js and run npx react-native-asset. Fonts are available instantly at launch. Load at runtime with useFonts or Font.loadAsync from expo-font. Nothing native changes, which suits Expo Go and quick experiments, but you must wait for loading before rendering text, usually behind the splash screen. The classic gotchas: fontWeight does not pick a weight from a custom family reliably, especially on Android. Register each weight as its own family name and switch fontFamily instead, often via a typography component. Names differ by platform when embedding. iOS looks the font up by its internal PostScript or family name, while Android uses the file name. Rename files to match the PostScript name to avoid "font not found" on one platform only. Variable fonts have patchy support across platforms; static files per weight are the safe choice. Rendering text before a runtime font loads causes a visible jump from the system font. Remember that users can scale text up for accessibility. A custom font does not change that, so test layouts with large font scaling.
jsonLd.description: Custom fonts are typeface files you bundle with a React Native app, either embedded at build time or loaded at runtime with expo-font, then used through fontFamily.
jsonLd.headline: What is Custom Fonts in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/custom-hook.title: Custom Hook in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A custom hook is your own function, named with a use prefix, that combines built-in hooks so several React Native components can reuse the same stateful logic.
og:description: A custom hook is your own function, named with a use prefix, that combines built-in hooks so several React Native components can reuse the same stateful logic.
og:title: Custom Hook in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A custom hook is your own function, named with a use prefix, that combines built-in hooks so several React Native components can reuse the same stateful logic.
jsonLd.name: Custom Hook

jsonLd.articleBody: A custom hook is a JavaScript function whose name starts with use and which calls other hooks. It is the standard way to extract stateful logic — a subscription, a form, a timer — out of a component so it can be shared and tested on its own. Any component can now call useKeyboardVisible() instead of repeating the listener setup and cleanup. React Native code is full of these: wrapping AppState, network status, permissions, or a data request behind a one-line call keeps screens readable. The key misconception: a custom hook shares logic, not state. Two components calling useKeyboardVisible() each get their own useState and their own listeners. If you want both to see the same value, put it in context or a store, and let the hook read from there. Other things to know: The use prefix is not decoration. It is how React’s lint rules recognise a hook and check the rules of hooks inside it. A function that calls useState but is named getKeyboardState escapes those checks. A function that calls no hooks should not be named use…; make it a plain utility instead. Return a stable shape. Returning a new object or function each render forces consumers to deal with changing identities; wrap returned callbacks in useCallback. Hooks are tested with renderHook from React Native Testing Library, without building a dummy component. See reusing logic with custom hooks.
jsonLd.description: A custom hook is your own function, named with a use prefix, that combines built-in hooks so several React Native components can reuse the same stateful logic.
jsonLd.headline: What is Custom Hook in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/deep-linking.title: Deep Linking in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Deep linking lets a URL open a React Native app on a specific screen, such as myapp://post/42, instead of just launching it on the home screen.
og:description: Deep linking lets a URL open a React Native app on a specific screen, such as myapp://post/42, instead of just launching it on the home screen.
og:title: Deep Linking in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Deep linking lets a URL open a React Native app on a specific screen, such as myapp://post/42, instead of just launching it on the home screen.
jsonLd.name: Deep Linking

jsonLd.articleBody: Deep linking maps a URL to a screen inside your app. Tapping myapp://post/42 in an email, a push notification or another app launches yours and lands the user on post 42 rather than the home screen. The simplest form is a custom URL scheme such as myapp://. You register it natively (CFBundleURLTypes in Info.plist, an intent-filter in AndroidManifest.xml, or the scheme field in an Expo app config), then teach your navigator how to turn paths into screens. In React Navigation that is the linking prop: Expo Router skips this step: every file is already a route, so every screen has a URL. Under the hood the app receives URLs two ways, which the Linking API exposes: getInitialURL() when the link cold-starts the app, and a url event when the app is already running. Handling only one of them is the classic bug where links work "sometimes". The misconception worth correcting: a custom scheme is not owned by you. Any app can register myapp://, and if your app is not installed the link simply fails. For links you share publicly, use verified https links instead: Universal Links on iOS and Android App Links. They open the app when installed and fall back to your website when not. Test without building a sharing flow: Treat every deep link as untrusted input: validate parameters and require authentication before showing private screens.

jsonLd.headline: What is Deep Linking in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/density-independe.title: Density-Independent Pixels in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Density-independent pixels are the unitless numbers React Native uses for sizes, mapped to iOS points and Android dp so layouts look the same size on any screen density.
og:description: Density-independent pixels are the unitless numbers React Native uses for sizes, mapped to iOS points and Android dp so layouts look the same size on any screen density.
og:title: Density-Independent Pixels in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Density-independent pixels are the unitless numbers React Native uses for sizes, mapped to iOS points and Android dp so layouts look the same size on any screen density.
jsonLd.name: Density-Independent Pixels

jsonLd.articleBody: Density-independent pixels are the unit behind every number in a React Native style. When you write width: 100 there is no px: the value is 100 logical pixels, which iOS calls points and Android calls dp. The platform multiplies it by the screen’s pixel density to get physical pixels. That is why the same layout looks roughly the same physical size on a budget Android phone and a high-end iPhone, even though one has far more physical pixels per inch. The multiplier is exposed by PixelRatio: Where it matters in practice: Images. A 100×100 slot on a 3× screen needs a 300×300 bitmap to look sharp, which is why bundled images come as @2x and @3x variants that Metro picks automatically. Thin borders. borderWidth: 0.5 renders differently across densities; StyleSheet.hairlineWidth gives a true one-pixel line. Pixel snapping. Fractional sizes are rounded to the physical grid, which can leave a sub-pixel gap between adjacent views. PixelRatio.roundToNearestPixel helps. The common misconception is that density-independent means screen-size-independent. It does not. A 400-wide view fills a phone and looks small on a tablet; adapting to screen size is a responsive design job. Text is a separate case. fontSize is also in logical pixels but is further multiplied by the user’s accessibility text size, so a 16 can render much larger. See font scaling before fixing heights around text.
jsonLd.description: Density-independent pixels are the unitless numbers React Native uses for sizes, mapped to iOS points and Android dp so layouts look the same size on any screen density.
jsonLd.headline: What is Density-Independent Pixels in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Design tokens are named values for colour, spacing, typography and radius that a React Native app’s theme reads, so one change updates the design everywhere.
og:description: Design tokens are named values for colour, spacing, typography and radius that a React Native app’s theme reads, so one change updates the design everywhere.
og:title: Design Tokens in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Design tokens are named values for colour, spacing, typography and radius that a React Native app’s theme reads, so one change updates the design everywhere.
jsonLd.name: Design Tokens

jsonLd.articleBody: Design tokens are the named values a design system is built from: colors.textPrimary, space.md, radius.card, font.heading. In a React Native app, a theme is a set of tokens, and components read tokens instead of hard-coding #1A1A1A or 16. Tokens usually come in two layers: Primitive tokens describe raw values: blue500, space4 = 16. Semantic tokens describe intent: colors.background, colors.danger, space.screenPadding. Components should use these, because a dark theme or a rebrand changes what they point to, not every component. React Native has no built-in theme system, so you supply one. The simplest pattern puts the active theme in Context, chosen from the system setting via Appearance or useColorScheme. Libraries such as Unistyles, Tamagui and NativeWind provide typed theming out of the box, and React Navigation accepts its own theme object that should be fed from the same tokens. Common gotchas: Static StyleSheet.create cannot switch themes. Values captured at module load stay fixed; styles that depend on the theme must be created from it, or use a library that does so. Only colours get tokenised. Spacing, radius, shadows and type scale drift just as fast without tokens. Native surfaces are separate. The splash screen, status bar and system navigation bar do not read your JavaScript theme and need matching native configuration. Teams sharing tokens with a web app or design tool often generate them from a single JSON source, so Figma, CSS and React Native stay in step.

author: David Leuliette
description: Detox is an end-to-end testing framework for React Native that drives a real app build on a simulator or emulator and automatically waits for the app to go idle.
og:description: Detox is an end-to-end testing framework for React Native that drives a real app build on a simulator or emulator and automatically waits for the app to go idle.
og:title: Detox in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Detox is an end-to-end testing framework for React Native that drives a real app build on a simulator or emulator and automatically waits for the app to go idle.
jsonLd.name: Detox

jsonLd.articleBody: Detox is an open-source end-to-end testing framework built by Wix specifically for React Native. It installs a real build of your app on an iOS Simulator or Android Emulator, then taps, types and scrolls through it while asserting what appears on screen. Tests are written in JavaScript, typically run by Jest: What sets Detox apart is that it is grey-box. Because it runs code inside your app, it knows when the app is busy: pending network requests, running animations, timers and work on the JavaScript thread. It waits until the app is idle before each action, instead of relying on fixed sleeps. That synchronisation is its main defence against flaky tests. It also has costs: Setup is the heaviest of the common options: a Detox configuration file, build commands for each platform, and native test configuration on Android. Detox tests need a build made for testing, so every run involves a native build or a cached one. Automatic idle detection can work against you. An infinite animation, a polling request or a long timer means the app never looks idle, and tests hang until they time out. You then have to disable synchronisation for that step or exclude specific URLs. Elements are best targeted with a testID prop, which keeps tests stable when copy or translations change. Teams choosing between Detox and Maestro usually trade Detox's tight synchronisation and JavaScript API against Maestro's simpler setup.
jsonLd.description: Detox is an end-to-end testing framework for React Native that drives a real app build on a simulator or emulator and automatically waits for the app to go idle.
jsonLd.headline: What is Detox in React Native?

jsonLd.articleBody: The dev menu is the overlay React Native shows in development builds, giving you the debugging controls that do not belong in a production app. Open it with: iOS Simulator — <kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>D</kbd> Android emulator — <kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>M</kbd> (macOS) or <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>M</kbd> A physical device — shake it, or run adb shell input keyevent 82 on Android What is inside: Reload — re-fetch the bundle from Metro, for when Fast Refresh gets out of sync Open Debugger — attach React Native DevTools Element Inspector — tap any view to see its component, props, and computed styles Performance Monitor — a live overlay of JS and UI frame rates Toggle Fast Refresh The menu is stripped from release builds, so it is not a leak risk. description: A development build is your app plus expo-dev-client: run any native library, load JS from Metro and outgrow Expo Go. When to switch and how to build one.
og:description: A development build is your app plus expo-dev-client: run any native library, load JS from Metro and outgrow Expo Go. When to switch and how to build one.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A development build is a debug build of your app with its native dependencies and the Expo dev client, so it loads JavaScript from Metro and runs any native library.
jsonLd.name: Development Build

jsonLd.articleBody: A development build is a debug build of your app that includes your project's native code plus a development client, letting it connect to Metro and load JavaScript at runtime. It replaces the old Expo Go workflow for any real project. Expo Go is a prebuilt sandbox app containing a fixed set of Expo SDK modules — great for a first tutorial, useless the moment you add a native module it does not include. A development build contains your dependencies, so nothing is off-limits. You produce one with eas build --profile development or locally with npx expo run:ios, install it once on a device or simulator, and from then on iterate in JavaScript with Fast Refresh. The rule that follows: rebuild only when native code changes. Adding a JavaScript-only package needs no rebuild; adding expo-camera does. Development builds also carry the dev menu and debugging tools that release builds strip. See development builds.

author: David Leuliette
description: A drawer navigator hides the app’s main destinations in a side panel that slides in from the screen edge, opened by a swipe or a menu button in the header.
og:description: A drawer navigator hides the app’s main destinations in a side panel that slides in from the screen edge, opened by a swipe or a menu button in the header.
og:title: Drawer Navigator in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A drawer navigator hides the app’s main destinations in a side panel that slides in from the screen edge, opened by a swipe or a menu button in the header.
jsonLd.name: Drawer Navigator

jsonLd.articleBody: A drawer navigator renders a panel, usually on the left, that slides over or pushes aside the current screen to list the app’s sections. It is the "hamburger menu" pattern, common on Android and in apps with more destinations than a tab bar can hold. In React Navigation it comes from @react-navigation/drawer. The drawer is driven by gestures and animation running on the UI thread, so it depends on Gesture Handler and Reanimated; a missing or mismatched version of either is the usual reason a fresh drawer crashes on launch. Useful details: drawerType chooses the motion: front overlays the screen, slide and back move the content, and permanent keeps the drawer always visible, which suits tablets and wide layouts. Open it from code with navigation.openDrawer() or toggleDrawer(), typically from a header button. On Android the hardware back button closes an open drawer before it navigates back. Replace the default list with drawerContent to add a profile header or sign-out button. The common gotcha is gesture conflict. The edge swipe that opens the drawer competes with horizontal carousels, maps and the iOS swipe-back gesture of a nested stack. Narrow the swipe area or disable swiping on screens that need horizontal gestures. The design caveat is discoverability: items hidden behind a menu get used less than visible tabs, so keep the most frequent destinations out of the drawer.
jsonLd.description: A drawer navigator hides the app’s main destinations in a side panel that slides in from the screen edge, opened by a swipe or a menu button in the header.

jsonLd.description: EAS (Expo Application Services) is Expo’s hosted cloud service for building, submitting and updating React Native apps without running your own Xcode and Gradle machines.
jsonLd.name: EAS

jsonLd.articleBody: EAS — Expo Application Services — is the hosted infrastructure that compiles, signs, ships, and updates React Native apps. It removes the need to keep a Mac with the right Xcode version around just to produce an iOS build. It is three services: EAS Build — compiles .ipa and .aab binaries in the cloud, managing signing certificates and provisioning profiles for you. eas build --platform ios is the whole workflow. EAS Submit — uploads a finished binary to App Store Connect and Google Play. EAS Update — delivers JavaScript-only changes over the air, skipping review for anything that lives in the bundle. The concept newcomers most need is the build profile, configured in eas.json: development produces a development build, preview an internal-distribution build, production the store artefact. EAS is optional — you can build locally with Xcode and Android Studio — but it is what most Expo teams use. See the EAS docs.

og:title: EAS Build in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: EAS Build is Expo’s cloud build service: it compiles and signs your React Native app into an installable .ipa, .apk or .aab on hosted macOS and Linux machines.
jsonLd.name: EAS Build

jsonLd.articleBody: EAS Build is the part of EAS that turns a React Native project into a signed binary. You run one command, the CLI uploads your project, and a hosted machine (macOS for iOS, Linux for Android) installs dependencies, generates native folders if needed, compiles, signs and hands you back an artefact. What it takes off your plate is mostly code signing. EAS can create and store iOS distribution certificates, provisioning profiles and the Android upload keystore, so a new teammate or a CI job builds without anyone emailing a .p12 file around. eas credentials lets you inspect or replace them. How a build behaves is set per profile in eas.json: distribution: "internal" gives an ad hoc iOS build or an .apk you can install from a link. On iOS each test device must be registered first (eas device:create). developmentClient: true produces a development build. autoIncrement bumps the build number for you, so store uploads stop failing on a duplicate version code. The gotcha that catches most teams: the build server only sees what is uploaded, and by default that follows your .gitignore. A local .env file, a generated config or a secret JSON file that is ignored by git simply does not exist on the build machine, so the build succeeds locally and fails (or silently misbehaves) in the cloud. Declare those values as EAS environment variables or secret files instead. The --local flag runs the same build pipeline on your own machine, which is the fastest way to debug a cloud-only failure. See the EAS Build docs.

jsonLd.headline: What is EAS Build in React Native?

author: David Leuliette

og:description: EAS Submit is Expo’s service for uploading a finished React Native binary to App Store Connect or Google Play from the command line or CI, without opening Xcode.
og:title: EAS Submit in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: EAS Submit is Expo’s service for uploading a finished React Native binary to App Store Connect or Google Play from the command line or CI, without opening Xcode.
jsonLd.name: EAS Submit

jsonLd.articleBody: EAS Submit is the part of EAS that takes a built .ipa or .aab and uploads it to the stores. It replaces dragging a file into Transporter or clicking through the Play Console upload form, and works with binaries from EAS Build or ones you built yourself. It authenticates differently on each store: iOS uses an App Store Connect API key, which EAS can generate and store for you. The binary lands in App Store Connect, processes, and appears in TestFlight. Android uses a Google Cloud service account JSON key with access to your Play developer account. A submit profile in eas.json chooses the track (internal, alpha, beta, production) and release status. Two misconceptions are worth clearing up. First, “submit” means upload, not review: on iOS you still pick the build, fill in release notes and press Submit for Review in App Store Connect, and on Android a draft release still has to be rolled out. Second, the very first Android upload for a new app cannot go through the API. Google requires one manual upload in the Play Console before any automated tool, EAS Submit included, can push to that package name. Most teams end up chaining build and submit, either with --auto-submit or as two jobs in a pipeline, so a merge to main ends with a binary waiting in TestFlight and the Play internal testing track. See the EAS Submit docs.
jsonLd.description: EAS Submit is Expo’s service for uploading a finished React Native binary to App Store Connect or Google Play from the command line or CI, without opening Xcode.
jsonLd.headline: What is EAS Submit in React Native?

og:description: EAS Update is Expo’s hosted over-the-air update service: the expo-updates library in your app downloads new JavaScript and assets published with eas update.
og:title: EAS Update in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: EAS Update is Expo’s hosted over-the-air update service: the expo-updates library in your app downloads new JavaScript and assets published with eas update.
jsonLd.name: EAS Update

jsonLd.articleBody: EAS Update is Expo’s implementation of an over-the-air update. It has two halves: the expo-updates library compiled into your app, and the hosted service you publish to with eas update. This entry is about how that particular service behaves. Every update is tagged with a runtime version, and a build only ever downloads updates whose runtime version matches its own. Builds find their updates through an update channel, which points at a branch of published updates. The default loading behaviour surprises people. On launch, expo-updates checks for a newer update and downloads it in the background, but the app keeps running the bundle it already has. The new code only runs on the next cold start. So a user who opens the app once after you publish sees the old version, and closing it from the app switcher is what picks up the fix. To apply critical fixes sooner, check yourself and reload: Other things that work differently from a plain bundle swap: Updates are disabled in development, so test them with a preview or production build. You can roll an update out to a percentage of users, and eas update:rollback points devices back to the previous update or the embedded bundle. The bundle shipped inside the binary is itself an update, which is what devices fall back to. See the EAS Update docs.

jsonLd.headline: What is EAS Update in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: EAS Workflows is Expo’s CI/CD service: YAML files in .eas/workflows chain builds, submissions, OTA updates and tests on Expo’s infrastructure when your repo changes.
og:description: EAS Workflows is Expo’s CI/CD service: YAML files in .eas/workflows chain builds, submissions, OTA updates and tests on Expo’s infrastructure when your repo changes.
og:title: EAS Workflows in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: EAS Workflows is Expo’s CI/CD service: YAML files in .eas/workflows chain builds, submissions, OTA updates and tests on Expo’s infrastructure when your repo changes.
jsonLd.name: EAS Workflows

jsonLd.articleBody: EAS Workflows is a CI/CD service built specifically for React Native release pipelines. You describe jobs in YAML files under .eas/workflows/, connect your GitHub repository in the Expo dashboard, and the workflow runs on Expo’s machines when you push, open a pull request, or trigger it with eas workflow:run. Where a generic CI provider makes you script the Expo CLI yourself, EAS Workflows has pre-packaged job types that already know about your project: build, submit and update wrap EAS Build, EAS Submit and EAS Update, using the profiles in eas.json. fingerprint hashes the native side of the project. maestro runs Maestro end-to-end tests against a build. Jobs declare needs to run in order and can read outputs from earlier jobs, such as passing a build id from the build job to the submit job. The pattern that makes it worth adopting is the fingerprint branch. A workflow computes the project fingerprint, looks for an existing build with that fingerprint, and then takes one of two paths: if native code is unchanged it publishes an over-the-air update in a minute or two; if native code changed it starts a new store build. That turns “do I need a new binary for this change?” from a judgement call into an automatic decision. The common misconception is that it replaces your test CI. EAS Workflows is strongest at the build-and-release end; many teams keep linting and unit tests on GitHub Actions and hand off to EAS Workflows for anything that produces a binary or an update. Builds triggered from a workflow also count against your EAS plan like any other build.

jsonLd.headline: What is EAS Workflows in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: End-to-end testing runs a real build of a React Native app on a simulator or device and drives it like a user, checking that whole flows work from screen to backend.
og:description: End-to-end testing runs a real build of a React Native app on a simulator or device and drives it like a user, checking that whole flows work from screen to backend.
og:title: End-to-End Testing in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: End-to-end testing runs a real build of a React Native app on a simulator or device and drives it like a user, checking that whole flows work from screen to backend.
jsonLd.name: End-to-End Testing

jsonLd.articleBody: End-to-end (E2E) testing checks a complete user journey in the real app: launch, sign in, add to cart, pay. A tool installs an actual build on a simulator, emulator or device, taps and types through the interface, and asserts on what appears on screen. It is the only kind of test that exercises everything together: JavaScript, native modules, navigation, permissions, the network and the backend. A Jest test can pass while the screen it covers crashes on launch because a native dependency is misconfigured; an E2E test catches that. The main options for React Native: Detox — grey-box, JavaScript tests, synchronises with the app's idle state. Maestro — black-box, YAML flows, quick to set up. Appium — a long-standing cross-platform option based on the WebDriver protocol. E2E tests are slow and expensive to maintain, so a sound strategy keeps them few and focused on flows that would lose money or users if they broke: onboarding, login, checkout. Business rules and edge cases belong in faster unit tests. The biggest practical problem is flakiness: a test that passes and fails on the same code. Common causes are fixed sleep calls instead of waiting for elements, tests that depend on each other's leftover state, live backends returning different data, and animations still running when an assertion fires. Seed predictable test data, reset app state between tests, and target elements by testID rather than copy. Run E2E tests against a release build where possible, because debug builds behave differently and are slower. For how this fits into a full strategy, see our React Native testing page.
jsonLd.description: End-to-end testing runs a real build of a React Native app on a simulator or device and drives it like a user, checking that whole flows work from screen to backend.
jsonLd.headline: What is End-to-End Testing in React Native?
