author: David Leuliette
description: Entitlements are signed key-value permissions in an iOS app that unlock Apple capabilities such as push notifications, App Groups, Sign in with Apple and Universal Links.
og:description: Entitlements are signed key-value permissions in an iOS app that unlock Apple capabilities such as push notifications, App Groups, Sign in with Apple and Universal Links.
og:title: Entitlements in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Entitlements are signed key-value permissions in an iOS app that unlock Apple capabilities such as push notifications, App Groups, Sign in with Apple and Universal Links.
jsonLd.name: Entitlements

jsonLd.articleBody: Entitlements are key-value pairs embedded in an iOS app’s code signature that grant it access to Apple services and system capabilities. They live in a .entitlements property list in your Xcode project, and Xcode’s "Signing & Capabilities" tab is a friendly editor for them. Typical entitlements a React Native app needs: aps-environment for push notifications. com.apple.developer.associated-domains for Universal Links and password autofill. App Groups, to share data with a widget or extension. Sign in with Apple, HealthKit, iCloud, Apple Pay and keychain sharing. What makes them different from Info.plist keys is that Apple checks them. Each entitlement must also be enabled on your App ID in the Apple Developer portal and be included in the provisioning profile used for code signing. If the app claims an entitlement its profile does not allow, signing fails at build time, or the feature silently does not work on device. With Expo you declare them in app config, and many library config plugins add their own: EAS Build can sync these capabilities to your App ID automatically; with manual signing you must enable them yourself and regenerate the profile. Common gotchas: enabling a capability in Xcode but not regenerating the profile on CI; a library that adds push entitlements you never asked for, which then triggers an App Store warning; and assuming Android has an equivalent file. It does not. Android grants comparable powers through AndroidManifest.xml permissions and features.
jsonLd.description: Entitlements are signed key-value permissions in an iOS app that unlock Apple capabilities such as push notifications, App Groups, Sign in with Apple and Universal Links.
jsonLd.headline: What is Entitlements in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: In React Native, environment variables are build-time values, such as an API URL, inlined into the JavaScript bundle; they configure an app but never keep a secret.
og:description: In React Native, environment variables are build-time values, such as an API URL, inlined into the JavaScript bundle; they configure an app but never keep a secret.
og:title: Environment Variables in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: In React Native, environment variables are build-time values, such as an API URL, inlined into the JavaScript bundle; they configure an app but never keep a secret.
jsonLd.name: Environment Variables

jsonLd.articleBody: Environment variables in React Native are configuration values, such as an API base URL, a feature flag or an analytics key, that differ between development, staging and production builds. Unlike on a server, they are read once at build time and written into the app. That is the single most important fact about them: the device has no environment to read from at runtime. Whatever value you use ends up as plain text inside the JavaScript bundle or the native binary. In Expo projects, variables prefixed with EXPO_PUBLIC_ in a .env file are inlined into your code when Metro bundles it: Projects without Expo often use react-native-config, which also exposes values to native code, or a Babel plugin that does similar inlining. Expo projects can also pass values to native configuration through dynamic app config. Common gotchas: They are not secrets. Anyone can unzip an app and read them. Private keys belong on a server; see API keys in mobile apps. Access must be static. Inlining finds process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL written out in full. Destructuring process.env or building the name dynamically returns undefined. Changes need a restart. Editing .env while Metro runs may not take effect until you restart it, sometimes with the cache cleared. Cloud builds do not see your local file if it is not committed. For EAS Build, define the values as EAS environment variables for each environment. An over-the-air update can change JavaScript values because they live in the bundle, while values baked into native code need a new build.
jsonLd.description: In React Native, environment variables are build-time values, such as an API URL, inlined into the JavaScript bundle; they configure an app but never keep a secret.
jsonLd.headline: What is Environment Variables in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/error-boundary.title: Error Boundary in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: An error boundary is a React component that catches errors thrown while rendering its children and shows a fallback UI instead of letting the whole app go down.
og:description: An error boundary is a React component that catches errors thrown while rendering its children and shows a fallback UI instead of letting the whole app go down.
og:title: Error Boundary in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An error boundary is a React component that catches errors thrown while rendering its children and shows a fallback UI instead of letting the whole app go down.
jsonLd.name: Error Boundary

jsonLd.articleBody: An error boundary is a component that catches JavaScript errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods or in constructors anywhere in the tree below it, and renders a fallback in place of the broken subtree. Without one, a single bad render unmounts the entire React tree, and in a React Native release build an unhandled JavaScript error can end with the app closing. It is still the one feature that needs a class component. There is no hook equivalent: getDerivedStateFromError switches to the fallback; componentDidCatch is where you send the error to your crash reporting tool. Most teams use the react-error-boundary package instead of writing the class, and Sentry ships its own boundary. In Expo Router, a route file can export an ErrorBoundary component that wraps just that route. What a boundary does not catch is where most surprises come from: Errors in event handlers, such as an onPress that throws. Errors in asynchronous code: a rejected promise, a setTimeout callback, a failed fetch. Errors thrown inside the boundary’s own render. Native crashes in Swift, Kotlin or C++ code, which never reach JavaScript. For handlers and async code, catch the error yourself, or move it into state and rethrow during render so the boundary sees it. Place boundaries deliberately. One at the root stops a white screen; one per screen or per widget lets the rest of the app keep working when, say, a recommendations carousel receives malformed data. In development LogBox still reports the error, so test your fallback in a release build to see what users get. See catching rendering errors.
jsonLd.description: An error boundary is a React component that catches errors thrown while rendering its children and shows a fallback UI instead of letting the whole app go down.
jsonLd.headline: What is Error Boundary in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/eslint.title: ESLint in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: ESLint is the JavaScript linter React Native projects use to catch bugs and enforce conventions, most importantly the Rules of Hooks and effect dependencies.
og:description: ESLint is the JavaScript linter React Native projects use to catch bugs and enforce conventions, most importantly the Rules of Hooks and effect dependencies.
og:title: ESLint in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: ESLint is the JavaScript linter React Native projects use to catch bugs and enforce conventions, most importantly the Rules of Hooks and effect dependencies.
jsonLd.name: ESLint

jsonLd.articleBody: ESLint is a static analysis tool that reads your JavaScript and TypeScript and reports patterns that are likely bugs or break team conventions. React Native projects use it to catch problems that type checking cannot see, such as a hook called inside a condition. Both main toolchains ship a ready-made config. Projects on the React Native CLI get @react-native/eslint-config, and Expo projects can run npx expo lint, which sets up eslint-config-expo on first use. Current ESLint versions use a flat eslint.config.js file rather than the older .eslintrc. The rules that earn their place in a React Native codebase come from eslint-plugin-react-hooks: rules-of-hooks stops hooks being called conditionally or in loops, which otherwise causes state to land in the wrong place. exhaustive-deps checks that every value used inside useEffect, useMemo and useCallback is listed as a dependency. Rules from the React Compiler team flag code the compiler cannot safely optimise, such as mutating props. The most common mistake is silencing exhaustive-deps with // eslint-disable-next-line whenever it complains. The warning usually points at a real stale-closure bug: an effect reading an old value of state, or a listener that never re-subscribes. Restructure the effect instead. Other practical points: Let a formatter such as Prettier handle formatting and keep ESLint for correctness, so the two do not fight over the same lines. Lint in CI and fail the build on errors. Warnings that nobody is forced to fix tend to grow into hundreds. ESLint does not replace tsc. Type-aware rules exist, but they do not type-check the project.
jsonLd.description: ESLint is the JavaScript linter React Native projects use to catch bugs and enforce conventions, most importantly the Rules of Hooks and effect dependencies.
jsonLd.headline: What is ESLint in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/event-emitter.title: Event Emitter in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: An event emitter lets native code push events to JavaScript, such as download progress or sensor readings, which components receive by subscribing to a listener.
og:description: An event emitter lets native code push events to JavaScript, such as download progress or sensor readings, which components receive by subscribing to a listener.
og:title: Event Emitter in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An event emitter lets native code push events to JavaScript, such as download progress or sensor readings, which components receive by subscribing to a listener.
jsonLd.name: Event Emitter

jsonLd.articleBody: An event emitter is how native code talks to JavaScript without being asked. A normal native module call goes from JavaScript to native and returns once; an emitter lets the native side send any number of events later — Bluetooth packets, location updates, download progress, an audio player finishing a track. The long-standing API is NativeEventEmitter, wrapping a native module that can emit: On iOS the module typically subclasses RCTEventEmitter, lists its event names in supportedEvents and calls sendEventWithName. On Android it emits through DeviceEventManagerModule.RCTDeviceEventEmitter, and the module should also implement addListener and removeListeners methods, or React Native logs a warning when you construct the emitter. Under the New Architecture, a TurboModule spec can also declare typed event emitters, so Codegen generates the plumbing and the payload type is checked instead of being an untyped string-named event. The common mistakes are all about lifetimes: Forgetting remove(). A listener added in a component and never removed keeps firing after the screen is gone, calling setState on an unmounted component and keeping its closure alive. Subscribe inside useEffect and remove in the cleanup. Duplicate listeners. Subscribing on every render, or in an effect with unstable dependencies, stacks handlers so one event runs your code several times. Emitting with nobody listening. Events sent before JavaScript subscribes, for example during start-up, are simply dropped. Native code should buffer them, or JavaScript should ask for the current state once it subscribes. Flooding the JavaScript thread. Emitting sensor data at 100 Hz means 100 callbacks a second competing with rendering. Throttle on the native side.
jsonLd.description: An event emitter lets native code push events to JavaScript, such as download progress or sensor readings, which components receive by subscribing to a listener.
jsonLd.headline: What is Event Emitter in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/event-loop.title: Event Loop in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The event loop is how React Native’s JavaScript thread schedules work: it runs one task at a time, drains the microtask queue after each, and then lets rendering update.
og:description: The event loop is how React Native’s JavaScript thread schedules work: it runs one task at a time, drains the microtask queue after each, and then lets rendering update.
og:title: Event Loop in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The event loop is how React Native’s JavaScript thread schedules work: it runs one task at a time, drains the microtask queue after each, and then lets rendering update.
jsonLd.name: Event Loop

jsonLd.articleBody: The event loop is the scheduler that decides what the JavaScript thread runs next. JavaScript never runs two things at once on that thread: it takes one task — a touch event, a timer callback, a network response — runs it to completion, then runs every pending microtask (resolved promise callbacks, queueMicrotask), and only then moves on. Under the New Architecture, React Native implements an event loop modelled on the web’s, with a defined order between tasks, microtasks and UI updates. That ordering is what lets useLayoutEffect read layout synchronously and have its changes applied before the user sees a frame, and it makes browser knowledge about promises and timers transfer to React Native with fewer surprises. Why it matters in practice: Long tasks freeze input. A 300 ms loop over data blocks every touch, scroll event and JavaScript-driven animation queued behind it. That is the root of most JavaScript-side jank. async is not background work. Marking a function async does not move it off the thread. CPU-heavy work inside it still blocks; the await only yields when it is waiting on something. Microtasks can starve the loop. A chain of promises that keeps scheduling more promises never lets the next task run. Chunking work with setTimeout gives the loop room to handle input between chunks. For heavy computation, the real options are leaving the thread entirely — a native module, a worklet on another runtime, or a library that runs work in C++ — or splitting the work into smaller tasks. The event loop belongs to the runtime setup React Native provides, not to the JavaScript language, which is why Node.js-specific scheduling such as process.nextTick does not exist here.
jsonLd.description: The event loop is how React Native’s JavaScript thread schedules work: it runs one task at a time, drains the microtask queue after each, and then lets rendering update.
jsonLd.headline: What is Event Loop in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Expo is a framework and toolchain built on React Native. It supplies routing, native modules, build services and updates so teams do not assemble that stack themselves.
og:description: Expo is a framework and toolchain built on React Native. It supplies routing, native modules, build services and updates so teams do not assemble that stack themselves.
og:title: Expo in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Expo is a framework and toolchain built on React Native. It supplies routing, native modules, build services and updates so teams do not assemble that stack themselves.
jsonLd.name: Expo

jsonLd.articleBody: Expo is a framework built on top of React Native. React Native gives you the renderer and the JavaScript-to-native bridge; Expo adds the parts every app ends up needing — routing, a large library of native modules, build infrastructure, and update delivery. The React Native documentation now recommends starting new apps with a framework, and Expo is the one it points to. In practice npx create-expo-app is the default entry point for newcomers. What you get beyond bare React Native: Expo Router — file-based navigation The Expo SDK — vetted native modules (expo-camera, expo-notifications, expo-sqlite) that version together EAS — hosted builds, store submission, and over-the-air updates Continuous Native Generation — ios/ and android/ folders generated from config rather than hand-maintained A common misconception is that Expo restricts you to its own APIs. That stopped being true with development builds: any native library works. Curious whether a published app uses Expo? The React Native app checker looks for Expo modules inside its Android APK.

author: David Leuliette
description: Expo Doctor is a command-line check, run with npx expo-doctor, that finds dependency, config and native setup problems in an Expo project before they break a build.
og:description: Expo Doctor is a command-line check, run with npx expo-doctor, that finds dependency, config and native setup problems in an Expo project before they break a build.
og:title: Expo Doctor in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Expo Doctor is a command-line check, run with npx expo-doctor, that finds dependency, config and native setup problems in an Expo project before they break a build.
jsonLd.name: Expo Doctor

jsonLd.articleBody: Expo Doctor is a diagnostic tool for Expo projects. Running npx expo-doctor in the project folder performs a series of checks and prints each problem it finds with a suggested fix. It needs no install and no configuration. What it looks for: Version mismatches. Libraries whose versions do not match what your Expo SDK version expects, the most common cause of native build failures after an upgrade. npx expo install --fix usually resolves them. Duplicate native modules. Two copies of the same native package in node_modules, often from a nested dependency, which breaks builds or crashes at runtime. Configuration conflicts. For example, native fields in app config that will be ignored because the project commits its own ios/ and android/ folders. Library health. Packages that React Native Directory marks as unmaintained, untested on the New Architecture or unknown. It matters because these problems often surface far from their cause: a cryptic Gradle error, a crash on launch, or an EAS Build that fails after twenty minutes. Doctor finds them in seconds on your own machine. Practical habits: Run it after every SDK upgrade and after adding a native dependency. Add it to CI. It exits with a failing status when a check fails, so it can block a merge before a broken build reaches the queue. When a warning is a deliberate choice, such as a library you know works despite its directory status, exclude it in your project configuration rather than learning to ignore the output. The common mistake is reading a clean result as proof that the app works. Doctor checks setup and versions, not behaviour. A project can pass every check and still crash, so it complements testing on a device rather than replacing it.
jsonLd.description: Expo Doctor is a command-line check, run with npx expo-doctor, that finds dependency, config and native setup problems in an Expo project before they break a build.
jsonLd.headline: What is Expo Doctor in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Expo DOM components are React files marked with a ‘use dom’ directive that render web DOM code inside a native WebView on iOS and Android, and as plain DOM on web.
og:description: Expo DOM components are React files marked with a ‘use dom’ directive that render web DOM code inside a native WebView on iOS and Android, and as plain DOM on web.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Expo DOM components are React files marked with a ‘use dom’ directive that render web DOM code inside a native WebView on iOS and Android, and as plain DOM on web.
jsonLd.name: Expo DOM Components

jsonLd.articleBody: Expo DOM components let you drop ordinary web React code, with <div>, CSS and browser-only libraries, into a native React Native app. You add the 'use dom' directive at the top of a file, and Expo bundles that component separately and renders it inside a WebView on iOS and Android. On web it renders as normal DOM with no WebView at all. From the native side you import and render it like any other component, passing props across the boundary. The dom prop accepts WebView options such as scrollEnabled or matchContents. It matters for two jobs: migrating a web app to native one screen at a time, and using web-only libraries that have no native equivalent (rich text editors, certain charting or syntax-highlighting packages). It requires react-native-webview to be installed. The boundary has rules that follow from it being a separate JavaScript context: Props must be serialisable. Plain data crosses; class instances and React elements do not. Functions passed as props become asynchronous calls back into native, so they should be async and return serialisable values. Native components cannot be rendered inside a DOM component; the tree is web-only from that point down. The misconception is that this is a free way to skip native UI. Each DOM component is a WebView with its own startup cost and memory, it does not get native gestures, scrolling or accessibility for free, and it will not feel native beside real native views. Treat it as a tool for islands of web content, not for building whole apps. See using React DOM in Expo native apps.

author: David Leuliette
description: Expo Go is a free sandbox app from the App Store and Google Play that runs Expo projects instantly, with a fixed set of native modules and no custom native code.
og:description: Expo Go is a free sandbox app from the App Store and Google Play that runs Expo projects instantly, with a fixed set of native modules and no custom native code.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Expo Go is a free sandbox app from the App Store and Google Play that runs Expo projects instantly, with a fixed set of native modules and no custom native code.
jsonLd.name: Expo Go

jsonLd.articleBody: Expo Go is a prebuilt app you download from the App Store or Google Play. It already contains the native code for the Expo SDK, so it can load your project’s JavaScript from Metro and run it with no Xcode or Android Studio install. You scan a QR code from npx expo start and the app opens. That makes it the fastest way to try React Native: a phone, Node.js and five minutes are enough. It is ideal for tutorials, workshops, quick prototypes and sharing a demo with a colleague on the same network. The trade-off is that the native side is frozen. Expo Go can only use the native modules compiled into it, so: Libraries with their own native code that Expo does not bundle, such as many payment, Bluetooth or analytics SDKs, will not work. Config plugins and changes to native configuration have no effect. App name, icon, bundle identifier and push notification setup are Expo Go’s, not yours. Each store release of Expo Go supports one Expo SDK version. When a new SDK ships and the store app updates, a project still on an older SDK stops opening in it. This catches people out after an automatic phone update. The most common misconception is that Expo Go is "how Expo apps run". It is not what you ship. Real projects move to a development build, which is your own app with your own native dependencies plus the same quick reload workflow. Expo’s own docs treat Expo Go as a learning tool, not a production workflow.

author: David Leuliette
description: The Expo Modules API is a Swift and Kotlin DSL for writing native modules and views for React Native, built on JSI and usable in Expo and bare React Native apps.
og:description: The Expo Modules API is a Swift and Kotlin DSL for writing native modules and views for React Native, built on JSI and usable in Expo and bare React Native apps.
og:title: Expo Modules API in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The Expo Modules API is a Swift and Kotlin DSL for writing native modules and views for React Native, built on JSI and usable in Expo and bare React Native apps.
jsonLd.name: Expo Modules API

jsonLd.articleBody: The Expo Modules API is Expo’s framework for writing native code that JavaScript can call. You describe a module in a declarative Swift or Kotlin DSL — its name, functions, constants, events and views — and Expo generates the binding to JavaScript over JSI. Every package in the Expo SDK is built with it. From JavaScript you call requireNativeModule('Greeter').greet('Ada'). The Kotlin version mirrors the Swift one almost line for line. Why React Native developers choose it over a hand-written TurboModule: Modern languages only. Swift and Kotlin, with no Objective-C++ or Java glue to maintain. Type conversion handled for you, including records, enums and optional arguments, with argument validation. Async functions, events and native views declared in the same definition. Lifecycle hooks for app delegate and activity events, without editing AppDelegate or MainActivity. Getting started is npx create-expo-module for a publishable library, or npx create-expo-module --local to add one under modules/ in your app. Pair it with a config plugin when the module also needs Info.plist or manifest changes. The common misconception is that it only works in Expo-managed apps. It runs in any React Native project that has the expo package installed, which npx install-expo-modules sets up in a bare app. It does not work in Expo Go, though: custom native code always needs a development build. It is not a TurboModule under the hood and does not use React Native’s Codegen; it reaches the same goal — fast, typed JSI calls — through its own runtime. Both approaches are supported by the New Architecture. See the Expo Modules API docs.

author: David Leuliette
description: The Expo SDK version is the numbered release of the expo package that pins a matching React Native version and a tested set of Expo library versions.
og:description: The Expo SDK version is the numbered release of the expo package that pins a matching React Native version and a tested set of Expo library versions.
og:title: Expo SDK Version in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The Expo SDK version is the numbered release of the expo package that pins a matching React Native version and a tested set of Expo library versions.
jsonLd.name: Expo SDK Version

jsonLd.articleBody: An Expo SDK version is a numbered release of the expo package, such as SDK 54. Each one targets a specific React Native version and ships a set of expo-* libraries that have been tested together with it. The major version of the expo package is the SDK number. Expo releases a new SDK roughly three times a year, each following a recent React Native minor. In practice the SDK is the unit you upgrade, not React Native itself: bumping the SDK moves React Native, React and every Expo module forward together. The upgrade flow looks like this: npx expo install reads the SDK’s compatibility list and picks the right version of each library, including popular third-party ones such as Reanimated. Expo Doctor then flags anything still out of range. Practical advice: Upgrade one SDK at a time and read that SDK’s changelog. Breaking changes and deprecations are listed per release. If you use Continuous Native Generation, regenerate the native folders after upgrading rather than patching them. Native code changed, so build a new binary. An over-the-air update cannot move a user from one SDK to another. The most common mistake is installing libraries with plain npm install, which grabs the latest version rather than the one matching your SDK. That is the usual cause of "works in a new project, crashes in mine" bugs and native build failures after an upgrade.

/react-native-glossary/fabric-native-com.title: Fabric Native Component in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A Fabric Native Component is a platform view, such as a map or video player, exposed to React Native as a component through a Codegen spec and the Fabric renderer.
og:description: A Fabric Native Component is a platform view, such as a map or video player, exposed to React Native as a component through a Codegen spec and the Fabric renderer.
og:title: Fabric Native Component in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A Fabric Native Component is a platform view, such as a map or video player, exposed to React Native as a component through a Codegen spec and the Fabric renderer.
jsonLd.name: Fabric Native Component

jsonLd.articleBody: A Fabric Native Component is a native view — a UIView subclass on iOS, an Android View — that you render from JavaScript like any other component. It is how libraries ship maps, video players, camera previews and charts that cannot be built from React Native’s core components. Where a native module exposes functions, a native component exposes a view with props and events. Under the New Architecture you describe it in a TypeScript spec file whose name ends in NativeComponent: Codegen generates the C++ props, event emitter and shadow node, plus the platform interfaces your Objective-C++ or Kotlin view implements. The Fabric renderer then creates and updates the real view as part of its normal render pipeline, including layout through Yoga. The legacy equivalent was requireNativeComponent('CustomWebView') with view managers registered over the bridge. That still appears in older libraries and runs through the interop layer, but new components should use a Codegen spec. Gotchas that catch first-time authors: A spec change needs a native rebuild. Adding a prop means Codegen has to run again; Fast Refresh cannot pick it up. Props are typed for Codegen, not for TypeScript in general. Only a subset is understood: no any or arbitrary unions, and numbers are declared with Codegen types such as Int32 and Double, events with DirectEventHandler. Sizing. Native views without an intrinsic size from the layout system get zero height. Give them an explicit size or flex in style. Commands need declaring. Imperative calls such as play() are declared with codegenNativeCommands, not by calling methods on a ref. In Expo projects the Expo Modules API offers an alternative way to write native views with less boilerplate.
jsonLd.description: A Fabric Native Component is a platform view, such as a map or video player, exposed to React Native as a component through a Codegen spec and the Fabric renderer.
jsonLd.headline: What is Fabric Native Component in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Fabric is React Native’s rendering system. It builds the view tree in C++ and mounts real native views, replacing the legacy Paper renderer.
og:description: Fabric is React Native’s rendering system. It builds the view tree in C++ and mounts real native views, replacing the legacy Paper renderer.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Fabric is React Native’s rendering system. It builds the view tree in C++ and mounts real native views, replacing the legacy Paper renderer.
jsonLd.name: Fabric Renderer

jsonLd.articleBody: Fabric is the renderer React Native uses to turn your component tree into real platform views. It replaced the legacy Paper renderer and is part of the New Architecture, default since React Native 0.76. What changed matters for performance: Shared C++ core. The view tree, the diffing, and Yoga layout all live in C++ shared by iOS and Android, instead of being reimplemented per platform. Synchronous access. Because it sits on JSI, JavaScript can read layout and dispatch updates without a round trip over the old async bridge. Concurrent-safe. Fabric supports React 18 features such as Suspense and transitions, which the old renderer could not express. In practice this shows up as fewer dropped frames when a list mounts and less flicker when a screen measures itself before painting. Fabric renders host views: a <View> becomes a genuine UIView or ViewGroup, never a web element. See the architecture overview.

author: David Leuliette
description: Fast Refresh reloads edited React components in a running app within a second, preserving component state where it safely can.
og:description: Fast Refresh reloads edited React components in a running app within a second, preserving component state where it safely can.
og:title: Fast Refresh in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Fast Refresh reloads edited React components in a running app within a second, preserving component state where it safely can.
jsonLd.name: Fast Refresh

jsonLd.articleBody: Fast Refresh is React Native's hot-reloading system. Save a file and Metro pushes just that module to the running app, which re-renders in well under a second — no rebuild, no navigating back to the screen you were testing. It is state-aware, which is the part that saves real time: Editing a component that only renders JSX → state is preserved, so you keep your form input and scroll position Editing a hook or a non-component export → the module is re-run, so state resets A syntax or runtime error → a red screen appears, and fixing the file recovers automatically Fast Refresh replaced the older Hot Reloading and Live Reload toggles in React Native 0.61 and is on by default; you can disable it from the dev menu. What it does not cover is anything outside the JavaScript bundle. Installing a native module, changing app config, or upgrading React Native needs a full rebuild. If refresh stops applying, reload from the dev menu or restart Metro with --clear.

author: David Leuliette
description: Fastlane is an open-source Ruby tool that automates building, signing and uploading iOS and Android apps, with scripted lanes that replace manual Xcode and store steps.
og:description: Fastlane is an open-source Ruby tool that automates building, signing and uploading iOS and Android apps, with scripted lanes that replace manual Xcode and store steps.
og:title: Fastlane in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Fastlane is an open-source Ruby tool that automates building, signing and uploading iOS and Android apps, with scripted lanes that replace manual Xcode and store steps.
jsonLd.name: Fastlane

jsonLd.articleBody: Fastlane automates the release chores of mobile apps: building, managing certificates, bumping build numbers, taking screenshots and uploading to the stores. You describe each workflow as a lane in a Ruby file called a Fastfile, then run it locally or in CI. Each line is an action, and the common ones carry older short names you will still see in guides: build_app (gym), upload_to_testflight (pilot), upload_to_app_store (deliver) and upload_to_play_store (supply). The piece React Native teams value most is match. It stores your iOS certificates and provisioning profiles, encrypted, in a private Git repository or cloud bucket, and installs them on any machine that runs the lane. That removes "it only signs on Dave’s laptop" from your team, which is the core problem of iOS code signing on CI. Where it fits today: if you use EAS Build, you mostly do not touch fastlane directly; EAS manages credentials and runs the iOS build steps for you. Bare React Native projects building on their own runners, or teams that need custom release steps, still rely on it heavily. Practical gotchas: It is a Ruby gem, so pin it in a Gemfile and run bundle exec fastlane to avoid "works on my machine" version drift. Authenticate with an App Store Connect API key rather than an Apple ID, which runs into two-factor prompts on CI. match nuke revokes every certificate of a type for the whole team. Read the prompt twice. See the fastlane docs.

/react-native-glossary/fetch-api.title: Fetch API in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The Fetch API is React Native’s built-in global fetch() for HTTP requests, implemented over the native networking stacks of iOS and Android rather than a browser.
og:description: The Fetch API is React Native’s built-in global fetch() for HTTP requests, implemented over the native networking stacks of iOS and Android rather than a browser.
og:title: Fetch API in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The Fetch API is React Native’s built-in global fetch() for HTTP requests, implemented over the native networking stacks of iOS and Android rather than a browser.
jsonLd.name: Fetch API

jsonLd.articleBody: fetch() is the global function React Native provides for HTTP requests, with the same promise-based API as in browsers. Underneath, it is not a browser: requests are handed to the platform’s native networking stack on iOS and Android, which explains most of the ways it behaves differently from the web. Differences that matter on mobile: No CORS on native. CORS is a browser rule, so native requests ignore it. The same code may fail on web, which is a server configuration problem, not a React Native one. Plain HTTP is blocked by default. iOS App Transport Security and Android (since Android 9) refuse cleartext http:// traffic unless you add an exception. A local API that works in the browser often fails on a device for this reason. localhost is the device, not your computer. From the Android emulator, your machine is 10.0.2.2; from a physical phone, use your machine’s LAN address. Streaming is limited. React Native’s built-in fetch does not expose response bodies as streams. Expo provides expo/fetch with streaming support for cases such as reading an LLM response token by token. The mistakes that show up in production are about the network, not the API. fetch only rejects on network failure; a 401 or 500 resolves normally, so always check res.ok. And there is no default timeout, so on a weak mobile connection a request can hang far longer than any user will wait; abort it yourself as above. For caching, retries and refetching, wrap fetch with TanStack Query rather than calling it directly from effects. For connections that must stay open, use a WebSocket. See networking.
jsonLd.description: The Fetch API is React Native’s built-in global fetch() for HTTP requests, implemented over the native networking stacks of iOS and Android rather than a browser.
jsonLd.headline: What is Fetch API in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/firebase.title: Firebase in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Firebase is Google’s app backend platform; React Native apps use it through React Native Firebase, which wraps the native SDKs, or through the Firebase JavaScript SDK.
og:description: Firebase is Google’s app backend platform; React Native apps use it through React Native Firebase, which wraps the native SDKs, or through the Firebase JavaScript SDK.
og:title: Firebase in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Firebase is Google’s app backend platform; React Native apps use it through React Native Firebase, which wraps the native SDKs, or through the Firebase JavaScript SDK.
jsonLd.name: Firebase

jsonLd.articleBody: Firebase is Google’s backend-as-a-service: authentication, Firestore and Realtime Database, Cloud Storage, Cloud Messaging for push notifications, Crashlytics for crash reporting, Analytics and Remote Config. A React Native app can talk to it in two quite different ways, and choosing between them is the first decision. React Native Firebase (the @react-native-firebase/* packages, installed per product) wraps Google’s official native iOS and Android SDKs. You get every product, including those that only exist natively (Crashlytics, native Analytics, Cloud Messaging), plus native performance and offline persistence for Firestore. The Firebase JavaScript SDK (the firebase package) is the web SDK running in React Native. It needs no native code, so it works in Expo Go, but products that depend on native SDKs are missing or limited. React Native Firebase needs native configuration: a GoogleService-Info.plist for iOS and a google-services.json for Android, downloaded from the Firebase console. In Expo projects its config plugins wire these in during prebuild, and you need a development build rather than Expo Go. Gotchas that come up often: Do not mix the two SDKs for the same product. Two auth instances, for example, means two separate sessions. With the JavaScript SDK, auth persistence is not automatic. Without configuring React Native persistence, users are logged out on every restart. Cloud Messaging on iOS still goes through APNs. You must upload an APNs key to Firebase and enable the push capability, or iOS notifications never arrive while Android works fine. Security rules are your backend. Firestore and Storage are accessed directly from the app, so the rules are the only thing standing between your data and anyone who extracts your config. Compared with Supabase, Firebase’s databases are document-based rather than relational. See the React Native Firebase docs.
jsonLd.description: Firebase is Google’s app backend platform; React Native apps use it through React Native Firebase, which wraps the native SDKs, or through the Firebase JavaScript SDK.
jsonLd.headline: What is Firebase in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/flashlist.title: FlashList in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: FlashList is Shopify’s high-performance list component for React Native. It recycles mounted cells instead of unmounting them, with an API close to FlatList.
og:description: FlashList is Shopify’s high-performance list component for React Native. It recycles mounted cells instead of unmounting them, with an API close to FlatList.
og:title: FlashList in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: FlashList is Shopify’s high-performance list component for React Native. It recycles mounted cells instead of unmounting them, with an API close to FlatList.
jsonLd.name: FlashList

jsonLd.articleBody: FlashList is an open-source list component from Shopify, installed as @shopify/flash-list. It replaces FlatList for long or complex lists, keeping a similar props API while changing how rows are managed underneath. The difference is cell recycling. A VirtualizedList unmounts rows that leave the window and mounts new ones as they enter. FlashList keeps a pool of mounted row components and re-renders them with new data as they scroll back into view, so the app avoids creating and destroying native views during a fling. On big feeds that means fewer blank areas and steadier frame rate, especially on mid-range Android phones. Version 2 was rewritten for the New Architecture and no longer needs the estimatedItemSize prop that v1 required, because it measures items synchronously. If you read an older tutorial that insists on it, it was written for v1. Recycling brings its own gotchas: Local state leaks between rows. A recycled component keeps its useState values, so row A’s “expanded” flag can appear on row D. Derive UI from item data, or reset state when the item id changes. Don’t put a key on the row’s root. That forces React to remount the component and throws away the recycling benefit. Keys on children inside the row are also worth avoiding. Use getItemType when rows have very different layouts, so a header cell is never recycled into a product card. FlashList is not magic: heavy row components still need memoising. It shines once rows are reasonably cheap and the list is long.
jsonLd.description: FlashList is Shopify’s high-performance list component for React Native. It recycles mounted cells instead of unmounting them, with an API close to FlatList.
jsonLd.headline: What is FlashList in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: FlatList is React Native’s virtualised list component. It renders only the rows near the viewport, keeping memory flat no matter how long the data is.
og:description: FlatList is React Native’s virtualised list component. It renders only the rows near the viewport, keeping memory flat no matter how long the data is.
og:title: FlatList in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: FlatList is React Native’s virtualised list component. It renders only the rows near the viewport, keeping memory flat no matter how long the data is.
jsonLd.name: FlatList

jsonLd.articleBody: FlatList renders long lists efficiently by only mounting the rows near the viewport and recycling them as the user scrolls. A ScrollView mounts every child immediately, so a thousand-row list built from one would allocate a thousand native views up front. The props that decide whether it performs: keyExtractor — stable ids, for the same reasons keys matter anywhere getItemLayout — skips measurement when rows are a fixed height initialNumToRender — how much to render before the first paint The usual newcomer mistake is an inline renderItem arrow that recreates every row component on each render; memoising the row is the standard fix. For heavy lists many teams use FlashList from Shopify, a drop-in-shaped alternative with better recycling. Rule of thumb: ScrollView for a handful of known items, FlatList for anything data-driven.

author: David Leuliette
description: Flexbox is the layout system React Native uses for every view. It matches CSS Flexbox closely, with a column default direction and a few React Native specific differences.
og:description: Flexbox is the layout system React Native uses for every view. It matches CSS Flexbox closely, with a column default direction and a few React Native specific differences.
og:title: Flexbox in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Flexbox is the layout system React Native uses for every view. It matches CSS Flexbox closely, with a column default direction and a few React Native specific differences.
jsonLd.name: Flexbox

jsonLd.articleBody: Flexbox is how you lay out every screen in React Native. There is no grid, no float, and no absolute positioning by default — layout is flex containers all the way down, computed by the Yoga engine. The three properties that do most of the work: flexDirection — the main axis, column (default) or row justifyContent — distribution along the main axis alignItems — alignment across the main axis Differences from web CSS that catch newcomers: Web CSS React Native Default flexDirection row column Default alignContent stretch flex-start flex value shorthand string a single number Units px, rem, % unitless density-independent numbers flex: 1 means "take all remaining space", which is why a root screen container almost always has it. If a view is invisible, the usual cause is a parent with no height rather than a styling mistake on the view itself. See layout with Flexbox.
jsonLd.description: Flexbox is the layout system React Native uses for every view. It matches CSS Flexbox closely, with a column default direction and a few React Native specific differences.
jsonLd.headline: What is Flexbox in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Flipper is Meta’s desktop debugging platform for mobile apps, once bundled with every React Native project and removed from the default template in 0.74.
og:description: Flipper is Meta’s desktop debugging platform for mobile apps, once bundled with every React Native project and removed from the default template in 0.74.
og:title: Flipper in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Flipper is Meta’s desktop debugging platform for mobile apps, once bundled with every React Native project and removed from the default template in 0.74.
jsonLd.name: Flipper

jsonLd.articleBody: Flipper is a desktop app from Meta for inspecting and debugging iOS and Android apps through plugins. For several years every new React Native project shipped with it preinstalled, giving developers a network inspector, layout viewer, log viewer, database browser and crash reporter in one window. React Native removed Flipper from the default project template in version 0.74, and React Native DevTools became the official debugger in 0.76. If you start a project today, you will not meet Flipper unless you add it yourself. Why it was dropped: It added native dependencies to every app, which slowed iOS builds and caused frequent CocoaPods and build failures after Xcode updates. Meta moved its investment to a debugger built into React Native itself, connected directly to Hermes. Plugin quality varied and many React Native plugins went unmaintained. You still meet it in two places. Older codebases may contain Flipper setup in the Podfile, AppDelegate or Android debug sources, which often breaks during upgrades. Removing it, following the diff in the Upgrade Helper, is usually the simplest fix. And years of blog posts and Stack Overflow answers say "open Flipper" for tasks that now belong elsewhere. The common misconception is that removing Flipper means losing network inspection or state viewing. The replacements are React Native DevTools for console, breakpoints, memory and components, Reactotron for state and custom logging, and the network tooling built into recent DevTools versions or into Expo’s dev tools plugins. Flipper itself continues as a general mobile debugging tool, but it is no longer part of the React Native story.

/react-native-glossary/flow.title: Flow in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Flow is Meta’s static type checker for JavaScript; React Native’s own source code is written in it, though most apps today use TypeScript instead.
og:description: Flow is Meta’s static type checker for JavaScript; React Native’s own source code is written in it, though most apps today use TypeScript instead.
og:title: Flow in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Flow is Meta’s static type checker for JavaScript; React Native’s own source code is written in it, though most apps today use TypeScript instead.
jsonLd.name: Flow

jsonLd.articleBody: Flow is a static type checker for JavaScript built by Meta. React Native itself is written in Flow, which is why files inside node_modules/react-native start with @flow and contain type annotations that look almost, but not quite, like TypeScript. For app developers Flow is mostly background knowledge. The community settled on TypeScript, new templates use it, and Meta now generates React Native’s TypeScript types from the Flow sources. You are unlikely to write Flow in an app in 2026. Where it still touches your work: Reading React Native internals. Stack traces and "go to definition" often land in Flow-typed files. The syntax (?string, $ReadOnly<{...}>, exact object types) is readable once you know it is Flow. Native module specs. Codegen accepts specs written in either Flow or TypeScript, so older libraries and Meta examples use Flow specs. Tooling that does not strip Flow. React Native’s packages ship Flow syntax untranspiled and rely on the toolchain to remove it. That last point is the common gotcha. Metro and the React Native Jest preset handle Flow automatically through Babel. A custom Jest transform, a web bundler or a test runner configured without the React Native preset will choke on it with errors such as "Unexpected token" pointing at import typeof or a type annotation inside node_modules/react-native. The fix is to use the React Native preset or make sure those packages are transformed, not to rewrite anything. A frequent misconception is that a library being written in Flow makes it incompatible with a TypeScript app. It does not: types are stripped at build time, and most libraries ship .d.ts files alongside.

jsonLd.headline: What is Flow in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/flutter.title: Flutter in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Flutter is Google’s open-source UI toolkit that builds cross-platform apps in Dart and draws its own widgets with its own rendering engine instead of native views.
og:description: Flutter is Google’s open-source UI toolkit that builds cross-platform apps in Dart and draws its own widgets with its own rendering engine instead of native views.
og:title: Flutter in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Flutter is Google’s open-source UI toolkit that builds cross-platform apps in Dart and draws its own widgets with its own rendering engine instead of native views.
jsonLd.name: Flutter

jsonLd.articleBody: Flutter is Google’s open-source framework for building apps for iOS, Android, the web and desktop from one codebase written in Dart. It is the framework most often compared with React Native, because both target the same problem: one team shipping a mobile app to both stores. The core technical difference is rendering. React Native’s Fabric renderer turns your components into real platform views, such as UIView on iOS and android.view.View on Android. Flutter draws every pixel itself with its own engine onto a canvas, using its own widget library (Material and Cupertino) that imitates platform controls. That leads to real trade-offs, not a winner: Consistency vs platform fidelity. Flutter looks identical everywhere and is unaffected by OS styling changes. React Native picks up native behaviour and new OS styling for free, but platforms can differ slightly. Language and ecosystem. Flutter uses Dart and pub.dev. React Native uses JavaScript or TypeScript, npm and React, so web teams can share skills and sometimes code. Compilation. Flutter compiles Dart ahead of time to machine code for release builds. React Native runs JavaScript on Hermes, which precompiles to bytecode. Native access. Both use plugins or modules written in Swift, Kotlin or C++ for device features. Both offer fast development reload loops, mature tooling and large production users, and both can deliver smooth 60 or 120 fps interfaces when written carefully. A common misconception is that one is "native" and the other is not. Both produce real compiled app binaries. What differs is who draws the UI: the operating system in React Native, Flutter’s engine in Flutter. Choose based on your team’s language, how closely you need to track platform UI, and whether sharing code with a React web app matters.
jsonLd.description: Flutter is Google’s open-source UI toolkit that builds cross-platform apps in Dart and draws its own widgets with its own rendering engine instead of native views.
jsonLd.headline: What is Flutter in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/font-scaling.title: Font Scaling in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Font scaling is React Native’s support for the user’s system text size, such as iOS Dynamic Type and Android font size, which enlarges Text by default.
og:description: Font scaling is React Native’s support for the user’s system text size, such as iOS Dynamic Type and Android font size, which enlarges Text by default.
og:title: Font Scaling in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Font scaling is React Native’s support for the user’s system text size, such as iOS Dynamic Type and Android font size, which enlarges Text by default.
jsonLd.name: Font Scaling

jsonLd.articleBody: Font scaling is how React Native respects the text size people choose in their device settings: Dynamic Type and Larger Text on iOS, Font size on Android. By default every Text and TextInput multiplies its fontSize by the system font scale, so a user at 150% sees 16-point text rendered at 24. That default is deliberate. A large share of users raise their text size, many of them older or with low vision, and an app that ignores the setting is hard or impossible for them to read. You can read the current scale to adapt layouts: useWindowDimensions updates when the setting changes; PixelRatio.getFontScale() returns the same value imperatively. Props that control scaling: allowFontScaling (default true) turns scaling on or off for one element. maxFontSizeMultiplier caps how far an element can grow, which is the right tool for a tab bar label or a badge that must stay compact. On iOS, dynamicTypeRamp on Text maps it to an iOS text style, such as body or caption, so it scales along the matching Dynamic Type curve. What breaks in practice is layout, not text. Fixed height values, numberOfLines={1} on important labels and rows that assume one line all clip or overlap at large sizes. Let containers grow with content, allow wrapping, and switch from a row to a column when the scale is high. The most common mistake is fixing those bugs by setting allowFontScaling={false} on every Text. It hides the problem by removing an accessibility feature users rely on. Cap specific elements with maxFontSizeMultiplier instead, and test the main screens at the largest setting on both platforms.
jsonLd.description: Font scaling is React Native’s support for the user’s system text size, such as iOS Dynamic Type and Android font size, which enlarges Text by default.
jsonLd.headline: What is Font Scaling in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/fragment.title: Fragment in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A Fragment groups several React elements without adding a wrapper, so a component can return siblings without creating an extra native View in the hierarchy.
og:description: A Fragment groups several React elements without adding a wrapper, so a component can return siblings without creating an extra native View in the hierarchy.
og:title: Fragment in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A Fragment groups several React elements without adding a wrapper, so a component can return siblings without creating an extra native View in the hierarchy.
jsonLd.name: Fragment

jsonLd.articleBody: A Fragment lets a component return more than one element without wrapping them in a container. JSX requires a single root, and before Fragments the usual workaround in React Native was an extra <View>. A Fragment satisfies the rule and leaves nothing behind in the native hierarchy. The two Text elements become direct children of whatever renders Price, so they take part in the parent’s flex layout as if they had been written there. That is the main reason to prefer a Fragment over a wrapper View in React Native: an extra View is an extra flex container. It changes how gap, justifyContent and flexDirection apply to its children, and it is a frequent cause of "why is this row not stretching" bugs. Use a View when you actually want a container to style or lay out; use a Fragment when you only need grouping. Things worth knowing: Keys need the long form. The <>…</> shorthand cannot take props. When mapping a list that returns several elements per item, write <Fragment key={item.id}>. Fragments accept no style or event props. There is nothing to style; it does not exist at runtime. The text rule still applies. A string inside a Fragment is still a raw string; if the Fragment ends up outside a Text component you get "Text strings must be rendered within a <Text> component". A Fragment is not quite free. React still tracks it during reconciliation, and toggling between returning a Fragment and returning a single element at the same position can reset the child’s state. In practice this rarely matters. See Fragment.

/react-native-glossary/frame-rate.title: Frame Rate in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Frame rate is how many frames per second a React Native app draws. At 60 FPS each frame has about 16.7 ms of work; on 120 Hz screens only 8.3 ms.
og:description: Frame rate is how many frames per second a React Native app draws. At 60 FPS each frame has about 16.7 ms of work; on 120 Hz screens only 8.3 ms.
og:title: Frame Rate in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Frame rate is how many frames per second a React Native app draws. At 60 FPS each frame has about 16.7 ms of work; on 120 Hz screens only 8.3 ms.
jsonLd.name: Frame Rate

jsonLd.articleBody: Frame rate is the number of frames your app renders each second, measured in FPS. Phones refresh at 60 Hz as a baseline, and many iPhones (ProMotion) and Android devices run at 90 or 120 Hz, so a frame must be ready in 16.7 ms, 11.1 ms or 8.3 ms. React Native has two frame rates worth watching, not one: UI FPS — how often the native UI thread produces a frame. If this drops, scrolling and native transitions visibly stutter. JS FPS — how often the JavaScript thread gets through its work. If this drops, taps feel slow, state updates lag and JS-driven animations freeze, even while native scrolling stays smooth. The Perf Monitor in the Dev Menu shows both numbers live, which makes it the quickest way to tell which side is struggling. The common mistake is judging frame rate in a debug build. Development mode adds runtime checks, warnings and an unoptimised bundle, so a screen that crawls at 30 FPS in development can be perfectly smooth in a release build. Always confirm on a release build and on a mid-range Android phone, not only on the latest iPhone. The second misconception is that 120 Hz is free. Higher refresh rates halve the time budget, so code that was just under 16 ms now misses every other frame. Work that must run every frame, such as gesture-driven animation, belongs on the UI thread through Reanimated worklets or the native driver, where a busy JavaScript thread cannot hold it back.
jsonLd.description: Frame rate is how many frames per second a React Native app draws. At 60 FPS each frame has about 16.7 ms of work; on 120 Hz screens only 8.3 ms.
jsonLd.headline: What is Frame Rate in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/garbage-collectio.title: Garbage Collection in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Garbage collection is how the JavaScript engine reclaims memory from objects nothing references any more. In React Native, Hermes runs a mostly concurrent collector.
og:description: Garbage collection is how the JavaScript engine reclaims memory from objects nothing references any more. In React Native, Hermes runs a mostly concurrent collector.
og:title: Garbage Collection in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Garbage collection is how the JavaScript engine reclaims memory from objects nothing references any more. In React Native, Hermes runs a mostly concurrent collector.
jsonLd.name: Garbage Collection

jsonLd.articleBody: Garbage collection (GC) is the automatic process that frees memory used by JavaScript objects your code can no longer reach. The engine periodically traces every object reachable from the roots — globals, the call stack, live closures — and reclaims the rest. In React Native that engine is usually Hermes, whose collector, called Hades, does most of its work on a background thread. Older collectors stopped the JavaScript thread for the whole collection, which on a large heap could show up as a dropped frame mid-scroll. Hades keeps those pauses short, so GC is rarely the cause of jank on its own. What GC cannot do is free memory you are still pointing at. That is what a JavaScript memory leak really is: an object kept reachable by mistake. The usual culprits in React Native: Event listeners and subscriptions never removed, holding closures that capture whole screens. setInterval timers still running after their component unmounted. Module-level caches, arrays or maps that only ever grow. Large responses stored in a global store long after they are needed. There is also a React Native-specific blind spot. Through JSI, a small JavaScript object can own a large native allocation — a decoded image, a Skia surface, a database handle. The collector only sees the small JavaScript side, so it feels no pressure to run, and the native memory waits until it does. Libraries that wrap native resources usually offer an explicit dispose() or release(); call it rather than relying on GC. To investigate, take heap snapshots in React Native DevTools and compare them before and after repeating an action several times, such as opening and closing a screen. Objects whose count keeps climbing are being retained. Remember that memory from native views, images and the native heap does not appear in a JavaScript heap snapshot; use Xcode Instruments or the Android Studio profiler for those.
jsonLd.description: Garbage collection is how the JavaScript engine reclaims memory from objects nothing references any more. In React Native, Hermes runs a mostly concurrent collector.
jsonLd.headline: What is Garbage Collection in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/gesture-handler.title: Gesture Handler in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: React Native Gesture Handler recognises touches and gestures natively on the UI thread, replacing the JS-based responder system for pans, swipes and pinches.
og:description: React Native Gesture Handler recognises touches and gestures natively on the UI thread, replacing the JS-based responder system for pans, swipes and pinches.
og:title: Gesture Handler in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: React Native Gesture Handler recognises touches and gestures natively on the UI thread, replacing the JS-based responder system for pans, swipes and pinches.
jsonLd.name: Gesture Handler

jsonLd.articleBody: React Native Gesture Handler (RNGH), from Software Mansion, is the standard library for gestures in React Native. It recognises touches using the platforms’ native gesture systems on the UI thread, instead of sending every touch to JavaScript to be interpreted, as the built-in PanResponder does. You describe a gesture with the Gesture builder and attach it with GestureDetector: With Reanimated installed, these callbacks run as worklets on the UI thread and write straight to shared values, so a dragged card tracks the finger with no JavaScript round trip even while the JS thread is busy. React Navigation’s stack and drawer, bottom sheets and swipeable list rows all depend on it. Composition is where it earns its place. Gesture.Simultaneous lets pinch and rotate run together, Gesture.Exclusive gives double-tap priority over single-tap, and Gesture.Race lets whichever gesture activates first win. Gestures can also be told to wait for, or run alongside, a native scroll view, which solves the classic “horizontal swipe inside a vertical list” conflict. The setup mistake almost everyone makes once: gestures only work inside a GestureHandlerRootView, which should wrap the whole app near the root. Forget it and gestures silently do nothing. On Android, content rendered in a React Native Modal sits outside that root, so the modal’s content needs its own GestureHandlerRootView. The other common surprise is mixing systems. A RNGH gesture and a Pressable or onTouchStart handler on the same area compete for the touch in ways that are hard to reason about; pick one system per interactive area. See the Gesture Handler docs.
jsonLd.description: React Native Gesture Handler recognises touches and gestures natively on the UI thread, replacing the JS-based responder system for pans, swipes and pinches.
jsonLd.headline: What is Gesture Handler in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/getitemlayout.title: getItemLayout in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: getItemLayout is a FlatList prop that tells the list each item’s height and offset in advance, so it can skip measuring rows and jump straight to any index.
og:description: getItemLayout is a FlatList prop that tells the list each item’s height and offset in advance, so it can skip measuring rows and jump straight to any index.
og:title: getItemLayout in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: getItemLayout is a FlatList prop that tells the list each item’s height and offset in advance, so it can skip measuring rows and jump straight to any index.
jsonLd.name: getItemLayout

jsonLd.articleBody: getItemLayout is an optional prop on FlatList and other lists built on VirtualizedList. You give it a function that returns the length, offset and index of any item, so the list knows the layout of every row without rendering and measuring it first. Why it matters: scrollToIndex works reliably. Without it, jumping to a row that has not been rendered yet fails or lands in the wrong place, because the list cannot know where that row is. initialScrollIndex opens the list at the right spot without a visible jump. Less layout work while scrolling fast, so fewer blank areas appear. It only makes sense when item sizes are known up front: fixed-height rows, or heights you can compute from the data without rendering. If rows vary with their text content, a wrong getItemLayout is worse than none, causing overlapping rows and scroll positions that drift. The classic gotcha is forgetting extras. If you use ItemSeparatorComponent, a header or content padding, the offset must include them, otherwise each row is off by a few pixels more than the last and long lists end up badly misaligned. In a SectionList, section headers and footers count as items in the index too. FlashList does not use getItemLayout; it has its own layout approach.

/react-native-glossary/google-play-conso.title: Google Play Console in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Google Play Console is Google’s web dashboard for publishing Android apps: it holds the store listing, release tracks, app signing, policy forms and Android vitals.
og:description: Google Play Console is Google’s web dashboard for publishing Android apps: it holds the store listing, release tracks, app signing, policy forms and Android vitals.
og:title: Google Play Console in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Google Play Console is Google’s web dashboard for publishing Android apps: it holds the store listing, release tracks, app signing, policy forms and Android vitals.
jsonLd.name: Google Play Console

jsonLd.articleBody: Google Play Console is where an Android build becomes a Play Store app. A developer account costs a one-time registration fee, and from there each app gets its own section for releases, listing, policy and quality data. What a React Native developer does there: Uploads releases as Android App Bundles to a track: internal, closed, open testing or production. See internal testing track. Manages Play App Signing, where Google holds the key that signs what users install and you sign uploads with a separate upload key. Completes policy declarations: the Data safety form, content rating questionnaire, target audience and, depending on the app, permission justifications. Watches Android vitals: crash rate, ANR rate and startup time from real devices. Crossing Google’s bad-behaviour thresholds can reduce the app’s visibility in the store. Controls rollout of production releases by percentage, the Android form of a staged rollout. Gotchas specific to Play: The first upload must be manual. The Play Developer API, which EAS Submit and fastlane use, cannot upload until the app exists and has had a release in the console. New personal developer accounts must run a closed test with a minimum number of opted-in testers for a set period before they can apply for production access. Plan for this weeks before launch. Google requires apps to target a recent Android API level. When the deadline passes, you cannot publish updates until you raise targetSdkVersion, which in React Native usually means upgrading React Native or the Expo SDK. A rejected or suspended release blocks every track, so read policy emails promptly. To automate uploads, create a Google Cloud service account, grant it access in Play Console and give its JSON key to your CI or EAS.

/react-native-glossary/gradle.title: Gradle in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Gradle is the build system that compiles the Android side of a React Native app, resolving native dependencies and producing the APK or AAB you install or ship.
og:description: Gradle is the build system that compiles the Android side of a React Native app, resolving native dependencies and producing the APK or AAB you install or ship.
og:title: Gradle in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Gradle is the build system that compiles the Android side of a React Native app, resolving native dependencies and producing the APK or AAB you install or ship.
jsonLd.name: Gradle

jsonLd.articleBody: Gradle is the build tool Android uses, and in a React Native project it compiles everything under android/: your app module, React Native, Hermes and the Android half of each native library. It plays the role on Android that Xcode’s build system plays on iOS. The files you will meet: android/app/build.gradle — the app module: applicationId, versionCode, versionName, signing configs and dependencies. android/build.gradle and settings.gradle — project-wide setup, including where autolinking plugs in native libraries. android/gradle.properties — flags such as hermesEnabled, newArchEnabled and the JVM memory Gradle may use. gradlew and gradle/wrapper/ — the Gradle wrapper, which downloads the exact Gradle version the project expects. Always run ./gradlew, never a globally installed gradle. The wrapper pins the version, and React Native, the Android Gradle Plugin and Gradle must be compatible with each other. npx react-native run-android and npx expo run:android call these tasks for you. The output lands in android/app/build/outputs/ as an APK or Android App Bundle. Gotchas worth knowing: The first build is slow because Gradle downloads dependencies and compiles every architecture. Later builds reuse its cache and daemon. “Could not resolve” errors usually mean a version mismatch between a library and your React Native version, not a network problem. ./gradlew clean fixes stale outputs, but deleting android/.gradle and android/app/build is sometimes needed after an upgrade. In Expo projects using Continuous Native Generation, edit Gradle settings through app.json or config plugins, because android/ is regenerated.
