/react-native-glossary/headless-js.title: Headless JS in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Headless JS is an Android-only React Native feature that runs a JavaScript task from a native service while no UI is showing, for work such as syncing data.
og:description: Headless JS is an Android-only React Native feature that runs a JavaScript task from a native service while no UI is showing, for work such as syncing data.
og:title: Headless JS in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Headless JS is an Android-only React Native feature that runs a JavaScript task from a native service while no UI is showing, for work such as syncing data.
jsonLd.name: Headless JS

jsonLd.articleBody: Headless JS is a React Native API for running JavaScript on Android without rendering any screen. Native code starts an Android service, the service asks React Native to run a named task, and your JavaScript function executes and resolves, all while the app may be in the background. On the JavaScript side you register an async function under a name, next to your app registration: On the native side you write a service extending HeadlessJsTaskService that returns a HeadlessJsTaskConfig with the task name, the data to pass, a timeout and whether the task may run while the app is in the foreground. Native code — a broadcast receiver for connectivity changes, a push notification handler, a scheduled job — then starts that service. Things that trip people up: It is Android-only. iOS has no equivalent mechanism; background work there goes through the platform’s own APIs, usually via libraries built for background tasks. No UI. The task cannot render; it can update storage, call APIs or schedule a notification. Foreground runs are refused by default. Unless the config allows it, starting the task while the app is visible fails, which surprises people testing with the app open. Android decides what is allowed. Modern Android versions restrict background services heavily, so long-running work has to be a foreground service with a visible notification or be scheduled through WorkManager. Headless JS does not exempt you from those rules. Keep it short. Tasks run on the JavaScript thread and are killed at the timeout. A task that never resolves holds the service and drains the battery. Most apps never write this by hand. Libraries for background fetch, geolocation and notifications use Headless JS internally to deliver events to JavaScript when the app is not open. See Headless JS.
jsonLd.description: Headless JS is an Android-only React Native feature that runs a JavaScript task from a native service while no UI is showing, for work such as syncing data.
jsonLd.headline: What is Headless JS in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/hermes.title: Hermes in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Hermes is the JavaScript engine Meta built for React Native. Default since version 0.70, it precompiles code to bytecode for faster startup and lower memory use.
og:description: Hermes is the JavaScript engine Meta built for React Native. Default since version 0.70, it precompiles code to bytecode for faster startup and lower memory use.
og:title: Hermes in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Hermes is the JavaScript engine Meta built for React Native. Default since version 0.70, it precompiles code to bytecode for faster startup and lower memory use.
jsonLd.name: Hermes

jsonLd.articleBody: Hermes is an open-source JavaScript engine Meta built specifically for running React Native on mobile. It has been the default engine since React Native 0.70, replacing JavaScriptCore. It is optimised for constraints a browser engine does not have: Ahead-of-time bytecode. Instead of parsing JavaScript on every launch, Hermes compiles the bundle to bytecode at build time. That removes parse cost from startup, which is the single biggest win on low-end Android devices. Smaller memory footprint, from a garbage collector tuned for mobile. No JIT. Hermes trades peak throughput for start-up speed and predictability — the right trade for UI code, less so for heavy computation. Two practical notes. Debugging targets React Native DevTools rather than a Chrome tab, because Hermes is not Chrome's V8. And engine gaps are real: an Intl or regex feature that works in a browser may be absent, so test on device rather than trusting a web preview. To see if a published app runs Hermes, paste its Google Play link in the React Native app checker. See Hermes.
jsonLd.description: Hermes is the JavaScript engine Meta built for React Native. Default since version 0.70, it precompiles code to bytecode for faster startup and lower memory use.
jsonLd.headline: What is Hermes in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/hermes-bytecode.title: Hermes Bytecode in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Hermes bytecode is the precompiled binary form of your JavaScript bundle that Hermes executes in release builds, so the device skips parsing source code at launch.
og:description: Hermes bytecode is the precompiled binary form of your JavaScript bundle that Hermes executes in release builds, so the device skips parsing source code at launch.
og:title: Hermes Bytecode in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Hermes bytecode is the precompiled binary form of your JavaScript bundle that Hermes executes in release builds, so the device skips parsing source code at launch.
jsonLd.name: Hermes Bytecode

jsonLd.articleBody: Hermes bytecode (HBC) is what Hermes actually runs in a production React Native app. During a release build, Metro produces the JavaScript bundle, then the Hermes compiler, hermesc, turns it into a compact binary file of bytecode instructions. That file is embedded in the app instead of readable source. The benefit is start-up time. A traditional engine must download, parse and compile the whole bundle on the device every launch. With bytecode, that work happened on your build machine, so the app can memory-map the file and start executing functions as they are needed. On low-end Android devices this is often the largest single start-up win available. How it behaves in practice: Development builds usually run plain JavaScript. Hermes can compile source on the device when you load the bundle from Metro, which keeps Fast Refresh quick. Bytecode is a release-build step, so start-up measured in debug mode is not representative. Bytecode is tied to the engine version. The bytecode format changes between Hermes versions, and a file compiled for one cannot be run by another. This is why an over-the-air update must target a binary with the matching React Native version: services such as EAS Update compile bytecode for the runtime that will load it. Stack traces need source maps. Errors from a release build point at bytecode offsets. Upload the Hermes source maps produced at build time to your crash reporter, or your production stack traces are unreadable. A common misconception is that bytecode protects your code. It is harder to read than minified JavaScript, but decompilers for Hermes bytecode exist, and string constants such as API endpoints and keys are visible in the file. Never treat it as a place to hide secrets. Bytecode does not make running code faster in general; Hermes still interprets it. The gain is skipping parse and compile at launch.
jsonLd.description: Hermes bytecode is the precompiled binary form of your JavaScript bundle that Hermes executes in release builds, so the device skips parsing source code at launch.
jsonLd.headline: What is Hermes Bytecode in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/hooks.title: Hooks in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Hooks are React functions such as useState and useEffect that let a function component hold state, run side effects and reach React features without a class.
og:description: Hooks are React functions such as useState and useEffect that let a function component hold state, run side effects and reach React features without a class.
og:title: Hooks in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Hooks are React functions such as useState and useEffect that let a function component hold state, run side effects and reach React features without a class.
jsonLd.name: Hooks

jsonLd.articleBody: Hooks are functions whose names start with use that let a function component tap into React: keep state between renders, run code after rendering, read context, or hold a mutable value. They are how every modern React Native component is written; class components still work but new code and new libraries assume hooks. The ones you will use daily: useState and useReducer for local state. useEffect for subscriptions and other side effects. useRef for a value that survives renders without causing one, including refs to native views. useContext (or use in React 19) for shared values. useMemo and useCallback for keeping values and functions stable. React Native adds its own, such as useWindowDimensions and useColorScheme, and most libraries expose their API as hooks too: useNavigation, useSharedValue, useQuery. Hooks rely on call order. React stores each hook's data in a list attached to the component and matches them up by position on every render, which is why the two rules exist: Call hooks only at the top level, never inside a condition, loop or after an early return. Call them only from components or from other hooks. Break the first rule and you get "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render" or, worse, state silently landing in the wrong variable. The classic slip in React Native is an early return <ActivityIndicator /> placed above a useEffect. Install eslint-plugin-react-hooks, which catches both rules and missing effect dependencies. Packaging your own combination of hooks into a reusable function gives you a custom hook. See the hooks reference.
jsonLd.description: Hooks are React functions such as useState and useEffect that let a function component hold state, run side effects and reach React features without a class.
jsonLd.headline: What is Hooks in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/host-platform.title: Host Platform in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The host platform is the operating system embedding React Native — iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, tvOS or the web — and the source of the real views your components render to.
og:description: The host platform is the operating system embedding React Native — iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, tvOS or the web — and the source of the real views your components render to.
og:title: Host Platform in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The host platform is the operating system embedding React Native — iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, tvOS or the web — and the source of the real views your components render to.
jsonLd.name: Host Platform

jsonLd.articleBody: The host platform is whatever operating system is hosting your React Native app and providing the real UI widgets it renders into. React Native itself is platform-agnostic; the host supplies the views, the threading model, and the APIs. The supported hosts split into two groups: Maintained by Meta — iOS and Android. Maintained by partners — macOS and Windows by Microsoft, tvOS, and visionOS, plus React Native Web for the browser. The concept matters because it explains React Native's core promise and its main caveat. A <View> is not one thing: it is a host component resolved to a UIView, a ViewGroup, or a <div> depending on where it runs. Shared code describes intent; the host decides the pixels. You handle host differences with the Platform module or platform-specific files, and you reach host capabilities that React Native does not wrap through a native module.

/react-native-glossary/hybrid-app.title: Hybrid App in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A hybrid app is a web app written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript that runs inside a WebView in a native shell, distributed through the app stores like any other app.
og:description: A hybrid app is a web app written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript that runs inside a WebView in a native shell, distributed through the app stores like any other app.
og:title: Hybrid App in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A hybrid app is a web app written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript that runs inside a WebView in a native shell, distributed through the app stores like any other app.
jsonLd.name: Hybrid App

jsonLd.articleBody: A hybrid app is a mobile app whose interface is a web page. The code is HTML, CSS and JavaScript, rendered by the system WebView inside a thin native container that is installed from the App Store or Google Play. A plugin layer gives the web code access to device features. Apache Cordova (and PhoneGap, built on it) popularised the approach; Capacitor is the main modern option. React Native is not a hybrid app in this sense, even though both use JavaScript. The distinction is where the UI is drawn: Hybrid: JavaScript builds a DOM, and a browser engine lays out and paints it. React Native: JavaScript describes a tree of components, and React Native creates real platform views. There is no DOM, no CSS engine and no WebView involved unless you add one. That difference explains the typical trade-offs. Hybrid apps reuse web skills and often an entire existing web app, and one codebase can also serve the browser. In return, scrolling physics, gestures, text inputs and transitions are web imitations of platform behaviour, and complex screens can feel less responsive than native ones, especially on low-end Android devices. Some people also call React Native apps "hybrid" simply because they are not fully native. That usage is loose and best avoided, since it blurs the meaningful difference above. The line also blurs in practice: many native apps and React Native apps embed WebViews for a help centre, checkout flow or legal pages. That makes them partly web-based, not hybrid apps. The useful question is not the label but which screens need native feel and which are fine as web content.
jsonLd.description: A hybrid app is a web app written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript that runs inside a WebView in a native shell, distributed through the app stores like any other app.
jsonLd.headline: What is Hybrid App in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/image-caching.title: Image Caching in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Image caching keeps downloaded images in memory or on disk so a React Native app can show them again instantly without re-downloading or re-decoding them.
og:description: Image caching keeps downloaded images in memory or on disk so a React Native app can show them again instantly without re-downloading or re-decoding them.
og:title: Image Caching in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Image caching keeps downloaded images in memory or on disk so a React Native app can show them again instantly without re-downloading or re-decoding them.
jsonLd.name: Image Caching

jsonLd.articleBody: Image caching is storing remote images after the first download so they can be displayed again without another network request. A good cache works at two levels: a memory cache of decoded images for instant display while scrolling, and a disk cache of the files that survives app restarts. The core Image component relies on the platform's networking and image pipeline, and its caching behaviour differs between iOS and Android and depends on the server's HTTP cache headers. That inconsistency is why many apps use expo-image, which is built on mature native image libraries and lets you choose a cachePolicy such as 'memory-disk', plus placeholders, transitions and prefetching. Things that commonly go wrong: Cache-busting URLs. Signed URLs or query strings that change on every request (?token=…, ?t=…) give each load a new cache key, so nothing is ever reused. Oversized images. Caching is not the only cost. A 4000 px photo displayed in a 48 px avatar is still decoded at full size, using far more memory than needed and causing jank and memory pressure in long lists. Ask your image server for the display size. Stale content. If the image behind a URL changes but the URL does not, users keep the old version. Version the URL when content changes. For lists of images, prefetch the next few items, give every image explicit dimensions to avoid layout jumps, and pair the cache with a recycling list such as FlashList.
jsonLd.description: Image caching keeps downloaded images in memory or on disk so a React Native app can show them again instantly without re-downloading or re-decoding them.
jsonLd.headline: What is Image Caching in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/image-component.title: Image Component in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Image is the React Native core component for displaying bundled, remote or base64 pictures; expo-image is the popular drop-in with stronger caching and placeholders.
og:description: Image is the React Native core component for displaying bundled, remote or base64 pictures; expo-image is the popular drop-in with stronger caching and placeholders.
og:title: Image Component in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Image is the React Native core component for displaying bundled, remote or base64 pictures; expo-image is the popular drop-in with stronger caching and placeholders.
jsonLd.name: Image Component

jsonLd.articleBody: <Image> is the core component that draws pictures in React Native, from three kinds of source: a static file pulled in with require(), a remote URI, or a base64 data URI. The two kinds of source behave very differently: Static images are resolved by Metro at build time. Their size is known, and Metro picks logo@2x.png or logo@3x.png to match the screen density. Remote images have no intrinsic size until they download, so they render as nothing unless you give them a width and height. This is the single most common “my image doesn’t show” bug. resizeMode (cover, contain, stretch, repeat, center) controls how the picture fills its box. Image.prefetch() warms the cache before a screen opens, and onLoad and onError let you react to the result. The built-in component leans on each platform’s networking stack for caching, which gives you little control over disk cache behaviour. That is why many apps switch to expo-image, which uses SDWebImage on iOS and Glide on Android. It adds a real memory and disk cache with a cachePolicy prop, blurhash and thumbhash placeholders, transitions, and formats such as WebP and AVIF. Its contentFit prop replaces resizeMode. It works in bare React Native projects too, not only Expo ones; see image caching for strategy. A frequent performance mistake is loading a 4000-pixel photo into a 100-point thumbnail. Decoding it costs memory on every render, so request a server-resized image sized for the device’s pixel density.
jsonLd.description: Image is the React Native core component for displaying bundled, remote or base64 pictures; expo-image is the popular drop-in with stronger caching and placeholders.
jsonLd.headline: What is Image Component in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/info-plist.title: Info.plist in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Info.plist is the iOS property list holding an app’s configuration: display name, version, URL schemes, fonts and the permission usage messages users see.
og:description: Info.plist is the iOS property list holding an app’s configuration: display name, version, URL schemes, fonts and the permission usage messages users see.
og:title: Info.plist in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Info.plist is the iOS property list holding an app’s configuration: display name, version, URL schemes, fonts and the permission usage messages users see.
jsonLd.name: Info.plist

jsonLd.articleBody: Info.plist is an XML property list in ios/YourApp/ that iOS reads to learn about your app before any code runs. It holds the display name, version numbers, supported orientations, URL schemes, custom fonts and the explanations shown in permission prompts. Android keeps similar information in AndroidManifest.xml. Keys React Native developers touch most: Usage descriptions such as NSCameraUsageDescription or NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription — the sentence iOS shows when asking for a permission. CFBundleShortVersionString and CFBundleVersion — the marketing version and build number. CFBundleURLTypes — custom URL schemes for deep links. LSApplicationQueriesSchemes — schemes Linking.canOpenURL is allowed to check. UIAppFonts — font files to register. The gotcha that bites everyone once: if your code, or a library, touches a protected resource without the matching usage description, iOS terminates the app immediately. App Review also rejects vague messages like “needs camera”, so write what the feature actually does. See App Permissions for the runtime request itself. Don’t confuse Info.plist with neighbouring files. Capabilities such as push notifications or associated domains live in the entitlements file, and the data-collection declarations Apple requires live in PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, the privacy manifest. In Expo projects, set these keys under ios.infoPlist in your app config instead of editing the file, because Continuous Native Generation regenerates it. Many Expo libraries add their own usage descriptions through config plugins, with defaults worth overriding.
jsonLd.description: Info.plist is the iOS property list holding an app’s configuration: display name, version, URL schemes, fonts and the permission usage messages users see.
jsonLd.headline: What is Info.plist in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: InteractionManager is a legacy React Native API that defers expensive JavaScript work until running animations and touches finish, using runAfterInteractions.
og:description: InteractionManager is a legacy React Native API that defers expensive JavaScript work until running animations and touches finish, using runAfterInteractions.
og:title: InteractionManager in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: InteractionManager is a legacy React Native API that defers expensive JavaScript work until running animations and touches finish, using runAfterInteractions.
jsonLd.name: InteractionManager

jsonLd.articleBody: InteractionManager is a core API for scheduling work after the current interactions are done. Its main method, runAfterInteractions, queues a callback that runs once any registered animations or touch handling have finished, so heavy work does not compete with them on the JavaScript thread. The classic use is a screen transition. The new screen mounts, its push animation plays, and only then does the expensive part render, such as a large list, a chart or a map. Without deferral, that work lands in the middle of the transition and causes visible jank. How it decides what counts as an “interaction”: JS-driven Animated animations register an interaction handle while they run. You can register your own with createInteractionHandle() and release it with clearInteractionHandle(). The common misconception is that it waits for everything visual to finish. Animations that run natively, via the native driver or Reanimated, do not necessarily register a handle, so the callback can fire immediately while the transition is still on screen. A handle that is created and never cleared does the opposite: deferred work never runs at all, which looks like a screen that never finishes loading. Treat it as a legacy tool. It predates the New Architecture and concurrent React, and recent guidance favours other approaches: React Navigation’s transition events, requestIdleCallback, startTransition for low-priority state updates, or simply making the expensive work cheaper. It still works, but check the React Native docs for its current status before building new code around it.
jsonLd.description: InteractionManager is a legacy React Native API that defers expensive JavaScript work until running animations and touches finish, using runAfterInteractions.
jsonLd.headline: What is InteractionManager in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/internal-testing-.title: Internal Testing Track in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The internal testing track is Google Play’s fastest release channel, delivering a build to up to 100 invited testers within minutes, ahead of the closed and open tracks.
og:description: The internal testing track is Google Play’s fastest release channel, delivering a build to up to 100 invited testers within minutes, ahead of the closed and open tracks.
og:title: Internal Testing Track in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The internal testing track is Google Play’s fastest release channel, delivering a build to up to 100 invited testers within minutes, ahead of the closed and open tracks.
jsonLd.name: Internal Testing Track

jsonLd.articleBody: Google Play distributes every release through a track, and the internal testing track is the first and fastest. A build uploaded there reaches up to 100 testers you name by email, usually within minutes. It plays the same role as internal testers in TestFlight. The full ladder in Google Play Console: Internal testing: up to 100 testers, minimal waiting, ideal for every merge to main. Closed testing: invite-only through email lists or Google Groups, with no small cap. You can run several closed tracks, for example one for QA and one for beta customers. Open testing: anyone can join from your store listing. Production: everyone, optionally through a staged rollout. A build moves up by being promoted from one track to the next, so the exact binary your testers approved is the one users get. How testers join: they open the track’s opt-in link while signed in to the same Google account the Play Store app uses, accept, then install from the store as normal. Most "I can’t see the update" reports come from testers using a different Google account, or from Play caching the listing for a while after the opt-in. The rule that trips up automated pipelines is version codes. Once a versionCode has been uploaded to any track it can never be uploaded again, even if that release was discarded. Increment it on every build; see app versioning. Two related features are easy to confuse: Internal app sharing lets you upload any build, even one with a reused version code, and share a link. It is for quick checks, not releases. The closed testing requirement for new personal accounts means a closed track, not the internal one, must run with enough testers before production access is granted.
jsonLd.description: The internal testing track is Google Play’s fastest release channel, delivering a build to up to 100 invited testers within minutes, ahead of the closed and open tracks.
jsonLd.headline: What is Internal Testing Track in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Internationalisation (i18n) is preparing a React Native app to support several languages and regions, and localisation (l10n) is adding the translations and formats.
og:description: Internationalisation (i18n) is preparing a React Native app to support several languages and regions, and localisation (l10n) is adding the translations and formats.
og:title: Internationalization in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Internationalisation (i18n) is preparing a React Native app to support several languages and regions, and localisation (l10n) is adding the translations and formats.
jsonLd.name: Internationalization

jsonLd.articleBody: Internationalisation (i18n) is the work of making a React Native app adaptable to any language and region: no hard-coded strings, dates, numbers or layout assumptions. Localisation (l10n) is the follow-up of supplying translations and regional formats for each market you ship to. React Native has no built-in translation system, so teams pick a library. Common choices are i18next with react-i18next, FormatJS (react-intl) and Lingui. To detect the user’s preferred languages and region, use expo-localization or react-native-localize. For formatting, the standard Intl API (Intl.NumberFormat, Intl.DateTimeFormat and others) is available in Hermes, although coverage of the newer Intl features can lag behind browsers, so check before relying on one. Mobile adds work that web i18n guides miss: Native strings. Permission prompts in Info.plist, the app name and notification text live outside JavaScript and must be localised natively, or through the locales field in Expo’s app config. Store listings in App Store Connect and Google Play are localised separately. Per-app language. iOS and recent Android versions let users pick a language for one app, so read the locale from the device instead of assuming the system language. Locale changes at runtime when the user switches settings while the app is in the background. The most common mistakes are building sentences by concatenation ("You have " + n + " messages"), which breaks word order and plurals in other languages, and designing layouts that only fit English. German and French text often runs noticeably longer, and Arabic or Hebrew need a right-to-left layout. Use message formats with placeholders and plural rules, and test with a long pseudo-locale early.
jsonLd.description: Internationalisation (i18n) is preparing a React Native app to support several languages and regions, and localisation (l10n) is adding the translations and formats.
jsonLd.headline: What is Internationalization in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/interop-layer.title: Interop Layer in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The interop layer lets native modules and view components written for the legacy architecture run unchanged inside a New Architecture React Native app.
og:description: The interop layer lets native modules and view components written for the legacy architecture run unchanged inside a New Architecture React Native app.
og:title: Interop Layer in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The interop layer lets native modules and view components written for the legacy architecture run unchanged inside a New Architecture React Native app.
jsonLd.name: Interop Layer

jsonLd.articleBody: The interop layer is compatibility code inside React Native that runs libraries built for the legacy architecture on top of the New Architecture. A native module written against the old bridge API, or a view component registered for the old Paper renderer, is wrapped so that TurboModules and Fabric can call it without the library author changing a line. It exists because the ecosystem could not migrate overnight. Thousands of packages expose native code, and many are maintained by one person or not at all. Without the interop layer, turning on the New Architecture would have required every dependency to ship a rewrite first. With it, apps could switch and migrate dependencies one at a time. It has been enabled automatically for both modules and components since the New Architecture became the default. What you should expect from it: Most legacy modules and components just work, including events and props. No New Architecture benefits for those libraries. A wrapped module does not get Codegen type checking, and a wrapped view does not take part in Fabric features the way a real Fabric Native Component does. Edge cases fail. Code that reaches into the bridge directly, relies on synchronous UIManager calls, or manipulates the native view hierarchy behind React’s back is the usual source of crashes, missing views or layout glitches. The common mistake is treating "it works through interop" as the end state. It is a transition aid, and React Native has been steadily removing legacy code paths. When you audit dependencies before an upgrade, prefer packages that implement the New Architecture natively — React Native Directory shows this for each library — and treat interop-only packages as candidates for replacement or a contribution upstream.
jsonLd.description: The interop layer lets native modules and view components written for the legacy architecture run unchanged inside a New Architecture React Native app.
jsonLd.headline: What is Interop Layer in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/ios-simulator.title: iOS Simulator in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The iOS Simulator is the Mac app bundled with Xcode that runs iPhone and iPad builds of your React Native app on your computer, without a physical device.
og:description: The iOS Simulator is the Mac app bundled with Xcode that runs iPhone and iPad builds of your React Native app on your computer, without a physical device.
og:title: iOS Simulator in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The iOS Simulator is the Mac app bundled with Xcode that runs iPhone and iPad builds of your React Native app on your computer, without a physical device.
jsonLd.name: iOS Simulator

jsonLd.articleBody: The iOS Simulator is a macOS app shipped with Xcode that runs iPhone, iPad and other Apple device builds on your Mac. It is where most React Native iOS development happens day to day, launched by npx expo run:ios or npx react-native run-ios. It is a simulator, not an emulator: it does not imitate iPhone hardware. Your app is compiled for the Mac’s own CPU against a simulator SDK and runs as a Mac process. That has practical consequences: It only exists on macOS. There is no official way to run it on Windows or Linux. Simulator builds cannot be installed on a phone, and device builds cannot run in the Simulator. A development build made for one will not work on the other. Performance is not representative. A fast Mac hides jank that a three-year-old iPhone will show, so profile on real hardware. localhost is your Mac, which is why the app reaches Metro with no extra setup, unlike the Android Emulator. Handy shortcuts: Cmd+D opens the Dev Menu, Cmd+R reloads, and Cmd+Shift+H goes to the home screen. The xcrun simctl command line tool can boot devices, open URLs to test deep links, grant permissions and send a fake push payload. The common misconception is that "it works in the Simulator" means it works on a device. Camera hardware, some sensors, real push delivery, Face ID behaviour, signing and entitlements, and memory limits all differ. Test anything touching those on a physical iPhone before release.
jsonLd.description: The iOS Simulator is the Mac app bundled with Xcode that runs iPhone and iPad builds of your React Native app on your computer, without a physical device.
jsonLd.headline: What is iOS Simulator in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/ipa.title: IPA in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: An IPA (.ipa) is the signed archive that packages an iOS app for distribution, the file you upload to App Store Connect or install on registered test devices.
og:description: An IPA (.ipa) is the signed archive that packages an iOS app for distribution, the file you upload to App Store Connect or install on registered test devices.
og:title: IPA in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An IPA (.ipa) is the signed archive that packages an iOS app for distribution, the file you upload to App Store Connect or install on registered test devices.
jsonLd.name: IPA

jsonLd.articleBody: An IPA is a ZIP file containing a Payload/ folder with your .app bundle inside: the compiled executable, Info.plist, assets, the embedded provisioning profile, the code signature and, for a React Native release build, main.jsbundle. It is the iOS counterpart of an Android APK, with one big difference: it only runs on devices its signature allows. In a bare React Native project you get one from Xcode by choosing Product → Archive, then distributing the archive, or from the command line with xcodebuild -exportArchive and an export options plist. EAS Build and fastlane run those same steps for you. During the archive, the "Bundle React Native code and images" build phase embeds the JavaScript, so the IPA does not need Metro. The export method decides who can install it: App Store Connect: uploaded for TestFlight and App Store release; it cannot be installed directly. Ad hoc: installs only on devices whose UDIDs are registered in the provisioning profile. Enterprise: for in-house distribution under the separate Apple Developer Enterprise Program. Development: for devices of team members, with debugging enabled. The misconception to drop: you cannot send an IPA to anyone and have them install it. Without their device in the profile, or distribution through Apple, iOS refuses it. That is code signing at work, not a broken file. The other gotcha is the simulator. The iOS Simulator cannot run an IPA at all; it needs a .app built for the simulator. A build meant for the simulator and one meant for devices are separate builds, which is why EAS build profiles have a simulator option.
jsonLd.description: An IPA (.ipa) is the signed archive that packages an iOS app for distribution, the file you upload to App Store Connect or install on registered test devices.
jsonLd.headline: What is IPA in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Jailbreak and root detection lets a React Native app check whether it runs on a modified iOS or Android device, where its security protections can be bypassed.
og:description: Jailbreak and root detection lets a React Native app check whether it runs on a modified iOS or Android device, where its security protections can be bypassed.
og:title: Jailbreak and Root Detection
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Jailbreak and root detection lets a React Native app check whether it runs on a modified iOS or Android device, where its security protections can be bypassed.
jsonLd.name: Jailbreak and Root Detection

jsonLd.articleBody: Jailbreak and root detection is a set of runtime checks that try to tell whether the device has been modified to give the user, or malware, full system access. A jailbroken iPhone or rooted Android phone lifts the sandbox your app relies on: other code can read your app's files, hook its functions and change its behaviour while it runs. Apps that handle money, health data or paid content use detection to reduce risk, typically by warning the user, disabling sensitive features or reporting the device to the backend. Classic local checks look for traces of modification: files and apps that only exist on modified devices, writable system paths, or a debugger attached. Community React Native libraries bundle these checks behind a simple JavaScript call. The essential gotcha is that local checks can always be bypassed. The user controls the device, so tools such as Frida or root-hiding modules can make any check return "clean". A boolean computed on the phone and then trusted by your app is easy to defeat. The stronger approach is attestation, where the platform vouches for the device and your server verifies it: Android: the Play Integrity API, which replaced SafetyNet Attestation. iOS: App Attest from the DeviceCheck framework. The app requests a signed token and sends it to your backend, which validates it before granting access. Because the decision is made on the server, tampering with the app alone is not enough. Also weigh the cost. Blocking every rooted device locks out legitimate users such as developers and enthusiasts, and false positives generate support tickets. Match the response to the risk, and combine detection with secure storage, SSL pinning and server-side validation.
jsonLd.description: Jailbreak and root detection lets a React Native app check whether it runs on a modified iOS or Android device, where its security protections can be bypassed.
jsonLd.headline: What is Jailbreak and Root Detection in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/jank.title: Jank in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Jank is visible stutter in a React Native app, caused when the UI or JavaScript thread misses its frame deadline and frames are dropped or delivered late.
og:description: Jank is visible stutter in a React Native app, caused when the UI or JavaScript thread misses its frame deadline and frames are dropped or delivered late.
og:title: Jank in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Jank is visible stutter in a React Native app, caused when the UI or JavaScript thread misses its frame deadline and frames are dropped or delivered late.
jsonLd.name: Jank

jsonLd.articleBody: Jank is the stutter a user sees when an app fails to produce a frame in time. Instead of smooth motion, a scroll or animation jumps, hitches or freezes for a moment because one or more frames were dropped. In React Native, jank has two different sources and the fix depends on which one you have: UI thread jank. Native work takes too long: laying out a huge view tree, decoding a large image, or mounting hundreds of views at once. Scrolling itself stutters. JavaScript thread jank. The JS thread is busy with a large re-render, a heavy JSON parse or a synchronous loop. Native scrolling may stay smooth, but taps respond late, lists show blank cells and JS-driven animations pause. A classic example is an animation started with the Animated API without the native driver: it runs on the JS thread, so the moment a screen fetches data and re-renders, the animation hitches. Typical fixes: Virtualise long lists with FlashList or a well-tuned FlatList instead of mapping over arrays in a ScrollView. Move animation and gesture work to the UI thread. Defer expensive work until after a navigation transition finishes. Resize images to the size they are displayed at. The usual mistake is guessing. Developers often add useMemo everywhere when the real cause is one oversized image or an unvirtualised list. Measure first with a profiler, in a release build, on a slow Android device, where jank shows up long before it does on a flagship phone.
jsonLd.description: Jank is visible stutter in a React Native app, caused when the UI or JavaScript thread misses its frame deadline and frames are dropped or delivered late.
jsonLd.headline: What is Jank in React Native?

jsonLd.description: The JavaScript bundle is the single file Metro produces from your source code. It ships inside the app binary and is what the JavaScript engine actually executes.

jsonLd.articleBody: The JavaScript bundle is the compiled output of your entire application's JavaScript — your code plus every npm dependency — collapsed by Metro into one file. Where it lives depends on the build: Development — served over HTTP by the Metro dev server and fetched on launch, which is why the app needs Metro running. Release — written into the binary as main.jsbundle (iOS) or index.android.bundle (Android), and precompiled to Hermes bytecode. Two consequences worth internalising as a newcomer. Bundle size affects startup, not download size, in the way you might expect — the bundle is a small fraction of an app binary, but everything in it is parsed or loaded at launch, so an unused 2MB dependency still costs you. And the JS/native split is exactly this file. Changing bundle contents can ship as an over-the-air update; changing anything outside it requires a new store build.

author: David Leuliette
description: The JavaScript runtime is the engine that executes your app’s JavaScript on the device. React Native ships Hermes by default, with JavaScriptCore as the alternative.
og:description: The JavaScript runtime is the engine that executes your app’s JavaScript on the device. React Native ships Hermes by default, with JavaScriptCore as the alternative.
og:title: JavaScript Runtime in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The JavaScript runtime is the engine that executes your app’s JavaScript on the device. React Native ships Hermes by default, with JavaScriptCore as the alternative.
jsonLd.name: JavaScript Runtime

jsonLd.articleBody: The JavaScript runtime is the engine embedded in your app that actually runs your code on the user's phone. Unlike a web app there is no browser here — React Native bundles an engine into the binary. Two engines matter: Hermes — built by Meta specifically for React Native and the default since React Native 0.70. It compiles JavaScript to bytecode ahead of time, which cuts start-up time and memory use on low-end devices. JavaScriptCore (JSC) — Apple's engine, the historical default and still selectable. The runtime executes the JavaScript bundle that Metro produced, on the JavaScript thread. Two consequences newcomers hit. First, Node.js APIs do not exist here — no fs, no Buffer unless polyfilled. Second, engine differences are real: a regex or Intl feature that works in Chrome may be missing in Hermes, which is why debugging in a browser can hide bugs that only appear on device.

author: David Leuliette
description: The JavaScript thread is where your React components, business logic and event handlers run. Blocking it makes the app feel frozen even though native rendering continues.
og:description: The JavaScript thread is where your React components, business logic and event handlers run. Blocking it makes the app feel frozen even though native rendering continues.
og:title: JavaScript Thread in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The JavaScript thread is where your React components, business logic and event handlers run. Blocking it makes the app feel frozen even though native rendering continues.
jsonLd.name: JavaScript Thread

jsonLd.articleBody: The JavaScript thread is the single thread where your application code executes: component renders, hooks, event handlers, network callbacks, and state updates all queue here. It is separate from the UI thread, which draws the actual pixels. That separation is why a React Native app can stay visually responsive — a scroll can keep moving natively — while your JavaScript is stuck. Because it is single-threaded, anything expensive blocks everything else: Parsing a large JSON payload A heavy map/filter over thousands of records on every render Synchronous work inside a useEffect that runs on mount Symptoms are a button that responds a second late, or a setState-driven animation that stutters. The fixes are to move work off the render path (useMemo, pagination, background native modules) or to move animation off this thread entirely with worklets. Profiling the JS thread is the first step in almost any React Native performance investigation.

/react-native-glossary/javascriptcore.title: JavaScriptCore in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: JavaScriptCore is Apple’s JavaScript engine from Safari. It was React Native’s original engine and is now an opt-in alternative to Hermes, maintained by the community.
og:description: JavaScriptCore is Apple’s JavaScript engine from Safari. It was React Native’s original engine and is now an opt-in alternative to Hermes, maintained by the community.
og:title: JavaScriptCore in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: JavaScriptCore is Apple’s JavaScript engine from Safari. It was React Native’s original engine and is now an opt-in alternative to Hermes, maintained by the community.
jsonLd.name: JavaScriptCore

jsonLd.articleBody: JavaScriptCore (JSC) is the JavaScript engine Apple builds for Safari and WebKit. React Native used it to run app code from the very beginning, on both platforms, until Hermes replaced it as the default. The two platforms got it differently: On iOS JSC is part of the operating system, so React Native could use the system copy at no extra size cost. The catch is that Apple does not allow third-party apps to use JIT compilation there, so JSC runs in interpreter mode inside a React Native app, unlike in Safari. On Android there is no system JSC, so React Native bundled its own build, which added several megabytes to every APK and was often years behind WebKit. Hermes won on the metrics that matter for mobile apps: start-up time through precompiled bytecode, lower memory use, smaller downloads on Android, and a debugger built for React Native. Meta also stopped maintaining JSC support inside the core repository. JSC now lives in a community package, @react-native-community/javascriptcore, for apps that opt out of Hermes. Why some teams still use it: They depend on a library or an Intl and regular expression behaviour that matches Safari more closely. They measured a CPU-heavy workload that runs faster on JSC in their case. The common misconception is that switching engines is a quick fix. Behaviour differs at the edges — date parsing, Intl support, error messages, stack trace format — so an app tested only on Hermes can break on JSC and vice versa. Debugging tools and performance tooling also centre on Hermes now. Treat moving to JSC as a deliberate decision you measure and test on devices, not a toggle to flip when a bug appears. Because React Native talks to the engine through JSI, your JavaScript code does not change between engines; only the runtime underneath does.
jsonLd.description: JavaScriptCore is Apple’s JavaScript engine from Safari. It was React Native’s original engine and is now an opt-in alternative to Hermes, maintained by the community.
jsonLd.headline: What is JavaScriptCore in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Jest is the JavaScript test runner most React Native projects use for unit and component tests. It runs tests in Node.js, not on a device, with mocks and snapshots.
og:description: Jest is the JavaScript test runner most React Native projects use for unit and component tests. It runs tests in Node.js, not on a device, with mocks and snapshots.
og:title: Jest in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Jest is the JavaScript test runner most React Native projects use for unit and component tests. It runs tests in Node.js, not on a device, with mocks and snapshots.
jsonLd.name: Jest

jsonLd.articleBody: Jest is a JavaScript testing framework: it finds your test files, runs them, and reports which assertions passed or failed. It is the default test runner in new React Native projects, and Expo projects use it through the jest-expo preset. A Jest test is plain JavaScript or TypeScript: Jest bundles everything a test suite needs in one tool: the runner, the expect assertion library, mocking with jest.fn() and jest.mock(), fake timers, snapshots and coverage reports. Watch mode re-runs only the tests affected by the files you change. The most important thing to understand is where Jest runs: in Node.js on your computer, not on a phone. There is no iOS or Android, no native views and no native modules. The react-native preset swaps core components for JavaScript stand-ins so components can render in a test, but anything that calls native code (camera, storage, a payments SDK) must be mocked. When a test fails with "native module cannot be null" or a similar error, a missing mock is almost always the cause. That also defines Jest's limits. It is excellent for business logic, hooks and component behaviour, which is where unit testing pays off most. It cannot tell you whether a screen looks right, scrolls smoothly or works on a real device; that is the job of end-to-end tools. Most teams pair Jest with React Native Testing Library to render components and interact with them the way a user would.

/react-native-glossary/jni.title: JNI in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: JNI (Java Native Interface) is the JVM bridge between Java or Kotlin and C++ code, which React Native’s Android side uses to reach Hermes, JSI and the Fabric renderer.
og:description: JNI (Java Native Interface) is the JVM bridge between Java or Kotlin and C++ code, which React Native’s Android side uses to reach Hermes, JSI and the Fabric renderer.
og:title: JNI in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: JNI (Java Native Interface) is the JVM bridge between Java or Kotlin and C++ code, which React Native’s Android side uses to reach Hermes, JSI and the Fabric renderer.
jsonLd.name: JNI

jsonLd.articleBody: JNI, the Java Native Interface, is the standard mechanism that lets code running on the Java Virtual Machine call into native C or C++ libraries, and lets C++ call back into Java or Kotlin. On Android, React Native relies on it constantly, because its engine room is C++. Here is why it matters. Hermes, JSI, the Fabric renderer and the TurboModule infrastructure are all C++, shared between iOS and Android. On iOS, Objective-C++ talks to C++ directly. On Android, the app’s Java and Kotlin layer has to cross JNI to reach that shared core, and every native view update and module call that involves C++ passes through it. Raw JNI is verbose and easy to get wrong: references must be managed manually, type signatures are written as strings, and mistakes crash the process instead of throwing a readable exception. Meta wrote fbjni, a C++ helper library, to make this safer, and React Native uses it internally. Most React Native developers never write JNI themselves: Kotlin or Java modules generated from Codegen specs are wired to C++ for you. A C++ TurboModule lets you write shared logic once in C++ and skip platform glue entirely. Libraries that ship C++ code handle JNI in their own Android build. Where it does surface is in errors. java.lang.UnsatisfiedLinkError means a native .so library the app expected is missing or was built for a different CPU architecture — often after excluding architectures to speed up builds, or when a library’s native code was not packaged. Native crashes from JNI code appear in Logcat as a SIGSEGV with a native backtrace rather than a JavaScript error, so you need symbol files to read them. If you do write JNI by hand, keep the surface small and pass simple types across it.
jsonLd.description: JNI (Java Native Interface) is the JVM bridge between Java or Kotlin and C++ code, which React Native’s Android side uses to reach Hermes, JSI and the Fabric renderer.
jsonLd.headline: What is JNI in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/jsi.title: JSI in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: JSI (JavaScript Interface) is a lightweight C++ API that lets JavaScript hold direct references to native objects and call them synchronously, replacing the bridge.
og:description: JSI (JavaScript Interface) is a lightweight C++ API that lets JavaScript hold direct references to native objects and call them synchronously, replacing the bridge.
og:title: JSI in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: JSI (JavaScript Interface) is a lightweight C++ API that lets JavaScript hold direct references to native objects and call them synchronously, replacing the bridge.
jsonLd.name: JSI

jsonLd.articleBody: JSI — the JavaScript Interface — is a small C++ API that lets the JavaScript engine and native code talk to each other directly. It is the foundation the whole New Architecture is built on. Under the legacy bridge, every call was converted to a JSON string, queued, and delivered asynchronously. With JSI, native code can expose a HostObject that JavaScript holds a real reference to and invokes like an ordinary object — no serialisation, no queue, and a synchronous return value when one is wanted. Three things this unlocks: TurboModules — native modules loaded lazily and called directly. Fabric — a renderer that can read layout synchronously. Engine independence — JSI is an abstraction over the engine, so React Native can run on Hermes or JavaScriptCore behind the same interface. Most app developers never write JSI by hand; they benefit from libraries built on it. See the New Architecture docs.
jsonLd.description: JSI (JavaScript Interface) is a lightweight C++ API that lets JavaScript hold direct references to native objects and call them synchronously, replacing the bridge.
jsonLd.headline: What is JSI in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that lets you write UI markup directly inside component code. React Native compiles it to plain function calls.
og:description: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that lets you write UI markup directly inside component code. React Native compiles it to plain function calls.
og:title: JSX in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that lets you write UI markup directly inside component code. React Native compiles it to plain function calls.
jsonLd.name: JSX

jsonLd.articleBody: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that lets you describe a screen using tag syntax inside your component code. It looks like HTML, but it is neither HTML nor a template language — a compiler rewrites every tag into a plain function call that returns a React element. In React Native the tags are not DOM tags. <View> and <Text> are core components that map to real native views, so <View><Text>Hi</Text></View> becomes a native UIView on iOS and a ViewGroup on Android. Three rules trip up newcomers: Every expression goes in braces: <Text>{user.name}</Text>. A component returns one root element — wrap siblings in a <View> or a fragment (<>…</>). Attributes use camelCase, and styles are objects, not strings: style={{ marginTop: 8 }}. You can write React Native without JSX by calling React.createElement yourself, but effectively nobody does.

author: David Leuliette
description: KeyboardAvoidingView is a React Native core component that moves or shrinks its content when the software keyboard opens, so inputs and buttons stay visible.
og:description: KeyboardAvoidingView is a React Native core component that moves or shrinks its content when the software keyboard opens, so inputs and buttons stay visible.
og:title: KeyboardAvoidingView in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: KeyboardAvoidingView is a React Native core component that moves or shrinks its content when the software keyboard opens, so inputs and buttons stay visible.
jsonLd.name: KeyboardAvoidingView

jsonLd.articleBody: KeyboardAvoidingView is a core component that adjusts its own height, padding or position when the on-screen keyboard appears. Without it, a TextInput near the bottom of the screen ends up hidden behind the keyboard. The behavior prop picks the strategy: padding adds bottom padding, height shrinks the view, position moves it. Which one works depends on the layout and platform, which is why the snippet above uses platform-specific code. keyboardVerticalOffset compensates for anything above the view, such as a navigation header; leaving it at zero under a header is the usual cause of the input stopping short of the keyboard. The two platforms start from different places. iOS never resizes your app for the keyboard, so you always need something. On Android, the window’s windowSoftInputMode (often adjustResize) traditionally resized the app for you, and adding a KeyboardAvoidingView on top could double the adjustment. Edge-to-edge display on recent Android versions changes that picture, so test on a current device rather than relying on old advice. The component sits beside the imperative Keyboard API: Keyboard.dismiss() closes the keyboard, and Keyboard.addListener('keyboardDidShow', …) reports its height. The keyboardWill… events fire on iOS only. For chat screens, forms in a ScrollView, and anything that must follow the keyboard frame by frame, many teams use the community library react-native-keyboard-controller, which tracks the keyboard animation natively and behaves consistently on both platforms.

author: David Leuliette
description: A key is a stable identifier you give each item in a rendered list so React can tell which item is which across renders instead of re-creating them all.
og:description: A key is a stable identifier you give each item in a rendered list so React can tell which item is which across renders instead of re-creating them all.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A key is a stable identifier you give each item in a rendered list so React can tell which item is which across renders instead of re-creating them all.
jsonLd.name: Keys

jsonLd.articleBody: A key is a string you attach to each element in a list so React can match items between renders. Without keys React compares by position, so inserting one row at the top makes it think every row changed. Rules that matter in practice: Use a value that is stable and unique among siblings — a database id, not a random number. Do not use the array index when the list can reorder, filter, or receive inserts. Index keys are the usual cause of "the wrong row kept its text input value". Keys only need to be unique within one list, not app-wide. In FlatList the same job is done by the keyExtractor prop rather than a key on the element. Getting keys wrong shows up as lost scroll position, wrong animations, and state landing on the wrong row. See rendering lists.

/react-native-glossary/kotlin.title: Kotlin in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Kotlin is Google’s preferred language for Android; React Native’s Android template is written in it, and it is the usual choice for writing Android native modules.
og:description: Kotlin is Google’s preferred language for Android; React Native’s Android template is written in it, and it is the usual choice for writing Android native modules.
og:title: Kotlin in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Kotlin is Google’s preferred language for Android; React Native’s Android template is written in it, and it is the usual choice for writing Android native modules.
jsonLd.name: Kotlin

jsonLd.articleBody: Kotlin is a statically typed language from JetBrains that runs on the Java Virtual Machine and is Google’s preferred language for Android. In a React Native project it is what MainActivity.kt and MainApplication.kt are written in, and what you use to write the Android half of a native module. Kotlin interoperates fully with Java, so React Native’s Java code, older libraries and Android’s own Java APIs can all be called from it. Practically, React Native developers meet it when they: Write an Android module with the Expo Modules API, whose Android side is a Kotlin DSL. Implement a TurboModule’s Android code from a Codegen-generated spec. Edit MainApplication.kt to register a package or initialise an SDK at startup. Read a library’s Android source to understand a crash. That snippet shows the classic module style; New Architecture modules extend a generated spec class instead, but the Kotlin is similar. A common misconception is that Kotlin talks to JavaScript directly. It does not: React Native’s core is C++, and Kotlin code reaches it through JNI, which React Native wraps so module authors rarely see it. The usual gotcha is versions. The Kotlin compiler version is set in the Gradle build, and a library compiled with a newer Kotlin than your project can fail with metadata or “incompatible version” errors. Upgrade through your React Native or Expo version rather than bumping Kotlin alone. Don’t confuse Kotlin with Kotlin Multiplatform, which shares Kotlin business logic across iOS and Android and is an alternative approach to cross-platform apps.

jsonLd.headline: What is Kotlin in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/kotlin-multiplatf.title: Kotlin Multiplatform in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) is JetBrains’ technology for sharing Kotlin code across Android, iOS and other targets, usually business logic, while keeping native UIs.
og:description: Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) is JetBrains’ technology for sharing Kotlin code across Android, iOS and other targets, usually business logic, while keeping native UIs.
og:title: Kotlin Multiplatform in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) is JetBrains’ technology for sharing Kotlin code across Android, iOS and other targets, usually business logic, while keeping native UIs.
jsonLd.name: Kotlin Multiplatform

jsonLd.articleBody: Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) is a JetBrains technology for compiling the same Kotlin code to several targets: the JVM for Android, native binaries for iOS, plus desktop and the web. Its most common use is sharing networking, data and business logic while each platform keeps its own native UI. It approaches cross-platform from the opposite side to React Native. React Native shares the UI layer and most logic in JavaScript; KMP typically shares the logic layer and leaves the UI to SwiftUI on iOS and Jetpack Compose on Android. On iOS, shared Kotlin is compiled to a native framework that Swift code calls like any other library. Compose Multiplatform is a related JetBrains framework that extends Jetpack Compose so the UI can be shared too, including on iOS. With it, KMP becomes closer to Flutter or React Native in scope, drawing its own UI rather than using native views on iOS. Points worth knowing when comparing it with React Native: Adoption path. KMP is easy to add gradually to existing native apps, one shared module at a time, which suits teams with strong Android and iOS developers. Skills. It favours Kotlin and Android experience; React Native favours JavaScript, TypeScript and React. Tooling. iOS developers still work in Xcode, while shared code is written in Android Studio or IntelliJ IDEA. Ecosystem. Its library ecosystem is younger than npm’s React Native packages but growing, and Google supports KMP for sharing logic in Android apps. A common misconception is that KMP and React Native are mutually exclusive. They can coexist: a native or brownfield app can share logic through KMP and still host React Native screens.

/react-native-glossary/layout-animations.title: Layout Animations in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Layout animations are Reanimated’s entering, exiting and layout props, which animate a component automatically when it mounts, unmounts or changes position in the layout.
og:description: Layout animations are Reanimated’s entering, exiting and layout props, which animate a component automatically when it mounts, unmounts or changes position in the layout.
og:title: Layout Animations in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Layout animations are Reanimated’s entering, exiting and layout props, which animate a component automatically when it mounts, unmounts or changes position in the layout.
jsonLd.name: Layout Animations

jsonLd.articleBody: Layout animations are a Reanimated feature that animates components through structural changes you could not otherwise animate: appearing, disappearing, and moving because something around them changed. You declare them as props on an animated component and Reanimated handles the rest. entering runs when the component mounts. exiting runs when it unmounts. Reanimated keeps the native view on screen until the animation finishes, which you cannot do with ordinary React rendering. layout runs when the component’s size or position changes, such as list items sliding up after one is deleted. Reanimated ships a large set of presets (fades, slides, zooms, bounces, flips) with chainable modifiers like .duration(), .delay() and .springify(), and you can write custom ones. This is different from React Native’s core LayoutAnimation API, which animates the next layout change for the whole tree at once and offers little control. Reanimated’s version is per component and supports exit animations. Gotchas to expect: Exiting needs a surviving parent. If the parent unmounts too, for example when the whole screen is popped, the child’s exit animation never plays. Entering runs on first mount. A list that fades in every row when the screen opens may not be what you want. Wrap it in LayoutAnimationConfig with skipEntering to animate only rows added later. Lists need the list-level prop. In an Animated.FlatList, item reordering is animated with itemLayoutAnimation rather than a layout prop on each row, because rows are wrapped in cells you do not render. See FlatList. Keys matter. Entering and exiting are tied to component identity, so unstable keys make every item exit and re-enter on each update.

author: David Leuliette
description: LayoutAnimation is a React Native API that animates every layout change in the next render automatically, with one line of code and no animated values to manage.
og:description: LayoutAnimation is a React Native API that animates every layout change in the next render automatically, with one line of code and no animated values to manage.
og:title: LayoutAnimation in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: LayoutAnimation is a React Native API that animates every layout change in the next render automatically, with one line of code and no animated values to manage.
jsonLd.name: LayoutAnimation

jsonLd.articleBody: LayoutAnimation is a core API that animates the next layout update across the whole app. You call it just before a state change, and every view that moves, resizes, appears or disappears in the resulting commit animates to its new position instead of jumping. There are three presets, easeInEaseOut, linear and spring, or you can pass your own config with a duration and separate create, update and delete settings. The animation runs natively, so it is smooth even while JavaScript is busy. Its appeal is the effort-to-result ratio: an accordion, a list item being removed, or a card growing to show more detail, with no animated components, shared values or measured heights. Its weakness is the same feature: it is global and one-shot. It animates everything that changes in that commit, including unrelated views that happen to re-render at the same moment, which can produce odd movement elsewhere on screen. It cannot be interrupted, reversed mid-way, or tied to a gesture. It applies to one commit only, so state changes that land in a later render jump without animating. Older tutorials say Android needs UIManager.setLayoutAnimationEnabledExperimental(true). That flag mattered under the legacy architecture; with the New Architecture, the default since React Native 0.76, it does nothing and can be removed. For anything that needs per-component control, use the entering, exiting and layout transitions from Reanimated, covered under layout animations. Keep LayoutAnimation for quick, self-contained transitions where “animate whatever changed” is exactly what you want.

/react-native-glossary/lazy-loading.title: Lazy Loading in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Lazy loading delays loading or running code until it is needed. In React Native that mostly means inline requires and React.lazy, which defer module evaluation.
og:description: Lazy loading delays loading or running code until it is needed. In React Native that mostly means inline requires and React.lazy, which defer module evaluation.
og:title: Lazy Loading in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Lazy loading delays loading or running code until it is needed. In React Native that mostly means inline requires and React.lazy, which defer module evaluation.
jsonLd.name: Lazy Loading

jsonLd.articleBody: Lazy loading means postponing work until the moment it is needed instead of doing it all at launch. In a React Native app, the work in question is usually running JavaScript modules: their top-level code, their imports and their side effects. This differs from the web in one important way. A browser can download extra chunks on demand (code splitting). A standard React Native release ships one JavaScript bundle inside the app, so all the code is already on the device. What you can defer is evaluation, and that alone can noticeably improve startup time. There are two main tools: Inline requires. A Metro transform that rewrites top-level imports into require() calls placed where the value is first used, so a module only runs when your code actually touches it. React.lazy. Wraps a dynamic import() so a component, usually a whole screen, is evaluated the first time it renders, with Suspense showing a fallback meanwhile. The gotcha with inline requires is code that depends on import side effects, such as a polyfill or a module that registers itself globally. Once imports are deferred, that side effect may run later than expected or not at all. Import such modules explicitly at the top of your entry file. Do not lazy-load the first screen a user sees, or you simply move the delay to behind a spinner. Defer settings screens, rarely used flows and heavy SDKs instead.

description: The New Architecture replaces the asynchronous bridge with JSI, Fabric and TurboModules. It has been the default since React Native 0.76.

jsonLd.name: Legacy vs New Architecture

jsonLd.articleBody: React Native has two architectures. The legacy architecture (often called Paper) sent every instruction between JavaScript and native code as serialised JSON over an asynchronous bridge. The New Architecture removes that bridge and lets the two sides call each other directly through JSI. Legacy (Paper) New Architecture JS ↔ native Async JSON bridge JSI, direct and synchronous Renderer Paper Fabric Native modules Loaded eagerly at startup TurboModules, loaded on demand Type safety Hand-written, unchecked Codegen from TypeScript specs Layout Yoga Yoga, integrated in C++ The New Architecture became the default in React Native 0.76 (October 2024), and 0.80 began winding down legacy support. New apps get it automatically; older apps migrate by upgrading and checking that each native dependency has a New Architecture build. For newcomers the practical takeaway is that tutorials written before late 2024 may describe bridge behaviour that no longer applies.

author: David Leuliette
description: Linking is the React Native API for opening URLs in other apps, such as the browser, phone or maps, and for receiving the URLs that open your own app via deep links.
og:description: Linking is the React Native API for opening URLs in other apps, such as the browser, phone or maps, and for receiving the URLs that open your own app via deep links.
og:title: Linking API in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Linking is the React Native API for opening URLs in other apps, such as the browser, phone or maps, and for receiving the URLs that open your own app via deep links.
jsonLd.name: Linking API

jsonLd.articleBody: Linking is the core API that connects your app to URLs in both directions. Outgoing, it hands a URL to the operating system so the right app opens: https: in the browser, tel: in the dialler, mailto: in mail, or another app’s custom scheme. Incoming, it tells you which URL launched or resumed your app, the raw material of deep linking. Other useful methods are Linking.openSettings(), which jumps to your app’s page in system Settings (the standard way to recover from a denied permission), and Linking.sendIntent() for Android intents. The classic gotcha is canOpenURL. It returns false for other apps’ schemes unless you declare them first: in LSApplicationQueriesSchemes in Info.plist on iOS, and in a <queries> element in AndroidManifest.xml on Android 11 and later. Many apps skip canOpenURL and simply call openURL inside a try/catch, since openURL rejects when nothing can handle the URL. Incoming links have two paths that must both work: getInitialURL() for a cold start and the url event while the app is running. Handling only one is why “the link works only when the app is already open” is such a common bug report. Routers such as React Navigation and Expo Router build on Linking to map URLs to screens automatically, so in most apps you configure linking rather than calling these methods by hand. Expo also offers expo-linking, which adds helpers like createURL for building links that work in development and production. Verified https links are covered separately under universal links and Android App Links.

author: David Leuliette
description: LogBox is React Native’s in-app overlay for development builds that shows errors full screen and warnings as dismissible notifications, with readable stack traces.
og:description: LogBox is React Native’s in-app overlay for development builds that shows errors full screen and warnings as dismissible notifications, with readable stack traces.
og:title: LogBox in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: LogBox is React Native’s in-app overlay for development builds that shows errors full screen and warnings as dismissible notifications, with readable stack traces.
jsonLd.name: LogBox

jsonLd.articleBody: LogBox is the overlay React Native draws on top of your app in development builds to surface errors and warnings. It replaced the older "red box" and "yellow box" screens in React Native 0.63, though many developers still use those names. It shows three kinds of message: Errors, such as an exception during render, open full screen with a symbolicated stack trace and the component stack. Warnings, such as a deprecated API or a missing key, appear as a small notification at the bottom that you can tap to expand. Syntax errors from Metro open full screen and clear automatically once you fix the file and Fast Refresh reloads. LogBox matters because it puts the cause of a problem in front of you in the app, collapsing React Native internals so the frames from your own code stand out. You can silence noise from libraries you do not control: Patterns match by substring or regular expression. LogBox.ignoreAllLogs() hides everything, which is useful for demo recordings and dangerous anywhere else. The common misconceptions: Ignoring a warning does not fix it. It only hides the overlay; the message still reaches the console and React Native DevTools. Deprecation warnings ignored today become crashes after the next upgrade. LogBox does not exist in release builds. An error that shows a dismissible overlay in development will close the app in production unless an error boundary catches it. Dismissing the red screen and carrying on hides how users will experience the bug.
