author: David Leuliette
description: Lottie is a format for vector animations exported from After Effects as JSON; lottie-react-native plays them in React Native apps using the native Lottie players.
og:description: Lottie is a format for vector animations exported from After Effects as JSON; lottie-react-native plays them in React Native apps using the native Lottie players.
og:title: Lottie in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Lottie is a format for vector animations exported from After Effects as JSON; lottie-react-native plays them in React Native apps using the native Lottie players.
jsonLd.name: Lottie

jsonLd.articleBody: Lottie is an animation format created at Airbnb: a designer builds an animation in Adobe After Effects, exports it as JSON with the Bodymovin plugin (or as a compressed .lottie file), and the app plays it back as resolution-independent vectors. lottie-react-native renders these in React Native by wrapping the official native players on iOS and Android. Lottie is the right tool for illustrative motion that a designer owns: onboarding illustrations, empty states, success checkmarks, loading characters. The animation is authored once and runs identically on both platforms, and replacing the file changes the animation without a developer touching code. You can control playback through a ref (play, pause, reset) or by passing a progress value, which lets you scrub the animation from a gesture or scroll position. Where it fits against other tools: interactive, state-driven UI motion (a button press, a sheet sliding up) belongs in Reanimated, because it responds to input and data. Lottie plays pre-authored timelines. Custom drawn graphics that react to data are better in Skia. Gotchas worth knowing: Not every After Effects feature is supported. Expressions, some effects and certain masks or blend modes render differently or not at all. Designers should check the Lottie feature support list and preview on real devices, not only in a web preview. File size. A complex animation can be hundreds of kilobytes of JSON, and embedded raster images inflate it further. Keep image layers out of the export, and prefer .lottie files, which are compressed. Android rendering cost. Very complex animations can drop frames on low-end Android devices; test there, and simplify layers if needed. See the lottie-react-native repository.

author: David Leuliette
description: Maestro is a mobile end-to-end testing tool where tests are short YAML flows that tap, type and assert on a running app, with no changes needed inside the app.
og:description: Maestro is a mobile end-to-end testing tool where tests are short YAML flows that tap, type and assert on a running app, with no changes needed inside the app.
og:title: Maestro in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Maestro is a mobile end-to-end testing tool where tests are short YAML flows that tap, type and assert on a running app, with no changes needed inside the app.
jsonLd.name: Maestro

jsonLd.articleBody: Maestro is an end-to-end testing framework for mobile apps in which each test is a flow written in YAML. It drives an installed app on a simulator, emulator or device from the outside, much as a user would. Run it with maestro test flow.yaml. Maestro also offers an interactive Studio for inspecting the screen and building flows. Why React Native teams adopt it: No app integration. Maestro is black-box: it works with any build, so there is no test library to link and no special test build. Built-in tolerance for flakiness. Commands retry and wait for elements to appear rather than failing immediately. Readable tests. Product people and QA can read, and often write, flows. Framework-agnostic. The same tool tests React Native, native and Flutter apps. Maestro finds elements by visible text, accessibility labels or testID. Text matching is convenient but brittle: a copy change or switching the device language breaks the flow. For anything beyond a quick smoke test, give key elements a testID. The trade-off against Detox is control. Maestro waits by observing the screen, not by knowing what the JavaScript thread is doing, and logic beyond YAML (loops, conditions, API calls to seed data) relies on its JavaScript scripting support rather than a full test framework. It runs well in CI, including in EAS Workflows, and is often the quickest way to get a first set of critical-path tests running.

/react-native-glossary/memoization.title: Memoization in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Memoization caches the result of a computation and reuses it while its inputs stay the same. In React Native it is used to skip wasted renders and repeated work.
og:description: Memoization caches the result of a computation and reuses it while its inputs stay the same. In React Native it is used to skip wasted renders and repeated work.
og:title: Memoization in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Memoization caches the result of a computation and reuses it while its inputs stay the same. In React Native it is used to skip wasted renders and repeated work.
jsonLd.name: Memoization

jsonLd.articleBody: Memoization is a caching technique: store the result of a function for a given set of inputs, and return the stored result instead of recomputing when the same inputs come back. In React Native apps it is the main tool for avoiding wasted re-renders and repeated expensive calculations. React gives you three forms of it: React.memo skips re-rendering a component when its props are shallowly equal to last time. useMemo caches a computed value, such as a filtered and sorted list. useCallback caches a function so its identity stays stable between renders. They work together. React.memo on a list row is useless if the parent passes a new inline function or object on every render, because shallow comparison sees a different reference each time: The misconception is that memoising everything makes an app faster. Every memo has a cost: storing values, comparing dependencies, and more code to read. For cheap components and trivial calculations the comparison can cost as much as the render it saves. Memoise where a profiler shows real waste, typically list items, heavy charts and context values. The React Compiler changes the picture: it inserts this memoisation automatically at build time. In a codebase using it, manual useMemo and useCallback become mostly unnecessary.

/react-native-glossary/memory-leak.title: Memory Leak in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A memory leak is memory a React Native app keeps holding after it is no longer needed, so usage grows until the app slows down or the OS kills it.
og:description: A memory leak is memory a React Native app keeps holding after it is no longer needed, so usage grows until the app slows down or the OS kills it.
og:title: Memory Leak in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A memory leak is memory a React Native app keeps holding after it is no longer needed, so usage grows until the app slows down or the OS kills it.
jsonLd.name: Memory Leak

jsonLd.articleBody: A memory leak is memory your app allocated and never releases, even though nothing will use it again. Each leak may be small, but repeated over many screen visits it adds up until the app becomes sluggish or the operating system terminates it for using too much memory. JavaScript has garbage collection, which surprises people who assume leaks are impossible. The collector only frees objects that are unreachable, so anything still referenced stays alive. The most common React Native leaks are references you forgot to remove: Event listeners and subscriptions (AppState, Keyboard, a WebSocket, a store) added in a useEffect without a cleanup function. setInterval timers that keep running, and keep their closures alive, after a screen unmounts. Module-level caches or arrays that only ever grow. Screens kept mounted in a navigation stack that keeps getting deeper instead of going back. Leaks can also be native. Large decoded images are the classic case: a bitmap held by the native side can be many megabytes even when the file was small, which is why long image grids crash on low-memory Android phones. Native modules that hold strong references to callbacks can leak too. To find a leak, repeat one action many times (open and close a screen twenty times) and watch whether memory returns to its baseline. Use the memory tools in React Native DevTools for the Hermes heap, and Xcode Instruments or the Android Studio Memory Profiler for native memory. A single high reading is not a leak; steady growth that never comes back down is.
jsonLd.description: A memory leak is memory a React Native app keeps holding after it is no longer needed, so usage grows until the app slows down or the OS kills it.
jsonLd.headline: What is Memory Leak in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Metro is React Native’s JavaScript bundler. It resolves imports, transforms code, serves the bundle to the app in development and powers Fast Refresh.
og:description: Metro is React Native’s JavaScript bundler. It resolves imports, transforms code, serves the bundle to the app in development and powers Fast Refresh.
og:title: Metro in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Metro is React Native’s JavaScript bundler. It resolves imports, transforms code, serves the bundle to the app in development and powers Fast Refresh.
jsonLd.name: Metro

jsonLd.articleBody: Metro is the bundler React Native uses, filling the role Webpack or Vite plays on the web. It takes your entry file, follows every import, transforms the code, and produces a single JavaScript bundle the app can execute. It runs in two modes: In development it is a server, usually on port 8081. The app fetches the bundle from it on launch and keeps a connection open for Fast Refresh. At build time it emits the static bundle that gets embedded in the .ipa or .aab you ship. Metro is mobile-specific in ways that surprise web developers: it resolves platform extensions such as Button.ios.tsx automatically (see platform-specific code), and it handles asset registration for images. Most React Native error messages a newcomer sees during setup come from Metro — "Unable to resolve module", or a stale cache that npx expo start --clear fixes. See the Metro docs.

/react-native-glossary/mmkv.title: MMKV in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: MMKV is a fast, synchronous key-value storage library for React Native, built on Tencent’s memory-mapped MMKV engine and exposed through JSI as react-native-mmkv.
og:description: MMKV is a fast, synchronous key-value storage library for React Native, built on Tencent’s memory-mapped MMKV engine and exposed through JSI as react-native-mmkv.
og:title: MMKV in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: MMKV is a fast, synchronous key-value storage library for React Native, built on Tencent’s memory-mapped MMKV engine and exposed through JSI as react-native-mmkv.
jsonLd.name: MMKV

jsonLd.articleBody: MMKV is a key-value store originally built by Tencent for the WeChat app, which memory-maps a file so reads and writes are close to the speed of working with memory. In React Native it means react-native-mmkv, maintained by Marc Rousavy, which exposes it to JavaScript through JSI rather than an asynchronous bridge call. The practical difference from AsyncStorage is that every call is synchronous. storage.getString('theme') returns the value immediately, so you can read persisted settings during the very first render with no loading state and no flash of the wrong theme. It also stores booleans, numbers and binary buffers natively instead of forcing everything through JSON, and it can encrypt its file with a key you supply. That makes it the common choice for: Persisting a Zustand or Redux store with instant hydration. Feature flags, settings and “has seen onboarding” style values read at startup. Caching small pieces of data that are read frequently. Things to know before adopting it: It contains native code, so it does not run in Expo Go; you need a development build. Recent major versions also require the New Architecture. The API changed shape between major versions, so check which version a tutorial is written for. Synchronous cuts both ways. Writing a multi-megabyte JSON blob blocks the JavaScript thread while it serialises; MMKV is for many small values, not one huge one. Encryption is only as strong as where you keep the key. Hard-coding it in the bundle protects nothing; generate it once and keep it in secure storage. MMKV is not a database. It has no queries, indexes or relations, so once you find yourself scanning keys to filter records, move that data to SQLite. See the react-native-mmkv repository.

/react-native-glossary/mocking.title: Mocking in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Mocking replaces a real dependency, such as a native module, network call or timer, with a controlled fake so React Native code can be tested in Jest without a device.
og:description: Mocking replaces a real dependency, such as a native module, network call or timer, with a controlled fake so React Native code can be tested in Jest without a device.
og:title: Mocking in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Mocking replaces a real dependency, such as a native module, network call or timer, with a controlled fake so React Native code can be tested in Jest without a device.
jsonLd.name: Mocking

jsonLd.articleBody: Mocking means swapping a real dependency for a fake one during a test. The fake returns whatever the test needs and records how it was called. In React Native it is not optional: Jest runs in Node.js, where no iOS or Android exists, so any code that reaches a native module has to be mocked to run at all. Jest provides the core tools: jest.fn() creates a fake function you can program and inspect. jest.mock('module-name', factory) replaces a whole module for every file in the test. jest.spyOn(object, 'method') watches or overrides a single method. Fake timers (jest.useFakeTimers()) control setTimeout and intervals. Many popular libraries ship an official Jest mock or setup file for exactly this reason. Check a library's documentation for a testing section before writing your own, and register shared mocks once in a setup file referenced from your Jest config rather than repeating them in every test. Typical errors that mean a mock is missing include "native module cannot be null", "TurboModuleRegistry.getEnforcing(...) could not be found", or an import failing with unexpected syntax because the package ships untransformed code (which is fixed with transformIgnorePatterns, not a mock). The gotcha is over-mocking. Mock the edges of your system, such as the network, native APIs, time and randomness, not your own modules. A test where every collaborator is mocked passes even when the real pieces no longer fit together. For network calls, mocking at the HTTP level with a tool such as Mock Service Worker keeps more of your real code under test than mocking your API client.

author: David Leuliette
description: Modal is React Native’s core component for presenting content above the rest of the app in a separate native window, with slide or fade animations and iOS sheet styles.
og:description: Modal is React Native’s core component for presenting content above the rest of the app in a separate native window, with slide or fade animations and iOS sheet styles.
og:title: Modal in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Modal is React Native’s core component for presenting content above the rest of the app in a separate native window, with slide or fade animations and iOS sheet styles.
jsonLd.name: Modal

jsonLd.articleBody: Modal is the core component that presents content on top of everything else in the app. It is controlled by a visible prop and renders its children in a separate native layer: a presented view controller on iOS and a dialog window on Android. The props that matter: animationType — none, slide or fade. transparent — draws a see-through backdrop so you can build your own dimmed overlay. presentationStyle (iOS) — fullScreen, pageSheet, formSheet or overFullScreen. Page sheets give the native card look with swipe-to-dismiss. onRequestClose — called when the user presses the Android back button, and when an iOS page sheet is swiped down. If you ignore it, the modal state and what is on screen drift apart. Because a Modal lives in its own native layer, a few things surprise people. Toasts, snackbars and portals rendered in your root view appear behind an open modal. On iOS, opening a second modal while one is animating closed can silently fail. The status bar and safe area also need handling inside the modal, since the modal does not inherit your screen’s layout. For full screens that are part of a flow, such as a checkout or a compose screen, a modal route in your stack navigator or Expo Router is often better. It participates in navigation state, deep links and the back stack. Keep the core Modal for self-contained overlays: a picker, a confirmation, a short form.

/react-native-glossary/monorepo.title: Monorepo in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A monorepo keeps a React Native app alongside other apps and shared packages in one repository, linked together with npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun workspaces.
og:description: A monorepo keeps a React Native app alongside other apps and shared packages in one repository, linked together with npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun workspaces.
og:title: Monorepo in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A monorepo keeps a React Native app alongside other apps and shared packages in one repository, linked together with npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun workspaces.
jsonLd.name: Monorepo

jsonLd.articleBody: A monorepo is a single repository that holds several projects, for example a React Native app, a Next.js site and shared packages for UI, types and API clients. The package manager’s workspaces feature links them so the app can import @acme/ui as if it came from the registry. Teams adopt it to share code between mobile and web, keep one version of TypeScript and lint config, and change an API client and its callers in one pull request. React Native makes monorepos harder than the web does, for three reasons: Metro must see the whole repository. It needs to watch and resolve files outside the app folder. Expo’s Metro config detects workspaces automatically; bare projects usually set watchFolders themselves. Native dependencies must be visible to the app. Autolinking only links native libraries the app depends on, so a library used by a shared package must also be listed in the app’s own package.json. There must be exactly one copy of React and React Native. Two copies cause "Invalid hook call" errors or native crashes. That last point is the classic failure. Different packages pin slightly different versions of react, the package manager installs both, and the app breaks in ways that look unrelated. Declare react and react-native as peer dependencies in shared packages, and keep a single version at the root. Hoisting also matters. Some React Native tooling still assumes packages live in a flat node_modules, so pnpm’s isolated layout may need node-linker=hoisted, depending on your toolchain version. Tools such as Nx and Turborepo add caching and task orchestration on top, but the workspace rules above apply whichever you pick.
jsonLd.description: A monorepo keeps a React Native app alongside other apps and shared packages in one repository, linked together with npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun workspaces.
jsonLd.headline: What is Monorepo in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/native-app.title: Native App in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A native app is a mobile app built with each platform’s own SDK and languages, Swift or Objective-C on iOS and Kotlin or Java on Android, installed from a store.
og:description: A native app is a mobile app built with each platform’s own SDK and languages, Swift or Objective-C on iOS and Kotlin or Java on Android, installed from a store.
og:title: Native App in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A native app is a mobile app built with each platform’s own SDK and languages, Swift or Objective-C on iOS and Kotlin or Java on Android, installed from a store.
jsonLd.name: Native App

jsonLd.articleBody: A native app is an application written directly against a platform’s own SDK: Swift or Objective-C with SwiftUI or UIKit on iOS, Kotlin or Java with Jetpack Compose or Android Views on Android. Each platform usually gets its own codebase and often its own team. The term is used in two ways, and confusing them causes most debates: Native development describes how the app is built: platform languages and tools, no cross-platform layer. Native app in the broader sense describes what the user gets: a compiled binary installed from the App Store or Google Play that uses real platform UI and APIs, as opposed to a website or a hybrid app in a WebView. A React Native app is native in the second sense but not the first. It ships as an .ipa and an .aab, renders platform views, and can call any native API, but its UI and logic are written in JavaScript or TypeScript. Why fully native development is still chosen: Day-one access to new OS features and frameworks, without waiting for wrappers. Apps dominated by platform-specific work, such as widgets, watch apps, advanced camera or audio pipelines. Teams that already have experienced iOS and Android engineers. The costs are two codebases, features that drift apart between platforms, and roughly double the effort for anything shared. The misconception to avoid is that "native" automatically means faster or better. A carefully built React Native app and a native app are often indistinguishable to users, and a poorly built native app can still stutter. Performance depends far more on how the app is written than on the label. Many large apps mix both, adding React Native to an existing native codebase as a brownfield app.
jsonLd.description: A native app is a mobile app built with each platform’s own SDK and languages, Swift or Objective-C on iOS and Kotlin or Java on Android, installed from a store.
jsonLd.headline: What is Native App in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/native-driver.title: Native Driver in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The native driver, useNativeDriver: true in React Native’s Animated API, hands an animation to native code once so it runs on the UI thread without JavaScript.
og:description: The native driver, useNativeDriver: true in React Native’s Animated API, hands an animation to native code once so it runs on the UI thread without JavaScript.
og:title: Native Driver in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The native driver, useNativeDriver: true in React Native’s Animated API, hands an animation to native code once so it runs on the UI thread without JavaScript.
jsonLd.name: Native Driver

jsonLd.articleBody: The native driver is a mode of React Native’s built-in Animated API. When you pass useNativeDriver: true, the whole animation (start value, end value, easing, duration) is described to native code once, before it starts, and then runs frame by frame on the UI thread. JavaScript is no longer involved until the animation ends. Without it, JavaScript calculates each frame and sends the new value across, so the animation stutters whenever the JavaScript thread is busy rendering a screen or parsing a response. With it, the animation stays smooth through that work. That difference is most of the story behind jank in older React Native apps. The constraint is what it can animate. The native driver only supports properties that do not affect layout: Supported: opacity, transform (translate, scale, rotate) and a handful of others such as some colour properties. Not supported: width, height, top, left, margin, padding, flex and anything that requires recalculating layout. Trying produces an error saying the style property is not supported by the native animated module. The usual workaround is to restate the animation in supported properties: animate scaleY instead of height, translateX instead of left. It also works with Animated.event for scroll-driven effects, such as a header that fades as the list scrolls, by passing useNativeDriver: true to the event mapping. Common gotchas: you cannot drive the same Animated.Value with both native and JavaScript animations; once a value has been used natively, mixing causes errors. Listeners and reading the current value need extra care because the value now lives on the native side. And React Native warns if you leave useNativeDriver unspecified, so set it explicitly every time. When you need to animate layout properties or respond to gestures continuously, Reanimated removes these limits by running full worklets on the UI thread. See the Animated docs.
jsonLd.description: The native driver, useNativeDriver: true in React Native’s Animated API, hands an animation to native code once so it runs on the UI thread without JavaScript.
jsonLd.headline: What is Native Driver in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: A native module is platform code — Swift, Kotlin, Objective-C, Java or C++ — exposed to JavaScript, letting an app reach APIs React Native does not wrap itself.
og:description: A native module is platform code — Swift, Kotlin, Objective-C, Java or C++ — exposed to JavaScript, letting an app reach APIs React Native does not wrap itself.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A native module is platform code — Swift, Kotlin, Objective-C, Java or C++ — exposed to JavaScript, letting an app reach APIs React Native does not wrap itself.
jsonLd.name: Native Module

jsonLd.articleBody: A native module is a piece of platform code exposed to JavaScript. React Native wraps a useful but finite set of APIs; anything beyond it — Bluetooth, biometrics, a payment SDK, an on-device ML model — reaches your app through a native module. Most developers consume rather than write them. Installing react-native-ble-plx or expo-camera adds native module code to the project, which is why those installs need a native rebuild and cannot be delivered by an over-the-air update. Under the New Architecture the modern form is a TurboModule, typed by Codegen and loaded on demand. Two things newcomers should recognise: "Autolinking" means the native build discovers installed modules automatically — no manual Xcode or Gradle wiring in almost all cases. A module needing a config change (permissions, entitlements) uses a config plugin in Expo projects rather than hand-edited native files. See native modules.

/react-native-glossary/nativewind.title: NativeWind in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: NativeWind lets you style React Native components with Tailwind CSS utility classes through a className prop, compiled into native styles at build time.
og:description: NativeWind lets you style React Native components with Tailwind CSS utility classes through a className prop, compiled into native styles at build time.
og:title: NativeWind in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: NativeWind lets you style React Native components with Tailwind CSS utility classes through a className prop, compiled into native styles at build time.
jsonLd.name: NativeWind

jsonLd.articleBody: NativeWind is a library that brings Tailwind CSS to React Native. Instead of a StyleSheet object, you write utility classes in a className prop, and NativeWind turns them into React Native style objects. It runs the real Tailwind compiler during bundling, wired in through Metro and Babel, so most of the class parsing happens at build time rather than on every render. Your tailwind.config provides the theme, which makes it a natural home for design tokens. It also supports modifiers such as dark:, platform variants, and responsive breakpoints. Why teams pick it: web developers already know the vocabulary, the same classes work on React Native Web, and styling stays next to the markup. Common gotchas: Setup is the usual failure point. NativeWind needs its Metro wrapper, a global CSS file imported at the root, and Tailwind’s content paths covering every file that uses classes. A class that silently does nothing usually means one of those is wrong, or the cache needs clearing. React Native is not the browser. Utilities with no native equivalent, such as CSS grid or many hover and pseudo-element styles, do not apply. Third-party components only accept className if NativeWind is told how to map it to their style props. Class names built with string concatenation at runtime cannot be seen by the compiler. Write full class names and switch between them. See the NativeWind docs.

jsonLd.headline: What is NativeWind in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/navigation-state.title: Navigation State in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Navigation state is the plain object a React Native navigator keeps describing which screens exist, which one is focused and the params each received.
og:description: Navigation state is the plain object a React Native navigator keeps describing which screens exist, which one is focused and the params each received.
og:title: Navigation State in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Navigation state is the plain object a React Native navigator keeps describing which screens exist, which one is focused and the params each received.
jsonLd.name: Navigation State

jsonLd.articleBody: Navigation state is the data structure React Navigation (and Expo Router on top of it) uses to describe where the user is. Each navigator owns an object listing its routes, the index of the focused one, and for each route a name, a unique key and its params. Nested navigators nest their state inside the parent route. The NavigationContainer at the root holds the whole tree. Every navigate, push or goBack is an action that produces a new state, a lot like a reducer. That design is what makes several features possible: Deep linking works by turning a URL into a state object. State persistence saves the state with onStateChange and restores it via initialState, useful in development so a reload keeps you on the screen you were editing. Hooks such as useNavigationState and useRoute let a screen read it. Route params are the part developers touch daily. Pass identifiers, not objects: Passing a full object gives the screen a frozen copy that will not update when the data changes, and it cannot be rebuilt from a URL. Passing functions or class instances triggers React Navigation’s "non-serializable values were found in the navigation state" warning, because persistence and linking need state that can round-trip through JSON. The misconception to drop: navigation state is not your app’s data store. Treat params like a URL’s query string, and keep shared data in a cache or state management library that each screen reads by id.
jsonLd.description: Navigation state is the plain object a React Native navigator keeps describing which screens exist, which one is focused and the params each received.
jsonLd.headline: What is Navigation State in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/node-js.title: Node.js in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Node.js is the JavaScript runtime that powers React Native’s development tools such as Metro, Expo CLI and the React Native CLI, though your app itself never runs on it.
og:description: Node.js is the JavaScript runtime that powers React Native’s development tools such as Metro, Expo CLI and the React Native CLI, though your app itself never runs on it.
og:title: Node.js in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Node.js is the JavaScript runtime that powers React Native’s development tools such as Metro, Expo CLI and the React Native CLI, though your app itself never runs on it.
jsonLd.name: Node.js

jsonLd.articleBody: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime for computers and servers. In React Native it is the engine behind your tooling: Metro, Expo CLI, the React Native CLI, package managers, Jest and the build scripts that Xcode and Gradle call during a native build all run on Node. Your app does not. On the device your code runs on Hermes, a different JavaScript runtime with no Node APIs. This is the most common misconception for developers arriving from backend or web tooling: fs, path and child_process do not exist in the app, and process.env only holds values inlined at build time. npm packages that depend on Node built-ins, such as many crypto or file libraries, will fail to bundle or crash when called. Look for React Native-specific alternatives. Buffer is not a global by default. React Native and Expo each declare a minimum Node version in their packages, and it rises over time. Use an active LTS release and pin it per project so everyone on the team, and CI, gets the same version. Version managers such as nvm, fnm or Volta read a file at the repository root: The classic setup gotcha: the app builds from the terminal but fails in Xcode with "node: command not found" or the wrong version. Xcode does not load your shell profile, so it cannot see a Node installed through a version manager. React Native projects solve this with ios/.xcode.env, and you can override it locally in ios/.xcode.env.local: Upgrading Node also changes the native modules your tooling depends on, so reinstall node_modules after switching major versions.

/react-native-glossary/objective-c.title: Objective-C in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Objective-C is Apple’s older iOS language; much of React Native’s iOS core and many libraries still use it, often as Objective-C++ to reach C++ code like JSI.
og:description: Objective-C is Apple’s older iOS language; much of React Native’s iOS core and many libraries still use it, often as Objective-C++ to reach C++ code like JSI.
og:title: Objective-C in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Objective-C is Apple’s older iOS language; much of React Native’s iOS core and many libraries still use it, often as Objective-C++ to reach C++ code like JSI.
jsonLd.name: Objective-C

jsonLd.articleBody: Objective-C is the language Apple platforms were built on before Swift arrived. It adds Smalltalk-style messaging to C, and React Native’s iOS code — the RCT classes, the app host and a large share of community libraries — is written in it. Its variant, Objective-C++, is why it remains relevant. A file with the .mm extension can mix Objective-C and C++ freely, and React Native’s New Architecture is C++ at its core: JSI, the Fabric renderer and TurboModules all expose C++ interfaces. Objective-C++ is the glue that lets iOS code plug into them, which is why generated TurboModule and Fabric component code on iOS is .mm, not Swift. What you will recognise in React Native code: .h header and .m or .mm implementation files. Macros such as RCT_EXPORT_MODULE() and RCT_EXPORT_METHOD(), from the classic native module system. Square-bracket method calls like [UIApplication sharedApplication]. That pattern is the thin Objective-C file that exposes a Swift class to React Native. The common gotcha is file extensions. Renaming an .m file to .mm changes the compiler used, so a module that suddenly needs to include a C++ header must become Objective-C++; forgetting this produces baffling errors about unknown C++ syntax. The reverse also matters: Swift cannot import C++ headers the same way, so you cannot simply rewrite every .mm file in Swift. You do not need to master Objective-C to work with React Native, but being able to read it makes library source code and native stack traces far less intimidating.
jsonLd.description: Objective-C is Apple’s older iOS language; much of React Native’s iOS core and many libraries still use it, often as Objective-C++ to reach C++ code like JSI.
jsonLd.headline: What is Objective-C in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/offline-first.title: Offline-First in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Offline-first is an architecture where a React Native app reads and writes a local database first and syncs in the background, so it works without a connection.
og:description: Offline-first is an architecture where a React Native app reads and writes a local database first and syncs in the background, so it works without a connection.
og:title: Offline-First in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Offline-first is an architecture where a React Native app reads and writes a local database first and syncs in the background, so it works without a connection.
jsonLd.name: Offline-First

jsonLd.articleBody: Offline-first means the app treats data on the device as its primary source of truth. Screens read from a local database and writes go there immediately; a sync process then exchanges changes with the server whenever a connection is available. The network becomes an optimisation rather than a requirement. It matters more on mobile than anywhere else. Phones spend real time in lifts, underground, on planes and on weak signal, and an app that shows a spinner or an error in those moments feels broken. Offline-first apps also feel faster online, because every screen renders from local data with no wait. There is a spectrum of approaches: Cached reads. Persist your TanStack Query cache so the last data shows offline, and queue mutations until the network returns. Cheap, and enough for many apps. Local database plus sync. Store data in SQLite and run a sync engine such as PowerSync, WatermelonDB’s sync protocol, or a custom one. This is true offline-first. Local-first with CRDTs. Data structures that merge concurrent edits automatically, suited to collaborative apps. The hard part is never storage; it is conflicts. If two devices edit the same record offline, something has to decide the result: last write wins, field-level merging, or asking the user. Decide this per data type before writing code, because retrofitting conflict rules onto a shipped schema is painful. The common technical gotcha is trusting the connectivity flag. Libraries such as NetInfo report isConnected when the device is attached to a network, which is not the same as being able to reach your server (captive portal Wi-Fi is the classic case). Check isInternetReachable, and design sync so a failed request is simply retried later rather than surfaced as an error.
jsonLd.description: Offline-first is an architecture where a React Native app reads and writes a local database first and syncs in the background, so it works without a connection.
jsonLd.headline: What is Offline-First in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: An out-of-tree platform is a React Native target maintained outside the core repository, such as React Native Windows, React Native macOS or react-native-tvos.
og:description: An out-of-tree platform is a React Native target maintained outside the core repository, such as React Native Windows, React Native macOS or react-native-tvos.
og:title: Out-of-Tree Platform in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An out-of-tree platform is a React Native target maintained outside the core repository, such as React Native Windows, React Native macOS or react-native-tvos.
jsonLd.name: Out-of-Tree Platform

jsonLd.articleBody: An out-of-tree platform is a React Native target that lives outside the main facebook/react-native repository. Core React Native ships iOS and Android; other targets are built and released separately by companies or the community, reusing React and the core renderer while supplying their own host platform implementation. The best-known examples: React Native Windows and React Native macOS, maintained by Microsoft for desktop apps. react-native-tvos, a community-maintained fork that adds Apple TV and Android TV support, including focus-based navigation for remotes. React Native visionOS, a community project for Apple Vision Pro. React Native Web is related but different: it reimplements React Native’s components on top of the DOM rather than plugging a native platform into the core renderer. In practice an out-of-tree platform behaves much like iOS and Android from your code’s point of view. Platform.OS reports values such as 'windows' or 'macos', and Metro can resolve platform extensions like Button.windows.tsx, so platform-specific code works the same way. The gotchas are about timing and libraries: Out-of-tree platforms follow core releases, so a new React Native version may take a while to be supported there. Check before upgrading. Third-party native libraries only work on a platform if their authors added native code for it. A package that supports iOS and Android often has no Windows or macOS implementation. react-native-tvos is installed in place of react-native, usually through a package alias in package.json, rather than alongside it. Check each library’s supported platforms before committing to a desktop or TV target.

author: David Leuliette
description: An over-the-air update ships new JavaScript and assets straight to installed apps, skipping app store review. Native code changes still require a new store build.
og:description: An over-the-air update ships new JavaScript and assets straight to installed apps, skipping app store review. Native code changes still require a new store build.
og:title: Over-the-Air Update in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An over-the-air update ships new JavaScript and assets straight to installed apps, skipping app store review. Native code changes still require a new store build.
jsonLd.name: Over-the-Air Update

jsonLd.articleBody: An over-the-air (OTA) update delivers a new JavaScript bundle and its assets to apps already installed on devices, without going through App Store or Play review. The app downloads the new bundle and runs it on next launch. The line that decides whether an OTA update is possible is exact: Change Ships over the air? Component, screen, business logic Yes Styles, copy, images bundled as assets Yes Adding a native module No — new store build Upgrading the React Native version No Permissions, app icon, entitlements No The main implementations are EAS Update (part of EAS) and, historically, Microsoft's CodePush, which was retired in 2025. Two constraints newcomers should know: both Apple and Google permit OTA updates for bug fixes and content, but not to substantially change what the app does. And the update must match the installed binary's runtime version — shipping a bundle that calls a native module the binary lacks crashes the app.

/react-native-glossary/owasp-masvs.title: OWASP MASVS in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: OWASP MASVS is the open Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, a checklist of security requirements used to audit iOS, Android and React Native apps.
og:description: OWASP MASVS is the open Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, a checklist of security requirements used to audit iOS, Android and React Native apps.
og:title: OWASP MASVS in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: OWASP MASVS is the open Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, a checklist of security requirements used to audit iOS, Android and React Native apps.
jsonLd.name: OWASP MASVS

jsonLd.articleBody: OWASP MASVS, the Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, is an open standard from the OWASP Mobile Application Security project that defines what a secure mobile app should do. It is the most common reference for mobile security audits, penetration tests and security questionnaires from enterprise customers. MASVS describes requirements, not tools. Its controls are grouped into areas that map directly onto a React Native app: MASVS-STORAGE: sensitive data stored securely, for example tokens in the Keychain or Keystore through secure storage, not in AsyncStorage. MASVS-CRYPTO: cryptography used correctly. MASVS-AUTH: authentication and session handling. MASVS-NETWORK: secure communication, including when to use SSL pinning. MASVS-PLATFORM: safe use of platform features such as deep links, WebViews and inter-app communication. MASVS-CODE: up-to-date dependencies, input validation and secure updates. MASVS-RESILIENCE: resistance to reverse engineering and tampering. MASVS-PRIVACY: data minimisation and user control. Its companion, the Mobile Application Security Testing Guide (MASTG), explains how to test each control on iOS and Android. For React Native developers, a useful way to read MASVS is as a map of where the framework does not protect you by default. React Native does not encrypt storage, pin certificates or keep API keys secret; those are your decisions. JavaScript dependencies also fall under MASVS-CODE, so a vulnerable npm package is an audit finding like any native one. The common misconception is that every app should meet every control. Resilience controls such as obfuscation and tamper detection add cost and matter mainly for apps handling money, health data or valuable content. Choose the controls that fit your risk profile. If you need an outside review against the standard, see our React Native security audit.
jsonLd.description: OWASP MASVS is the open Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, a checklist of security requirements used to audit iOS, Android and React Native apps.
jsonLd.headline: What is OWASP MASVS in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/package-manager.title: Package Manager in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A package manager such as npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun installs a React Native project’s dependencies into node_modules and records exact versions in a lockfile.
og:description: A package manager such as npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun installs a React Native project’s dependencies into node_modules and records exact versions in a lockfile.
og:title: Package Manager in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A package manager such as npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun installs a React Native project’s dependencies into node_modules and records exact versions in a lockfile.
jsonLd.name: Package Manager

jsonLd.articleBody: A package manager installs the libraries your project depends on, resolves their own dependencies, and writes a lockfile so every machine installs the same versions. React Native projects can use npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun. The choice matters less for features than for consistency. Whichever you pick, one rule applies: one package manager, one lockfile. The tool is detected from the lockfile you commit (package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml or bun.lock), including by build services such as EAS Build. Two lockfiles in the same repository mean CI and teammates may install different versions without anyone noticing. React Native adds constraints a web project does not have: Native code lives in packages. Installing a library with native code means a new native build, not just a reload. Metro needs a real node_modules folder. Yarn’s Plug’n’Play mode is not supported, so Yarn Berry projects set nodeLinker: node-modules. Version alignment matters. Expo projects should add libraries with npx expo install, which calls your package manager but picks the version that matches your Expo SDK version. The common gotcha is "fixing" an install failure by deleting the lockfile. That silently upgrades every dependency in the tree at once and is a frequent cause of builds that break the next day. Resolve the specific conflict instead, often a peer dependency mismatch. Each manager also has its own way to override a nested dependency version (overrides in npm and Bun, resolutions in Yarn, pnpm.overrides in pnpm) and to patch packages, which teams otherwise do with patch-package. In a monorepo, workspace and hoisting behaviour differs between them, which is where the choice really shows.
jsonLd.description: A package manager such as npm, Yarn, pnpm or Bun installs a React Native project’s dependencies into node_modules and records exact versions in a lockfile.
jsonLd.headline: What is Package Manager in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/panresponder.title: PanResponder in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: PanResponder is React Native’s built-in API for tracking drag gestures in JavaScript, wrapping the gesture responder system to report distance and velocity.
og:description: PanResponder is React Native’s built-in API for tracking drag gestures in JavaScript, wrapping the gesture responder system to report distance and velocity.
og:title: PanResponder in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: PanResponder is React Native’s built-in API for tracking drag gestures in JavaScript, wrapping the gesture responder system to report distance and velocity.
jsonLd.name: PanResponder

jsonLd.articleBody: PanResponder is a core API for building drag and swipe interactions. It sits on top of React Native’s gesture responder system, the mechanism that decides which view “owns” a touch, and turns raw touch events into a gestureState with useful numbers: dx and dy (distance since the touch began) and vx and vy (velocity). The responder system works by negotiation. On touch start and move, each view is asked whether it wants to become the responder (onStartShouldSetPanResponder, onMoveShouldSetPanResponder). Once granted, another view, such as a parent ScrollView, can ask to take over, and onPanResponderTerminationRequest decides whether to let go. onPanResponderTerminate fires if you lose the gesture, which is why drags inside scroll views sometimes stop halfway. Common mistakes: Creating it on every render. PanResponder.create inside the component body without useRef or useMemo rebuilds the handlers each render, and handlers capture stale state. Expecting it to stay smooth under load. Every move event runs on the JavaScript thread. When that thread is busy, the drag stutters, even if the animation itself uses the native driver. Fighting native scroll views and system gestures, which the responder system cannot coordinate well. PanResponder still works and needs no dependency, which suits a simple draggable. For production gesture work, such as swipeable rows, bottom sheets or pinch-to-zoom, most apps use Gesture Handler, which recognises gestures natively and can drive Reanimated animations on the UI thread.

You edit the library’s files in node_modules, run one command, and it records the difference as a patch file that is reapplied after every install. This creates patches/some-library+1.2.3.patch, which you commit. A postinstall script in package.json then applies it on every machine and in CI: It is common in React Native because libraries often need a small fix that cannot wait for a release: a crash on a new Android version, a build error after an Xcode update, a missing New Architecture tweak. Most package managers now offer built-in equivalents, such as yarn patch, pnpm patch and bun patch, which record patches in package.json without an extra dependency. The idea is identical. How it behaves in practice: Patches are tied to the version in the file name. After upgrading the library, patch-package warns or fails when the patch no longer applies, which is your cue to check whether the fix landed upstream. Patching a library’s native code, under its ios/ or android/ folder, needs a new native build. On iOS, reinstall CocoaPods dependencies so the change is picked up. Patch the files the app actually loads. Many libraries ship both src/ and compiled output such as lib/, so check which one the package’s entry point uses before editing. The common mistake is treating a patch as permanent. Patches accumulate quietly and then all break during a React Native upgrade. Open an issue or pull request upstream, link it in a comment at the top of the patch, and delete the patch once the fixed version is out.

author: David Leuliette
description: Peer dependencies are packages a library expects your app to provide, such as react and react-native, so that only one shared copy exists in the project.
og:description: Peer dependencies are packages a library expects your app to provide, such as react and react-native, so that only one shared copy exists in the project.
og:title: Peer Dependencies in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Peer dependencies are packages a library expects your app to provide, such as react and react-native, so that only one shared copy exists in the project.
jsonLd.name: Peer Dependencies

jsonLd.articleBody: A peer dependency is a package that a library needs but does not install for itself. The library declares it in peerDependencies, and your app is expected to supply it. Almost every React Native library lists react and react-native this way, and many list others, such as react-native-reanimated or react-native-gesture-handler. The reason is that some packages must exist exactly once. Two copies of React break hooks with "Invalid hook call". Two copies of a native module lead to duplicate symbols at build time or crashes at runtime. Peer dependencies make the app the single owner of those shared packages. In practice modern npm installs missing peers automatically and refuses to continue when ranges conflict, printing an ERESOLVE error. Yarn and pnpm warn instead, and pnpm has settings to make peer rules stricter. The most common mistake is reaching for npm install --legacy-peer-deps or --force the moment ERESOLVE appears. That makes the error go away by ignoring the declared ranges. Sometimes that is fine, because a library simply has not widened its range for a new React version yet. Sometimes it installs a library that really is incompatible with your React Native version and fails at build time, which is harder to diagnose. A better sequence: Read the conflict. It names the library and the range it expects. Check for a newer release of that library that supports your version. In Expo projects, use npx expo install and Expo Doctor, which know the compatible versions for your SDK. If you must override, use your package manager’s overrides or resolutions field so the decision is visible in package.json, not hidden in an install flag.

author: David Leuliette
description: PixelRatio is the React Native API that exposes the device’s pixel density and font scale, used to request sharp images and to round layout values to physical pixels.
og:description: PixelRatio is the React Native API that exposes the device’s pixel density and font scale, used to request sharp images and to round layout values to physical pixels.
og:title: PixelRatio in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: PixelRatio is the React Native API that exposes the device’s pixel density and font scale, used to request sharp images and to round layout values to physical pixels.
jsonLd.name: PixelRatio

jsonLd.articleBody: PixelRatio is a core API that tells you how many physical pixels make up one layout unit on the current device. React Native lays everything out in density-independent pixels; PixelRatio is the bridge to the real screen underneath. Its methods: PixelRatio.get() — the density: 1 on old low-density Android phones, 2 or 3 on most modern iPhones and Android flagships, and fractional values such as 2.625 on many Android devices. PixelRatio.getFontScale() — the user’s text size multiplier from accessibility settings. PixelRatio.getPixelSizeForLayoutSize(size) — converts layout units to physical pixels. PixelRatio.roundToNearestPixel(size) — snaps a value to a whole physical pixel. The main practical use is requesting the right image size. A 100-point avatar on a 3x screen needs a 300-pixel image to look sharp; asking a CDN for exactly that avoids both blur and wasted bandwidth. roundToNearestPixel solves a subtler problem. On fractional-density Android screens, a layout value like 33.3 can land between physical pixels, producing blurry 1-pixel borders or a hairline gap between adjacent views. Rounding fixes it. For the thinnest possible line, StyleSheet.hairlineWidth already gives you one physical pixel. A common misconception is using PixelRatio to make layouts “scale” across devices by multiplying every size by the density. React Native already does that conversion; multiplying again makes everything huge on dense screens. Layout should stay in layout units, with PixelRatio reserved for images, borders and the occasional pixel-perfect alignment. getFontScale() returns the same value as fontScale from useWindowDimensions, but the hook updates when the setting changes, so prefer it inside components.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The Podfile is the Ruby file in ios/ that tells CocoaPods which native iOS dependencies to install; Podfile.lock records the exact versions it resolved.
jsonLd.name: Podfile

jsonLd.articleBody: The Podfile is a Ruby file at ios/Podfile that tells CocoaPods what to install into your iOS app. In a React Native project you rarely list libraries in it yourself: a few helper calls do the work. use_native_modules! runs autolinking, adding every native library found in node_modules, and use_react_native! adds React Native’s own pods. Expo projects call use_expo_modules! for Expo modules as well. The surrounding code sets the minimum iOS version, applies post-install fixes and passes build flags. Podfile.lock is the iOS equivalent of your JavaScript lockfile: it pins the exact version of every pod, including transitive ones. Commit it. Without it, two developers running pod install on the same commit can end up with different native code, and CI can break on a dependency nobody touched. When does a React Native developer edit the Podfile directly? Raising the iOS deployment target a library requires. Adding a post_install tweak to work around a build error in a dependency. Enabling options a library documents, such as static frameworks. The main gotcha is Expo’s Continuous Native Generation. If ios/ is generated by npx expo prebuild and not committed, hand edits to the Podfile disappear on the next prebuild. Make those changes through a config plugin or the expo-build-properties plugin instead. A merge conflict in Podfile.lock is usually safest to resolve by taking either side and re-running pod install, then committing what it produces.

author: David Leuliette
description: Pressable is React Native’s core component for handling taps and long presses, exposing a pressed state for feedback; it supersedes the older Touchables.
og:description: Pressable is React Native’s core component for handling taps and long presses, exposing a pressed state for feedback; it supersedes the older Touchables.
og:title: Pressable in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Pressable is React Native’s core component for handling taps and long presses, exposing a pressed state for feedback; it supersedes the older Touchables.
jsonLd.name: Pressable

jsonLd.articleBody: Pressable is a core component that detects presses on whatever it wraps. It is the modern replacement for the Touchable* family (TouchableOpacity, TouchableHighlight, TouchableWithoutFeedback), which still exist but are no longer where new features land. Unlike the Touchables, Pressable gives no visual feedback by default. You add it yourself, usually by passing a function as style or children that receives the pressed state: The press lifecycle is onPressIn, then either onPress or onLongPress (after delayLongPress, 500 ms by default), then onPressOut. Two props solve most “my button is hard to hit” complaints: hitSlop enlarges the touchable area without changing layout, useful for small icons. pressRetentionOffset controls how far the finger can drift before the press is cancelled. On Android, android_ripple gives the native Material ripple, which is often a better choice than an opacity change. A common gotcha is forgetting accessibility. A Pressable is just a View to a screen reader until you set an accessibility role such as button and, for icon-only buttons, a label. Pressable is built on the JavaScript responder system, the same one PanResponder uses. For presses inside complex gesture surfaces, such as a swipeable row or a bottom sheet, the buttons from Gesture Handler coordinate better with native gestures.

author: David Leuliette
description: A privacy manifest is the PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file Apple requires in iOS apps and SDKs, declaring the data they collect and why they use certain sensitive APIs.
og:description: A privacy manifest is the PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file Apple requires in iOS apps and SDKs, declaring the data they collect and why they use certain sensitive APIs.
og:title: Privacy Manifest in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A privacy manifest is the PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file Apple requires in iOS apps and SDKs, declaring the data they collect and why they use certain sensitive APIs.
jsonLd.name: Privacy Manifest

jsonLd.articleBody: A privacy manifest is a property list file named PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy that Apple requires in iOS apps and in many third-party SDKs. It declares what data the app collects, whether it is used for tracking, and why the code calls certain APIs Apple considers open to fingerprinting. Those are the required reason APIs. Calling them is allowed, but each category must be listed with an approved reason code. Categories include UserDefaults, file timestamps, system boot time, disk space and active keyboards. React Native itself, and libraries such as AsyncStorage, touch several of them, so practically every React Native app needs a manifest even if your own code never mentions these APIs. If something is missing, App Store Connect emails you an ITMS-91053: Missing API declaration warning or rejects the upload, naming the API category. The fix is to add the category and reason to your app’s manifest. With Expo you declare it in your app config and prebuild writes the file: Common gotchas: Libraries installed through CocoaPods may ship their own manifest that does not reach your final app correctly. If Apple flags an API you never call directly, copy the dependency’s declaration into your app manifest. The manifest is separate from the App Store privacy "nutrition label" you fill in online. Keep the two consistent. It is not Info.plist. Permission prompt strings still go there. See Apple’s privacy manifest documentation.

/react-native-glossary/profiling.title: Profiling in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Profiling is measuring where a React Native app spends time and memory, using tools that record JS, React renders and native threads, so you fix real bottlenecks.
og:description: Profiling is measuring where a React Native app spends time and memory, using tools that record JS, React renders and native threads, so you fix real bottlenecks.
og:title: Profiling in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Profiling is measuring where a React Native app spends time and memory, using tools that record JS, React renders and native threads, so you fix real bottlenecks.
jsonLd.name: Profiling

jsonLd.articleBody: Profiling is recording what your app actually does over a period of time, then reading the recording to find what is slow. It replaces guessing with evidence: which function blocked the thread, which component rendered forty times, which allocation kept growing. A React Native app runs on several layers, and each has its own profiler: React renders. The React Profiler in React Native DevTools records every commit and shows which components rendered, how long they took and why. This is the place to hunt unnecessary re-renders. JavaScript execution. Sampling the Hermes runtime shows which functions consume time on the JavaScript thread. Native threads. Xcode Instruments (Time Profiler, Allocations) on iOS and the Android Studio profilers or Perfetto on Android show the UI thread, rendering and native memory. The usual workflow is: reproduce one specific slow interaction, record only that interaction, find the single most expensive item, fix it, then record again to confirm the improvement. The most common mistake is profiling a debug build. Development mode runs extra checks, warnings and unoptimised code, which inflates render times and can point you at problems that do not exist in production. Absolute numbers from a debug build are misleading; use a release or profiling build on a real, preferably low-end, device when timing matters. The second mistake is optimising before profiling. Wrapping everything in React.memo or useCallback adds complexity and sometimes cost. Profile first, and fix the one thing the recording points at.

jsonLd.headline: What is Profiling in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: A Progressive Web App (PWA) is a website that can be installed to the home screen and work offline, using a web app manifest and a service worker instead of a store.
og:description: A Progressive Web App (PWA) is a website that can be installed to the home screen and work offline, using a web app manifest and a service worker instead of a store.
og:title: Progressive Web App in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A Progressive Web App (PWA) is a website that can be installed to the home screen and work offline, using a web app manifest and a service worker instead of a store.
jsonLd.name: Progressive Web App

jsonLd.articleBody: A Progressive Web App (PWA) is a website built to behave like an installed app. A web app manifest gives it a name, icon and full-screen display mode so users can add it to their home screen, and a service worker caches assets and data so it can load offline and, where supported, receive push notifications. For a React Native team, PWAs come up in two ways. First, as an alternative. A PWA skips App Store and Google Play review, updates instantly, and is reachable through a URL. In exchange it runs in the browser, has limited or no access to many device APIs (Bluetooth, background tasks, widgets and deeper system integration vary by browser), and is less discoverable for people who look for apps in a store. Support is notably uneven on iOS, where installation and web push have historically arrived later and with more restrictions than on Android. Second, as an extra target. With React Native Web, often through Expo’s web support, the same components can run in the browser. Turning that web build into a PWA is a separate step: you add the manifest and a service worker yourself, just as for any web app. Shared code makes this practical, but it is not automatic. The common misconception is that a PWA is a cheaper version of the same product. It is a different distribution model with different limits. It suits tools people open from a link, internal apps and content sites. It suits less well apps that depend on reliable push, background work, payments through store billing, or deep OS features. Many products ship both: a PWA for reach and a React Native app for engaged users. Design the offline-first data layer once and both benefit.

og:description: Props are the read-only inputs a component receives from its parent. State is the data a component owns and can change, triggering a re-render.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.name: Props and State

jsonLd.articleBody: Props and state are the two ways data reaches a React Native component, and the difference decides where a value should live. Props are arguments passed down from a parent. They are read-only: a component must never write to its own props. Changing a prop is the parent's job, and doing so re-renders the child. State is data a component owns, created with the useState hook. Calling the setter schedules a re-render with the new value: The practical rule newcomers ask about: if two components need the same value, lift the state up to their closest common parent and pass it down as props. If a value changes but should not trigger a re-render — a timer id, a scroll offset — it belongs in a ref instead.

/react-native-glossary/push-notification.title: Push Notifications in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Push notifications are messages a server sends to a device through Apple’s APNs or Google’s FCM, shown by the OS even when the React Native app is closed.
og:description: Push notifications are messages a server sends to a device through Apple’s APNs or Google’s FCM, shown by the OS even when the React Native app is closed.
og:title: Push Notifications in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Push notifications are messages a server sends to a device through Apple’s APNs or Google’s FCM, shown by the OS even when the React Native app is closed.
jsonLd.name: Push Notifications

jsonLd.articleBody: Push notifications are messages sent from your server to a user’s device and displayed by the operating system, even when your React Native app is not running. Your server never talks to the phone directly: it goes through the platform’s delivery service. APNs (Apple Push Notification service) delivers to iPhones and iPads. FCM (Firebase Cloud Messaging) delivers to Android devices with Google Play Services. The flow is always the same. The app asks for permission, registers with the platform, and receives a device token. You send that token to your backend, which later calls APNs or FCM with the token and a payload. In React Native the usual options are expo-notifications, which works with Expo’s push service (one ExponentPushToken that fans out to APNs and FCM) or with raw native tokens, and @react-native-firebase/messaging, often paired with Notifee for rich local display. Gotchas that cost people days: iOS needs the Push Notifications capability, which adds the aps-environment entitlement and must be in your provisioning profile, plus an APNs key uploaded to whoever sends the pushes. Android 13 and later require the runtime notification permission; older versions granted it silently. Expo Go is not a reliable test bed: remote push on Android is no longer supported there. Use a development build. Foreground behaviour is opt-in. By default a notification arriving while the app is open may not be shown; you decide with a handler such as setNotificationHandler. Tokens change. Refresh and re-send them on every launch rather than storing one forever. See the Expo push notifications guide.

/react-native-glossary/r8-proguard.title: R8 and ProGuard in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: R8 is Android’s code shrinker and obfuscator, the successor to ProGuard; it removes unused Java and Kotlin code from release builds and renames what remains.
og:description: R8 is Android’s code shrinker and obfuscator, the successor to ProGuard; it removes unused Java and Kotlin code from release builds and renames what remains.
og:title: R8 and ProGuard in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: R8 is Android’s code shrinker and obfuscator, the successor to ProGuard; it removes unused Java and Kotlin code from release builds and renames what remains.
jsonLd.name: R8 and ProGuard

jsonLd.articleBody: R8 is the tool the Android build uses to shrink, optimise and obfuscate Java and Kotlin bytecode in a release build. It replaced ProGuard as the default years ago but still reads ProGuard’s configuration format, which is why the file is called proguard-rules.pro and people use the names interchangeably. In a bare React Native project it is switched off by default. The template’s android/app/build.gradle has a flag, enableProguardInReleaseBuilds, that turns on minifyEnabled for release; in Expo projects the same setting is exposed through the expo-build-properties config plugin. Turning it on typically trims the native part of the app and makes the Java side harder to reverse-engineer. What it does not touch is your JavaScript. The bundle is minified by Metro and compiled to bytecode by Hermes; R8 never sees it. For protecting JavaScript, see code obfuscation. The gotcha is reflection. R8 deletes or renames anything it cannot see being used, and some libraries look classes up by name at runtime. The result is a release build that crashes with ClassNotFoundException or a missing method, while the debug build works perfectly. The fix is a keep rule in android/app/proguard-rules.pro, such as -keep class com.example.sdk.** { *; }. Well-maintained libraries ship their own consumer rules, so check the library’s docs before writing rules by hand. Two habits avoid pain: Test the release build with minification on before every store upload, not just once. Keep the mapping.txt file R8 writes for each build. Without it, Java stack traces from production are full of names like a.b.c. Upload it to Play Console and your crash reporting service so they can translate the names back.

/react-native-glossary/re-render.title: Re-render in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A re-render is React calling a component function again to compute new output. It does not always change the screen, but too many of them slow a React Native app.
og:description: A re-render is React calling a component function again to compute new output. It does not always change the screen, but too many of them slow a React Native app.
og:title: Re-render in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A re-render is React calling a component function again to compute new output. It does not always change the screen, but too many of them slow a React Native app.
jsonLd.name: Re-render

jsonLd.articleBody: A re-render is React running a component function again after the first render, to work out what the UI should look like now. Only after that does reconciliation decide whether any native view actually needs to change. A component re-renders for three reasons: Its own state changed (setState, a reducer dispatch). Its parent re-rendered. By default every child re-renders with it, whether or not its props changed. A context it reads changed value. Notice what is missing: "its props changed" is not a trigger on its own. Props only change because a parent re-rendered. Re-rendering is normal and usually cheap. It becomes a problem in React Native because all of it runs on the single JavaScript thread. When a keystroke in a search box re-renders a screen with a hundred list rows, the thread is busy while touches and scroll events queue up, and the user feels lag. A wasted render is one where the component ran but produced identical output. To find them, turn on "Highlight updates when components render" in React DevTools, or record a session in the profiler, which also reports why each component rendered. Typical fixes, in order of preference: Move state down, closer to where it is used, so less of the tree depends on it. Pass expensive subtrees as children, so they are not recreated when the wrapper’s state changes. Memoise list rows with React.memo and stabilise their props. Enable the React Compiler, which memoises automatically. The common mistake is optimising by instinct. A re-render is not the same as a native view update, and a hundred cheap re-renders can cost less than one memo comparison you added to the wrong component. Measure first.

jsonLd.headline: What is Re-render in React Native?

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that memoises components and hooks automatically, removing most hand-written useMemo, useCallback and memo.
jsonLd.name: React Compiler

jsonLd.articleBody: React Compiler is an optimising compiler that runs on your components while the app is being built. It analyses each component and hook, works out which values depend on which inputs, and inserts caching so unchanged parts are not recomputed or re-rendered. It was developed at Meta under the codename React Forget and reached a stable 1.0 release in 2025. For a React Native developer the appeal is direct. Avoiding wasted re-renders on the JavaScript thread used to mean sprinkling useMemo and useCallback and React.memo by hand, keeping dependency arrays correct, and debugging the cases where an inline object silently defeated it all. The compiler does that bookkeeping for you, often at a finer grain than people manage manually, including memoising individual JSX elements. It ships as a Babel plugin, babel-plugin-react-compiler, which slots into Metro’s Babel pipeline. Expo projects can turn it on from the app config with the experiments.reactCompiler flag rather than editing Babel themselves. The catch is that it relies on the Rules of React: components and hooks must be pure during render, props and state must not be mutated, and hooks must follow the call rules. When the compiler cannot prove a component is safe it skips it, so code that bends the rules does not get faster and does not break either. Code that breaks the rules in ways the compiler cannot detect can behave differently once compiled, which is why the React team recommends: Running the React Compiler rules in eslint-plugin-react-hooks first and fixing what they report. Keeping Strict Mode on to surface impure renders. Rolling it out gradually on a large codebase, directory by directory. Existing useMemo and memo calls keep working alongside it, so there is no need to strip them out on day one. See the React Compiler docs.
jsonLd.description: React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that memoises components and hooks automatically, removing most hand-written useMemo, useCallback and memo.
jsonLd.headline: What is React Compiler in React Native?
