jsonLd.articleBody: React DevTools is the React team’s inspector for React apps. In React Native it shows the live component tree of your running app, lets you select any component to read its props, state and hook values, and records profiles of every render. Today it is built into React Native DevTools as the Components and Profiler panels, so there is nothing extra to install. The standalone app, started with npx react-devtools, still exists for setups that need it. It answers two questions you cannot answer from logs alone: What is on screen and with which data? The Components panel shows the tree as React sees it, including context values and custom hook state, and you can edit props live to test a theory. Why did this render? The Profiler records a session commit by commit, shows how long each component took and, with "record why each component rendered" turned on, whether props, state, hooks or a parent caused it. That second question is the heart of most re-render investigations. Turning on "Highlight updates when components render" is a fast way to spot a whole screen flashing on every keystroke. The common mistake is reading absolute timings from a development build as real performance. Development mode adds checks and runs much slower than a release build, so the Profiler is best for relative comparisons and finding which components render too often. Measure actual frame rates and startup time on a release build with a dedicated profiling tool. Another gotcha: the component tree shows React components, not native views. A component that renders nothing visible still appears, and layout problems are better explored with the Element Inspector.

jsonLd.articleBody: A React element is a plain JavaScript object describing what you want on screen — a type, some props, and children. It is a description, not the thing itself: creating an element costs almost nothing and touches no native view. <Text>Hello</Text> compiles to roughly: On each render React builds a fresh tree of these objects and diffs it against the previous one. Only the differences are turned into real native operations, which is why re-rendering a component is cheap and re-creating a native UIView is not. Two distinctions newcomers conflate: a component is the function you write, an element is what calling it produces, and an instance is the native view the Fabric renderer eventually mounts. Keys are what let React match elements across renders inside a list. See createElement for the underlying API.

author: David Leuliette
description: React.memo wraps a component so React skips re-rendering it when its props are shallowly equal to last time, a common fix for slow lists in React Native.
og:description: React.memo wraps a component so React skips re-rendering it when its props are shallowly equal to last time, a common fix for slow lists in React Native.
og:title: React.memo in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: React.memo wraps a component so React skips re-rendering it when its props are shallowly equal to last time, a common fix for slow lists in React Native.
jsonLd.name: React.memo

jsonLd.articleBody: React.memo is a function that wraps a component and tells React it may reuse the previous render output when the new props are the same as the old ones. It is the function-component equivalent of the old PureComponent class. It matters most in React Native lists. When a screen holding a FlatList updates — a search box, a selection — every visible row re-renders by default. Memoised rows skip that work, which keeps scrolling and typing smooth on mid-range Android devices. The comparison is shallow: each prop is checked with Object.is. That is where most memo wrappers quietly stop working: An inline style object, style={{ padding: 8 }}, is a new object every render. An inline arrow function, onPress={() => ...}, is a new function every render. JSX passed as children is a new element every render, so a memoised component that takes children almost never skips. Stabilise those props with StyleSheet.create, useMemo and useCallback, or by passing ids instead of objects. You can also pass a custom arePropsEqual(prev, next) as the second argument, but a comparator that ignores a prop which does change causes stale UI that is hard to trace. Two limits worth knowing. memo only guards against parent-driven re-renders: the component still re-renders when its own state changes or a context it reads changes. And memoising cheap leaf components often costs more in comparisons than it saves. The React Compiler applies equivalent memoisation automatically, which makes hand-written memo largely unnecessary in projects that enable it. See memo.

jsonLd.headline: What is React.memo in React Native?

jsonLd.articleBody: The React Native CLI is the command-line tool, published as @react-native-community/cli, that scaffolds a plain React Native project and drives it day to day: starting Metro, building and installing the native app, and wiring up native dependencies. A project created this way is often called "bare" React Native. You own the ios/ and android/ folders outright and edit them by hand, rather than generating them from configuration. Behind those commands the CLI does real work. It reads each package’s native configuration for autolinking, runs CocoaPods on iOS, invokes Gradle on Android, and offers npx react-native doctor to check your machine setup. Why it matters now: the official React Native docs recommend starting new apps with a framework, which in practice means Expo. The CLI remains the right fit for teams that want no framework layer, for libraries, and for adding React Native to an existing native app. Common gotchas: The old npx react-native init command is deprecated. Use the community CLI package directly as shown above. "Bare" does not mean "cannot use Expo". Any CLI project can install the expo package and use Expo modules. Upgrades are manual. Every native template change has to be merged into your own ios/ and android/ folders, which is what the Upgrade Helper exists for.

jsonLd.articleBody: React Native DevTools is the official debugging tool for React Native, the default since React Native 0.76. It opens a desktop window built on the Chrome DevTools front end and connects directly to the Hermes engine running inside your app. Open it by pressing j in the terminal running Metro, or pick the debugger entry in the Dev Menu. What you get: Console showing your app’s logs, with objects you can expand and inspect. Sources with breakpoints, stepping and debugger; statements, mapped back to your original files. Memory for heap snapshots when you suspect a leak. Components and Profiler panels from React DevTools, built in. Newer releases keep adding panels, such as network and performance tooling, so check the docs for your version. It matters because it replaced a fragmented history. Earlier, developers juggled Chrome remote debugging, Flipper and standalone tools, each with its own setup. Now one tool ships with React Native and needs no extra install. The biggest misconception comes from that history. The old "Debug JS Remotely" option ran your JavaScript inside Chrome rather than on the device. Timing, available APIs and even bugs differed from the real app, and synchronous native calls did not work at all. React Native DevTools debugs the code where it actually runs, on Hermes, which is also why it requires Hermes and does not support JavaScriptCore. A common gotcha: breakpoints that never hit or land on the wrong line usually mean the debugger is attached to a stale bundle. Reload the app with DevTools open. See the debugging docs.

jsonLd.articleBody: React Native Directory is a community-run website, at reactnative.directory, that lists React Native libraries with the details you need before adding one to a project. It is the closest thing the ecosystem has to an official package index. Each entry shows: Platforms supported: iOS, Android, web, and others such as Windows, macOS or TV. New Architecture compatibility. Whether it works in Expo Go or needs a development build. Maintenance signals: last release, recent commits, open issues and download counts, combined into a quality score. It matters because choosing a library is one of the riskiest decisions in a React Native project. A package with native code that stops being maintained can block a React Native upgrade years later. Since the New Architecture became the default, compatibility with it is the first thing to check, and the directory shows it at a glance alongside alternatives. Expo Doctor uses the same data to warn about dependencies that are unmaintained or untested on the New Architecture. How it works: libraries are added by pull request to the directory’s GitHub repository, and most metadata is then fetched automatically from npm and GitHub. Maintainers can add details such as supported platforms themselves. The common misconception is treating the directory as a guarantee. Some fields come from the library’s own maintainers, popularity does not equal quality, and "unmaintained" sometimes means "finished". Before adopting a native module, still open its repository, read recent issues, check it supports your React Native version and, ideally, try it in a throwaway project. Absence from the directory does not mean a library is bad either; it may simply never have been submitted.

author: David Leuliette
description: A renderer is the part of React that turns components into output for one platform. React Native ships its own renderer, so the same React core drives native views.
og:description: A renderer is the part of React that turns components into output for one platform. React Native ships its own renderer, so the same React core drives native views.
og:title: Renderer in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A renderer is the part of React that turns components into output for one platform. React Native ships its own renderer, so the same React core drives native views.
jsonLd.name: Renderer

jsonLd.articleBody: In React, a renderer is the layer that connects the platform-independent core to a real output. The react package only knows about components, hooks and state; it does not know what a view is. A renderer supplies that knowledge. react-dom renders to the browser DOM, and React Native’s renderer renders to native views. All renderers share the same engine, the reconciler, which does reconciliation, scheduling and hooks. Each renderer plugs in a host config: a set of functions that tell the reconciler how to create an instance, append a child, update props and commit changes on its platform. That design is why React’s model shows up in unexpected places — Ink renders to the terminal, React Three Fiber to a WebGL scene, and React Native Skia uses its own reconciler to draw to a canvas. React Native’s renderer is the JavaScript half of the Fabric renderer. Its host config does not create views directly; it builds shadow nodes in C++ through JSI, and Fabric takes over from there. Host components such as View, Text and Image are the elements it understands; your own components are resolved down to those. Why this matters day to day: react and react-native versions are locked together. The renderer is built from the React repository and shipped inside the react-native package, so it expects one exact React version. Upgrading react on its own produces an "Incompatible React versions" error at start-up. Upgrade both together, as the release notes specify. Not everything from React DOM applies. APIs that belong to react-dom, such as portals created with createPortal or DOM form actions, do not exist in React Native. One codebase, several renderers. React Native Web maps React Native’s components onto react-dom, which is how an app can target the browser without a new renderer. When you read "React is platform-agnostic", the renderer is the reason that is true.
jsonLd.description: A renderer is the part of React that turns components into output for one platform. React Native ships its own renderer, so the same React core drives native views.
jsonLd.headline: What is Renderer in React Native?

jsonLd.articleBody: React Native SVG (react-native-svg) is the community library that brings SVG to React Native. React Native has no built-in SVG support, and the core Image component cannot display .svg files, so this package fills the gap by drawing vector shapes with native code. It mirrors SVG markup as components, so icons, charts and illustrations can be written or pasted in almost directly: Most icon libraries for React Native are built on top of it. To import .svg files as components rather than hand-converting them, teams add react-native-svg-transformer to the Metro config, or convert them ahead of time with a tool such as SVGR. Practical notes: Always set viewBox. Without it, changing width and height crops the drawing instead of scaling it. currentColor picks up the color prop, which makes recolouring icons for themes easy. Not every SVG feature is supported. Some filters, CSS inside <style> blocks and certain masks render differently or not at all, so check exported files from design tools. Shapes can be animated with Reanimated by making them animated components, but hundreds of animated nodes get expensive. The usual misconception is that it is the right tool for every graphic. For complex, frequently updating drawings, Skia renders faster on the GPU; for displaying a static remote SVG, expo-image can render it like any other image.

author: David Leuliette
description: React Native Testing Library (RNTL) renders components in Jest and queries them by text, role or label, so tests check what users see rather than internal state.
og:description: React Native Testing Library (RNTL) renders components in Jest and queries them by text, role or label, so tests check what users see rather than internal state.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: React Native Testing Library (RNTL) renders components in Jest and queries them by text, role or label, so tests check what users see rather than internal state.
jsonLd.name: React Native Testing Library

jsonLd.articleBody: React Native Testing Library, published as @testing-library/react-native and often shortened to RNTL, is a library for testing React Native components inside Jest. It renders a component, lets you find elements the way a user would, and lets you fire events like presses and typing. Its guiding principle comes from the wider Testing Library family: the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give. So instead of reaching into component state or props, you query what is on screen: Prefer queries in roughly this order: by role, by label, by text, and only then by testID. Querying by role and label has a useful side effect: if a test cannot find your button by its role, a screen reader probably cannot either. Common gotchas: getBy versus findBy. getBy* looks synchronously; findBy* waits, and is what you need after a fetch or any async state update. Act warnings. Updates that happen after the test finishes trigger warnings about act. Await the UI change you expect instead of ignoring them. It is not a device. RNTL renders in Node.js, so layout, styles and native behaviour are not real. It verifies behaviour and content, not appearance. RNTL is maintained by Callstack and has become the standard way to write component tests in React Native.

description: React Native Web is a library that implements React Native’s components and APIs with React DOM, so the same View, Text and StyleSheet code renders as a website.
og:description: React Native Web is a library that implements React Native’s components and APIs with React DOM, so the same View, Text and StyleSheet code renders as a website.

jsonLd.description: React Native Web is a library that implements React Native’s components and APIs with React DOM, so the same View, Text and StyleSheet code renders as a website.
jsonLd.name: React Native Web

jsonLd.articleBody: React Native Web is a compatibility layer that lets React Native code run in a browser. It reimplements View, Text, Image, ScrollView, StyleSheet and many core APIs on top of React DOM, and the bundler aliases imports of react-native to react-native-web when building for web. The output is real HTML and CSS, not a canvas and not a WebView. A View becomes a div, StyleSheet styles are compiled into atomic CSS classes, and accessibility props map to ARIA attributes. That is why sites built with it are indexable and work with browser text selection and screen readers. When people say “Expo web” they mean this: Expo’s web target and Expo Router’s web output are built on React Native Web, with Metro doing the bundling. You rarely install or configure it yourself in an Expo project. How it behaves in practice: Layout uses React Native’s Flexbox defaults (column direction, position: relative), so screens look the same on web without CSS rewrites. Platform.OS is 'web', and files ending in .web.tsx are picked up for web-only implementations. See platform-specific code. Mouse and keyboard concerns, such as hover styles and focus rings, need explicit handling that mobile code never needed. The most common gotcha is third-party libraries. Anything that wraps a native module (camera, secure storage, many map or payment SDKs) has no web implementation unless the library ships one, and the build fails or the import returns undefined on web. Check each dependency’s web support before promising a web version, and put web fallbacks behind a .web.tsx file. See the React Native Web docs.

jsonLd.name: Reactotron

jsonLd.articleBody: Reactotron is an open-source desktop app from Infinite Red that connects to your React Native app while it runs in development and shows a timeline of what is happening inside it. It complements, rather than replaces, React Native DevTools. Its strengths are app-level insight that a general debugger does not give you out of the box: A timeline of logs, network requests and responses, and async events. State inspection and subscriptions for Redux and MobX-State-Tree, including dispatching actions and restoring snapshots. A view of AsyncStorage contents. Custom commands: buttons in the desktop app that run code in your app, such as "reset onboarding" or "log in as test user". Unlike a debugger, Reactotron is set up in code with the reactotron-react-native package and a small config file, imported only in development: That guard matters. The most common mistake is importing the config unconditionally, which ships the client in production builds where it tries to reach a desktop that is not there. Other practical gotchas: On a physical Android device the app cannot reach localhost on your computer. Forward the port with adb reverse tcp:9090 tcp:9090, or point the client at your machine’s IP address. Network logging works by intercepting the app’s requests, so the configuration order relative to your HTTP client setup can matter. Reactotron shows what your code reports. It does not set breakpoints or inspect native views. Teams that relied on Flipper for state and network plugins often move to Reactotron for that part of the workflow.

author: David Leuliette
description: Reanimated is the standard React Native animation library. It runs animation logic as worklets on the UI thread, so motion stays smooth while JavaScript is busy.
og:description: Reanimated is the standard React Native animation library. It runs animation logic as worklets on the UI thread, so motion stays smooth while JavaScript is busy.

jsonLd.articleBody: Reanimated is the animation library most production React Native apps use. Its defining idea is that animation logic should not live on the JavaScript thread at all. Instead you write worklets — functions that run on the UI thread — driven by shared values that both threads can see: Because the style is recomputed natively every frame, the animation keeps running at full frame rate even while JavaScript is parsing a large response — the exact case where a setState animation visibly stutters. It pairs with react-native-gesture-handler, which delivers touch events on the same thread, so drag-to-dismiss and swipeable rows track your finger without a round trip. Newcomers should be aware that Reanimated 2 and 3 APIs differ substantially from version 1, so old tutorials mislead. See the Reanimated docs.

author: David Leuliette
description: Reconciliation is React’s process of comparing the new element tree with the previous one to work out the minimal set of changes to apply to the native views.
og:description: Reconciliation is React’s process of comparing the new element tree with the previous one to work out the minimal set of changes to apply to the native views.
og:title: Reconciliation in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Reconciliation is React’s process of comparing the new element tree with the previous one to work out the minimal set of changes to apply to the native views.
jsonLd.name: Reconciliation

jsonLd.articleBody: Reconciliation is the step where React compares the elements your components just returned with the ones from the previous render and decides what actually changed. In React Native the result is a set of create, update and delete operations that the renderer turns into native view changes. A full tree diff would be too slow, so React relies on two shortcuts: Different type, different subtree. If a position held a <View> and now holds a <ScrollView>, or <ProfileCard> becomes <SettingsCard>, React throws the old subtree away — state included — and mounts the new one from scratch. Keys identify siblings. In a list, React matches children by their key rather than their index, so a moved item keeps its state. Same type and same position means React keeps the component instance and its state, and only updates the props that differ. The most common bug this explains is defining a component inside another component: Because Field is a new function each time Screen renders, React sees a different type, unmounts the old input and mounts a new one. The keyboard closes after every keystroke and the text resets. Move Field to module level. You can also use this rule deliberately: changing a component’s key forces React to discard it and start fresh, a clean way to reset a form when the user switches account. In React Native under the New Architecture, React’s output feeds the Shadow Tree in C++, which does its own diff to produce the final mount instructions for the UI thread. See preserving and resetting state.

author: David Leuliette
description: Redux is a predictable global state library where a single store is updated by dispatched actions. Redux Toolkit is its official, modern way to write it in React Native.
og:description: Redux is a predictable global state library where a single store is updated by dispatched actions. Redux Toolkit is its official, modern way to write it in React Native.
og:title: Redux in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Redux is a predictable global state library where a single store is updated by dispatched actions. Redux Toolkit is its official, modern way to write it in React Native.
jsonLd.name: Redux

jsonLd.articleBody: Redux is a library for global state in which the whole app’s shared data lives in one store, and the only way to change it is to dispatch an action that a reducer turns into new state. In React Native it works exactly as on the web, connected to components through react-redux. Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official way to write Redux today. It replaces the hand-written action types, switch statements and immutable spread updates of older tutorials with configureStore and createSlice, and it uses Immer so reducers can look like mutations: Components read with useSelector and write with useDispatch. RTK also ships RTK Query, a data-fetching and caching layer comparable to TanStack Query, which is the right place for API data if you are already on Redux. Why teams still choose it: strict, traceable updates, middleware for side effects, and excellent time-travel debugging, which in React Native usually means a tool such as Reactotron. Large teams value the enforced structure. For a small app, a lighter store like Zustand is often enough. The common performance gotcha is a selector that returns a new object or array on every call, for example useSelector((s) => s.items.filter(...)). Because the result is never referentially equal, every dispatch anywhere in the app re-renders that component. Use memoised selectors (createSelector) or select primitives. The second gotcha is persistence: on mobile the store is wiped when the app is killed, so anything that must survive a restart needs explicit persistence to device storage, and that layer then needs migrations when the state shape changes. See the Redux Toolkit docs.

jsonLd.articleBody: A ref is a container for a value that survives re-renders but does not cause one. It has two everyday uses in React Native. Reaching a component imperatively. Attach a ref to a core component and you can call its methods: That is the supported way to focus a field, scroll a list to an offset, or measure a view — actions that have no declarative equivalent. Storing mutable data. A timer id, a previous value, or a "has this already fired" flag belongs in useRef rather than useState, precisely because writing to it should not re-render. The guidance is to reach for refs sparingly: if a value affects what the user sees, it should be state, not a ref. See referencing values with refs.

/react-native-glossary/release-build.title: Release Build in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A release build is the optimised, production-signed React Native app with JavaScript bundled in and developer tooling removed, unlike the debug build you develop with.
og:description: A release build is the optimised, production-signed React Native app with JavaScript bundled in and developer tooling removed, unlike the debug build you develop with.
og:title: Release Build in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A release build is the optimised, production-signed React Native app with JavaScript bundled in and developer tooling removed, unlike the debug build you develop with.
jsonLd.name: Release Build

jsonLd.articleBody: React Native apps compile in two main modes. A debug build loads JavaScript from Metro, enables Fast Refresh, LogBox and the Dev Menu, and runs React in development mode with its extra checks. A release build embeds the JavaScript bundle in the binary, compiles it to Hermes bytecode, sets __DEV__ to false, strips the developer tooling and turns on native compiler optimisations. On Android these modes are build variants (build types, optionally combined with product flavours); on iOS they are build configurations, Debug and Release, selected by a scheme. Running one locally: Why it matters: Never judge performance in debug. Development-mode React and the absence of bytecode precompilation make debug builds much slower. Profile release builds. Some bugs exist only in release: code that relies on __DEV__, a native library broken by R8 shrinking, a missing environment variable, or a JavaScript error that LogBox showed politely in debug but that crashes the app in release. console.log calls still run in release. They cost time and can leak data to device logs; strip them with a Babel plugin if that matters to you. The gotcha in a fresh bare project: Android’s release build type is signed with the debug keystore by default. It installs and runs, but the store will not accept it. Configure a real signing key before your first upload. A development build is a debug build with your native code included; it is not a release build, and testing in one does not replace a pass on a real release candidate.

/react-native-glossary/responsive-design.title: Responsive Design in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Responsive design in React Native means layouts that adapt to window size, orientation and device type, from small phones to tablets, foldables and split screens.
og:description: Responsive design in React Native means layouts that adapt to window size, orientation and device type, from small phones to tablets, foldables and split screens.
og:title: Responsive Design in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Responsive design in React Native means layouts that adapt to window size, orientation and device type, from small phones to tablets, foldables and split screens.
jsonLd.name: Responsive Design

jsonLd.articleBody: Responsive design in React Native is building screens that adapt to the space they are given: a small Android phone, a large iPhone, an iPad in landscape, a foldable opening up, or an app sharing the screen in split view. There are no CSS media queries in core React Native, so you combine layout primitives with runtime measurements. The tools, from most to least preferred: Flexbox first. flex, flexWrap, percentages, maxWidth and aspectRatio handle most variation without any code. useWindowDimensions for structural changes, such as switching from one column to two above a width threshold. It updates on rotation and window resize. Breakpoint helpers from styling libraries such as Unistyles, Tamagui or NativeWind, if you already use one. Base decisions on the window, not the device. An iPad running your app in a narrow split view should get the phone layout, and checking "is this a tablet" gets that wrong. Common gotchas: Dimensions.get('window') called at module level reads the size once and never updates. Use the hook inside components. Scaling every size by screen width with helper libraries makes text and touch targets huge on tablets and ignores the user’s font scaling preference. Adapt layout; keep sizes in density-independent pixels. iPad support is a build setting. Expo apps opt in with ios.supportsTablet, and iPad apps are expected to handle every orientation unless you require full screen. Do not forget safe areas, which change with orientation.

/react-native-glossary/right-to-left.title: Right-to-Left Layout in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Right-to-left (RTL) layout mirrors a React Native interface for languages such as Arabic and Hebrew, controlled through the I18nManager API and start/end styles.
og:description: Right-to-left (RTL) layout mirrors a React Native interface for languages such as Arabic and Hebrew, controlled through the I18nManager API and start/end styles.
og:title: Right-to-Left Layout in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Right-to-left (RTL) layout mirrors a React Native interface for languages such as Arabic and Hebrew, controlled through the I18nManager API and start/end styles.
jsonLd.name: Right-to-Left Layout

jsonLd.articleBody: Right-to-left (RTL) layout is the mirrored interface used for languages written from right to left, such as Arabic, Hebrew, Persian and Urdu. In React Native the whole layout flips: rows run from right to left, navigation moves to the other side, and text aligns to the right. React Native handles most of this automatically when the app runs in RTL mode, because Yoga resolves flexDirection: 'row' relative to the layout direction. You control the mode with I18nManager: The direction is applied when the app starts, so changing it requires a full app restart, not a Fast Refresh. On Android, the manifest must also declare android:supportsRtl="true", which the default template already does. How to write styles that mirror correctly: Use start and end instead of left and right, and marginStart, paddingEnd, borderStartWidth and similar instead of their left and right versions. Physical left and right stay where they are. Use textAlign: 'auto' or omit it rather than 'left'. Mirror directional icons, such as back arrows, chevrons and progress indicators, for example with transform: [{ scaleX: -1 }] when isRTL is true. Do not mirror logos, media controls or clocks. Absolute positions written with left will not flip, so overlays and badges are a frequent source of bugs. The common misconception is that translating strings into Arabic is enough. Without testing in RTL mode, screens built with physical left and right values end up half mirrored. Gesture direction in custom swipes and carousels is another one to check, since users expect "next" to move the other way. Force RTL in a development build early in a project; retrofitting it later means touching nearly every stylesheet. See internationalisation for the wider work.

/react-native-glossary/runtime-version.title: Runtime Version in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A runtime version is a label describing an app binary’s native layer. Expo’s OTA updates only install on builds with the exact same runtime version string.
og:description: A runtime version is a label describing an app binary’s native layer. Expo’s OTA updates only install on builds with the exact same runtime version string.
og:title: Runtime Version in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A runtime version is a label describing an app binary’s native layer. Expo’s OTA updates only install on builds with the exact same runtime version string.
jsonLd.name: Runtime Version

jsonLd.articleBody: A runtime version is the compatibility contract between a native binary and the JavaScript that runs inside it. In Expo it is the runtimeVersion field in app config: every build records one, every EAS Update is published with one, and a device only accepts updates whose string matches its own exactly. It exists because JavaScript can only call native code that is actually compiled into the app. An update that imports a native module added last week will crash every binary built before it. The runtime version is how you tell the update service “these binaries are safe to receive this bundle”. You rarely type the value by hand. Instead you choose a policy: appVersion uses your app’s version, so you must bump the version whenever native code changes. nativeVersion combines the version and build number. fingerprint hashes the native-relevant parts of the project (native dependencies, config plugins, native folders) and changes automatically when they do. The gotcha is treating it like the marketing version. With the appVersion policy, installing a library with native code and shipping an update without bumping version is the classic way to push a crashing update to production. The fingerprint policy removes that human step, at the cost of an opaque hash and the occasional surprise when a change you thought was JavaScript-only turns out to alter the fingerprint. The runtime version is not the store version users see; that is app versioning. Several store versions can share one runtime version, and one store version can never have two. See runtime versions.

jsonLd.headline: What is Runtime Version in React Native?

jsonLd.articleBody: The safe area is the region of the screen that system UI does not obscure — everything inside the notch or Dynamic Island, the status bar, the home indicator, and rounded display corners. Ignore it and your header slides under the clock while your bottom button sits beneath the home indicator. The fix is to inset content by the device's safe area insets. The standard tool is react-native-safe-area-context, which works on both platforms and exposes the values as a hook: Two things newcomers should know. React Native's built-in SafeAreaView is iOS-only and applies padding bluntly, so the community package is the usual choice. And insets are dynamic — they change on rotation and differ per device — so hardcoding paddingTop: 44 breaks on the next phone. React Navigation applies safe-area handling to its headers and tab bars automatically, so you mostly deal with this in custom full-screen layouts.

/react-native-glossary/screen-reader.title: Screen Reader in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A screen reader is assistive software, VoiceOver on iOS and TalkBack on Android, that speaks the interface aloud and lets people navigate an app by swipes and taps.
og:description: A screen reader is assistive software, VoiceOver on iOS and TalkBack on Android, that speaks the interface aloud and lets people navigate an app by swipes and taps.
og:title: Screen Reader in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A screen reader is assistive software, VoiceOver on iOS and TalkBack on Android, that speaks the interface aloud and lets people navigate an app by swipes and taps.
jsonLd.name: Screen Reader

jsonLd.articleBody: A screen reader is assistive software that reads the interface aloud for blind and low-vision users. On iOS it is VoiceOver; on Android it is TalkBack. Users move focus from element to element with swipes, hear each one’s label, role and state, and double-tap anywhere to activate the focused item. React Native has no screen reader logic of its own: because it renders native views, it maps your accessibility props onto each platform’s accessibility APIs. That is good news, but it means the reader only knows what you tell it. An accessibility label, an accessibility role and state such as accessibilityState={{ selected: true }} are what turn a tree of views into something navigable. The AccessibilityInfo API lets your code react to the screen reader: Use announcements for changes that happen without focus moving, such as a toast or a saved form. On Android, accessibilityLiveRegion on a view does the same job for content that updates. Behaviour that surprises developers: Gestures change. With the reader on, a single tap selects rather than activates, and custom swipe gestures may never fire. Offer an alternative, for example with accessibilityActions. Focus order follows the view tree, which is not always visual order. Absolutely positioned overlays can be read in the wrong place. Custom modals can leak focus to the screen behind them; on iOS accessibilityViewIsModal helps contain it. The biggest mistake is never testing with the real thing. VoiceOver is not available in the iOS Simulator, so test on a device (Xcode’s Accessibility Inspector helps for a quick check), and turn TalkBack on an Android device or a Google Play emulator image. Ten minutes navigating your main flow eyes-closed finds most issues.

jsonLd.headline: What is Screen Reader in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/scrollview.title: ScrollView in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: ScrollView is React Native’s generic scrolling container. It renders all of its children at once, which suits short content but not long data-driven lists.
og:description: ScrollView is React Native’s generic scrolling container. It renders all of its children at once, which suits short content but not long data-driven lists.
og:title: ScrollView in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: ScrollView is React Native’s generic scrolling container. It renders all of its children at once, which suits short content but not long data-driven lists.
jsonLd.name: ScrollView

jsonLd.articleBody: ScrollView is the core component that wraps content in a native scrolling container (UIScrollView on iOS, ScrollView or HorizontalScrollView on Android). It is the right choice for a settings page, a form or an article, where the content is finite and known. Its defining trait is that it mounts every child immediately. Twenty rows is fine; two thousand means two thousand native views in memory before the user sees anything. For data-driven lists, use FlatList or another virtualised list. Layout rules that confuse newcomers: A ScrollView needs a bounded height to scroll. Inside a parent without flex: 1 it grows to fit its content and never scrolls. Alignment of the content goes in contentContainerStyle, not style. Putting justifyContent: 'center' on style throws an error. To centre short content but still scroll when it overflows, use contentContainerStyle={{ flexGrow: 1 }}. Useful props include horizontal, pagingEnabled for carousels, refreshControl for pull-to-refresh, stickyHeaderIndices, and keyboardShouldPersistTaps. That last one matters on forms: by default a tap outside a focused TextInput only dismisses the keyboard, so the user taps “Submit” twice. Set it to 'handled'. The classic warning, “VirtualizedLists should never be nested inside plain ScrollViews with the same orientation”, appears when a FlatList sits inside a vertical ScrollView. The inner list loses virtualisation because the outer view gives it unlimited height. Use the list’s ListHeaderComponent and ListFooterComponent instead of wrapping it.

/react-native-glossary/sectionlist.title: SectionList in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: SectionList is React Native’s virtualised list for grouped data, rendering section headers and rows from an array of sections, like a contacts list or settings screen.
og:description: SectionList is React Native’s virtualised list for grouped data, rendering section headers and rows from an array of sections, like a contacts list or settings screen.
og:title: SectionList in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: SectionList is React Native’s virtualised list for grouped data, rendering section headers and rows from an array of sections, like a contacts list or settings screen.
jsonLd.name: SectionList

jsonLd.articleBody: SectionList is the core component for long lists split into groups: contacts by letter, transactions by day, settings by category. Like FlatList, it is built on VirtualizedList, so only rows near the viewport are mounted. Its data shape is the part to learn. Instead of a flat array, you pass sections, where each section has a data array plus any extra fields you want for the header: Things worth knowing in practice: Sticky headers are controlled by stickySectionHeadersEnabled. It is on by default on iOS, where that is the platform convention, and off on Android, so the two platforms look different until you set it explicitly. A section can override renderItem and keyExtractor for its own rows, which is handy for mixed content. SectionSeparatorComponent sits between sections, while ItemSeparatorComponent sits between rows within a section. scrollToLocation({ sectionIndex, itemIndex }) replaces FlatList’s scrollToIndex. The common mistake is building sections inside the render function on every pass, for example grouping a large array with reduce without memoising it. That hands the list new section objects every render and defeats its optimisations. Group once with useMemo, keep keys stable, and memoise row components. When a grouped list gets heavy, FlashList handles the same case with a flat array of mixed header and row items and getItemType, which many teams find faster than SectionList.

/react-native-glossary/secure-storage.title: Secure Storage in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Secure storage keeps small secrets such as auth tokens encrypted on the device, using the iOS Keychain and Android Keystore through libraries like expo-secure-store.
og:description: Secure storage keeps small secrets such as auth tokens encrypted on the device, using the iOS Keychain and Android Keystore through libraries like expo-secure-store.
og:title: Secure Storage in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Secure storage keeps small secrets such as auth tokens encrypted on the device, using the iOS Keychain and Android Keystore through libraries like expo-secure-store.
jsonLd.name: Secure Storage

jsonLd.articleBody: Secure storage is where a React Native app keeps secrets: refresh tokens, session tokens, encryption keys for other stores. It is backed by each platform’s hardware-protected key store, the Keychain on iOS and the Android Keystore on Android, so values are encrypted at rest with keys that never leave the secure hardware. The common libraries are expo-secure-store and react-native-keychain. Both expose a small asynchronous key-value API: It matters because the default places to put data, AsyncStorage and MMKV without encryption, are plain files. Anyone with a rooted device or an unencrypted backup can read a token stored there. Secure storage also supports options such as requiring biometric authentication before a value is returned, and controlling whether a value is available while the device is locked. Things that catch developers out: It is for small values. It is designed for tokens and keys, not JSON documents or caches, and large values can be slow or rejected. Store a key in secure storage and encrypt bulk data elsewhere with it. iOS Keychain items survive uninstall. Delete and reinstall the app and the old token is still there, so the app can appear logged in on a fresh install. Many apps clear the keychain on the first launch after install. Android removes the data with the app. It does not protect secrets you ship. Secure storage protects data the app receives at runtime. An API key hard-coded in your bundle is readable regardless; see API keys in mobile apps. See the expo-secure-store docs.

/react-native-glossary/shadow-tree.title: Shadow Tree in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The Shadow Tree is the C++ tree of shadow nodes Fabric builds from your React components, where layout is computed before changes are applied to real native views.
og:description: The Shadow Tree is the C++ tree of shadow nodes Fabric builds from your React components, where layout is computed before changes are applied to real native views.
og:title: Shadow Tree in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The Shadow Tree is the C++ tree of shadow nodes Fabric builds from your React components, where layout is computed before changes are applied to real native views.
jsonLd.name: Shadow Tree

jsonLd.articleBody: The Shadow Tree is the intermediate representation the Fabric renderer keeps between React and the platform. Each host component you render, such as a <View> or <Text>, gets a shadow node in C++ holding its props, its layout and any native state. Real UIView and Android View objects are created later from this tree. Rendering a frame goes through three phases: Render. React’s output creates or clones shadow nodes on the JavaScript thread. Nodes are immutable, so an update clones only the changed path and shares the rest with the previous tree. Commit. The new tree is promoted to current and Yoga computes every node’s size and position. Mount. Fabric diffs the new tree against the one currently on screen and applies the resulting mutations on the UI thread. Immutability is what makes the New Architecture’s features possible. Several tree revisions can exist at once, so React can prepare an update in the background for concurrent rendering, and layout can be read synchronously because it lives in C++ rather than behind an asynchronous bridge. The gotcha is that shadow nodes and native views are not one-to-one. Fabric performs view flattening: a <View> that only affects layout, with no background, border or event handler, is dropped from the native hierarchy and its children are positioned directly in its parent. That saves memory and draw time, but it surprises code that expects a native view to exist, such as a native library looking up a view by tag or a measurement on a wrapper. Setting collapsable={false} on the <View> keeps it. When a React Native talk mentions "shadow threads" or "the shadow queue", it is describing the legacy architecture, which built a similar tree per platform in Objective-C and Java. See render, commit and mount.
jsonLd.description: The Shadow Tree is the C++ tree of shadow nodes Fabric builds from your React components, where layout is computed before changes are applied to real native views.
jsonLd.headline: What is Shadow Tree in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/shadows-and-eleva.title: Shadows and Elevation in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Shadows in React Native come from iOS shadow props, Android elevation, or the cross-platform boxShadow style available on the New Architecture.
og:description: Shadows in React Native come from iOS shadow props, Android elevation, or the cross-platform boxShadow style available on the New Architecture.
og:title: Shadows and Elevation in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Shadows in React Native come from iOS shadow props, Android elevation, or the cross-platform boxShadow style available on the New Architecture.
jsonLd.name: Shadows and Elevation

jsonLd.articleBody: Shadows are one of the few places React Native styling has historically split by platform. There are three ways to draw one. iOS shadow props: shadowColor, shadowOffset, shadowOpacity and shadowRadius. They map to the native layer’s shadow and give fine control, but only render on iOS. Android elevation: a single number that raises the view on the Material z-axis, and the system draws a shadow based on a light source. You cannot set offset or blur, and the view needs a backgroundColor or no shadow appears. boxShadow: a CSS-style property, added in React Native 0.76 for the New Architecture, that works the same on both platforms and supports spread, inset and multiple shadows. On current React Native, boxShadow is the simplest choice for new code. Older codebases usually combine the iOS props and elevation with Platform.select. Common gotchas: overflow: 'hidden' clips the shadow on iOS. To have rounded, clipped content and a shadow, wrap it: the outer view casts the shadow, the inner one clips. No background colour on iOS means the shadow is drawn around every child, so text gets a blurry halo. Elevation changes stacking on Android, so a raised card can cover siblings regardless of zIndex; see absolute positioning. Many large, blurred shadows in a long list cost rendering time. Keep them subtle and consistent, ideally as a few shared design tokens.

/react-native-glossary/share-api.title: Share API in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Share is the React Native API that opens the native share sheet so users can send a message or link to other apps, returning a promise that reports the outcome.
og:description: Share is the React Native API that opens the native share sheet so users can send a message or link to other apps, returning a promise that reports the outcome.
og:title: Share API in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Share is the React Native API that opens the native share sheet so users can send a message or link to other apps, returning a promise that reports the outcome.
jsonLd.name: Share API

jsonLd.articleBody: Share is the core API that opens the system share sheet: the UIActivityViewController on iOS and the Android share chooser. One call lets the user send content to Messages, WhatsApp, email, notes or any app that accepts shares. The content object is less portable than it looks: message works on both platforms and is the safe default. url is iOS only. On Android it is ignored, so put the link inside message if it must appear everywhere. title is Android only and sets the chooser’s title; subject is used by email targets. iOS-specific options include excludedActivityTypes to hide targets such as “Add to Reading List”. The returned promise resolves with sharedAction or dismissedAction. That result is not reliable analytics on Android, where the promise always resolves with sharedAction, whether or not the user actually sent anything. iOS can also tell you which activity was chosen. The biggest limitation is files. The core API shares text and links, not images, PDFs or videos from local storage on Android. For that, use expo-sharing from Expo, which shares a local file URI on both platforms, or the community library react-native-share for richer options. Shared links are only useful if they open the right screen. Pair the share sheet with proper deep linking, ideally verified https links, so a recipient who taps an invite lands inside the app, or on a web page when it is not installed, rather than on a dead custom scheme.

author: David Leuliette
description: A shared value is Reanimated’s animatable state container, created with useSharedValue, readable and writable from both the JavaScript thread and the UI thread.
og:description: A shared value is Reanimated’s animatable state container, created with useSharedValue, readable and writable from both the JavaScript thread and the UI thread.
og:title: Shared Value in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A shared value is Reanimated’s animatable state container, created with useSharedValue, readable and writable from both the JavaScript thread and the UI thread.
jsonLd.name: Shared Value

jsonLd.articleBody: A shared value is the piece of state that drives a Reanimated animation. You create it with useSharedValue, and unlike React state it can be read and written from both the JavaScript thread and the UI thread, where worklets run every frame. The defining behaviour: changing a shared value does not re-render the component. Instead, any animated style, derived value or animated reaction that reads it is re-evaluated on the UI thread. That is how a gesture can update a position 120 times a second without React doing any work. Assigning an animation function such as withTiming or withSpring to a shared value starts the animation, and assigning a new one interrupts it smoothly from wherever it currently is. Derived values (useDerivedValue) compute one shared value from others, such as turning a scroll offset into a header opacity. Mistakes that silently break things: Mutating nested fields. pos.value.x = 10 changes the object without Reanimated noticing. Assign a new object (pos.value = { ...pos.value, x: 10 }) or use modify. Destructuring. const { value } = progress takes a snapshot; later updates never reach it. Reading .value during render. It works, but the component will not re-render when the value changes, so the output goes stale. If React needs to display it, mirror it into React state deliberately, or keep the display inside an animated style. Using it as general app state. Shared values are for things that change every frame. Data your screens render belongs in React state or a store. The get() and set() methods exist alongside .value because the React Compiler treats property writes on hook results as mutations it may optimise away.

author: David Leuliette
description: React Native Skia is Shopify’s library that brings Google’s Skia 2D graphics engine to React Native, for drawing custom shapes, charts, shaders and effects on a canvas.
og:description: React Native Skia is Shopify’s library that brings Google’s Skia 2D graphics engine to React Native, for drawing custom shapes, charts, shaders and effects on a canvas.
og:title: Skia in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: React Native Skia is Shopify’s library that brings Google’s Skia 2D graphics engine to React Native, for drawing custom shapes, charts, shaders and effects on a canvas.
jsonLd.name: Skia

jsonLd.articleBody: Skia is the open-source 2D graphics engine Google uses in Chrome, Android and Flutter. React Native Skia (@shopify/react-native-skia) exposes it as React components, so you can draw directly onto a GPU-backed canvas: paths, gradients, blurs, image filters, text along a path and custom shaders, all things ordinary views cannot do. It is what you reach for when a design goes beyond rectangles and borders: animated charts, generative backgrounds, image editors, glass and noise effects, or games. Shaders are written in Skia’s shading language and run on the GPU, so effects that would be impossible with views are cheap. It integrates directly with Reanimated. Skia component props accept shared values, so a circle’s radius or a shader uniform can be driven by a gesture or animation on the UI thread without React re-rendering. How it compares with React Native SVG: SVG maps shapes to native views and is the right tool for icons and static vector graphics. Skia draws everything into one canvas, which scales much better to hundreds of animated shapes and offers effects SVG cannot. What to weigh before adopting it: Bundle size. It ships the Skia engine as native binaries, adding several megabytes to the app. For a single gradient, that is a poor trade. It is not a layout system. Content inside a canvas has no Flexbox, no native accessibility tree and no text selection. Keep ordinary UI in views and use Skia for the drawn parts. Fonts are explicit. Text needs a font loaded through Skia’s own APIs, such as useFont; system fonts are not used automatically. Web needs extra setup. On web it runs on CanvasKit, a WebAssembly build of Skia that must be loaded before rendering. See the React Native Skia docs.
jsonLd.description: React Native Skia is Shopify’s library that brings Google’s Skia 2D graphics engine to React Native, for drawing custom shapes, charts, shaders and effects on a canvas.
jsonLd.headline: What is Skia in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/snapshot-testing.title: Snapshot Testing in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Snapshot testing saves a serialised copy of a rendered React Native component to a file and fails the test whenever later output differs from that stored copy.
og:description: Snapshot testing saves a serialised copy of a rendered React Native component to a file and fails the test whenever later output differs from that stored copy.
og:title: Snapshot Testing in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Snapshot testing saves a serialised copy of a rendered React Native component to a file and fails the test whenever later output differs from that stored copy.
jsonLd.name: Snapshot Testing

jsonLd.articleBody: Snapshot testing is a Jest feature that records the output of a value, typically a rendered component tree, and compares future runs against that recording. The first run writes a .snap file into a __snapshots__ folder; every later run fails if the output changes. When a change is intentional, you update the stored snapshot with jest -u (or press u in watch mode). toMatchInlineSnapshot() stores the snapshot inside the test file itself, which keeps small snapshots visible in code review. The misconception to avoid: a React Native snapshot is not a screenshot. It is a text serialisation of the component tree, with element types, props and style objects. It does not run layout, so it cannot tell you whether something overlaps, is cut off or looks right on a small screen. Visual regression needs real screenshots taken on a device or simulator. The bigger problem in practice is snapshot fatigue. Large snapshots of whole screens change with every small edit, so developers learn to run jest -u without reading the diff, and the test stops protecting anything. Signs you are there: snapshots hundreds of lines long, and pull requests where snapshot updates are the noisiest part. Snapshots work best when they are small and focused: a serialised data transformation, an error message, a single small component with a stable output. For behaviour, an explicit assertion such as "the error text is shown" with React Native Testing Library says far more about intent than a 300-line snapshot.

jsonLd.headline: What is Snapshot Testing in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/source-maps.title: Source Maps in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A source map is a file that maps positions in a compiled React Native bundle back to your original source, so stack traces and debuggers show real file names and lines.
og:description: A source map is a file that maps positions in a compiled React Native bundle back to your original source, so stack traces and debuggers show real file names and lines.
og:title: Source Maps in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A source map is a file that maps positions in a compiled React Native bundle back to your original source, so stack traces and debuggers show real file names and lines.
jsonLd.name: Source Maps

jsonLd.articleBody: A source map is a JSON file that records how each position in a compiled JavaScript bundle corresponds to a line and column in your original files. Tools use it to turn index.android.bundle:1:48213 into CheckoutScreen.tsx:42. In development you rarely think about them. Metro serves source maps alongside the bundle, which is why breakpoints in React Native DevTools and stack traces in LogBox point at your real code. Release builds are where they matter. The shipped bundle is minified and, with Hermes, compiled to Hermes bytecode. A production crash report without source maps is a list of meaningless offsets. To make it readable you generate maps at build time and upload them to your crash reporting service: How it behaves in practice: With Hermes there are two maps, one from Metro and one from the Hermes compiler. They have to be composed into one, which the React Native build scripts and crash reporting SDKs’ plugins usually handle. A source map is only valid for the exact bundle it was generated with. Rebuild, even with no code change, and the old map no longer matches. That second point causes the classic gotcha: crash reports that stay unreadable or point at the wrong lines. The cause is almost always a map from a different build, or a missing upload for an over-the-air update. Each OTA update is a new bundle and needs its own maps uploaded. Finally, source maps contain your original code. Upload them to your error tracker, but do not ship them inside the app or host them publicly.

author: David Leuliette
description: A splash screen is the static native image the OS shows while a React Native app launches, covering the gap until JavaScript loads and the first screen renders.
og:description: A splash screen is the static native image the OS shows while a React Native app launches, covering the gap until JavaScript loads and the first screen renders.
og:title: Splash Screen in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A splash screen is the static native image the OS shows while a React Native app launches, covering the gap until JavaScript loads and the first screen renders.
jsonLd.name: Splash Screen

jsonLd.articleBody: A splash screen, called a launch screen on iOS, is the static image the operating system displays the instant a user taps your app icon. In React Native it hides the time spent starting the native app, loading the JavaScript bundle and rendering the first React screen. It is native, not React. On iOS it is a storyboard compiled into the app; on Android 12 and later it uses the system SplashScreen API, which shows a centred icon on a solid background and does not allow a full-screen image. You cannot animate it with JavaScript or change it with an over-the-air update, because it is shown before any JavaScript exists. The useful trick is to keep it visible until the app is truly ready, rather than letting it disappear onto a blank screen while fonts and stored data load: With Expo you configure the image and colours through the expo-splash-screen config plugin; bare apps often use react-native-bootsplash, which generates the native assets for you. Common gotchas: A white or black flash between splash and first screen means the background colours of the splash and your root view do not match, or you hid it too early. Changes need a new native build; reloading Metro shows nothing new. A long splash is a symptom, not a fix. If users stare at it for seconds, work on startup time.

/react-native-glossary/spring-animation.title: Spring Animation in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A spring animation moves a value using simulated spring physics instead of a fixed duration and curve, so motion feels natural and can carry velocity from a gesture.
og:description: A spring animation moves a value using simulated spring physics instead of a fixed duration and curve, so motion feels natural and can carry velocity from a gesture.
og:title: Spring Animation in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A spring animation moves a value using simulated spring physics instead of a fixed duration and curve, so motion feels natural and can carry velocity from a gesture.
jsonLd.name: Spring Animation

jsonLd.articleBody: A spring animation drives a value towards its target as if it were attached by a spring: it accelerates, may overshoot, and settles. In React Native you meet it as withSpring in Reanimated and Animated.spring in the built-in Animated API. Most native iOS and Android motion is spring-based, which is why springs make a React Native app feel native. Instead of a duration and an easing curve, a physical spring is described by three parameters: Stiffness: how strongly it pulls towards the target. Higher is snappier. Damping: how quickly oscillation dies out. Low damping bounces; high damping settles without overshoot. Mass: how heavy the moving object feels. Higher is slower and more momentous. Reanimated also accepts a duration plus a damping ratio, which is easier to reason about when matching a design spec. The feature that makes springs essential is velocity. A spring can start already moving, so when a user flings a card, the release velocity from Gesture Handler becomes the starting speed of the spring: The card continues the user’s motion instead of stopping dead and restarting, and if it is grabbed again mid-flight, a new spring takes over smoothly from the current position and speed. Timing animations cannot do this. Gotchas to know: There is no fixed duration. A physical spring ends when its motion becomes negligible, so do not chain the next step with a setTimeout. Use the completion callback. Defaults differ between libraries and versions. withSpring and Animated.spring feel different out of the box, and Reanimated has changed its defaults between major versions, so set parameters explicitly when the feel matters. Overshoot can go out of bounds. A bouncy spring on opacity or a scale can briefly exceed its target; clamp it or increase damping for those properties.

jsonLd.headline: What is Spring Animation in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/sqlite.title: SQLite in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: SQLite is an embedded relational database stored as a single file on the device; React Native apps use it through libraries such as expo-sqlite and op-sqlite.
og:description: SQLite is an embedded relational database stored as a single file on the device; React Native apps use it through libraries such as expo-sqlite and op-sqlite.
og:title: SQLite in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: SQLite is an embedded relational database stored as a single file on the device; React Native apps use it through libraries such as expo-sqlite and op-sqlite.
jsonLd.name: SQLite

jsonLd.articleBody: SQLite is a full SQL database engine that runs inside your app and keeps everything in one file on the device. Both iOS and Android ship it, and React Native reaches it through a library: expo-sqlite in most Expo projects, or op-sqlite, a JSI-based library focused on raw speed. You reach for SQLite when key-value storage stops being enough: you need to filter, sort, join or paginate thousands of records locally, which is the foundation of any offline-first app. Many teams put a typed layer on top. Drizzle ORM supports both libraries and offers live queries that re-render a component when its rows change, and sync engines such as PowerSync use SQLite as their local store. The mistakes that bite in production: No migration plan. The schema you ship in version 1 lives on users’ devices forever. Every later change needs a migration that runs on launch, typically tracked with PRAGMA user_version or an ORM’s migration system. Editing the CREATE TABLE statement does nothing for existing installs. String-built SQL. Interpolating user input into a query invites injection and quoting bugs. Always use ? placeholders. Large writes one row at a time. Wrap bulk inserts in a transaction; the difference can be orders of magnitude. SQLite data is not encrypted by default. If the database holds sensitive information, use an encrypted build such as SQLCipher, which both libraries can be configured for, and keep the key in secure storage. See the expo-sqlite docs.
jsonLd.description: SQLite is an embedded relational database stored as a single file on the device; React Native apps use it through libraries such as expo-sqlite and op-sqlite.
jsonLd.headline: What is SQLite in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/ssl-pinning.title: SSL Pinning in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: SSL pinning makes a React Native app trust only specific certificates or public keys for its API, blocking interception even by certificates the device trusts.
og:description: SSL pinning makes a React Native app trust only specific certificates or public keys for its API, blocking interception even by certificates the device trusts.
og:title: SSL Pinning in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: SSL pinning makes a React Native app trust only specific certificates or public keys for its API, blocking interception even by certificates the device trusts.
jsonLd.name: SSL Pinning

jsonLd.articleBody: SSL pinning, more accurately TLS or certificate pinning, means your app only accepts a connection to your server if the server presents a certificate or public key you embedded in the app. A certificate that is merely valid in the eyes of the operating system is not enough. Normal HTTPS already encrypts traffic, so why pin? Because the device decides which certificate authorities to trust, and that list can be changed. An attacker, a corporate proxy or a researcher with a tool such as mitmproxy can install their own root certificate, then read and modify your app's API traffic. Pinning makes that interception fail. In practice, pin the public key hash (SPKI) rather than the whole certificate, because a renewed certificate can keep the same key. Both platforms support it natively: Android: a <pin-set> in the Network Security Config XML. iOS: NSPinnedDomains under App Transport Security in Info.plist. Community libraries wrap these so the Fetch API and libraries built on it are covered from JavaScript. The dangerous gotcha is bricking your own app. If the server's key changes and the app only knows the old pin, every request fails for every user on that version, and an over-the-air update cannot help if the pins live in native configuration. Always include at least one backup pin for a key you hold in reserve, and coordinate certificate rotation with app releases. Also be realistic about what pinning achieves. It protects users on hostile networks and slows down people reverse engineering your API, but on a rooted or jailbroken device tools like Frida can disable it. It is one layer of defence, not a reason to trust the client.

jsonLd.headline: What is SSL Pinning in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/stack-navigator.title: Stack Navigator in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A stack navigator shows one screen at a time and pushes new screens on top of a history stack, giving the familiar slide-in and swipe-back behaviour of mobile apps.
og:description: A stack navigator shows one screen at a time and pushes new screens on top of a history stack, giving the familiar slide-in and swipe-back behaviour of mobile apps.
og:title: Stack Navigator in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A stack navigator shows one screen at a time and pushes new screens on top of a history stack, giving the familiar slide-in and swipe-back behaviour of mobile apps.
jsonLd.name: Stack Navigator

jsonLd.articleBody: A stack navigator manages screens as a last-in, first-out history. Opening a screen pushes it on top; going back pops it off. It is the navigator behind almost every "list → detail" flow in a React Native app, and it is usually the outermost navigator in the tree. React Navigation offers two versions: Native Stack (@react-navigation/native-stack) hands transitions to UINavigationController on iOS and fragments on Android, so the swipe-back gesture, large titles and header behave exactly like a native app. Stack (@react-navigation/stack) draws transitions in JavaScript. It is more customisable but costs performance; reach for it only when you need an animation the native one cannot do. The calls on the navigation object behave differently, and mixing them up is a common source of duplicate screens: The gotcha that catches most people: screens underneath stay mounted. When the user comes back to a screen, its useEffect does not run again, because nothing remounted. Use useFocusEffect or the focus event to refresh data on return, and remember that a deep stack keeps every screen’s state in memory. In Expo Router, a Stack exported from a _layout.tsx file is this same native stack, configured by the files beside it. What the stack holds at any moment is visible in the navigation state.

/react-native-glossary/staged-rollout.title: Staged Rollout in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A staged rollout releases a new app version to a growing percentage of users over time, so a crash or bug reaches a small group before everyone receives it.
og:description: A staged rollout releases a new app version to a growing percentage of users over time, so a crash or bug reaches a small group before everyone receives it.
og:title: Staged Rollout in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A staged rollout releases a new app version to a growing percentage of users over time, so a crash or bug reaches a small group before everyone receives it.
jsonLd.name: Staged Rollout

jsonLd.articleBody: A staged rollout limits how many users get a new release, then widens it as confidence grows. Both stores support it for store builds, and over-the-air update services offer the same idea for JavaScript updates, but the three behave differently. Google Play staged rollout. In Google Play Console you release to production at a percentage you choose, say 5%, then raise it whenever you like. You can halt a rollout, which stops new users receiving it. Apple phased release. In App Store Connect a phased release spreads an update over seven days on a fixed schedule, starting at 1% of users and ending at 100%. You can pause it, release to everyone early, but not pick the percentages. It only affects users with automatic updates turned on; anyone can still download the new version from the App Store at any time. Over-the-air updates. Services such as EAS Update can roll out a new JavaScript bundle to a percentage of users and, unlike the stores, roll it back by pointing users to the previous update. The misconception that causes trouble: halting is not rolling back. Users who already installed the faulty store version keep it. On both stores the only fix is a new build with a higher version number. That is why many React Native teams pair a slow store rollout with OTA updates for fast JavaScript fixes. A rollout is only useful if someone is watching. Before widening, compare the new version’s crash-free sessions in your crash reporting tool and ANR rate in Android vitals against the previous release. A 1% rollout with no monitoring is just a slow release.
