/react-native-glossary/startup-time.title: Startup Time in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Startup time is how long a React Native app takes from the user tapping its icon to a usable first screen, covering native launch, bundle loading and first render.
og:description: Startup time is how long a React Native app takes from the user tapping its icon to a usable first screen, covering native launch, bundle loading and first render.
og:title: Startup Time in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Startup time is how long a React Native app takes from the user tapping its icon to a usable first screen, covering native launch, bundle loading and first render.
jsonLd.name: Startup Time

jsonLd.articleBody: Startup time is the delay between a user tapping your icon and the app being usable. For React Native the key metric is time to interactive (TTI): the moment the first real screen is rendered and responds to touch, not merely when the splash screen appears. A React Native launch happens in stages: The operating system starts the native process and runs native initialisation. The JavaScript runtime starts and loads the JavaScript bundle. The bundle's top-level code runs: every imported module executes its side effects. React renders the first screen, often after reading storage or fetching data. A cold start runs all of this from nothing; a warm start reuses a process the OS kept in memory and is much faster. Measure cold starts, because that is what new users and anyone whose app was killed in the background experience. Hermes helps the most at stage 2, because release builds ship precompiled bytecode instead of JavaScript source that must be parsed on the device. Stage 3 is where most apps lose time they could win back: importing a large SDK, a date library or every screen of the app at launch means all that code runs before anything appears. Lazy loading with inline requires defers modules until they are first used. The common mistake is measuring in development. Debug builds load the bundle from Metro over the network and skip bytecode, so their startup numbers say nothing about production. Measure a release build on a low-end Android phone, and keep the splash screen up only until the first screen is actually ready.
jsonLd.description: Startup time is how long a React Native app takes from the user tapping its icon to a usable first screen, covering native launch, bundle loading and first render.
jsonLd.headline: What is Startup Time in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/state-management.title: State Management in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: State management is how a React Native app stores, shares and updates data across screens, from local component state to global stores, server caches and persistence.
og:description: State management is how a React Native app stores, shares and updates data across screens, from local component state to global stores, server caches and persistence.
og:title: State Management in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: State management is how a React Native app stores, shares and updates data across screens, from local component state to global stores, server caches and persistence.
jsonLd.name: State Management

jsonLd.articleBody: State management is the set of decisions about where each piece of data in your app lives and who is allowed to change it. In React Native it covers everything from a text field’s value to the logged-in user, a cached API response and the data that must survive the app being killed. The useful move is to stop thinking of “state” as one thing. Most apps have five kinds, and each has a natural home: Local UI state (is this sheet open?) belongs in useState inside the component. Server state (the list of orders) is a cache of data owned by a backend. Tools like TanStack Query handle fetching, caching and refetching far better than a hand-rolled store. Global client state (theme, cart, onboarding progress) goes in a store such as Zustand or Redux, or in Context when it rarely changes. Persisted state has to outlive a cold start and is written to storage such as MMKV or SQLite. Navigation state (which screen, with which params) is owned by your navigation library. Mobile adds pressures the web rarely has. The OS can kill a backgrounded app at any time, so anything the user would be annoyed to lose must be persisted, not just kept in memory. Apps also live for days between launches, so cached server data goes stale in ways a page refresh would normally hide. The most common mistake is putting server data into a global client store: fetching in a useEffect, dispatching the result into Redux, then writing loading flags, error flags and refresh logic by hand for every endpoint. The second is using a single Context for frequently changing values, which re-renders every consumer on each update. Pick the home by the kind of state, and most “which library?” debates resolve themselves.
jsonLd.description: State management is how a React Native app stores, shares and updates data across screens, from local component state to global stores, server caches and persistence.
jsonLd.headline: What is State Management in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/static-hermes.title: Static Hermes in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Static Hermes is Meta’s next-generation Hermes compiler. It can use type annotations to compile JavaScript ahead of time to native code, and underpins Hermes V1.
og:description: Static Hermes is Meta’s next-generation Hermes compiler. It can use type annotations to compile JavaScript ahead of time to native code, and underpins Hermes V1.
og:title: Static Hermes in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Static Hermes is Meta’s next-generation Hermes compiler. It can use type annotations to compile JavaScript ahead of time to native code, and underpins Hermes V1.
jsonLd.name: Static Hermes

jsonLd.articleBody: Static Hermes is the project Meta’s Hermes team has been building to take the Hermes engine beyond interpreting bytecode. Its headline idea: when code carries sound type information, the compiler can skip the dynamic checks JavaScript normally needs and emit native machine code ahead of time, reaching speeds closer to C than to a typical interpreter. It changes the trade-off Hermes made originally. Classic Hermes compiles your bundle to bytecode for fast start-up but has no JIT, so CPU-heavy JavaScript runs slower than in a browser engine. Static Hermes aims to keep the fast start-up and add ahead-of-time speed for the code that needs it, without shipping a JIT. "Hermes V1" is the name used for the new generation of the engine that grew out of this work, with a rebuilt compiler and virtual machine that are faster even on untyped code. React Native has started offering it as an opt-in, and it is on the path to becoming the default engine. Before getting excited: Types must be sound, not just present. TypeScript types are erased and allow escape hatches such as any and unchecked casts, so the compiler cannot trust them blindly. The native-compilation mode relies on a stricter, checked subset; ordinary TypeScript does not automatically become native code. Typed native compilation is still experimental. The speed-ups you can count on today come from the improved engine running your existing bundle, not from rewriting code with stricter types. Your code does not change. It remains standard JavaScript, so adopting the new engine is a build setting plus testing, not a migration. Static Hermes is not a separate language or runtime to choose; it is the evolution of the engine React Native already ships. Watch the React Native release notes for when the new engine becomes the default,, and benchmark your own start-up and hot paths rather than trusting headline numbers.

jsonLd.articleBody: StatusBar controls the strip at the top of the screen that shows the time, battery and signal. React Native offers it both as a component you render and as static methods you call imperatively. The main prop is barStyle: light-content for white icons on a dark background, dark-content for dark icons on a light one, or default. Other props include hidden, animated and showHideTransition. Two Android-only props, backgroundColor and translucent, come from the era when the status bar was a coloured band above the app. Recent Android versions draw apps edge to edge, behind the status bar, so those props no longer have the effect old tutorials promise. Treat the status bar as transparent on both platforms and pad your content with safe area insets instead. StatusBar.currentHeight exists on Android only and is no substitute for insets. The component behaves like a stack. You can render several <StatusBar> elements in different screens, and the most recently mounted one wins; when it unmounts, the previous one’s props take over again. That is convenient per screen, but with tab and stack navigators some screens stay mounted when hidden, so the bar does not change when you expect. React Navigation’s docs suggest rendering it only in the focused screen. The most common bug is unreadable icons: dark icons on a dark header after switching to dark mode. Tie barStyle to the colour scheme from Appearance, or use expo-status-bar, whose style="auto" picks the contrasting style for you. Remember that a Modal may need its own status bar settings.

jsonLd.name: Storybook

jsonLd.articleBody: Storybook is a tool for building and reviewing UI components outside the screens that use them. Each component gets one or more stories: small, named examples of the component in a specific state, such as a button that is loading, disabled or showing a very long label. React Native Storybook, the @storybook/react-native package, renders those stories inside your app on a simulator, emulator or phone. You switch from the real app to a Storybook UI, pick a story, and adjust its props live with controls. Because it runs natively, you see real fonts, shadows, safe areas and platform differences, which a browser cannot show you faithfully. Stories use the Component Story Format shared with web Storybook: Why teams use it: Build a component without navigating five screens deep or faking backend data to reach the right state. Give designers and reviewers a catalogue of every component and variant, which keeps a design system built on design tokens honest. Reuse stories as test fixtures, so tests render the same states you review visually. Teams can also render stories in a browser through React Native Web for easier sharing, at the cost of not seeing true native rendering. The usual gotcha is shipping Storybook to users. It must be switched on by an environment variable or a development-only entry point, and excluded from production builds, or it adds weight and exposes internal screens. The other is stories that silently rot: components that need providers such as a theme or navigation must be wrapped with decorators, or the stories break the moment those dependencies change.

/react-native-glossary/strict-mode.title: Strict Mode in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Strict Mode is a development-only React wrapper that double-invokes renders and effects and flags deprecated APIs, so bugs in impure components show up early.
og:description: Strict Mode is a development-only React wrapper that double-invokes renders and effects and flags deprecated APIs, so bugs in impure components show up early.
og:title: Strict Mode in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Strict Mode is a development-only React wrapper that double-invokes renders and effects and flags deprecated APIs, so bugs in impure components show up early.
jsonLd.name: Strict Mode

jsonLd.articleBody: Strict Mode is a component, <StrictMode>, that turns on extra checks for everything inside it during development. It renders nothing itself and is completely inert in a release build. What it does to your components while you develop: Renders twice. Each component function, initialiser and reducer runs an extra time, and the second result is discarded. A component that mutates a variable outside itself or pushes to an array during render will show the duplicate. Runs effects twice on mount. React mounts, runs every effect, simulates an unmount by running the cleanups, then runs the effects again. A subscription without a cleanup ends up registered twice; a Keyboard or AppState listener fires two callbacks. Warns about legacy APIs, such as string refs and old lifecycle methods like componentWillMount. The point is to simulate what React may do anyway. Under concurrent rendering a render can be started and thrown away, and a component can be unmounted and restored with its previous state. Code that survives Strict Mode survives those. The common reaction is to remove Strict Mode because "my API call fires twice" or "my logs are doubled". That hides the bug rather than fixing it. Two requests on mount mean the effect has no way to cancel or ignore a stale response, which will bite in production when a user navigates quickly. Add the cleanup instead. (React DevTools dims the logs from the second render so you can tell them apart.) Strict Mode also matters for the React Compiler: the compiler assumes components are pure, and Strict Mode’s double render is the cheapest way to find the ones that are not. In an Expo or React Native CLI project, wrap your root component yourself, since the templates may not add it for you. See StrictMode.

jsonLd.headline: What is Strict Mode in React Native?

jsonLd.articleBody: StyleSheet is how you style a React Native app. There is no CSS file and no cascade: styles are JavaScript objects attached to a component through its style prop. A color on a <View> does not reach the <Text> inside it; text styles must go on the text Arrays compose and later entries win: style={[styles.card, isActive && styles.active]} StyleSheet.create is largely a validation and readability convention now — plain objects work too. /react-native-glossary/supabase.title: Supabase in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Supabase is an open-source backend platform built on Postgres; React Native apps use its supabase-js client for auth, database queries, storage and realtime updates.
og:description: Supabase is an open-source backend platform built on Postgres; React Native apps use its supabase-js client for auth, database queries, storage and realtime updates.
og:title: Supabase in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Supabase is an open-source backend platform built on Postgres; React Native apps use its supabase-js client for auth, database queries, storage and realtime updates.
jsonLd.name: Supabase

jsonLd.articleBody: Supabase is a backend-as-a-service built around a hosted Postgres database, with authentication, file storage, edge functions and realtime subscriptions alongside it. React Native apps use the same @supabase/supabase-js client as web apps, which is pure JavaScript and works in Expo Go. The React Native-specific part is setting up the client. On the web it stores the session in localStorage; on a phone you must give it storage and turn off URL session detection: Supabase’s guides also recommend calling supabase.auth.startAutoRefresh() when AppState becomes active and stopAutoRefresh() when it goes to the background, because timers do not run reliably in a suspended app. Teams that want the session encrypted swap AsyncStorage for an adapter built on secure storage. Why teams choose it: data is relational and queryable with SQL, the platform is open source and self-hostable, and Postgres row-level security lets the app query the database directly without a custom API. That last point is also the biggest gotcha. The public key in your app is extractable by anyone, so row-level security is not optional. A table without RLS policies is readable and writable by anyone holding that key. The service-role (secret) key bypasses RLS entirely and must never appear in app code; keep it on a server. See API keys in mobile apps. Realtime features run over a WebSocket, so expect to resubscribe after the app returns from the background. Compared with Firebase, Supabase is relational rather than document-based. See the Supabase docs.

/react-native-glossary/suspense.title: Suspense in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Suspense is a React component that shows a fallback, such as a spinner, while something inside it is still loading code or data, then swaps in the real content.
og:description: Suspense is a React component that shows a fallback, such as a spinner, while something inside it is still loading code or data, then swaps in the real content.
og:title: Suspense in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Suspense is a React component that shows a fallback, such as a spinner, while something inside it is still loading code or data, then swaps in the real content.
jsonLd.name: Suspense

jsonLd.articleBody: Suspense is a built-in React component that lets part of the tree declare "I am not ready yet". When a child suspends, React renders the nearest <Suspense> boundary’s fallback instead, and retries the child once the thing it was waiting for has resolved. Components do not suspend by themselves. Something has to throw a pending promise to React on their behalf, and in practice that is a library or a React API: Data libraries with a Suspense mode, such as TanStack Query’s useSuspenseQuery or Relay. React 19’s use(promise). React.lazy for code that has not loaded yet. That last one is less useful in React Native than on the web. A release build ships one JavaScript bundle already on the device, so there is rarely code to wait for. Suspense in React Native is mostly about data. Its value is moving loading states out of components. Instead of every screen juggling isLoading flags, the component is written as if the data were there, and the boundary decides where the spinner appears. Nesting boundaries lets a header show while a list below it is still loading. Gotchas: No boundary, no fallback. A component that suspends with no <Suspense> above it suspends the closest boundary higher up — possibly the whole screen. Content flashing back to a spinner. If already-visible content suspends again, for example on a new search query, React replaces it with the fallback. Wrap the update in startTransition to keep the old content on screen while the new data loads. That behaviour depends on concurrent rendering, so it needs the New Architecture. Suspense does not handle failures. A rejected promise is an error; pair boundaries with an error boundary. See Suspense.
jsonLd.description: Suspense is a React component that shows a fallback, such as a spinner, while something inside it is still loading code or data, then swaps in the real content.
jsonLd.headline: What is Suspense in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Swift is Apple’s modern programming language for iOS; React Native developers use it to write native modules, Expo modules and app delegate code on the iOS side.
og:description: Swift is Apple’s modern programming language for iOS; React Native developers use it to write native modules, Expo modules and app delegate code on the iOS side.
og:title: Swift in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Swift is Apple’s modern programming language for iOS; React Native developers use it to write native modules, Expo modules and app delegate code on the iOS side.
jsonLd.name: Swift

jsonLd.articleBody: Swift is Apple’s programming language for iOS, macOS and its other platforms, introduced in 2014 as the successor to Objective-C. In React Native work it is the language you reach for when JavaScript cannot do the job: calling an iOS SDK, wrapping a native view or handling app lifecycle events. Where Swift shows up in a React Native app: Native modules you write yourself, most comfortably with the Expo Modules API, whose iOS side is Swift-first. The app delegate — recent React Native and Expo templates generate it in Swift rather than Objective-C. Third-party SDKs, which are increasingly Swift-only. The important nuance is how Swift reaches JavaScript. React Native’s core is Objective-C++ and C++, and JSI is a C++ API. For a classic native module or TurboModule, a Swift implementation typically needs a thin Objective-C or Objective-C++ layer that exposes it to React Native, since Swift classes must be visible to the Objective-C runtime. The Expo Modules API hides that glue, which is a large part of its appeal. Two practical gotchas. UIKit work must happen on the main thread, while React Native may call your module from another queue, so dispatch to DispatchQueue.main when touching views. And mixing Swift into an Objective-C project needs a bridging header; if Xcode reports that Swift symbols are missing, that header is the first place to look. Swift is the iOS counterpart of Kotlin: learning a little of both covers most of the native code a React Native developer ever needs to write.
jsonLd.description: Swift is Apple’s modern programming language for iOS; React Native developers use it to write native modules, Expo modules and app delegate code on the iOS side.
jsonLd.headline: What is Swift in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/swift-package-man.title: Swift Package Manager in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Swift Package Manager is Apple’s built-in dependency manager for Swift and iOS code, integrated into Xcode and the long-term successor to CocoaPods for React Native.
og:description: Swift Package Manager is Apple’s built-in dependency manager for Swift and iOS code, integrated into Xcode and the long-term successor to CocoaPods for React Native.
og:title: Swift Package Manager in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Swift Package Manager is Apple’s built-in dependency manager for Swift and iOS code, integrated into Xcode and the long-term successor to CocoaPods for React Native.
jsonLd.name: Swift Package Manager

jsonLd.articleBody: Swift Package Manager (SPM) is Apple’s official tool for distributing and consuming Swift, Objective-C and C/C++ code. Packages are described by a Package.swift manifest and added from a Git URL, and Xcode resolves them natively, with no Ruby or separate install step. For React Native developers it matters because it is where iOS dependency management is heading. Most native iOS SDKs — analytics, payments, maps — now publish SPM packages first, and some have stopped updating their CocoaPods versions. Meanwhile React Native itself and the vast majority of community libraries have historically shipped as podspecs, installed through CocoaPods. In practice today: React Native’s own build and autolinking still revolve around CocoaPods, while support for SPM is being added gradually. Check the docs for your React Native and Expo versions rather than assuming either way. You can add an SPM package to your app target in Xcode and call it from your own Swift or Objective-C code, alongside your Pods. Library authors wrapping an SPM-only SDK sometimes have to vendor the binary or ask for a podspec. The common trap is Expo’s Continuous Native Generation. If ios/ is regenerated by npx expo prebuild, a package you added through Xcode’s user interface is wiped next time. Add it through a config plugin that edits the Xcode project, or keep ios/ committed. Another misconception is that SPM replaces npm for React Native libraries. It does not: the JavaScript half of a library still comes from your package manager, and SPM only concerns the native iOS half.

author: David Leuliette
description: Switch is React Native’s core on/off toggle, rendering UISwitch on iOS and a Material switch on Android, driven by a value prop and an onValueChange callback.
og:description: Switch is React Native’s core on/off toggle, rendering UISwitch on iOS and a Material switch on Android, driven by a value prop and an onValueChange callback.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Switch is React Native’s core on/off toggle, rendering UISwitch on iOS and a Material switch on Android, driven by a value prop and an onValueChange callback.
jsonLd.name: Switch

jsonLd.articleBody: Switch is the core component for a boolean toggle. It renders the native control, UISwitch on iOS and a Material switch on Android, so it gets the platform’s look, haptics and accessibility behaviour for free. It is a controlled component: it displays whatever value you pass and reports taps through onValueChange. If you forget to update state in onValueChange, the switch animates across and then snaps back, because the next render still says false. That snap-back is the classic sign of a missing state update, and also what users see when an optimistic toggle is reverted after a failed API call. Styling is limited on purpose: trackColor takes separate false and true colours. thumbColor sets the knob. ios_backgroundColor fills the track on iOS when it is off, which trackColor.false alone does not fully cover. Size is fixed by the platform; scaling with transform is the usual workaround, and is a hint that a custom component may fit the design better. Because the native controls differ in size and shape, a row that lines up perfectly on iOS can look off on Android. Test both, and use platform-specific code for spacing if needed. For accessibility, the native control already announces itself as a switch with its on/off state. Give it a label, either through accessibilityLabel or by making the whole row pressable with an accessibility role of switch, so the tap target is larger than the small knob.

/react-native-glossary/tab-navigator.title: Tab Navigator in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: A tab navigator switches between a few top-level sections with a persistent tab bar, keeping each section’s screen alive so users can return without losing their place.
og:description: A tab navigator switches between a few top-level sections with a persistent tab bar, keeping each section’s screen alive so users can return without losing their place.
og:title: Tab Navigator in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A tab navigator switches between a few top-level sections with a persistent tab bar, keeping each section’s screen alive so users can return without losing their place.
jsonLd.name: Tab Navigator

jsonLd.articleBody: A tab navigator shows a row of tabs, usually at the bottom of the screen, each leading to one top-level section of the app: Home, Search, Profile. Unlike a stack navigator, switching tabs does not build history; it swaps which section is visible. In React Navigation the common choice is createBottomTabNavigator from @react-navigation/bottom-tabs, which draws the bar in React Native components. Both React Navigation and Expo Router have also added options that render the platform’s own tab bar (UITabBarController on iOS, Material bottom navigation on Android), so the bar picks up system styling such as iOS translucency for free. Those APIs are newer and have moved between releases, so check the current docs before adopting them. How tabs behave in practice: Screens are lazy by default: a tab renders the first time it is opened, then stays mounted. Switching back keeps scroll position and form input. Each tab usually contains its own stack, so Home can drill into a detail screen while Profile keeps its own history. The bar sits above the home indicator, so it must respect the safe area. The classic mistake is wanting the tab bar to disappear on detail screens while nesting a stack inside each tab. The documented fix is to invert the structure: put the tab navigator as one screen of a root stack, and push detail screens on that root stack so they cover the bar naturally. Keep tabs to roughly three to five destinations. Anything beyond that tends to move into a "More" screen or a drawer.

/react-native-glossary/tamagui.title: Tamagui in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Tamagui is a styling library, UI kit and optimising compiler for React Native and web that shares typed components, tokens and themes across platforms.
og:description: Tamagui is a styling library, UI kit and optimising compiler for React Native and web that shares typed components, tokens and themes across platforms.
og:title: Tamagui in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Tamagui is a styling library, UI kit and optimising compiler for React Native and web that shares typed components, tokens and themes across platforms.
jsonLd.name: Tamagui

jsonLd.articleBody: Tamagui is an open-source styling system for React Native and the web. It combines three layers you can adopt separately: a core styled() API with style props, a set of ready-made UI components built on it, and an optional compiler that optimises styles ahead of time. You start by defining a configuration with createTamagui: design tokens for space, size, colour and radius, fonts, media queries, and named themes such as light and dark. Components then reference tokens by name and receive typed autocompletion. Its distinguishing feature is the compiler. At build time it analyses styled components and, where values are static, flattens them into plain React Native views or atomic CSS on the web, removing runtime styling cost. Without the compiler everything still works, just with more work at runtime. Teams choose it mainly for universal apps that share one design system between Expo and a Next.js site, often in a monorepo, using React Native Web underneath. Common gotchas: Version alignment. Tamagui is split into many @tamagui/* packages; mismatched versions cause confusing type and runtime errors. Upgrade them together. Setup cost. Configuring the bundler plugins and the compiler for both Metro and a web bundler is more involved than a plain StyleSheet. Theme scope. Values like $background resolve from the nearest theme, so a component can change colour when moved under a different theme provider. It is a significant dependency. For a mobile-only app with a small design system, simpler options may be enough. See the Tamagui docs.

/react-native-glossary/tanstack-query.title: TanStack Query in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: TanStack Query, formerly React Query, manages server state in React Native: it fetches, caches, deduplicates and refetches API data through hooks like useQuery.
og:description: TanStack Query, formerly React Query, manages server state in React Native: it fetches, caches, deduplicates and refetches API data through hooks like useQuery.
og:title: TanStack Query in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: TanStack Query, formerly React Query, manages server state in React Native: it fetches, caches, deduplicates and refetches API data through hooks like useQuery.
jsonLd.name: TanStack Query

jsonLd.articleBody: TanStack Query (still widely called React Query) is a library for server state: data your app shows but a backend owns. You describe a query with a key and a function that returns a promise, and the library handles caching, loading and error states, request deduplication, background refetching and retries. Two screens that use the same queryKey share one request and one cache entry, and useMutation plus invalidateQueries refreshes affected data after a write. It is network-agnostic, so it works with fetch, axios, GraphQL clients or Supabase calls. The React Native gotcha is that two of its best features are browser-driven and do nothing on mobile by default. “Refetch on window focus” listens for browser focus events, and “online” status comes from the browser’s connectivity events. On a phone you wire them to AppState and a network library yourself: With that in place, returning to the app after an hour refreshes stale screens automatically; without it, users see hour-old data until they pull to refresh. Connectivity is wired the same way through onlineManager, typically fed by NetInfo. Other things to know: staleTime defaults to zero, so data is considered stale immediately and refetched often, which is usually more traffic than you want on mobile; set it per query. The cache lives in memory, so for offline-first behaviour add a persister that writes it to device storage. See the TanStack Query React Native guide.

/react-native-glossary/testflight.title: TestFlight in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: TestFlight is Apple’s beta testing service: builds uploaded to App Store Connect are installed by internal and external testers through the TestFlight app before release.
og:description: TestFlight is Apple’s beta testing service: builds uploaded to App Store Connect are installed by internal and external testers through the TestFlight app before release.
og:title: TestFlight in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: TestFlight is Apple’s beta testing service: builds uploaded to App Store Connect are installed by internal and external testers through the TestFlight app before release.
jsonLd.name: TestFlight

jsonLd.articleBody: TestFlight is how iOS apps reach testers before the App Store. You upload a build to App Store Connect, invite people, and they install it through Apple’s TestFlight app. It is the iOS counterpart of Google Play’s testing tracks. There are two kinds of tester: Internal testers are members of your App Store Connect team, up to 100. Builds reach them as soon as processing finishes, with no review. External testers are anyone else, up to 10,000, invited by email or through a public link. The first build of each version goes through a lighter Beta App Review before they can install it. Builds expire 90 days after upload, so a long-running beta needs fresh uploads. What makes TestFlight valuable for React Native teams is that the build is the real thing: release-signed, with the JavaScript bundled into the app, not loaded from Metro. It is where you catch problems that only appear in a release build, such as a missing environment variable or a crash on startup that debug builds hide. Common surprises: TestFlight builds use Apple’s production push notification environment. A backend still sending to the sandbox environment makes notifications silently fail in TestFlight even though they worked in development. Testers report feedback and screenshots from inside the TestFlight app, and crash reports appear in App Store Connect and Xcode’s Organizer. Uploading with EAS Submit or fastlane still needs a unique build number every time. For quick internal builds that do not need Apple processing at all, an ad hoc or internal-distribution development build is often faster; use TestFlight when you want the build your users will actually get.
jsonLd.description: TestFlight is Apple’s beta testing service: builds uploaded to App Store Connect are installed by internal and external testers through the TestFlight app before release.
jsonLd.headline: What is TestFlight in React Native?

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Text is the React Native core component that displays strings. It is the only place raw text may appear, and nested Text elements inherit their parent’s styles.
jsonLd.name: Text Component

jsonLd.articleBody: <Text> is the core component for showing strings in React Native. Every character on screen must sit inside one: a bare string placed directly in a View throws Text strings must be rendered within a <Text> component. Text behaves differently from a web paragraph in ways that catch people out: Styles inherit only through nested Text. There is no CSS cascade from a parent View, so setting color on a container does nothing to the text inside it. Nest <Text> elements to bold one word in a sentence, and the inner one inherits font, colour and size from the outer. Nested Text is inline, not a box. Inside a <Text>, children flow as one paragraph and do not take part in Flexbox layout, so margins and padding on inner Text are ignored. Truncation is explicit. numberOfLines plus ellipsizeMode controls how long text is cut. Text respects the user’s system font size by default. allowFontScaling and maxFontSizeMultiplier let you cap it, which is better than switching it off, as covered in font scaling. Text can also take onPress, so a link inside a sentence is just nested Text with a handler. selectable enables long-press copy. The most common gotcha is cross-platform metrics: the same fontSize and lineHeight render with slightly different vertical spacing on iOS and Android, and Android adds font padding unless you set includeFontPadding: false. Check typography-heavy screens on both platforms before calling them pixel-perfect.

jsonLd.articleBody: TextInput is the core component that lets the user type. It wraps UITextField (or UITextView when multiline) on iOS and EditText on Android, so the keyboard, cursor, selection and autofill are the real platform ones. It is usually used as a controlled component, with value and onChangeText: The props that make a form feel native: keyboardType and inputMode choose numeric, email, phone or URL keyboards. autoComplete (both platforms) and textContentType (iOS) enable password managers and one-time-code autofill. secureTextEntry hides passwords. returnKeyType plus onSubmitEditing move focus from field to field through refs, which expose focus(), blur() and clear(). Platform defaults differ more than for most components. Android adds internal padding and, depending on the theme, an underline; multiline inputs centre text vertically on Android until you set textAlignVertical: 'top'. iOS shows no border at all until you style one. A common gotcha is reformatting input inside onChangeText, such as masking a phone number. Because the value makes a round trip through JavaScript, aggressive transforms can make the cursor jump or characters flicker. Keep transforms simple, or use an uncontrolled input with defaultValue and read the text on submit. The input does not move itself out of the keyboard’s way. That is a separate problem, covered by KeyboardAvoidingView and ScrollView’s keyboardShouldPersistTaps.

author: David Leuliette
description: Tree shaking is a build step that removes code you export but never import. Metro has traditionally not done it, so unused React Native code often still ships.
og:description: Tree shaking is a build step that removes code you export but never import. Metro has traditionally not done it, so unused React Native code often still ships.
og:title: Tree Shaking in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Tree shaking is a build step that removes code you export but never import. Metro has traditionally not done it, so unused React Native code often still ships.
jsonLd.name: Tree Shaking

jsonLd.articleBody: Tree shaking is the removal of unused code at build time. A bundler follows import and export statements, works out which exports are never used, and leaves them out of the final file. The name comes from shaking a dependency tree until the dead leaves fall off. On the web, bundlers such as Webpack, Rollup and Vite do this by default for ES modules. React Native developers often assume the same is true for them, and that is the key gotcha: Metro has historically bundled whole modules rather than individual exports. If you import one helper from a large utility library through its main entry point, the entire library can end up in your JavaScript bundle. Expo has added experimental tree-shaking support to its Metro configuration for production builds, but it depends on your setup and on packages publishing ES modules without side effects, so check the current Expo docs before relying on it. Until then, write code that does not need tree shaking: Prefer packages with per-function entry points or small, focused dependencies. Avoid barrel files (index.ts that re-exports everything) in large internal folders. Remove dead feature flags and unused screens rather than hiding them. Native code has its own dead-code removal, separate from JavaScript. On Android, R8 strips unused Java and Kotlin classes when shrinking is enabled; on iOS, the linker removes unreferenced symbols. Neither touches your JavaScript, so a large bundle size on the JS side needs JS-side fixes.

jsonLd.headline: What is Tree Shaking in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: TurboModules are the New Architecture's native modules: typed by Codegen, built on JSI and loaded lazily. How they replace the bridge and when to migrate.
og:description: TurboModules are the New Architecture's native modules: typed by Codegen, built on JSI and loaded lazily. How they replace the bridge and when to migrate.
og:title: TurboModules in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: TurboModules are the New Architecture’s native modules. They are typed by Codegen, built on JSI, and loaded lazily so startup only pays for what the app actually uses.
jsonLd.name: TurboModules

jsonLd.articleBody: TurboModules are the New Architecture replacement for classic native modules. They do the same job — expose platform capabilities to JavaScript — with three differences that matter. Lazy loading. Legacy native modules were all initialised at startup, whether or not the app used them. A TurboModule is instantiated the first time JavaScript touches it, so an app with 40 dependencies no longer pays for 40 modules on launch. Direct invocation. They sit on JSI, so calls skip JSON serialisation and can return synchronously. Generated type safety. You declare the interface once in a TypeScript spec file and Codegen produces the C++, Java, and Objective-C bindings, so a signature mismatch is a build error rather than a runtime crash. For app developers the practical impact is upgrade-shaped: when a library says it "supports the New Architecture", this is largely what it means. Libraries that were never migrated fail on modern React Native versions.

author: David Leuliette
description: Typed routes is an Expo Router feature that generates TypeScript types from your app directory, so a link to a route that does not exist fails type-checking.
og:description: Typed routes is an Expo Router feature that generates TypeScript types from your app directory, so a link to a route that does not exist fails type-checking.
og:title: Typed Routes in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Typed routes is an Expo Router feature that generates TypeScript types from your app directory, so a link to a route that does not exist fails type-checking.
jsonLd.name: Typed Routes

jsonLd.articleBody: Typed routes is an Expo Router feature that turns the files in your app/ directory into TypeScript types. Every href you pass to <Link>, router.push() or router.replace() is checked against the routes that actually exist, including the names of dynamic segments. It matters because navigation strings are the one part of a React Native app the compiler usually cannot see. Renaming profile.tsx to account.tsx used to leave broken links that only showed up when someone tapped them, or when a push notification deep link silently landed on a not-found screen. With typed routes the rename produces a list of type errors. How it works in practice: It is switched on in app config (historically under experiments.typedRoutes; check the Expo Router docs for your SDK). The Expo CLI writes the generated declarations into the .expo folder and references them from an expo-env.d.ts file in the project root. The types are regenerated while the dev server runs, so adding a file updates autocomplete straight away. The gotcha is that the types are generated, not written. On a fresh clone or in CI, a type-check can fail with errors about every href until the Expo CLI has produced the declarations, and committing a stale copy causes the opposite problem. Run the generation step before tsc in CI rather than checking the files in. Typed routes check the shape of URLs your code builds. They cannot validate URLs that arrive from outside at runtime, such as links from emails, so the not-found route still matters. See typed routes.

/react-native-glossary/typescript.title: TypeScript in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: TypeScript is the typed superset of JavaScript that new React Native and Expo projects use by default, catching prop and API mistakes before the app runs.
og:description: TypeScript is the typed superset of JavaScript that new React Native and Expo projects use by default, catching prop and API mistakes before the app runs.
og:title: TypeScript in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: TypeScript is the typed superset of JavaScript that new React Native and Expo projects use by default, catching prop and API mistakes before the app runs.
jsonLd.name: TypeScript

jsonLd.articleBody: TypeScript is JavaScript with static types. It is the default language for new React Native and Expo projects, and React Native ships its own type definitions, so <View>, StyleSheet and every core API are typed without installing extra packages. For a React Native developer the payoff is concrete: a typo in a style property, a missing required prop or a wrong navigation parameter shows up in the editor instead of on a device. Libraries such as Expo Router build on this with typed routes, and TypeScript specs can drive Codegen for native modules. The key fact about how it runs: Metro does not run the TypeScript compiler. Babel simply deletes the type annotations and bundles what is left. That keeps reloads fast but means type errors never stop the app from starting. So type checking needs its own step: Run it in your editor, a pre-commit hook or CI. Many teams discover months of hidden errors the first time they add it to a pipeline. Other gotchas: tsconfig.json should extend the preset your toolchain provides (expo/tsconfig.base or @react-native/typescript-config) rather than a web or Node config, which brings in DOM types that do not exist in React Native. Path aliases in tsconfig.json only affect type checking. The bundler needs to resolve them too, which Expo handles automatically and bare projects usually do with a Babel plugin. Typing any on API responses silently removes the protection where you need it most.
jsonLd.description: TypeScript is the typed superset of JavaScript that new React Native and Expo projects use by default, catching prop and API mistakes before the app runs.
jsonLd.headline: What is TypeScript in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: The UI thread is the platform thread that measures, lays out and draws native views. Everything the user sees is painted here, at 60 or 120 frames per second.
og:description: The UI thread is the platform thread that measures, lays out and draws native views. Everything the user sees is painted here, at 60 or 120 frames per second.
og:title: UI Thread (Main Thread) in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The UI thread is the platform thread that measures, lays out and draws native views. Everything the user sees is painted here, at 60 or 120 frames per second.
jsonLd.name: UI Thread (Main Thread)

jsonLd.articleBody: The UI thread — the main thread in iOS and Android terminology — is where the operating system measures, lays out, and draws native views. Every frame the user sees is produced here, which on a modern phone means a budget of about 16ms per frame at 60Hz, or 8ms at 120Hz. React Native runs your code on the separate JavaScript thread and hands the results to the UI thread through the Fabric renderer. Two distinct kinds of jank follow from that split: JS-thread jank — logic is slow, so new frames are described too late. The screen keeps scrolling but content arrives blank. UI-thread jank — the view hierarchy itself is expensive: huge images, heavy shadows, deeply nested layouts. Frames are dropped even with idle JavaScript. Knowing which thread is saturated decides the fix, and they are opposite fixes. Worklets exist precisely so animations can run on this thread and survive a busy JavaScript thread.

description: Unistyles is a StyleSheet replacement for React Native that adds themes, breakpoints and variants, updating styles natively without re-rendering components.
og:description: Unistyles is a StyleSheet replacement for React Native that adds themes, breakpoints and variants, updating styles natively without re-rendering components.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Unistyles is a StyleSheet replacement for React Native that adds themes, breakpoints and variants, updating styles natively without re-rendering components.
jsonLd.name: Unistyles

jsonLd.articleBody: Unistyles (react-native-unistyles) is a styling library that keeps the familiar StyleSheet API and adds what the built-in one lacks: themes, breakpoints, variants and access to runtime values such as insets and screen size inside your styles. You register themes and breakpoints once, then pass a function to StyleSheet.create that receives the active theme: The object for padding is a breakpoint map: the right value is picked for the current window width. What sets the current major version apart is how changes are applied. Its core is written in C++ and, when the theme, orientation or breakpoint changes, it updates the affected views directly in the Shadow Tree instead of triggering a React re-render. Switching to dark mode does not re-run your components. The trade-off is that this version requires the New Architecture and a Babel plugin that rewrites your components so it can track which styles each view uses. When it fits: teams who like plain style objects rather than utility classes, want typed design tokens and theming, and care about avoiding re-renders on theme change. Common gotchas: Forgetting the Babel plugin, or excluding a folder from it, means styles stop reacting to theme changes in those files. Copying style values out into new objects or variables can break the link the library tracks; pass the style references to the style prop. Older tutorials describe a hook-based API from previous versions. Check which major version a guide targets before copying code.

/react-native-glossary/unit-testing.title: Unit Testing in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: Unit testing checks one small piece of a React Native app, such as a function, hook or component, in isolation and in milliseconds, usually with Jest.
og:description: Unit testing checks one small piece of a React Native app, such as a function, hook or component, in isolation and in milliseconds, usually with Jest.
og:title: Unit Testing in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Unit testing checks one small piece of a React Native app, such as a function, hook or component, in isolation and in milliseconds, usually with Jest.
jsonLd.name: Unit Testing

jsonLd.articleBody: Unit testing means testing a single unit of code on its own: a pure function, a custom hook, a reducer or one component. Anything outside the unit, such as the network, storage or native modules, is replaced with a controlled stand-in so the test is fast and deterministic. In React Native, unit tests run in Jest under Node.js, not on a device. That makes them quick enough to run hundreds on every save, but it also sets their boundary: they verify logic and behaviour, not native integration or visual appearance. In practice there are two flavours: Logic tests for code with no UI: price calculations, date formatting, validation rules, state machines, API response mapping. These give the best return of any test you can write. Component tests that render a component with React Native Testing Library, interact with it, and assert on the output: the error message appears, the button is disabled, the callback fires. The common mistake is testing implementation details: asserting on internal state, on how many times a private helper was called, or on the exact component tree. Such tests break every time you refactor even though the behaviour is unchanged, and teams end up deleting them. Test inputs and outputs, and what the user would observe. A second mistake is mocking so much that the test only checks the mocks. If a test replaces every dependency, it can pass while the real code is broken. Push logic into plain functions that need no mocks, and keep UI components thin.
jsonLd.description: Unit testing checks one small piece of a React Native app, such as a function, hook or component, in isolation and in milliseconds, usually with Jest.
jsonLd.headline: What is Unit Testing in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: Universal Links are Apple’s verified https links that open your iOS app when installed and your website when not, proven by an apple-app-site-association file.
og:description: Universal Links are Apple’s verified https links that open your iOS app when installed and your website when not, proven by an apple-app-site-association file.
og:title: Universal Links in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Universal Links are Apple’s verified https links that open your iOS app when installed and your website when not, proven by an apple-app-site-association file.
jsonLd.name: Universal Links

jsonLd.articleBody: Universal Links are ordinary https:// URLs that iOS routes to your app instead of Safari, once Apple has verified that you control both the domain and the app. They are the iOS half of public deep linking; the Android equivalent is Android App Links. Verification needs two pieces that point at each other: An Associated Domains entitlement in the app, such as applinks:example.com. In Expo this is ios.associatedDomains in the app config. An apple-app-site-association (AASA) file on the domain at /.well-known/apple-app-site-association, served over HTTPS with no redirects and a JSON content type, with no .json extension. The app ID is your Team ID followed by the bundle identifier. A typo in either fails silently. Once the link reaches the app, React Native handles it like any other deep link, through the same navigation linking config. The gotchas that make Universal Links feel broken when they are not: Apple caches the AASA file through its own CDN, so a fixed file can take a while to be picked up. Changes are not instant. Typing or pasting the URL into Safari’s address bar does not open the app. Neither does tapping a link to the same domain while already on that site. Test from Notes or Messages. If the user long-presses and chooses to open in Safari, iOS remembers that choice for the domain. A wildcard path that also matches your login or password-reset pages will hijack them into the app. Keep a working web page at every linked path: users without the app installed will land there.

/react-native-glossary/update-channel.title: Update Channel in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: An update channel is a name baked into an Expo build that decides which branch of OTA updates it receives, so you can retarget installed apps without rebuilding.
og:description: An update channel is a name baked into an Expo build that decides which branch of OTA updates it receives, so you can retarget installed apps without rebuilding.
og:title: Update Channel in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: An update channel is a name baked into an Expo build that decides which branch of OTA updates it receives, so you can retarget installed apps without rebuilding.
jsonLd.name: Update Channel

jsonLd.articleBody: An update channel is the label a binary uses to ask for updates. In EAS Update every build is given a channel at build time, usually from the channel field of its profile in eas.json, and it keeps that channel for its whole life. Channels sit on top of a second concept, the branch. The two are easy to confuse: A branch is an ordered list of published updates, like a git branch of bundles. eas update --branch staging adds to it. A channel is a pointer from builds to a branch. production builds ask the production channel, which by default points at a branch with the same name. That indirection is the whole point. Because builds are tied to the channel and not the branch, you can repoint the channel without touching any installed app: This is how you promote a tested set of updates from staging to production in one step, or roll back by pointing production at the previous branch. A channel can also split traffic between two branches for a percentage rollout. The mistake people make is publishing to a branch that no channel points at, then wondering why nobody received the update. The command succeeds, the update exists, and no device ever asks for it. The second is assuming a channel can be fixed after the fact: it is compiled into the binary, so unless the app contains code to override it at runtime, a build made with the wrong profile needs a rebuild. Remember that the runtime version must also match; the channel decides where a device looks, the runtime version decides what it may install.
jsonLd.description: An update channel is a name baked into an Expo build that decides which branch of OTA updates it receives, so you can retarget installed apps without rebuilding.
jsonLd.headline: What is Update Channel in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/upgrade-helper.title: Upgrade Helper in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: The Upgrade Helper is a community web tool that shows the exact template changes between two React Native versions, so you can apply them to your own native project.
og:description: The Upgrade Helper is a community web tool that shows the exact template changes between two React Native versions, so you can apply them to your own native project.
og:title: Upgrade Helper in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: The Upgrade Helper is a community web tool that shows the exact template changes between two React Native versions, so you can apply them to your own native project.
jsonLd.name: Upgrade Helper

jsonLd.articleBody: The Upgrade Helper is a web tool maintained by the React Native community. You pick your current version and the target version, and it shows a file-by-file diff of everything that changed in the default project template between them: package.json, the Podfile, Gradle files, AppDelegate, MainApplication and the rest. It is built on rn-diff-purge, a repository that generates a fresh project for every React Native release and stores the differences, which is where the alias comes from. It matters because a project created with the React Native CLI owns its ios/ and android/ folders. Upgrading the react-native package alone is not enough; the native files must change too, and the Upgrade Helper is the canonical list of what to change. How to use it well: Commit everything first and upgrade on a dedicated branch. Apply the diff by hand, file by file, keeping your own customisations. Files you never touched can usually be copied wholesale. Expand the release notes links shown alongside the diff for breaking changes in JavaScript APIs. Clean native caches afterwards: reinstall pods and run a clean Gradle build. The common misconceptions: It only covers the template. Your third-party libraries need their own upgrades, and they are usually the harder part. Check each native library supports the target version first. Skipping many versions makes the diff huge. Large jumps are possible, but going a few versions at a time keeps each step debuggable. Expo projects using Continuous Native Generation rarely need it. They regenerate native folders from config, so upgrading the Expo SDK version and running prebuild replaces the manual diff. See the Upgrade Helper.
jsonLd.description: The Upgrade Helper is a community web tool that shows the exact template changes between two React Native versions, so you can apply them to your own native project.
jsonLd.headline: What is Upgrade Helper in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/useanimatedstyle.title: useAnimatedStyle in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: useAnimatedStyle is a Reanimated hook returning a style computed on the UI thread from shared values, updating an Animated component without re-rendering.
og:description: useAnimatedStyle is a Reanimated hook returning a style computed on the UI thread from shared values, updating an Animated component without re-rendering.
og:title: useAnimatedStyle in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: useAnimatedStyle is a Reanimated hook returning a style computed on the UI thread from shared values, updating an Animated component without re-rendering.
jsonLd.name: useAnimatedStyle

jsonLd.articleBody: useAnimatedStyle is the Reanimated hook that connects shared values to what you see on screen. You give it a function that returns a style object; Reanimated runs that function as a worklet on the UI thread and re-runs it whenever a shared value it reads changes, applying the result directly to the native view. The style only works on an animated component: Animated.View, Animated.Text, or anything wrapped with createAnimatedComponent. Passing it to a plain View does not animate anything, which is the most common first mistake. Practices that keep it fast and correct: Keep static styles out. Put padding, colours and layout in a StyleSheet and combine them in an array, as above. The animated function should return only the properties that change. Prefer transform and opacity. Animating width, height or top triggers layout on every frame. It works, but scale and translate are much cheaper. Use interpolate and interpolateColor to map one driving value onto several properties instead of creating a shared value for each. Be careful with React state inside. Values captured from the component scope are copied into the worklet when the style is created; if they change on every render, the style is rebuilt on every render. For props that are not styles, such as an SVG path’s d or a TextInput’s text, the counterpart is useAnimatedProps. For simple state-driven changes, where a prop flips and the view should transition, recent Reanimated versions also offer CSS-style transitions and animations that need no shared value at all. useAnimatedStyle remains the tool when motion is driven continuously, by gestures, scroll position or physics.
jsonLd.description: useAnimatedStyle is a Reanimated hook returning a style computed on the UI thread from shared values, updating an Animated component without re-rendering.
jsonLd.headline: What is useAnimatedStyle in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/useeffect.title: useEffect in React Native, Explained — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: useEffect is the React hook that runs code after a component renders, used to subscribe to native events, start timers or fetch data, with optional cleanup.
og:description: useEffect is the React hook that runs code after a component renders, used to subscribe to native events, start timers or fetch data, with optional cleanup.
og:title: useEffect in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: useEffect is the React hook that runs code after a component renders, used to subscribe to native events, start timers or fetch data, with optional cleanup.
jsonLd.name: useEffect

jsonLd.articleBody: useEffect is the hook for synchronising a component with something outside React: a native event, a timer, a socket, a network request. React runs the effect after the render is committed, and runs the function you return as cleanup before the next run and when the component unmounts. The dependency array controls when it re-runs: No array: after every render. []: once on mount, cleaned up on unmount. [userId]: whenever userId changes between renders. In React Native, effects are mostly about native subscriptions — AppState, Keyboard, Linking, Dimensions — each of which returns an object with remove(). Forgetting that cleanup is the most common source of a memory leak and of handlers firing twice after a screen remounts. Gotchas that bite in practice: Objects and functions in the dependency array are new on every render, so the effect re-runs every time. Depend on primitives, or stabilise the value with useMemo or useCallback. Race conditions when fetching. If the user switches screens quickly, an old response can overwrite a new one. Set an ignore flag or abort the request in cleanup. It runs twice in development under Strict Mode. That is deliberate: if the double run breaks something, your cleanup is incomplete. Measuring layout. For reading a view's size before the user sees it, useLayoutEffect runs before paint; on the New Architecture it can measure synchronously without a visible jump. Many effects are unnecessary. Values you can compute from props or state during render do not belong in an effect plus setState. See useEffect.
jsonLd.description: useEffect is the React hook that runs code after a component renders, used to subscribe to native events, start timers or fetch data, with optional cleanup.
jsonLd.headline: What is useEffect in React Native?

/react-native-glossary/usememo-usecallba.title: useMemo and useCallback in React Native — weshipit.today

author: David Leuliette
description: useMemo caches a computed value and useCallback caches a function between renders, so they keep the same identity until one of their dependencies changes.

jsonLd.description: useMemo caches a computed value and useCallback caches a function between renders, so they keep the same identity until one of their dependencies changes.
jsonLd.name: useMemo and useCallback

jsonLd.articleBody: useMemo and useCallback are React hooks that remember something between renders. useMemo(() => compute(a), [a]) returns the cached result until a changes; useCallback(fn, [a]) returns the same function object until a changes. useCallback(fn, deps) is simply useMemo(() => fn, deps). They solve two different problems: Expensive work. Sorting or filtering a few thousand items on every keystroke can block the JavaScript thread. useMemo skips the work when the inputs have not changed. Referential stability. JavaScript compares objects and functions by identity, so an inline () => {} is a brand new value each render. That breaks React.memo on children, re-runs effects that list it as a dependency, and makes FlatList treat renderItem as changed. The most common misconception is that wrapping everything makes an app faster. useCallback on a handler passed to a plain, non-memoised component achieves nothing, because the child re-renders anyway when its parent does. The hooks also cost a little: a dependency comparison and retained memory on every render. Use them where a profiler or a memoised consumer gives them something to do. The second trap is a wrong dependency array. Omit a dependency and you read stale values, a bug that only shows up later; the react-hooks/exhaustive-deps lint rule catches it. With the React Compiler enabled, most manual useMemo and useCallback calls become unnecessary, since the compiler inserts equivalent caching at build time. See useMemo.
jsonLd.description: useMemo caches a computed value and useCallback caches a function between renders, so they keep the same identity until one of their dependencies changes.
jsonLd.headline: What is useMemo and useCallback in React Native?

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: useWindowDimensions is a React Native hook returning the window’s width, height, scale and font scale, re-rendering the component when rotation or resizing changes them.
jsonLd.name: useWindowDimensions

jsonLd.articleBody: useWindowDimensions is a core hook that returns the size of the app’s window in density-independent pixels, plus scale (pixel density) and fontScale (the user’s text size setting). It re-renders the component whenever those values change. It replaced the older imperative Dimensions API as the recommended approach. Dimensions.get('window') still exists, but the value is a snapshot, which leads to the most common bug in this area: Code like that, often found in StyleSheet.create files, computes layout once at import time. Rotate the device, open split-screen on an iPad, resize a foldable or a desktop window, and the layout stays at the old size. The hook avoids it because it subscribes for you. Things worth knowing: Window, not screen. The hook reports the window your app occupies. Dimensions.get('screen') reports the whole display. In split-screen or freeform modes they differ a lot. It does not subtract system UI. The notch, home indicator, and on edge-to-edge Android the status and navigation bars can all overlap the window. Use safe area insets for that, not arithmetic on height. Prefer layout over measurement. Flexbox and percentage widths handle most sizing without reading dimensions at all. Reach for the hook when you need breakpoints, such as switching columns or showing a side panel. For multiplying sizes by screen density or rounding to physical pixels, see PixelRatio. For a broader approach to adapting layouts, see responsive design.

jsonLd.headline: What is useWindowDimensions in React Native?

jsonLd.articleBody: View is the fundamental layout container in React Native. It draws nothing by itself; it exists to group children, apply layout, and carry styling such as background colour, padding, and borders. It maps to UIView on iOS, android.view on Android, and behaves roughly like a <div> on the web. Every View is a flexbox container by default, and unlike the web the default flexDirection is column, not row. Views nest freely, and nesting is how you build layout: Deeply nested views used to cost real performance on the old architecture. With the Fabric renderer the cost is far lower, but a flatter tree is still easier to reason about. See the View documentation for the full prop list.

author: David Leuliette
description: VirtualizedList is the React Native base component behind FlatList and SectionList, mounting only items inside a window around the viewport to keep long lists fast.
og:description: VirtualizedList is the React Native base component behind FlatList and SectionList, mounting only items inside a window around the viewport to keep long lists fast.
og:title: VirtualizedList in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: VirtualizedList is the React Native base component behind FlatList and SectionList, mounting only items inside a window around the viewport to keep long lists fast.
jsonLd.name: VirtualizedList

jsonLd.articleBody: VirtualizedList is the core component that implements list virtualisation in React Native. FlatList and SectionList are thin wrappers around it. Virtualisation, also called windowing, means only the items in a region around the viewport are mounted; everything outside is replaced by empty space of the right size. You rarely use it directly. The case for it is data that is not a plain array, such as an immutable collection, because it takes getItem and getItemCount instead of requiring data to be an array. Understanding it explains how its children behave. The tuning props live here: windowSize — how many viewport-heights stay mounted. The default of 21 means ten screens above, ten below and the current one. initialNumToRender — items rendered for the first paint. maxToRenderPerBatch and updateCellsBatchingPeriod — how quickly new items fill in while scrolling. removeClippedSubviews — detaches off-screen native views, with occasional rendering bugs. Lowering windowSize saves memory but makes blank areas more likely during a fast fling, because rendering happens on the JavaScript thread and cannot keep up. Raising it does the opposite. Fixed-height rows with getItemLayout help more than either, because the list skips measuring. The biggest misconception is that items keep their state. When an item scrolls out of the window it is unmounted, so local state such as an expanded row or a half-typed input is lost when it comes back. Store that state above the list, keyed by item id. VirtualizedList unmounts and remounts items; FlashList instead recycles a pool of mounted cells, which is why it often scrolls more smoothly on large lists.

og:title: Watchman in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Watchman is Meta’s file-watching service that Metro can use to detect file changes quickly, recommended on macOS for faster and more reliable reloads.
jsonLd.name: Watchman

jsonLd.articleBody: Watchman is a file-watching service from Meta. It runs in the background, tracks changes across large directory trees efficiently, and answers queries such as "which files changed since my last check". Metro uses it when it is installed to know when to rebuild and trigger Fast Refresh. It is optional. Without it, Metro falls back to Node’s own file watching. On macOS the React Native docs recommend installing it, usually with Homebrew: Why it matters: a React Native project, with node_modules and native folders, contains a very large number of files. Watchman handles that scale with a single daemon and keeps its own index, so Metro starts faster and picks up edits reliably, especially in large repositories and monorepos. How it shows up in practice: A "Recrawl" warning in the Metro output means Watchman lost track of changes and re-scanned the tree. The message itself suggests the fix. "EMFILE: too many open files" errors on macOS usually mean Metro is falling back to Node’s watcher without Watchman, and installing it resolves them. Watchman’s view of the project can go stale after moving or renaming large folders, switching branches with many changes, or restoring a project from backup. The common gotcha is assuming a Metro cache reset clears everything. If edits are not detected or Metro keeps resolving deleted files, reset Watchman too: Then restart Metro with its cache cleared. Together those two commands fix a surprising share of "it works on my colleague’s machine" bundler problems.

jsonLd.headline: What is Watchman in React Native?

author: David Leuliette
description: WebSocket is a persistent two-way connection between app and server; React Native ships a built-in global WebSocket class used for chat, live data and realtime updates.
og:description: WebSocket is a persistent two-way connection between app and server; React Native ships a built-in global WebSocket class used for chat, live data and realtime updates.
og:title: WebSocket in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: WebSocket is a persistent two-way connection between app and server; React Native ships a built-in global WebSocket class used for chat, live data and realtime updates.
jsonLd.name: WebSocket

jsonLd.articleBody: A WebSocket is a long-lived connection over which client and server can both send messages at any time, instead of the app asking with a new HTTP request each time. React Native provides the same global WebSocket class as browsers, implemented natively on iOS and Android, so standard WebSocket client code works unchanged. It powers chat, live scores, collaborative editing, delivery tracking and most hosted “realtime” features, including those of Supabase and Firebase, which manage the connection for you. The mobile reality is that connections drop constantly, and code written for a desktop browser does not expect it: Backgrounding kills it. When the app goes to the background, iOS suspends it within seconds and the socket dies. Listen to AppState and reconnect when the app becomes active again. Network changes kill it. Moving from Wi-Fi to cellular or through a tunnel drops the connection, sometimes without a clean onclose for a while. Use heartbeats (ping messages with a timeout) to detect dead connections. Reconnect with backoff. Retrying instantly in a loop drains battery and can hammer your server when it comes back up. Increase the delay between attempts. Resync after reconnecting. Messages sent while the app was disconnected are gone. Fetch what you missed over HTTP when the socket reopens. Two misconceptions: Socket.IO is its own protocol on top of WebSockets, so a plain WebSocket cannot talk to a Socket.IO server; and a WebSocket cannot keep running in the background to deliver messages. For reaching a user when the app is closed, use push notifications.
jsonLd.description: WebSocket is a persistent two-way connection between app and server; React Native ships a built-in global WebSocket class used for chat, live data and realtime updates.
jsonLd.headline: What is WebSocket in React Native?
