author: David Leuliette
description: A WebView is a native component that renders web content inside an app; in React Native it is provided by the community package react-native-webview, not by core.
og:description: A WebView is a native component that renders web content inside an app; in React Native it is provided by the community package react-native-webview, not by core.
og:title: WebView in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A WebView is a native component that renders web content inside an app; in React Native it is provided by the community package react-native-webview, not by core.
jsonLd.name: WebView

jsonLd.articleBody: A WebView is an embedded browser view that loads HTML, CSS and JavaScript inside a native screen. In React Native you get one from react-native-webview, a community-maintained package that wraps WKWebView on iOS and android.webkit.WebView on Android. It used to ship in core but was moved out, so it is not one of the core components today. Typical uses are pages you do not want to rebuild natively: payment and identity flows, help centres, terms of service, rich articles or an existing web dashboard. The page and the app talk through messages. Inside the page, window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage() sends data to onMessage; in the other direction you can inject JavaScript with injectedJavaScript or a ref’s injectJavaScript(). Gotchas that catch most teams: Messages are strings. Pass objects through JSON.stringify and parse them on the other side. Cookies and storage are separate from your app’s networking, so a user logged in through fetch is not automatically logged in inside the WebView. Navigation escapes. Links can leave your site unless you filter them with onShouldStartLoadWithRequest; hand external links and custom schemes to the system with the Linking API. Each WebView is a full browser engine, with its own memory cost and start-up delay. Do not render one per list row. A WebView screen will not feel like the rest of the app: scrolling, text selection and the keyboard behave like a browser. If you want web code inside an Expo app with a simpler model, Expo DOM components build on the same package. When a whole app is a WebView, it becomes a hybrid app.
jsonLd.description: A WebView is a native component that renders web content inside an app; in React Native it is provided by the community package react-native-webview, not by core.
jsonLd.headline: What is WebView in React Native?

og:title: Worklet in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: A worklet is a small JavaScript function marked to run on the UI thread instead of the JavaScript thread, so animations and gestures stay smooth while JS is busy.
jsonLd.name: Worklet

jsonLd.articleBody: A worklet is a JavaScript function that has been marked to run on the UI thread rather than the main JavaScript thread. It is the core idea behind Reanimated. You mark one with the 'worklet' directive, though in practice the Babel plugin adds it for you inside hooks like useAnimatedStyle: Because the worklet executes on the UI thread, it can compute a new style every frame even while JavaScript is blocked parsing a large API response. That is why a Reanimated gesture keeps tracking your finger when a setState-driven animation would freeze. The trade-off is isolation: a worklet runs in a separate context, so it can only use values explicitly captured from the enclosing scope, plus shared values. Calling back into normal JS needs runOnJS. See the Reanimated glossary.

author: David Leuliette
description: Xcode is Apple’s macOS IDE and toolchain that compiles the iOS side of a React Native app, runs it on simulators and devices, and signs it for the App Store.
og:description: Xcode is Apple’s macOS IDE and toolchain that compiles the iOS side of a React Native app, runs it on simulators and devices, and signs it for the App Store.
og:title: Xcode in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Xcode is Apple’s macOS IDE and toolchain that compiles the iOS side of a React Native app, runs it on simulators and devices, and signs it for the App Store.
jsonLd.name: Xcode

jsonLd.articleBody: Xcode is Apple’s integrated development environment and build toolchain. In a React Native project it compiles everything under the ios/ folder — your app target, React Native itself and every native library — into a binary that runs on the iOS Simulator or a real iPhone. You need it even if you never open its editor. npx react-native run-ios and npx expo run:ios both drive Xcode’s command-line tools (xcodebuild) behind the scenes, and the simulator ships inside Xcode. It only runs on macOS, which is why building iOS locally requires a Mac; cloud services such as EAS Build rent you one instead. Places a React Native developer actually visits in Xcode: Signing & Capabilities, to choose a team, fix provisioning errors and add capabilities such as push notifications. Build Settings, for the bundle identifier, deployment target and build configurations (Debug and Release). The scheme menu, to switch between Debug and Release or pick a device. The build log, which shows the real native error when the CLI only prints “build failed”. The classic gotcha: when the project uses CocoaPods, open ios/YourApp.xcworkspace, not YourApp.xcodeproj. The project file alone does not know about the Pods, so you get hundreds of “module not found” errors that have nothing to do with your code. When builds fail mysteriously after an upgrade, clearing Xcode’s DerivedData folder and re-running pod install resolves a surprising share of cases. Apple also raises the minimum Xcode and iOS SDK required for App Store uploads periodically, so an old Xcode can block a release even if the app builds fine. See Code Signing for the certificate side of shipping.

author: David Leuliette
description: Yoga is the C++ Flexbox engine behind every React Native layout. Why styles render the same on iOS and Android, and where it differs from CSS on the web.
og:description: Yoga is the C++ Flexbox engine behind every React Native layout. Why styles render the same on iOS and Android, and where it differs from CSS on the web.
og:title: Yoga Layout Engine in React Native
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Yoga is the cross-platform C++ layout engine React Native uses to implement Flexbox, producing identical layout results on iOS and Android.
jsonLd.name: Yoga

jsonLd.articleBody: Yoga is the layout engine that turns your style props into concrete positions and sizes. Written in C++ and shared by both platforms, it is the reason a flex: 1 layout measures the same on an iPhone and a Pixel. It implements a subset of the CSS Flexbox specification — enough for app layout, without the parts that only make sense in a document. Yoga knows nothing about React: it receives a tree of nodes with style properties and returns a tree of rectangles, which the Fabric renderer then mounts as native views. Differences from web Flexbox that Yoga enforces, and that catch newcomers: flexDirection defaults to column, not row alignContent defaults to flex-start flex takes a number, not the CSS shorthand string There is no float, no grid, and no percentage-based gap on older versions Yoga is used outside React Native too, which is why you will see it referenced by other frameworks. See Yoga.
jsonLd.description: Yoga is the cross-platform C++ layout engine React Native uses to implement Flexbox, producing identical layout results on iOS and Android.

author: David Leuliette

og:description: Zustand is a small React state library where a global store is a hook created with create(); components subscribe to slices through selectors, with no provider needed.
og:title: Zustand in React Native, Explained
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

jsonLd.description: Zustand is a small React state library where a global store is a hook created with create(); components subscribe to slices through selectors, with no provider needed.
jsonLd.name: Zustand

jsonLd.articleBody: Zustand is a minimal global state library that has become a popular default in React Native apps. A store is created with create(), and what you get back is a hook. There is no provider to wrap the app in, no actions or reducers to declare, and the store can also be read and updated outside React, for example from a notification handler. The selector is the important part. A component re-renders only when the value its selector returns changes, so useCart((s) => s.items.length) ignores every unrelated update. That fine-grained subscription is the main reason teams pick Zustand over Context, which re-renders every consumer. Persistence comes from the persist middleware with a storage adapter. On React Native that is usually AsyncStorage or a faster synchronous store such as MMKV, passed through createJSONStorage. Gotchas that come up repeatedly: Calling useCart() with no selector subscribes to the whole store, so the component re-renders on every change. A selector that builds a new object, such as (s) => ({ a: s.a, b: s.b }), returns a fresh reference each time. Wrap it in useShallow or select fields separately. With an asynchronous storage adapter, persisted state is hydrated after the first render, so a logged-in user can briefly see the logged-out screen. Wait for hydration, or use a synchronous adapter. See the Zustand docs.
jsonLd.description: Zustand is a small React state library where a global store is a hook created with create(); components subscribe to slices through selectors, with no provider needed.

jsonLd.description: Productized end-to-end testing setup for React Native apps using Maestro: YAML flows for your 5 core user journeys, CI/CD integration, a tailored runbook, and a recorded team handoff — delivered in 2 weeks for a flat fee.
jsonLd.name: React Native End-to-End Testing with Maestro

offers.description: Flat-fee productized engagement: Maestro installed and wired, 5 core user-journey flows, CI/CD integration, runbook & README, recorded handoff session, and 14 days of follow-up support.

acceptedAnswer.text: One number, agreed upfront, covers everything in scope: setup, the 5 flows, CI wiring, runbook, recorded handoff session, and 14 days of post-handoff support. No hourly billing, no scope-creep invoices. If the work takes longer than 2 weeks because of something on our end, that's our problem, not yours. The exact number depends on your app's complexity — book a 30-minute call and we'll quote on the spot.

mainEntity.name: What does "flat fee" actually mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: You own the test suite outright — it's YAML files in your repo. The runbook we wrote makes adding new flows a copy-paste-tweak operation that any teammate can do. If you'd rather we keep maintaining or extending the suite, you can book a follow-up engagement or fold it into a weshipit.today subscription. There's never a renewal lock-in.

mainEntity.name: What happens after the 14-day support window ends?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flows usually break because the UI changed — a renamed test ID, a new modal in the navigation path, a redesigned login screen. The runbook walks your team through diagnosing and fixing common breakages in under 10 minutes. For deeper issues, ping me directly — most one-off fixes take less than an hour and we keep DMs open even after the engagement.

mainEntity.name: What if my flows break after the support window?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both. Maestro tests the running app, not the build system — as long as your app boots on an iOS simulator or Android emulator, we can wire it up. We've set Maestro up for Expo managed workflow, Expo bare workflow, and bare React Native indistinguishably. EAS Build, Fastlane, or a hand-rolled CI all work too.

mainEntity.name: Does this work with Expo, bare React Native, or both?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but the 5-flow productized scope is the sharpest one — it's the smallest set that meaningfully covers your highest-risk user journeys, which is where E2E tests pay back fastest. If you need 10, 20, or a full regression suite, we'll scope a custom engagement on the discovery call. Same flat-fee philosophy, just a bigger number and longer timeline.

mainEntity.name: Can you cover more than 5 flows?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most of our clients hadn't. Maestro flows are YAML — closer to a step-by-step checklist than test code. The 30-minute recorded handoff session and the runbook are designed so a non-expert teammate can add their first flow within an afternoon. No prior Maestro experience required from your side.

twitter:creator: @flexbox_

acceptedAnswer.text: Non. Le Sprint est justement conçu pour les freelances et solopreneurs qui ne sont pas développeurs. Le live 2 installe avec toi tout le setup technique (base de données type Supabase, déploiement, sécurité) que les non-devs ne comprennent pas seuls. Ensuite tu construis en vibe coding, c'est-à-dire en décrivant ce que tu veux à Claude ou Codex. Le prérequis, c'est d'être à l'aise avec les outils IA au quotidien, pas de savoir écrire du code.

mainEntity.name: Faut-il savoir coder pour suivre le Sprint Solo SaaS ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Deux familles. Le SaaS back-office : un logiciel que tu ne vends à personne mais qui automatise ce que tu refais chaque mois pour tes clients (reporting, suivi, onboarding, livraison de mission). Flavie a construit le back-office de l'Incubateur de cette façon. Ou le SaaS produit : un outil que tu vends pour générer des revenus scalables, comme plusieurs incubés le font déjà. Le Sprint accepte les deux profils.

mainEntity.name: Quel type de SaaS peut-on construire en 4 semaines ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Un ancien incubé du bootcamp de Flavie devenu développeur agentique, c'est-à-dire spécialisé dans la construction de logiciels avec des agents IA. Il co-anime les 4 lives du Sprint : idée, setup, features, bêta-test. Les incubés qui rejoignent via un parrainage peuvent aussi demander une session de roast de 30 minutes où Pierre passe leur SaaS au crible.

mainEntity.name: Qui est Pierre Thomassina ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flavie vend chaque Sprint à deux prix : le Sprint seul (1 mois) autour de 1 490 € HT, ou le Sprint + 12 mois d'Incubateur autour de 1 990 € HT. Les prix exacts sont sur sa page de vente. Via le lien de parrainage de cette page, tu paies 1 490 € HT pour les 12 mois complets, Sprint Solo SaaS inclus : le prix du Sprint seul, mais avec l'année entière et les 11 autres Sprints.

mainEntity.name: Combien coûte le Sprint Solo SaaS ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Non, et Flavie le dit elle-même : c'est un Sprint avancé. Il faut déjà avoir eu plusieurs clients et trouvé sa niche pour identifier une offre réplicable qui mérite d'être outillée. Quelqu'un qui relance son bootcamp pour la deuxième fois, qui livre le même reporting chaque mois ou qui gère un produit avec des sponsors est dans la cible. Quelqu'un qui cherche encore ses premiers clients devrait plutôt viser le Sprint suivant, « Client Express ».

mainEntity.name: Ce Sprint est-il adapté à un débutant en freelancing ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tous les lives sont enregistrés et disponibles en replay dans l'espace live de la communauté. Avec une journée tranquille, tu peux rattraper deux replays et leurs exercices d'affilée. Les lives ont lieu le vendredi midi, le Sprint court du 9 au 30 octobre 2026.

mainEntity.name: Que se passe-t-il si je rate un live ?

acceptedAnswer.text: Flavie anime une masterclass gratuite le jeudi midi avant le lancement du Sprint, ouverte à tout le monde. Elle y aide à trouver une idée de SaaS back-office, puis présente le Sprint. C'est le meilleur moyen de voir sa façon de travailler avant de t'engager. Écris-moi si tu veux le lien de la prochaine session.

mainEntity.name: Comment tester sans payer ?

acceptedAnswer.text: L'Incubateur programme 12 Sprints par an. Après Solo SaaS viennent « Client Express » (4 semaines pour trouver 10 clients) en novembre et « Indé blindé » (fiscalité, finances, rémunération) en fin d'année. Tu rejoins pour le Sprint qui te parle, les autres sont inclus dans les 12 mois. Beaucoup d'incubés découvrent qu'un Sprint qu'ils jugeaient inutile était exactement ce dont ils avaient besoin.

author: David Leuliette
description: Xcode 27 replaced Simulator.app with Device Hub. Compare 4 alternatives for iOS simulators: Siniulator, simslim, agent-sim and Expo Simulators.
og:description: Xcode 27 replaced Simulator.app with Device Hub. Compare 4 alternatives for iOS simulators: Siniulator, simslim, agent-sim and Expo Simulators.
og:title: Xcode Device Hub alternatives (2026)
twitter:creator: @flexbox_

acceptedAnswer.text: Siniulator is the closest match. It is an open source macOS app that gives each iOS simulator its own window again, with slow animations, shake, screenshots and drag and drop install. iPad, tvOS, watchOS and visionOS support is still incomplete.

mainEntity.name: What is the best alternative to Xcode Device Hub?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Xcode 27 removed the standalone Simulator.app and opens Device Hub when you run an app on a simulator. The simulators themselves and xcrun simctl still work, which is why tools like Siniulator and simslim can drive them.

mainEntity.name: Can I get Simulator.app back in Xcode 27?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, once you upgrade. Expo CLI detects Device Hub from SDK 56, and on SDK 58 expo start, expo run:ios and expo start --ios all handle Xcode 27.

mainEntity.name: Does expo run:ios work with Device Hub?

acceptedAnswer.text: agent-sim runs iOS simulators on an x86-64 Linux machine and exposes them through an MCP server. Expo Simulators runs them in the cloud and starts them from the EAS CLI. Both suit agents and CI better than a desktop window.

mainEntity.name: Can I run an iOS simulator without a Mac?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use simslim. It turns off background daemons a simulator does not need and cuts each one from about 4 GB to under 1 GB of memory, so a 16 GB Mac runs about 12 simulators instead of 5.

mainEntity.name: How do I run more simulators on one Mac?
